The case of *Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine* originated from 20 applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were 19 Ukrainian nationals and one Russian national. The central issue in all applications was the lengthy failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions that had been issued in the applicants' favour. The Ukrainian Government attempted to resolve the cases by submitting unilateral declarations, but the Court rejected these requests, noting that the legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law.

The key facts revolve around the non-enforcement of domestic judgments. Between 1998 and 2007, various Ukrainian courts issued decisions entitling each applicant to receive specific pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These judgments became final and legally enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The primary reason for this failure was not the absence of a legal entitlement, but systemic issues within the state apparatus. The authorities failed to take the necessary budgetary or regulatory measures to facilitate payment. Furthermore, the enforcement process was obstructed by the introduction of bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or controlled companies, which were the debtors in many of these cases. This pattern of conduct by the state resulted in significant delays, with some decisions remaining unenforced for years, forming the basis of the applicants' complaints.

While the majority of the domestic decisions remained unenforced in full, the Court's facts note four exceptions. In applications no. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09, and 64583/09, the judgments in the applicants' favour were eventually enforced on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009, and 18 January 2011, respectively. However, even in these cases, the enforcement occurred long after the judgments became final, leading to the complaints of excessive delay.

The factual details from the appended table highlight the breadth of the problem. The applicants hailed from various regions across Ukraine, including Novogrodovka, Sumy, Kirovograd, and Kyiv. The domestic decisions at issue were delivered by a wide range of courts, from local district courts to the Higher Administrative Court, over a span of nearly a decade. The dates of the final domestic decisions ranged from 17 September 1998 to 12 November 2007. For instance, the lead applicant, Mr. Ternovik, obtained a judgment in his favour in September 1998, yet the decision had not been enforced by the time his application was lodged in April 2006, illustrating a delay of over seven years. This pattern was repeated across the other applications, where applicants waited years to receive what they were legally owed. Some applicants also raised additional, unrelated factual and legal matters, but the non-enforcement of final judgments was the common and primary grievance brought before the European Court of Human Rights.

**Summary of the Case of Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine**

The case of *Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications) was a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 11 April 2013. The case originated from 20 separate applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were primarily Ukrainian nationals, with one applicant being a Russian national.

The central factual issue common to all applications was the lengthy failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions that had been issued in the applicants' favour. Between 1998 and 2008, various domestic courts in Ukraine (including those in Novogrodivka, Sumy, Kirovograd, Makeyivka, Mariupol, and Kyiv) delivered judgments entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or to specific actions being taken. These judgments became final and enforceable.

Despite the final nature of these decisions, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The judgment identifies the root causes for this failure as twofold: first, the authorities' failure to take necessary budgetary or regulatory measures; and second, the introduction of legal bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or controlled companies. This systemic non-enforcement was the primary subject of the complaints communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The facts note that the underlying legal issue had already been addressed in the Court's well-established case-law, specifically referencing *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04). While the Ukrainian Government submitted unilateral declarations in an attempt to resolve the non-enforcement issues, the Court rejected these requests to strike the cases out of its list. In the majority of the applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. The judgment table indicates that enforcement was eventually achieved in only four instances: applications nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09, and 64583/09 were enforced on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009, and 18 January 2011, respectively. For all other applications, the decisions remained unenforced. Some applicants also raised additional factual and legal submissions unrelated to the primary non-enforcement issue. The case was brought by individuals ranging from those born in the 1920s to the 1980s, residing in various regions across Ukraine and one in Russia, highlighting the widespread and systemic nature of the problem within the Ukrainian legal system.

**Case Summary: Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications)**

The case of *Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine* was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in a Committee of the Fifth Section, with a judgment delivered on April 11, 2013. The case originated from 20 separate applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were primarily Ukrainian nationals, with one applicant being a Russian national. The central issue in all applications was the lengthy failure by Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions that had been issued in the applicants’ favor.

The core facts of the case are consistent across the various applications. On various dates, domestic courts in Ukraine delivered judgments granting the applicants entitlement to specific pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favor. These judgments became final and legally enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement of these decisions. The primary reason for the non-enforcement was the authorities’ failure to take the necessary budgetary or regulatory measures. Furthermore, the process was obstructed by the introduction of bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or controlled companies, which prevented the satisfaction of the judgments.

While the majority of the decisions remained unenforced, there were a few exceptions. In applications nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09, and 64583/09, the domestic judgments in the applicants’ favor were eventually enforced on various dates: June 2, 2011; April 18, 2008; July 9, 2009; and January 18, 2011, respectively. The judgments in all other applications had not been enforced in full at the time of the proceedings.

During the proceedings, the Ukrainian Government submitted a number of unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that the Court strike the applications out of its list of cases. The Court examined these declarations but decided to reject the Government's request.

The Court noted that the underlying legal issue concerning the lengthy non-enforcement of domestic decisions was already the subject of well-established case-law, referencing the case of *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. The Russian Government, given that one applicant was a Russian national, was informed of its right to intervene but declined to do so.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the existence of final and binding domestic court decisions in favor of the applicants, the failure of the respondent State to enforce those decisions within a reasonable time, and the systemic reasons for this failure, namely the lack of budgetary measures and the imposition of bans on property attachment and sale. These facts formed the basis for the applicants' complaints under the Convention, leading the Court to find violations related to the right to a fair trial and the protection of property, specifically the right of access to a court to have a final judgment enforced.

**Case: Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine (App. no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications)**  
**Court: European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section**  
**Date: 11 April 2013**

This case concerned twenty applications lodged under Article 34 of the Convention against Ukraine. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals, except for one applicant in application no. 64583/09, who was a Russian national. The applications mainly raised the issue of the Ukrainian authorities’ lengthy failure to enforce final domestic court decisions given in the applicants’ favour. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, particularly *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

The key facts were that domestic courts, on various dates, had delivered judgments entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The failure was attributed to the authorities’ failure to take specific budgetary or regulatory measures, and to the introduction of bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or State-controlled companies. As a result, valid and binding court decisions in the applicants’ favour remained unexecuted or were executed only after significant delay.

Most of the applications concerned prolonged non-enforcement. In four applications—nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09 and 64583/09—the domestic decisions were eventually enforced, on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009 and 18 January 2011 respectively. In all other applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. The appended table identified the applicants, their dates of birth, places of residence, relevant domestic decisions and dates of introduction. The domestic decisions dated from as early as 1998 to 2008 and came from various courts, including district courts in Novogrodovka, Sumy, Kirovograd, Makeyivka, Mariupol, Krasnyy Luch, Sevastopol, Kozelets, Kolomyya, Konotop, Torez, Kyiv and Cherkasy, as well as the Higher Administrative Court.

The Ukrainian Government submitted a number of unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that the Court strike the applications concerned out of its list of cases under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined those declarations but decided to reject the Government’s request. The case therefore continued, and the Court considered the merits in light of its established case-law. The Russian Government, in the application involving a Russian national, informed the Court on 4 February 2013 that it did not wish to intervene under Article 36 § 1.

Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues. However, the central factual complaint remained the State’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, either promptly or at all. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: final and enforceable domestic judgments in favour of the applicants; non-enforcement or delayed enforcement by State authorities; systemic causes such as lack of budgetary or regulatory measures and bans on attachment and sale of State-owned property; and the Government’s unsuccessful attempt to resolve the cases through unilateral declarations. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints that Ukraine’s prolonged failure to execute the domestic awards violated their Convention rights.

**Case Summary: Varava and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 12405/06 and 118 other applications)**

**Procedural Background**
The case originated in 119 applications lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals, Ukraine-based companies, and one Russian national. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. The Russian Government declined its right to intervene in one application (no. 12172/08). The case was heard by a Committee of the Fifth Section, which noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law (citing *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*, no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

**Key Facts**
The central factual pattern across all applications was the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions given in the applicants' favour. Between 1997 and 2009, various Ukrainian courts and labour dispute commissions issued decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts and/or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable under domestic law.

Despite the binding nature of these decisions, the applicants were unable to secure their enforcement in full or within a reasonable time. The failure was attributed to the national authorities' inaction—specifically, the State authorities' failure to take the necessary steps to execute the judgments. This pattern of non-enforcement affected a large number of applicants across different regions of Ukraine, involving various types of domestic bodies (district courts, town courts, administrative courts, courts of appeal, and labour dispute commissions).

Some applicants also raised submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues. Additionally, one applicant (Mr Borovskyy, application no. 39477/07) died during the proceedings, and his wife expressed the wish to pursue the application.

**Government's Position**
The Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues in seventeen of the applications, requesting that those applications be struck out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined these declarations and rejected the Government's request, meaning those applications proceeded to judgment on the merits.

**Alleged Violations**
The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are:
1. **Non-enforcement of final domestic decisions**: The applicants held final and enforceable domestic decisions in their favour, but the State failed to enforce them, either fully or at all.
2. **Excessive delays in enforcement**: Even where some enforcement occurred, the delays were excessive and unjustified.
3. **State responsibility**: The failure resulted from the national authorities' failure to take appropriate action, engaging Ukraine's responsibility under the Convention.

These facts gave rise to violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the Convention, consistent with the Court's well-established case-law on non-enforcement of domestic decisions in Ukraine.

Case Varava and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 12405/06 and 118 other applications) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, delivered on 17 January 2013. The case concerns 119 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention by numerous Ukrainian nationals, Ukrainian companies, and one Russian national. The applicants’ principal complaint was the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour and excessive delays in enforcing those decisions.

According to the facts set out in the appended tables, domestic courts and commissions on labour disputes issued decisions on various dates entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts and/or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and therefore enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to secure their enforcement, either in full or within a reasonable time, because the national authorities failed to take the necessary action. Many of the enforceable decisions dated from the late 1990s and 2000s, while the applications were introduced between 2006 and 2011. The table identifies each application, the applicant’s name and date of birth, and the relevant domestic decision. For example, the lead application, Varava and Others, concerned a decision of the Oktyabyrskyy District Court of Poltava of 5 August 2004. Other applications involved decisions of district courts, town courts, regional administrative courts, courts of appeal, and labour dispute commissions, often in labour-related matters.

The procedural history is also relevant to the alleged violations. The Ukrainian Government was represented by their Agent. The applications were communicated to the Government on various dates. During the proceedings, one applicant, Mr Borovskyy (application no. 39477/07), died, and his wife expressed the wish to pursue the application. The Government submitted unilateral declarations in seventeen applications, asking the Court to strike them out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined those declarations and rejected the Government’s request. The Russian Government was informed of its right to intervene in application no. 12172/08, concerning a Russian national, but declined to do so. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

The Court noted that the underlying legal issue in the applications was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring to Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009). That case concerned similar systemic problems of non-enforcement of domestic decisions in Ukraine. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the existence of final and enforceable domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, the authorities’ failure to enforce them fully or in due time, and the resulting excessive delay. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property. Article 13, the right to an effective remedy, is also relevant in the Court’s established case-law on non-enforcement. The Court’s reference to well-established case-law indicates that the applications raised repetitive issues already found to constitute violations of the Convention. The case thus illustrates a pattern of non-enforcement of domestic judicial and labour-dispute decisions by Ukrainian authorities, rather than isolated individual failures.

Varava and Others v. Ukraine (application no. 12405/06 and 118 other applications) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, delivered on 17 January 2013. The case concerned 119 applications against Ukraine brought by Ukrainian nationals, companies based in Ukraine, and one Russian national. The central complaint was that final domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour were not enforced, or were enforced only after excessive delays, because the Ukrainian authorities failed to take the necessary action. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

In each application, domestic courts or commissions on labour disputes had delivered decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts and/or requiring certain actions in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to secure enforcement in full or in due time. The appended table sets out numerous domestic decisions dating from 1997 to 2009, issued by courts and labour dispute commissions across Ukraine, including in Poltava, Kyiv, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsya, Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Crimea. Some applicants relied on multiple decisions. For example, Polezhay relied on labour dispute commission decisions from 1998; Popov relied on four labour dispute commission decisions from 2000–2002; Kyryk on a 2004 Kyiv court decision; and many others on court judgments from 2000–2008. The delays therefore varied, but in many cases final and binding awards remained unenforced for years.

The applicants also complained about excessive delays in the enforcement proceedings. Some applicants made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main communicated issue was the national authorities’ failure to enforce final decisions in full or in due time. These facts are relevant to the alleged violations, which principally concerned the right of access to court and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and the protection of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In many similar Ukrainian non-enforcement cases, Article 13 issues regarding effective remedies were also raised.

Procedurally, the Ukrainian Government submitted unilateral declarations in seventeen applications, seeking to have them struck out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention on the basis that the declarations resolved the non-enforcement complaints. The Court examined those declarations but rejected the Government’s request. One applicant, Mr Borovskyy (application no. 39477/07), died during the proceedings, and his wife, Ms Borovska, expressed the wish to pursue the application. The Russian Government was informed of its right to intervene in application no. 12172/08, which concerned the Russian national applicant, but indicated that it did not wish to exercise that right.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants held final and binding domestic decisions awarding them money or requiring action; the Ukrainian authorities failed to enforce those decisions fully or promptly; and the resulting delays formed the basis of the non-enforcement complaints. The case is therefore a repetitive non-enforcement case against Ukraine, raising Convention issues concerning timely execution of final domestic decisions and effective protection of applicants’ rights.

Case Varava and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 12405/06 and 118 other applications) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered by the Fifth Section on 17 January 2013. It concerned 119 applications lodged under Article 34 of the Convention by Ukrainian nationals, Ukraine-based companies, and one Russian national. The applicants complained mainly about the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour and about excessive delays in enforcing those decisions.

The domestic decisions came from various Ukrainian courts and labour dispute commissions between 1997 and 2008. They included judgments of district, town, regional, and administrative courts, as well as courts of appeal and labour dispute commissions. These decisions entitled the applicants to various pecuniary amounts and/or required certain actions to be taken in their favour. The decisions became final and therefore enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain full or timely enforcement because national authorities failed to act.

The core alleged violation was therefore the failure of the Ukrainian authorities to enforce final and binding domestic decisions. This non-enforcement and delay formed the basis of the applications. Some applicants also submitted complaints about factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main subject of the case remained the prolonged failure to execute decisions already issued in the applicants’ favour. The underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established Court case-law, particularly Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

Procedurally, the Government submitted unilateral declarations in seventeen applications, seeking to have those applications struck out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention on the basis that the declarations resolved the non-enforcement complaints. The Court examined the declarations but rejected the Government’s request to strike out those applications. In one application, no. 12172/08, the Russian Government was informed of its right to intervene because the applicant was a Russian national, but it declined to exercise that right. In application no. 39477/07, the applicant Mr Borovskyy died during the proceedings, and his wife expressed a wish to continue the application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that final domestic decisions had been issued in the applicants’ favour, that those decisions were enforceable, and that the applicants could not secure their enforcement in full or within a reasonable time due to the national authorities’ failure to take action. The case did not concern the merits of the original domestic awards, which had already been resolved in the applicants’ favour. Instead, it concerned Ukraine’s failure to ensure the timely execution of final decisions and, where relevant, the absence of an effective remedy for that non-enforcement. The Court noted that the legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, and the judgment was adopted on 18 December 2012.

case_name: CASE OF TERNOVIK AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
This case arises from 20 applications against Ukraine (application no. 19430/06 and 19 others). The applicants are Ukrainian nationals, except the applicant in application no. 64583/09, who is a Russian national. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy. On 4 February 2013 the Russian Government informed the Court that it did not wish to exercise its right under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention to intervene in the proceedings concerning application no. 64583/09. The applications mainly concerned the lengthy failure to enforce domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour; they were communicated to the Government on various dates.

On the dates set out in the appended table, domestic courts delivered judgments according to which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. Those judgments became final and enforceable. The applicants were unable to obtain enforcement in due time because of the authorities’ failure to take specific budgetary or regulatory measures, and because of the introduction of bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or controlled companies. In applications nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09, and 64583/09, the judgments in the applicants’ favour were enforced on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009, and 18 January 2011 respectively. In all other applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

summary:
The case originated in 119 applications against Ukraine: application no. 12405/06 and 118 other applications. The applicants are Ukrainian nationals, companies based in Ukraine, and one Russian national, with details set out in appended tables. The applications mainly concern the alleged non-enforcement of domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour and excessive delays in enforcement. The applications were communicated to the Government on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was represented by its Agent, Mr N. Kultchytskyy. During the proceedings, Mr Borovskyy (application no. 39477/07) died; his wife, Ms Borovska, expressed the wish to pursue that application. The Russian Government, having been informed of its right to intervene in application no. 12172/08 concerning the Russian national applicant, stated that it did not wish to exercise that right. The Government submitted unilateral declarations in seventeen applications aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that those applications be struck out. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

The appended table records each application’s introduction date, applicant details, and the final, enforceable domestic decisions that allegedly were not enforced. The decisions were delivered by domestic courts and labour-dispute commissions across Ukraine. They entitled the applicants to various pecuniary amounts and/or required certain actions in their favour. The table contains many similar entries. For example, application no. 12405/06, introduced on 17 March 2006, was brought by Nina Varava and eight other applicants and concerned an Oktyabyrskyy District Court of Poltava decision of 5 August 2004. Application no. 42557/06, introduced on 18 October 2006 by Viktor Kyryk, concerned a Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv decision of 1 November 2004. Application no. 48587/06, introduced on 14 November 2006 by Oleksandr Polezhay, concerned two Labour Disputes Commission decisions of the company “Chysti Metaly” dated 21 January 1998 and 14 August 1998. Application no. 6761/08, introduced on 17 January 2008 by Viktor Khapun, concerned Torez Court decisions of 6 May 2003 and 6 November 2006 and a Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal decision of 11 February 2008. Application no. 12172/08, introduced on 19 February 2008 by Dagir Kogermanov, concerned a Mukachevo Town Court decision of 18 July 2006. Other examples include application no. 55854/07, introduced on 20 November 2007 by Tetyana Dudina, concerning a Vinnytsya Regional Administrative Court decision of 14 September 2007; application no. 24392/08, introduced on 15 May 2008 by Antonina Golubnycha and Alla Shevchuk, concerning several decisions of the Korolovskyy District Court of Zhytomyr and Zhytomyr Regional Administrative Court dated 2006–2008; and application no. 23348/09, introduced on 15 April 2009 by Vasiliy Gabov, concerning Krasnoarmiysk Town Court decisions of 23 May 2008 and 11 June 2008.

The domestic decisions listed in the table range in date from 1997 to 2008, and the applications were introduced between 2006 and 2011. According to the applicants, those decisions became final and enforceable, but they were unable to secure enforcement in full or in due time because the national authorities failed to take action. The applicants therefore complained of non-enforcement and excessive delays.

case_name: CASE OF ĐUKOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO
summary:
The application was brought by Mr Batrić Đuković, a Montenegrin and Serbian national born in 1939. At the time of the proceedings he was serving his sentence in the Spuž Penitentiary. The Montenegrin Government were represented by their Agent, Ms V. Pavličić. On 13 November 2013 the application was communicated to the Government.

The factual record, as submitted by the parties, concerns two sets of civil proceedings before the domestic courts.

In the first set, on 25 March 1996 the applicant filed a compensation claim with the Court of First Instance (Osnovni sud) in Bar against the Municipality of Bar and one of the local primary schools. He sought damages for loss allegedly suffered as a consequence of the expropriation of his property. On 11 April 1996 the applicant’s representative informed the Court of First Instance that he had initiated a separate set of proceedings to determine the value of those damages. The Court of First Instance then suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that separate valuation matter. According to the record, no document was submitted by the parties showing whether the compensation proceedings had ended in the meantime. It therefore appeared that the two sets of proceedings were still pending before the Court of First Instance.

In the second set, on 2 February 2004 the applicant instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Bar against his neighbour. He sought a demarcation between their two plots of land. On 25 March 2004 the applicant amended his proposal in those proceedings. On 14 September 2004 the applicant and the respondent reached an agreement, which was approved by the Court of First Instance on the same day.

The supplied record does not set out any further factual allegations or arguments by the parties, nor does it describe additional concrete events or domestic decisions beyond those above. The case is identified as Đuković v. Montenegro, Application no. 38419/08.

case_name: CASE OF SARGSYAN AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
Three applications were lodged against Ukraine: no. 54012/07 by Vartan Sargsyan on 26 November 2007; no. 25697/08 by Igor Gordus on 9 May 2008; and no. 17361/10 by Konstantin Kravets on 7 October 2010. All applicants were Ukrainian nationals, represented by lawyers, and complained of police ill-treatment and ineffective investigation of their allegations.

Sargsyan alleged ill-treatment on 24–25 April 2007 at Chervonozavodskiy district police station in Kharkiv, where officers allegedly forced him to confess to murdering O. He described repeated face-pushing into foam rubber, twisting of handcuffed hands, being made to sit naked while officers squeezed his genitals with a plastic bag, head blows with a folder, spitting, threats, and electric current applied to wet rags on his ears, chin and head. He was placed under administrative arrest on 24 April, confessed on 25 April, met a lawyer on 27 April and retracted, and was released on 28 April. On 7 May 2007 the prosecutor decided not to institute criminal proceedings over O.’s murder for insufficient evidence. Medical evidence included a 24 April report of no injuries, a 29 April hospital certificate noting contusions, abrasions and painful genitals, and a 21 May forensic report of no injuries. He complained on 28 April 2007. Decisions not to institute proceedings were issued on 4 May, 8 May and 18 June 2007. On 18 August 2009 a district court dismissed his appeal concerning the 8 May decision because only a copy was available. On 24 February 2009 an administrative court allowed his complaint about prosecutor inactivity. He learned of some decisions late.

Gordus alleged two episodes. On 8 April 2006 at Debaltseve City Police office no. 35, after arrest on drug suspicion and questioning without a lawyer, police allegedly handcuffed him to a radiator for twelve hours, punched and hit him with truncheons, including blows to the mouth, kidneys and arms/shoulders; he fell and scratched his knees. On 18 June 2006 in Debaltseve ITT, three plainclothes officers allegedly hit his arms and shoulders and threatened to place him, a former policeman, with ordinary detainees. Medical reports of 12–13 April noted bruises, abrasions and lip erosion, minor and possibly self-inflicted; a 20 June certificate noted bruises on arrival at SIZO. Complaints were made on 11 April/5 June and 27 June 2006. Decisions not to institute proceedings were issued in 2006–2009; later decisions found injuries self-inflicted. One 2009 decision was communicated in 2011; an appeal against a 2006 decision was examined only in 2008 after delays.

Kravets alleged ill-treatment from 28 January to 1 February 2008 at Dniprovskiy district police station and Dniprodzerzhinsk ITT. He said he was detained from 28 to 30 January without procedural status, denied contact with relatives and a lawyer, and pressed to confess to inflicting fatal injuries on X. Officers allegedly tied him to a chair, punched his chest and head, suffocated him with smoke in a gas mask, threatened him, denied food, made him sleep on chairs, forced him to memorise a confession and sign blank papers, removed his boots and trousers, and made him participate in investigative actions in underpants. After confessing on 30 January, he was formally arrested and placed in ITT, where cellmate A. allegedly kicked and punched his chest and stomach. A 1 February forensic report noted bruises; a 28 February hospital certificate confirmed bruises and inpatient treatment for neurasthenia and hypertension. He was released on 1 February, retracted his confession, and on 19 October 2011 proceedings against him were terminated for lack of evidence. He complained on 30 January 2008. Repeated decisions not to institute proceedings were issued in 2008–2010. Criminal proceedings were initiated in 2010, closed and reopened, and finally closed on 29 February 2016, finding injuries inflicted by cellmate A. (then deceased) during a conflict. Decisions were often notified late; Kravets was mostly questioned as a witness and had victim status only briefly.

He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer.

At the police station he was taken into police custody. Before he had consulted his lawyer, who was not immediately available, but with his consent, police began a social interview concerning his personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He told officers he had cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord. He said this did not affect his functioning except possibly his trust in others, and that although he could play football he could not head the ball. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. Afterwards he said his lawyer would visit later that afternoon and that, on the lawyer’s advice, he would answer no further questions. The interview ended, and he met his lawyer later that day.

On 20 August 2009 the applicant was interviewed twice, including about the suspected distribution of child pornography. At the beginning he said he would prefer to have his lawyer present. He was told this was not possible, and the interview began. He answered questions. During questioning, officers noticed a spasm-like movement of his arm and asked if he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed that he was. The interview was interrupted and a doctor was called. He said the seizure could have been caused by stress and other factors. The interview then resumed. A final interview took place on 21 August 2009. Audio recordings were made of all interviews. He was released from police custody on 21 August 2009.

In the domestic proceedings, on 25 March 2011 the Regional Court of The Hague found him guilty of distribution of child pornography and sentenced him to a suspended two-week prison sentence and eighty hours’ community service. It considered that he should have been able to consult a lawyer before his first police interview. However, it found that the later interviews did not appear to have been conducted without his having been able to consult a lawyer, and that their content did not substantially differ from the interview conducted without legal assistance; it therefore considered a finding of procedural non-compliance sufficient. The applicant appealed.

On 3 July 2013 the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed the Regional Court’s decision, convicted him of the same offence, and sentenced him to forty hours’ community service. On his complaint about lack of legal assistance during police interviews, counsel argued that the suspect had the mental age of a fifteen- or sixteen-year-old and a brain disorder that might cause epileptic seizures, but submitted no medical data. The Court of Appeal found no indication to the interviewing officers of such mental age or that the disorder could cause a seizure. It considered that, after the spastic movement, the officers had correctly consulted a physician before resuming. It did not agree that they should reasonably have regarded him as vulnerable or underage. Accordingly, as an adult at the time, he was not entitled to have a lawyer present during interview under the Salduz case-law. The conviction relied on, among other evidence, the victim’s complaint and further police statement, the applicant’s 20 August 2009 statement that he had sent photographs and uploaded them, a third party’s statement about receiving two photographs, and a police record showing the photographs were accessible via a profile name on an image-hosting website.

The applicant appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court, complaining about the refusal to allow him legal assistance during police questioning. On 18 November 2014 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal with summary reasoning under section 81 of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act.

Under domestic law at the relevant time, following the earlier Salduz judgment of 27 November 2008, the Supreme Court held on 30 June 2009 that an arrested suspect could derive an entitlement to consult a lawyer before police interview, but not to have a lawyer present during police interviews; underage suspects were additionally entitled to a lawyer or confidant during interviews. On 22 December 2015, after the national proceedings, the Supreme Court accepted a right to legal assistance during police interviews, expected to apply from 1 March 2016. Article 457 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows revision of final convictions on the basis of a European Court of Human Rights ruling finding a violation in the proceedings leading to conviction, if necessary for legal redress.

case_name: CASE OF CĒSNIEKS v. LATVIA
summary:
Valters Cēsnieks, a Latvian national born in 1975 and later detained in Matīsa Prison, complained that after being summoned to a State Police station on 21 March 2002 he was ill-treated by police, that no effective investigation followed, and that evidence obtained through that ill-treatment was used at his trial.

On 21 March 2002 the police telephoned the applicant and asked him to come to the station. According to him, before formal charges were laid, officers accused him of murdering Ģ.Č. and used physical force to make him confess; he made a written confession. On 23 March 2002 he was transferred to a short-term detention facility. On 23 May 2002 the police opened an investigation into the alleged police misconduct. On 25 June 2005 a prosecutor concluded that the complaint was no longer subject to review, referring to the Supreme Court’s judgment of 26 April 2005.

The file included a typewritten witness statement of 21 March 2002 (5.20–6.40 p.m.), a handwritten confession dated 22 March 2002, a suspect interview on 22 March 2002 (11 a.m.–12.30 p.m.), and a further suspect interview that night (11.30 p.m.–12.50 a.m.). The transcripts recorded that he wished to give statements without a lawyer. In these statements he described financial difficulties, contacts with Z.K. and Ģ.Č., travel to Moscow with O.O., money transfers, and O.O.’s alleged role. In a further statement he said he had asked O.O. to kill Ģ.Č. to obtain LVL 17,000.

The applicant and co-accused O.O., V.Z. and J.G. were tried before the Riga Regional Court on charges relating to Ģ.Č.’s murder. On 11 October 2004 the Regional Court convicted V.Z. and J.G. of aggravated murder, but could not establish the guilt of the applicant or O.O. The applicant had pleaded not guilty and retracted his police statements, saying they were given after police beat him and broke his nose. The Regional Court found Article 3 violated, noting he remained at the Riga police station from 21 March until transfer on 23 March and that expert reports confirmed injuries. It found his 22 March 2002 statements contradictory, rejected an expert report finding no signs of anxiety, fear or ill-treatment, and ruled those statements could not be used for conviction. It found no other evidence that he had organised, assisted or incited the murder. The prosecution, victim and convicted co-accused appealed.

On 26 April 2005 the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder. It held that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected his confession and the expert report, that there was no impartial evidence the statements resulted from ill-treatment, and that the criminal case against police officers had been terminated. It admitted the 22 March 2002 statement in evidence and relied on it. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, confiscation of property and police control for two years.

The defence appealed on points of law, arguing that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because the confession and statements had been obtained through ill-treatment, the injuries were unexplained, and there was no other evidence of guilt. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, stating that it sought re-evaluation of evidence and that the Convention reference was formal.

case_name: CASE OF TERNOVIK AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
The case comprises twenty applications against Ukraine, introduced between 20 April 2006 and 7 September 2010. The applicants are Ukrainian nationals, except the applicant in application no. 64583/09, who is a Russian national. The applications mainly concern the lengthy failure to enforce final domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour. Domestic courts delivered judgments entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. The applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement because of the authorities’ failure to take specific budgetary or regulatory measures and because bans were introduced on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or controlled companies.

case_name: CASE OF HALIMI AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA
summary:
The application was brought against the Republic of Albania by nine Albanian nationals. Their details are said to be set out in Appendix No. 1 to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the supplied text. The applicants were represented before the European Court of Human Rights by Mr S. Puto, a lawyer practising in Tirana. The Albanian Government were represented by Ms A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. On 20 December 2013 the application was communicated to the Government.

The supplied factual record is brief. It states that on 30 May 1995 the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 sq. m. Since the plot was occupied, the applicants would be compensated in one of the ways provided by law. The record further states that, to date, no compensation has been paid.

No further particulars are given in the supplied text. The record does not identify the exact location or cadastral details of the plot, the person or entity occupying it, the compensation method selected or owed, any amount claimed, any later administrative or court decisions, or any concrete steps taken by the applicants to enforce the 1995 recognition. It also does not set out the applicants’ specific factual allegations beyond the recognition of inherited property rights and the non-payment of compensation, nor does it set out the Government’s factual response.

As regards domestic proceedings, the only domestic decision expressly mentioned in the factual circumstances is the Vlora Commission’s decision of 30 May 1995. The record does not describe subsequent domestic proceedings, decisions, appeals, or enforcement attempts. Under the heading “Relevant domestic law”, the supplied text does not reproduce the relevant provisions. Instead, it refers to descriptions of domestic law and practice in earlier judgments: Ramadhi v. Albania (no. 38222/02, 13 November 2007), Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania (nos. 604/07, 43628/07, 46684/07 and 34770/09, 31 July 2012), and Sharra and Others v. Albania [Committee] (nos. 25038/08, 64376/09, 64399/09, 347/10, 1376/10, 4036/10, 12889/10, 20240/10, 29442/10, 29617/10, 33154/11 and 2032/12, 10 November 2015). Those references are to earlier proceedings and prior descriptions of domestic law, not to findings in the present case.

The record also notes that relevant Council of Europe materials were referred to in earlier judgments: Sharra and Others, cited above; Metalla and Others v. Albania [Committee] (nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08, 16 July 2015); Siliqi and Others v. Albania [Committee] (nos. 37295/05 and 42228/05, 10 March 2015); and Karagjozi and Others v. Albania [Committee] (nos. 25408/06, 37419/06, 49121/06, 1504/07, 19772/07, 46685/07, 49411/07, 27242/08, 61912/08 and 15075/09, 8 April 2014). The supplied text does not set out the contents of those materials.

The record therefore contains little beyond the procedural communication and the core facts of the 1995 recognition, the occupied status of the land, the entitlement to compensation in one of the ways provided by law, and the continued absence of payment. It does not state the Convention provision invoked or the precise legal issue in the supplied text. No further dates, events, domestic rulings, or party arguments are provided in the factual record as supplied.

case_name: CASE OF EPNERS-GEFNERS v. LATVIA
summary:
The applicant, a Latvian national, lodged application no. 37862/02 against Latvia on 2 October 2002. He alleged that he had not received appropriate dental treatment and had not been able to receive long-term family visits in detention.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, the applicant was arrested on 1 October 1999 on suspicion of aggravated robbery. On 11 April 2002 the Kurzeme Regional Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to six years and one month’s imprisonment. On 5 June 2002 the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment on appeal. On 20 September 2002 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law at a preparatory meeting. On 23 August 2004 the Jelgava Court applied a pre-release scheme and ordered his release before the end of his sentence.

As to family visits, the applicant’s wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During pre-trial detention he received two short-term visits from his wife, on 16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001, and four short-term visits from his aunt. He was able to receive long-term visits while serving his sentence from 5 October 2002. Until his release on 23 August 2004 he received six long-term visits from his wife, each lasting about sixteen hours. Under the domestic rules in force until 14 May 2001, a Minister of the Interior instruction required approval for short-term visits and allowed one short-term visit of up to one hour per month with written permission. From 14 May 2001 a transitional instruction of the Minister of Justice allowed one short-term visit per month with written permission. Later rules included Cabinet Regulation no. 211 (2003), Cabinet Regulation no. 288 (2006) and the Law on Custody Procedure of 18 July 2006. In a domestic judgment of 19 December 2001, the Constitutional Court found that the transitional instruction and internal remand-prison regulations had not been made public and were internal normative acts; some rules were unconstitutional, but not those concerning short-term visits. In a domestic judgment of 23 April 2009, the Constitutional Court found no State obligation to ensure long-term visits and considered the restriction of such visits compatible with the Constitution, but held that the blanket one-hour monthly restriction on short-term visits was disproportionate. That restriction was abrogated from 1 December 2009, and since 11 August 2011 detainees have been entitled to visits of at least one hour from relatives or other persons at least once a month.

As to dental treatment, according to the Government the applicant first complained on 29 June 2000; a prison doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and advised him to consult a dentist. On 16 August 2000 he complained of toothache; the doctor prescribed Analgin and advised a dentist. On 18 August 2000 a dentist found caries in one tooth and noted two missing teeth and remains of twenty-one damaged teeth, with eight healthy teeth; the applicant refused the recommended treatment. On 10 August 2001 he again complained of toothache and was prescribed Analgin. On 19 September 2001 a psychiatrist considered his headaches related to dental cavity problems and advised a dentist. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease and four teeth were extracted. On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate that he had not received appropriate dental care and needed prosthetics; the complaint was transferred to the Prisons Administration. On 11 December 2001 the Prisons Administration replied that several extractions had been made free, eight teeth remained, and it was presumed he had not taken appropriate care before detention; prosthetics could be provided only at his own expense and no funds were allocated. On 27 December 2001 he complained to the President’s Chancery; the complaint was transferred via the Ministry of Justice and General Inspectorate to the Prisons Administration. On 12 February 2002 the Prisons Administration stated it had already answered on 11 December 2001 and reiterated that prosthetics could not be provided free in prisons. Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999), in force until 28 March 2007, provided that convicted persons receive minimum free health care and that the Prisons Administration provide emergency dental care within its budget; detained persons received care excluding planned in-patient treatment, with in-patient treatment only in acute circumstances.

case_name: CASE OF BRADARIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
summary:
The application was brought by Mr Nedžad Bradarić, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1954, who lives in Tuzla. Before the European Court of Human Rights he was represented by Zajednička advokatska kancelarija Jezdić & Matuzović, a law firm based in Tuzla. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were represented by their Agent, Ms B. Skalonjić. The applicant lodged application no. 84721/17 against Bosnia and Herzegovina on 14 December 2017. The complaint before the Court concerned the non-enforcement of a domestic settlement. On 13 November 2018 notice of that complaint was given to the Government.

The relevant domestic background began on 26 April 2012, when the applicant and his former employer, a private company based in Tuzla, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning the applicant’s severance pay. On 29 August 2012 the applicant filed a request with the Tuzla Municipal Court for enforcement of that settlement.

On 20 March 2017 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining about the non-enforcement of the settlement in question. On 15 June 2017 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in those domestic proceedings, found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court also awarded the applicant 1,000 convertible marks (BAM; approximately EUR 500) in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

On 27 September 2017, following a request submitted by a third party — a company which had brought a civil action against the applicant’s former employer in a separate set of proceedings — the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed the enforcement proceedings until the end of the proceedings initiated by that third party. The applicant appealed against that decision.

On 15 November 2017 the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned the decision of 27 September 2017 and rejected the third party’s request. It furthermore ordered the third party to pay the applicant BAM 1,053 in legal costs.

At the date of the latest information available to the Court (28 June 2019), the enforcement proceedings in the applicant’s case were still pending. The applicant’s complaint before the Court therefore concerned the continued non-enforcement of the settlement concluded on 26 April 2012, notwithstanding the earlier domestic proceedings and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 15 June 2017.

The relevant domestic background began on 26 April 2012, when the applicant and his former employer, a private company based in Tuzla, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning the applicant’s severance pay. On 29 August 2012 the applicant filed a request with the Tuzla Municipal Court for enforcement of that settlement.

On 20 March 2017 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining about the non-enforcement of the settlement in question. On 15 June 2017 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in those domestic proceedings, found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court also awarded the applicant 1,000 convertible marks (BAM; approximately EUR 500) in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

On 27 September 2017, following a request submitted by a third party — a company which had brought a civil action against the applicant’s former employer in a separate set of proceedings — the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed the enforcement proceedings until the end of the proceedings initiated by that third party. The applicant appealed against that decision.

On 15 November 2017 the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned the decision of 27 September 2017 and rejected the third party’s request. It furthermore ordered the third party to pay the applicant BAM 1,053 in legal costs.

At the date of the latest information available to the Court (28 June 2019), the enforcement proceedings in the applicant’s case were still pending. The applicant’s complaint before the Court therefore concerned the continued non-enforcement of the settlement concluded on 26 April 2012, notwithstanding the earlier domestic proceedings and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 15 June 2017.

case_name: CASE OF MAŽUKNA v. LITHUANIA
summary:
The application concerned Aleksandras Mažukna, a Lithuanian welder born in 1959, who alleged that Lithuania had failed to conduct an effective investigation into a workplace accident in which he was injured. In February 2007 he began working for company N. On 17 April 2007, while working at a factory construction site in Klaipėda, he and two co-workers were on scaffolding about two metres high when it broke and they fell. The applicant alleged he fell on his back, hit his head on concrete, lost consciousness, was moved away from the scene on his employer’s orders, and that traces of the accident were removed. An ambulance was called at 4:53 p.m. and he was taken to hospital.

The same day, a State Labour Inspectorate inspector examined the site. He found the scaffolding intact and no workers present. The site manager, V.J.S., said he had not seen the accident; a work-safety officer said initial medical examination showed no serious injury. The inspector decided the Inspectorate would not investigate. On 31 May 2007 another inspector concluded the applicant had fallen because of his own recklessness. After the applicant complained, on 15 July 2007 the Inspectorate issued a new conclusion attributing the accident to inappropriate organisation of dangerous work, particularly non-compliant scaffolding.

On 10 September 2007, at the applicant’s request, a pre-trial investigation was opened. Medical reports initially classified his head and face injuries as minor and chest injury as negligible; a later report found facial scarring causing disfigurement and classified the injury as serious. Witnesses interviewed generally said they had not seen the fall; some said no metal platform had been carried that day. On 6 October 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, relying on the initial Inspectorate finding and witness testimony, and suggested the applicant may have fallen due to recklessness or numbness in his legs. On 5 December 2008 the Klaipėda District Court reopened the investigation, criticising that conclusion as speculative.

In May 2009, co-worker V.K. stated that the workers had been ordered by V.J.S. to attach a metal platform to a reservoir tank, that the scaffolding was made of thin wood, that the company director told workers to repair it after the accident, and that he had earlier testified under employer pressure. On 17 June 2009 the Inspectorate concluded the scaffolding did not comply with safety requirements, the applicant had not received proper instructions, and the employer had breached safety law. On 3 July 2009 the prosecutor again discontinued the investigation, finding the scaffolding had been used safely before, that V.J.S. had been absent, and that workers acted recklessly. On 13 October 2009 the District Court reopened it, finding the employer had duties to ensure safety and supervise the platform work. On 28 October 2009 the Klaipėda Regional Court upheld that decision, noting the precise cause remained undetermined and that alleged false testimony under employer pressure required investigation.

In 2010, a forensic report found the platform exceeded the scaffolding’s weight limit, the scaffolding was unsuitable, workers lacked safety information, and the employer breached requirements. On 19 May 2010 the prosecutor discontinued again, concluding V.J.S. had not ordered the work and the accident resulted from workers’ recklessness; the employer might face only administrative liability. On 9 August 2010 the District Court reopened the case, finding the platform work was inherent to the job and the employer had failed to ensure safety. On 15 October 2010 V.J.S. was notified he was suspected under Article 176 §1 of the Criminal Code.

The pre-trial investigation was completed on 14 February 2011. On 1 April 2011 an indictment against V.J.S. was issued and transferred to the Klaipėda District Court. Hearings from June 2011 were adjourned due to absent witnesses and then V.J.S.’s repeated illness from December 2011. On 16 January 2012 the applicant filed a civil claim for LTL 300,000. On 8 May 2012 the prosecutor asked the court to terminate the case as time-barred; on 14 May 2012 the District Court terminated it, finding the five-year limitation period for negligent crimes could not be suspended, and did not examine the civil claim. The applicant’s later complaint to the Regional Court was not admitted as an appeal due to procedural defects; he did not submit another appeal. V.J.S.’s appeal was dismissed on 13 June 2012. On 22 November 2012 the Prosecutor General’s Office found no substantial procedural violations. The applicant died on 9 January 2016; his son Marius Mažukna wished to pursue the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF YAVOROVENKO AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
The case originated in 31 applications against Ukraine. The applicants were Ukrainian and Russian nationals and companies based in Ukraine, Cyprus and Romania. They were identified in the appended table. The applications were introduced between 21 June 2002 (no. 25663/02) and 1 March 2010 (no. 16112/10).

According to the appended table, domestic courts and arbitration bodies delivered decisions in the applicants’ favour. These included district and commercial courts, regional courts of appeal, the Higher Arbitration Court, and the International Commercial Arbitration Court at the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce. The decisions concerned various dates and applicants. For example, in no. 25663/02 the relevant decisions were given by the Zamostyanskyy and Leninskyy District Courts of Vinnytsya on 1 March 2004, 28 March 2006, 16 October 2006, 27 November 2006 and 6 April 2007. In no. 23581/03, the Odesa Regional Commercial Court gave decisions on 14 December 2000, rectified on 23 April 2001, and on 17 December 2001, as amended on 20 January 2003, 11 February 2004 and 12 May 2004. In no. 22422/05, the International Commercial Arbitration Court at the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce issued an award on 20 February 1997, in the light of a Kyiv City Commercial Court judgment of 29 August 2007. In no. 24245/10, the applicant complained of non-enforcement of an Oleksandriya Court judgment dated 22 October 2010; the appended table lists an Oleksandriya Court order of 22 October 2008.

The table also lists decisions in many other applications, including those of the Crimea Commercial Court, Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv, Chornomorskyy District Court of Crimea, Higher Arbitration Court, Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal, Donetsk Regional Commercial Court, Frankivskyy District Court of Lviv, Cherkasy Regional Court of Arbitration, Crimea Court of Appeal, Kyiv City Commercial Court, Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernigiv, Chuguyev Court, Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv, Leninskyy District Court of Lugansk, Minskyy District Court of Kyiv, Vyshgorodskyy District Court, Dnipropetrovsk Commercial Court of Appeal, Zaporizhzhya Regional Commercial Court, Lviv Circuit Administrative Court, Slovyansk Court, Kirovograd Regional Commercial Court, Novogorodivka Court, and others.

The domestic decisions entitled the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. The decisions became final and enforceable. The applicants alleged that they were unable to obtain enforcement of the decisions in due time. Some applicants also made submissions on factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

In application no. 23056/07, the applicant complained of non-enforcement of the Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv judgment dated 4 February 2005. The Government confirmed that the relevant domestic judgments remained unenforced. Later, according to the Government’s letter of 19 September 2013 and a Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv judgment of 9 July 2013, the enforcement proceedings in that application were terminated on 17 April 2013 and the decision was fully enforced. In application no. 24245/10, the Government also confirmed that the relevant judgment remained unenforced.

case_name: CASE OF EPNERS-GEFNERS v. LATVIA
summary:
The applicant, a Latvian national, lodged application no. 37862/02 against Latvia on 2 October 2002. He alleged that he had not received appropriate dental treatment and had not been able to receive long-term family visits in detention.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, the applicant was arrested on 1 October 1999 on suspicion of aggravated robbery. On 11 April 2002 the Kurzeme Regional Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to six years and one month’s imprisonment. On 5 June 2002 the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment on appeal. On 20 September 2002 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law at a preparatory meeting. On 23 August 2004 the Jelgava Court applied a pre-release scheme and ordered his release before the end of his sentence.

As to family visits, the applicant’s wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During pre-trial detention he received two short-term visits from his wife, on 16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001, and four short-term visits from his aunt. He was able to receive long-term visits while serving his sentence from 5 October 2002. Until his release on 23 August 2004 he received six long-term visits from his wife, each lasting about sixteen hours. Under the domestic rules in force until 14 May 2001, a Minister of the Interior instruction required approval for short-term visits and allowed one short-term visit of up to one hour per month with written permission. From 14 May 2001 a transitional instruction of the Minister of Justice allowed one short-term visit per month with written permission. Later rules included Cabinet Regulation no. 211 (2003), Cabinet Regulation no. 288 (2006) and the Law on Custody Procedure of 18 July 2006. In a domestic judgment of 19 December 2001, the Constitutional Court found that the transitional instruction and internal remand-prison regulations had not been made public and were internal normative acts; some rules were unconstitutional, but not those concerning short-term visits. In a domestic judgment of 23 April 2009, the Constitutional Court found no State obligation to ensure long-term visits and considered the restriction of such visits compatible with the Constitution, but held that the blanket one-hour monthly restriction on short-term visits was disproportionate. That restriction was abrogated from 1 December 2009, and since 11 August 2011 detainees have been entitled to visits of at least one hour from relatives or other persons at least once a month.

As to dental treatment, according to the Government the applicant first complained on 29 June 2000; a prison doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and advised him to consult a dentist. On 16 August 2000 he complained of toothache; the doctor prescribed Analgin and advised a dentist. On 18 August 2000 a dentist found caries in one tooth and noted two missing teeth and remains of twenty-one damaged teeth, with eight healthy teeth; the applicant refused the recommended treatment. On 10 August 2001 he again complained of toothache and was prescribed Analgin. On 19 September 2001 a psychiatrist considered his headaches related to dental cavity problems and advised a dentist. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease and four teeth were extracted. On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate that he had not received appropriate dental care and needed prosthetics; the complaint was transferred to the Prisons Administration. On 11 December 2001 the Prisons Administration replied that several extractions had been made free, eight teeth remained, and it was presumed he had not taken appropriate care before detention; prosthetics could be provided only at his own expense and no funds were allocated. On 27 December 2001 he complained to the President’s Chancery; the complaint was transferred via the Ministry of Justice and General Inspectorate to the Prisons Administration. On 12 February 2002 the Prisons Administration stated it had already answered on 11 December 2001 and reiterated that prosthetics could not be provided free in prisons. Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999), in force until 28 March 2007, provided that convicted persons receive minimum free health care and that the Prisons Administration provide emergency dental care within its budget; detained persons received care excluding planned in-patient treatment, with in-patient treatment only in acute circumstances.

case_name: CASE OF VAN DE KOLK v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
The applicant, Hugo Johannes Charles van de Kolk, is a Dutch national born in 1990 who lives in Alphen aan den Rijn. On 19 August 2009, when he was nineteen, he was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography—three pictures of a sixteen-year-old girl—in April of that year. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer.

At the police station he was taken into police custody. Before he had consulted his lawyer, who was not immediately available, but with his consent, police began a social interview concerning his personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He told officers he had cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord. He said this did not affect his functioning except possibly his trust in others, and that although he could play football he could not head the ball. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. Afterwards he said his lawyer would visit later that afternoon and that, on the lawyer’s advice, he would answer no further questions. The interview ended, and he met his lawyer later that day.

On 20 August 2009 the applicant was interviewed twice, including about the suspected distribution of child pornography. At the beginning he said he would prefer to have his lawyer present. He was told this was not possible, and the interview began. He answered questions. During questioning, officers noticed a spasm-like movement of his arm and asked if he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed that he was. The interview was interrupted and a doctor was called. He said the seizure could have been caused by stress and other factors. The interview then resumed. A final interview took place on 21 August 2009. Audio recordings were made of all interviews. He was released from police custody on 21 August 2009.

In the domestic proceedings, on 25 March 2011 the Regional Court of The Hague found him guilty of distribution of child pornography and sentenced him to a suspended two-week prison sentence and eighty hours’ community service. It considered that he should have been able to consult a lawyer before his first police interview. However, it found that the later interviews did not appear to have been conducted without his having been able to consult a lawyer, and that their content did not substantially differ from the interview conducted without legal assistance; it therefore considered a finding of procedural non-compliance sufficient. The applicant appealed.

On 3 July 2013 the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed the Regional Court’s decision, convicted him of the same offence, and sentenced him to forty hours’ community service. On his complaint about lack of legal assistance during police interviews, counsel argued that the suspect had the mental age of a fifteen- or sixteen-year-old and a brain disorder that might cause epileptic seizures, but submitted no medical data. The Court of Appeal found no indication to the interviewing officers of such mental age or that the disorder could cause a seizure. It considered that, after the spastic movement, the officers had correctly consulted a physician before resuming. It did not agree that they should reasonably have regarded him as vulnerable or underage. Accordingly, as an adult at the time, he was not entitled to have a lawyer present during interview under the Salduz case-law. The conviction relied on, among other evidence, the victim’s complaint and further police statement, the applicant’s 20 August 2009 statement that he had sent photographs and uploaded them, a third party’s statement about receiving two photographs, and a police record showing the photographs were accessible via a profile name on an image-hosting website.

The applicant appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court, complaining about the refusal to allow him legal assistance during police questioning. On 18 November 2014 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal with summary reasoning under section 81 of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act.

Under domestic law at the relevant time, following the earlier Salduz judgment of 27 November 2008, the Supreme Court held on 30 June 2009 that an arrested suspect could derive an entitlement to consult a lawyer before police interview, but not to have a lawyer present during police interviews; underage suspects were additionally entitled to a lawyer or confidant during interviews. On 22 December 2015, after the national proceedings, the Supreme Court accepted a right to legal assistance during police interviews, expected to apply from 1 March 2016. Article 457 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows revision of final convictions on the basis of a European Court of Human Rights ruling finding a violation in the proceedings leading to conviction, if necessary for legal redress.

case_name: CASE OF CĒSNIEKS v. LATVIA
summary:
Valters Cēsnieks, a Latvian national born in 1975 and later detained in Matīsa Prison, complained that after being summoned to a State Police station on 21 March 2002 he was ill-treated by police, that no effective investigation followed, and that evidence obtained through that ill-treatment was used at his trial.

On 21 March 2002 the police telephoned the applicant and asked him to come to the station. According to him, before formal charges were laid, officers accused him of murdering Ģ.Č. and used physical force to make him confess; he made a written confession. On 23 March 2002 he was transferred to a short-term detention facility. On 23 May 2002 the police opened an investigation into the alleged police misconduct. On 25 June 2005 a prosecutor concluded that the complaint was no longer subject to review, referring to the Supreme Court’s judgment of 26 April 2005.

The file included a typewritten witness statement of 21 March 2002 (5.20–6.40 p.m.), a handwritten confession dated 22 March 2002, a suspect interview on 22 March 2002 (11 a.m.–12.30 p.m.), and a further suspect interview that night (11.30 p.m.–12.50 a.m.). The transcripts recorded that he wished to give statements without a lawyer. In these statements he described financial difficulties, contacts with Z.K. and Ģ.Č., travel to Moscow with O.O., money transfers, and O.O.’s alleged role. In a further statement he said he had asked O.O. to kill Ģ.Č. to obtain LVL 17,000.

The applicant and co-accused O.O., V.Z. and J.G. were tried before the Riga Regional Court on charges relating to Ģ.Č.’s murder. On 11 October 2004 the Regional Court convicted V.Z. and J.G. of aggravated murder, but could not establish the guilt of the applicant or O.O. The applicant had pleaded not guilty and retracted his police statements, saying they were given after police beat him and broke his nose. The Regional Court found Article 3 violated, noting he remained at the Riga police station from 21 March until transfer on 23 March and that expert reports confirmed injuries. It found his 22 March 2002 statements contradictory, rejected an expert report finding no signs of anxiety, fear or ill-treatment, and ruled those statements could not be used for conviction. It found no other evidence that he had organised, assisted or incited the murder. The prosecution, victim and convicted co-accused appealed.

On 26 April 2005 the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder. It held that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected his confession and the expert report, that there was no impartial evidence the statements resulted from ill-treatment, and that the criminal case against police officers had been terminated. It admitted the 22 March 2002 statement in evidence and relied on it. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, confiscation of property and police control for two years.

The defence appealed on points of law, arguing that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because the confession and statements had been obtained through ill-treatment, the injuries were unexplained, and there was no other evidence of guilt. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, stating that it sought re-evaluation of evidence and that the Convention reference was formal.
