summary:
The case originated in 16 applications against Ukraine lodged by Ukrainian nationals and companies. The applications were communicated to the Government on various dates; the Government were represented by their Agent. In applications nos. 12424/06 and 23509/08, the applicants died during the Court proceedings, and their next-of-kin expressed the wish to pursue the applications.

The table also lists decisions in many other applications, including those of the Crimea Commercial Court, Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv, Chornomorskyy District Court of Crimea, Higher Arbitration Court, Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal, Donetsk Regional Commercial Court, Frankivskyy District Court of Lviv, Cherkasy Regional Court of Arbitration, Crimea Court of Appeal, Kyiv City Commercial Court, Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernigiv, Chuguyev Court, Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv, Leninskyy District Court of Lugansk, Minskyy District Court of Kyiv, Vyshgorodskyy District Court, Dnipropetrovsk Commercial Court of Appeal, Zaporizhzhya Regional Commercial Court, Lviv Circuit Administrative Court, Slovyansk Court, Kirovograd Regional Commercial Court, Novogorodivka Court, and others.

The domestic decisions entitled the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. The decisions became final and enforceable. In application no. 24245/10, the Government also confirmed that the relevant judgment remained unenforced.

case_name: CASE OF SARGSYAN AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
Three applications were lodged against Ukraine: no. 54012/07 by Vartan Sargsyan on 26 November 2007; no. 25697/08 by Igor Gordus on 9 May 2008; and no. 17361/10 by Konstantin Kravets on 7 October 2010. All applicants were Ukrainian nationals, represented by lawyers, and complained of police ill-treatment and ineffective investigation of their allegations.

Sargsyan alleged ill-treatment on 24–25 April 2007 at Chervonozavodskiy district police station in Kharkiv, where officers allegedly forced him to confess to murdering O. He described repeated face-pushing into foam rubber, twisting of handcuffed hands, being made to sit naked while officers squeezed his genitals with a plastic bag, head blows with a folder, spitting, threats, and electric current applied to wet rags on his ears, chin and head. He was placed under administrative arrest on 24 April, confessed on 25 April, met a lawyer on 27 April and retracted, and was released on 28 April. On 7 May 2007 the prosecutor decided not to institute criminal proceedings over O.’s murder for insufficient evidence. Medical evidence included a 24 April report of no injuries, a 29 April hospital certificate noting contusions, abrasions and painful genitals, and a 21 May forensic report of no injuries. He complained on 28 April 2007. Decisions not to institute proceedings were issued on 4 May, 8 May and 18 June 2007. On 18 August 2009 a district court dismissed his appeal concerning the 8 May decision because only a copy was available. On 24 February 2009 an administrative court allowed his complaint about prosecutor inactivity. He learned of some decisions late.

case_name: CASE OF MAŽUKNA v. LITHUANIA
summary:
The application concerned Aleksandras Mažukna, a Lithuanian welder born in 1959, who alleged that Lithuania had failed to conduct an effective investigation into a workplace accident in which he was injured. In February 2007 he began working for company N. On 17 April 2007, while working at a factory construction site in Klaipėda, he and two co-workers were on scaffolding about two metres high when it broke and they fell. The applicant alleged he fell on his back, hit his head on concrete, lost consciousness, was moved away from the scene on his employer’s orders, and that traces of the accident were removed. An ambulance was called at 4:53 p.m. and he was taken to hospital.

The same day, a State Labour Inspectorate inspector examined the site. He found the scaffolding intact and no workers present. The site manager, V.J.S., said he had not seen the accident; a work-safety officer said initial medical examination showed no serious injury. The inspector decided the Inspectorate would not investigate. On 31 May 2007 another inspector concluded the applicant had fallen because of his own recklessness. After the applicant complained, on 15 July 2007 the Inspectorate issued a new conclusion attributing the accident to inappropriate organisation of dangerous work, particularly non-compliant scaffolding.

On 10 September 2007, at the applicant’s request, a pre-trial investigation was opened. Medical reports initially classified his head and face injuries as minor and chest injury as negligible; a later report found facial scarring causing disfigurement and classified the injury as serious. Witnesses interviewed generally said they had not seen the fall; some said no metal platform had been carried that day. On 6 October 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, relying on the initial Inspectorate finding and witness testimony, and suggested the applicant may have fallen due to recklessness or numbness in his legs. On 5 December 2008 the Klaipėda District Court reopened the investigation, criticising that conclusion as speculative.

In May 2009, co-worker V.K. stated that the workers had been ordered by V.J.S. to attach a metal platform to a reservoir tank, that the scaffolding was made of thin wood, that the company director told workers to repair it after the accident, and that he had earlier testified under employer pressure. On 17 June 2009 the Inspectorate concluded the scaffolding did not comply with safety requirements, the applicant had not received proper instructions, and the employer had breached safety law. On 3 July 2009 the prosecutor again discontinued the investigation, finding the scaffolding had been used safely before, that V.J.S. had been absent, and that workers acted recklessly. On 13 October 2009 the District Court reopened it, finding the employer had duties to ensure safety and supervise the platform work. On 28 October 2009 the Klaipėda Regional Court upheld that decision, noting the precise cause remained undetermined and that alleged false testimony under employer pressure required investigation.

In 2010, a forensic report found the platform exceeded the scaffolding’s weight limit, the scaffolding was unsuitable, workers lacked safety information, and the employer breached requirements. On 19 May 2010 the prosecutor discontinued again, concluding V.J.S. had not ordered the work and the accident resulted from workers’ recklessness; the employer might face only administrative liability. On 9 August 2010 the District Court reopened the case, finding the platform work was inherent to the job and the employer had failed to ensure safety. On 15 October 2010 V.J.S. was notified he was suspected under Article 176 §1 of the Criminal Code.

The pre-trial investigation was completed on 14 February 2011. On 1 April 2011 an indictment against V.J.S. was issued and transferred to the Klaipėda District Court. Hearings from June 2011 were adjourned due to absent witnesses and then V.J.S.’s repeated illness from December 2011. On 16 January 2012 the applicant filed a civil claim for LTL 300,000. On 8 May 2012 the prosecutor asked the court to terminate the case as time-barred; on 14 May 2012 the District Court terminated it, finding the five-year limitation period for negligent crimes could not be suspended, and did not examine the civil claim. The applicant’s later complaint to the Regional Court was not admitted as an appeal due to procedural defects; he did not submit another appeal. V.J.S.’s appeal was dismissed on 13 June 2012. On 22 November 2012 the Prosecutor General’s Office found no substantial procedural violations. The applicant died on 9 January 2016; his son Marius Mažukna wished to pursue the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF ĐUKOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO
summary:
The application was brought by Mr Batrić Đuković, a Montenegrin and Serbian national born in 1939. At the time of the proceedings he was serving his sentence in the Spuž Penitentiary. The Montenegrin Government were represented by their Agent, Ms V. Pavličić. On 13 November 2013 the application was communicated to the Government.

The factual record, as submitted by the parties, concerns two sets of civil proceedings before the domestic courts.

In the first set, on 25 March 1996 the applicant filed a compensation claim with the Court of First Instance (Osnovni sud) in Bar against the Municipality of Bar and one of the local primary schools. He sought damages for loss allegedly suffered as a consequence of the expropriation of his property. On 11 April 1996 the applicant’s representative informed the Court of First Instance that he had initiated a separate set of proceedings to determine the value of those damages. The Court of First Instance then suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that separate valuation matter. According to the record, no document was submitted by the parties showing whether the compensation proceedings had ended in the meantime. It therefore appeared that the two sets of proceedings were still pending before the Court of First Instance.

In the second set, on 2 February 2004 the applicant instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Bar against his neighbour. He sought a demarcation between their two plots of land. On 25 March 2004 the applicant amended his proposal in those proceedings. On 14 September 2004 the applicant and the respondent reached an agreement, which was approved by the Court of First Instance on the same day.

The supplied record does not set out any further factual allegations or arguments by the parties, nor does it describe additional concrete events or domestic decisions beyond those above. The case is identified as Đuković v. Montenegro, Application no. 38419/08.

case_name: CASE OF BRADARIĆ v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
summary:
The application was brought by Mr Nedžad Bradarić, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1954, who lives in Tuzla. Before the European Court of Human Rights he was represented by Zajednička advokatska kancelarija Jezdić & Matuzović, a law firm based in Tuzla. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were represented by their Agent, Ms B. Skalonjić. The applicant lodged application no. 84721/17 against Bosnia and Herzegovina on 14 December 2017. The complaint before the Court concerned the non-enforcement of a domestic settlement. On 13 November 2018 notice of that complaint was given to the Government.

The relevant domestic background began on 26 April 2012, when the applicant and his former employer, a private company based in Tuzla, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning the applicant’s severance pay. On 29 August 2012 the applicant filed a request with the Tuzla Municipal Court for enforcement of that settlement.

On 20 March 2017 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining about the non-enforcement of the settlement in question. On 15 June 2017 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in those domestic proceedings, found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court also awarded the applicant 1,000 convertible marks (BAM; approximately EUR 500) in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

On 27 September 2017, following a request submitted by a third party — a company which had brought a civil action against the applicant’s former employer in a separate set of proceedings — the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed the enforcement proceedings until the end of the proceedings initiated by that third party. The applicant appealed against that decision.

On 15 November 2017 the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned the decision of 27 September 2017 and rejected the third party’s request. It furthermore ordered the third party to pay the applicant BAM 1,053 in legal costs.

At the date of the latest information available to the Court (28 June 2019), the enforcement proceedings in the applicant’s case were still pending. The applicant’s complaint before the Court therefore concerned the continued non-enforcement of the settlement concluded on 26 April 2012, notwithstanding the earlier domestic proceedings and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 15 June 2017.

case_name: CASE OF GAZSÓ v. HUNGARY
summary:
The factual record concerns an application brought by Mr György Gazsó, a Hungarian national born in 1963 who lives in Telki, against Hungary. The applicant, represented by Mr D. Karsai, a Budapest lawyer, lodged application no. 48322/12 under Article 34 of the Convention on 24 July 2012. The Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent at the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that litigation in his labour dispute had lasted an unreasonably long time and that there was no effective remedy available to him in that regard. He relied on Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention. On 13 November 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. At the same time, the Court proposed the pilot judgment procedure under Rule 61 of the Rules of Court to the parties, and the parties submitted comments in that respect.

The domestic facts concern a labour dispute between the applicant and his former employer. Between 25 February 2002 and 18 May 2005, litigation was in progress between the applicant and his former employer. That litigation eventually obliged the former employer to re-employ the applicant. The applicant did not accept the position that was offered to him in pursuit of the re-employment order. New litigation therefore started on 5 January 2006.

On 18 November 2008, the Budapest Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s action. On appeal, on 9 July 2010, the Budapest Regional Court reversed that decision and found for the applicant. The respondent then pursued a petition for review before the Kúria. On 29 February 2012, the Kúria reversed the appeal judgment and found for the respondent. These are the domestic decisions and dates identified in the supplied record.

The applicant’s factual allegations are framed around the overall duration of the labour dispute, including the earlier litigation period from 25 February 2002 to 18 May 2005 and the new litigation beginning on 5 January 2006, which continued through the domestic decisions up to 29 February 2012. The alleged lack of an effective remedy relates to that same labour dispute. The record does not set out further details of the domestic proceedings, such as the specific delays attributable to each stage, the reasons for the duration, the exact claims and defences in the labour dispute beyond the re-employment issue, or the content of the parties’ submissions beyond the fact that they commented on the proposed pilot judgment procedure. The application number, lodging date, representation details, communication date, and the domestic decisions listed above are the principal factual elements stated in the record relevant to the alleged violations.

case_name: CASE OF VLAD AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
summary:
Three Romanian nationals—Mihai Vlad, Flaviu Plaţa and Vasilica Bratu—lodged applications against Romania on 5 October 2006, 14 September 2007 and 9 November 2007. The applications concerned the length of domestic proceedings and the alleged absence of remedies in that respect; they were communicated to the Government and later joined.

Mr Vlad (born 1945, Bucharest) was detained on 30 January 1994 on suspicion of first-degree murder; the prosecutor opened an investigation and authorised his detention the next day. He was indicted on 18 November 1994 for murder and aggravated theft. Hearings before the Timiş County Court ran from February to December 1995. The case was remitted to the prosecution on 13 December 1995, but that was reversed on appeal on 22 April 1996. On 22 November 1996 he was convicted and sentenced to 18 years. On 14 April 1997 the appeal court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 15 September 1997 he was again convicted and sentenced to 18 years; his appeal was dismissed on 12 March 1998. On 28 October 1998 the ICCJ allowed a further appeal and returned the case to the prosecution because the investigation was incomplete. A new indictment followed on 8 July 1999. His requests for a counter forensic report and removal of the panel were rejected. On 5 May 2000 he was convicted and sentenced to 15 years; the ICCJ allowed an appeal on 9 November 2000 and returned the case to the prosecution. A new indictment was issued on 15 October 2001. On 12 April 2002 the ICCJ transferred the case to Dolj County Court. On 9 September 2003 that court convicted him and sentenced him to 15 years. Five appeal hearings were adjourned for failure to properly summon him. On 16 May 2005 the Craiova Court of Appeal rejected leave to appeal as time-barred; the ICCJ quashed that and ordered retrial. On 2 November 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and on 6 April 2006 the ICCJ dismissed his appeal on points of law.

Mr Plaţa (born 1969, Bucharest) learned on 6 March 1997 of a civil estate-division suit brought by his aunt before Bucharest District Court no. 2. On 19 May 1998 the ICCJ transferred it to District Court no. 6. Hearings were adjourned because authorities failed to submit documents. On 21 January 1999 the proceedings were stayed at his request and resumed on 22 November 1999. After a dispute about service in China, the court on 6 September 2001 annulled procedural acts from 16 December 1999 to 22 February 2001. On 13 December 2001 the action was allowed in part. An appeal led to a constitutional review; on 11 February 2003 the Constitutional Court upheld the relevant provision. On 18 November 2003 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the appeal. On 27 January 2005 the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal on points of law and sent the case back for retrial. On 28 October 2005 the County Court again quashed and remitted. On 21 June 2006 the District Court ruled in part, upheld on 15 November 2006 and 29 March 2007. Enforcement later stalled: on 7 September 2011 a bailiff declared he could not enforce the judgment, and a complaint remained pending before District Court no. 6.

Mrs Bratu (born 1964, Bucharest) was questioned by police on 4 May 1998 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and indicted on 30 June 1998 before Bucharest District Court no. 1. A new forensic accounting report was ordered on 26 May 1999 and submitted in November 1999. On 24 May 2000 the State’s civil claim was dismissed as time-barred; on 20 July 2000 she was convicted and given a suspended one-year sentence. On 29 June 2001 the county court upheld the criminal part but ordered retrial on the civil part; on 13 December 2001 the Court of Appeal rejected her appeal on points of law on the conviction. On 31 May 2002 the District Court allowed the civil action in part. After an appeal in June 2002, the Bucharest County Court scheduled 22 hearings pending documents from public authorities; on 8 November 2004 it increased compensation. On 28 January 2005 the Court of Appeal set aside the appeal decision and ordered a new appeal trial. The retrial was adjourned 17 times for improper service and missing documents. On 9 September 2005 the court fined the chief prosecutor; the documents arrived 19 months later. On 23 March 2007 the County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the 31 May 2002 decision. On 11 May 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on points of law.

The record also contains domestic law on reasonable time, tort liability and disciplinary liability, Law no. 202/2010, and a civil complaint about protraction of proceedings from 15 February 2013. The Government argued that existing remedies and case-law could expedite proceedings or compensate delays; Council of Europe materials noted structural delay problems and reforms.

case_name: CASE OF A AND B v. GEORGIA
summary:
The applicants, A and B, are Georgian nationals living in Georgia. A is C’s mother, and B is C’s son. C was born on 24 November 1994 and killed on 25 July 2014 by her partner D, B’s father and a police officer.

In 2011, when C was 17, D kidnapped her for marriage. Under constant threat, she cohabited with him from December 2011 until June 2012, when she returned to her parents’ home pregnant after physical and psychological harassment. From December 2011, C and her family allegedly suffered regular verbal and physical abuse from D, who threatened to kill C and her parents and referred to his police status and connections. In July 2012 C called police about a threat to kill A; no response followed. On 31 August 2013, after an argument over child support, D beat C at her parents’ house. Three patrol officers, D’s acquaintances and colleagues, interviewed C in D’s presence, dismissed wife-beating as commonplace, allowed D to interfere and prepared a report inaccurately describing a “minor family altercation”. C refused to sign, but D forced her to sign while threatening to kill her, which officers overheard. An officer warned her not to contact police without valid reason. D left with the officers.

The same day C filed a criminal complaint with a local prosecutor against D and the officers. On 4 September 2013 a prosecutor interviewed C, D and one officer; D denied ill-treatment. On 9 September 2013 D gave a written undertaking not to abuse C or her family; the prosecution decided not to open a criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014 C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her in public on 3 and 5 July 2014. Witness statements allegedly confirmed that between April 2011 and July 2014 D used his official position to abuse C: flaunting his service pistol at least seven times, threatening false charges against C’s father and brother, and saying he was part of law enforcement. On 20 July 2014 D was promoted to senior police lieutenant. On 25 July 2014 the General Inspectorate interviewed C about her complaint. She reiterated systematic physical and psychological harassment but asked that D not be treated too harshly because he was the father of her child. Shortly after, D stalked her; eyewitnesses saw a loud argument in a public park. D drew his service pistol and fired five shots at C’s chest and stomach at close range, killing her instantly.

Criminal proceedings against D began that day. He was charged with murder and told investigators the relationship had been strained by jealousy and that C had provoked and humiliated him by saying her private and sex life did not concern him. On 17 April 2015 the Kutaisi City Court convicted D of premeditated murder of a family member, sentencing him to 11 years. His insanity defence was rejected by forensic examination. The conviction became final on 15 February 2016 and did not refer to gender-based discrimination.

On 22 January 2015 A, for herself and B, asked the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office to open a criminal investigation into police and prosecutors’ failure to protect C and respond to domestic-violence reports, arguing negligence may have been influenced by gender-based discrimination. On 19 February 2015 a criminal case was opened into the police officers’ alleged failure; they said they did not think the incident was violent. A was interviewed on 27 February 2015. Between March and August 2015 five witnesses were interviewed; most described the 31 August 2013 incident as particularly violent. A repeatedly enquired about progress; on 20 March 2015 she was told an investigation into police negligence had been launched. She received no response about her complaint against prosecutors. In March 2016 a regional prosecutor said the police-negligence investigation was pending, no charges had been brought and victim status was not then necessary. A again received no response concerning prosecutors.

On 22 January 2015 A also sued the Ministry of the Interior and Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office under Article 1005 of the Civil Code, claiming GEL 120,000 non-pecuniary damage for failure to protect C’s life. On 24 July 2015 the Tbilisi City Court partly allowed the claim, awarding GEL 20,000. It found a causal link between police/prosecutor inactivity and C’s killing; noted police did not interview C or witnesses, did not issue a restraining order and did not restrict D’s service pistol; and found prosecutors failed to investigate adequately. The judgment became final on 29 June 2017 after the Supreme Court terminated proceedings.

Mr Vlad (born 1945, Bucharest) was detained on 30 January 1994 on suspicion of first-degree murder; the prosecutor opened an investigation and authorised his detention the next day. He was indicted on 18 November 1994 for murder and aggravated theft. Hearings before the Timiş County Court ran from February to December 1995. The case was remitted to the prosecution on 13 December 1995, but that was reversed on appeal on 22 April 1996. On 22 November 1996 he was convicted and sentenced to 18 years. On 14 April 1997 the appeal court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 15 September 1997 he was again convicted and sentenced to 18 years; his appeal was dismissed on 12 March 1998. On 28 October 1998 the ICCJ allowed a further appeal and returned the case to the prosecution because the investigation was incomplete. A new indictment followed on 8 July 1999. His requests for a counter forensic report and removal of the panel were rejected. On 5 May 2000 he was convicted and sentenced to 15 years; the ICCJ allowed an appeal on 9 November 2000 and returned the case to the prosecution. A new indictment was issued on 15 October 2001. On 12 April 2002 the ICCJ transferred the case to Dolj County Court. On 9 September 2003 that court convicted him and sentenced him to 15 years. Five appeal hearings were adjourned for failure to properly summon him. On 16 May 2005 the Craiova Court of Appeal rejected leave to appeal as time-barred; the ICCJ quashed that and ordered retrial. On 2 November 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and on 6 April 2006 the ICCJ dismissed his appeal on points of law.

Mr Plaţa (born 1969, Bucharest) learned on 6 March 1997 of a civil estate-division suit brought by his aunt before Bucharest District Court no. 2. On 19 May 1998 the ICCJ transferred it to District Court no. 6. Hearings were adjourned because authorities failed to submit documents. On 21 January 1999 the proceedings were stayed at his request and resumed on 22 November 1999. After a dispute about service in China, the court on 6 September 2001 annulled procedural acts from 16 December 1999 to 22 February 2001. On 13 December 2001 the action was allowed in part. An appeal led to a constitutional review; on 11 February 2003 the Constitutional Court upheld the relevant provision. On 18 November 2003 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the appeal. On 27 January 2005 the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal on points of law and sent the case back for retrial. On 28 October 2005 the County Court again quashed and remitted. On 21 June 2006 the District Court ruled in part, upheld on 15 November 2006 and 29 March 2007. Enforcement later stalled: on 7 September 2011 a bailiff declared he could not enforce the judgment, and a complaint remained pending before District Court no. 6.

Mrs Bratu (born 1964, Bucharest) was questioned by police on 4 May 1998 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and indicted on 30 June 1998 before Bucharest District Court no. 1. A new forensic accounting report was ordered on 26 May 1999 and submitted in November 1999. On 24 May 2000 the State’s civil claim was dismissed as time-barred; on 20 July 2000 she was convicted and given a suspended one-year sentence. On 29 June 2001 the county court upheld the criminal part but ordered retrial on the civil part; on 13 December 2001 the Court of Appeal rejected her appeal on points of law on the conviction. On 31 May 2002 the District Court allowed the civil action in part. After an appeal in June 2002, the Bucharest County Court scheduled 22 hearings pending documents from public authorities; on 8 November 2004 it increased compensation. On 28 January 2005 the Court of Appeal set aside the appeal decision and ordered a new appeal trial. The retrial was adjourned 17 times for improper service and missing documents. On 9 September 2005 the court fined the chief prosecutor; the documents arrived 19 months later. On 23 March 2007 the County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the 31 May 2002 decision. On 11 May 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on points of law.

The record also contains domestic law on reasonable time, tort liability and disciplinary liability, Law no. 202/2010, and a civil complaint about protraction of proceedings from 15 February 2013. The Government argued that existing remedies and case-law could expedite proceedings or compensate delays; Council of Europe materials noted structural delay problems and reforms.

case_name: CASE OF A AND B v. GEORGIA
summary:
The applicants, A and B, are Georgian nationals living in Georgia. A is C’s mother, and B is C’s son. C was born on 24 November 1994 and killed on 25 July 2014 by her partner D, B’s father and a police officer.

In 2011, when C was 17, D kidnapped her for marriage. Under constant threat, she cohabited with him from December 2011 until June 2012, when she returned to her parents’ home pregnant after physical and psychological harassment. From December 2011, C and her family allegedly suffered regular verbal and physical abuse from D, who threatened to kill C and her parents and referred to his police status and connections. In July 2012 C called police about a threat to kill A; no response followed. On 31 August 2013, after an argument over child support, D beat C at her parents’ house. Three patrol officers, D’s acquaintances and colleagues, interviewed C in D’s presence, dismissed wife-beating as commonplace, allowed D to interfere and prepared a report inaccurately describing a “minor family altercation”. C refused to sign, but D forced her to sign while threatening to kill her, which officers overheard. An officer warned her not to contact police without valid reason. D left with the officers.

The same day C filed a criminal complaint with a local prosecutor against D and the officers. On 4 September 2013 a prosecutor interviewed C, D and one officer; D denied ill-treatment. On 9 September 2013 D gave a written undertaking not to abuse C or her family; the prosecution decided not to open a criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014 C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her in public on 3 and 5 July 2014. Witness statements allegedly confirmed that between April 2011 and July 2014 D used his official position to abuse C: flaunting his service pistol at least seven times, threatening false charges against C’s father and brother, and saying he was part of law enforcement. On 20 July 2014 D was promoted to senior police lieutenant. On 25 July 2014 the General Inspectorate interviewed C about her complaint. She reiterated systematic physical and psychological harassment but asked that D not be treated too harshly because he was the father of her child. Shortly after, D stalked her; eyewitnesses saw a loud argument in a public park. D drew his service pistol and fired five shots at C’s chest and stomach at close range, killing her instantly.

Criminal proceedings against D began that day. He was charged with murder and told investigators the relationship had been strained by jealousy and that C had provoked and humiliated him by saying her private and sex life did not concern him. On 17 April 2015 the Kutaisi City Court convicted D of premeditated murder of a family member, sentencing him to 11 years. His insanity defence was rejected by forensic examination. The conviction became final on 15 February 2016 and did not refer to gender-based discrimination.

On 22 January 2015 A, for herself and B, asked the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office to open a criminal investigation into police and prosecutors’ failure to protect C and respond to domestic-violence reports, arguing negligence may have been influenced by gender-based discrimination. On 19 February 2015 a criminal case was opened into the police officers’ alleged failure; they said they did not think the incident was violent. A was interviewed on 27 February 2015. Between March and August 2015 five witnesses were interviewed; most described the 31 August 2013 incident as particularly violent. A repeatedly enquired about progress; on 20 March 2015 she was told an investigation into police negligence had been launched. She received no response about her complaint against prosecutors. In March 2016 a regional prosecutor said the police-negligence investigation was pending, no charges had been brought and victim status was not then necessary. A again received no response concerning prosecutors.

On 22 January 2015 A also sued the Ministry of the Interior and Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office under Article 1005 of the Civil Code, claiming GEL 120,000 non-pecuniary damage for failure to protect C’s life. On 24 July 2015 the Tbilisi City Court partly allowed the claim, awarding GEL 20,000. It found a causal link between police/prosecutor inactivity and C’s killing; noted police did not interview C or witnesses, did not issue a restraining order and did not restrict D’s service pistol; and found prosecutors failed to investigate adequately. The judgment became final on 29 June 2017 after the Supreme Court terminated proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF PILETIĆ v. MONTENEGRO
summary:
Application no. 53044/13 originated in an application against Montenegro lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on 12 July 2013. The applicant was Draga Piletić, born on 4 January 1928. She was represented by Ana Đukanović, a lawyer practising in Podgorica. The Montenegrin Government were given notice of the application. Draga Piletić died on 22 December 2015. The application was thereafter pursued by her heirs, Nina Đikanović, born on 4 December 1959, and Jelka Tomašević, born on 2 June 1954.

The applicant complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings. The appended factual table identifies the relevant starting date for the domestic civil proceedings as 3 March 2004. That date is described in the table as either the start of the proceedings or the date of entry into force of the Convention in respect of Montenegro. The domestic proceedings ended on 18 October 2011. The total length of the proceedings was recorded as 7 years, 7 months and 15 days. The proceedings took place before three levels of jurisdiction. The relevant domestic decision is identified as a decision of the Supreme Court of Montenegro, Rev.U.no. 18/10/2011.

Beyond those entries, the supplied record does not describe the subject matter of the civil dispute, the parties to the domestic civil case, the claims or relief sought, the procedural steps taken before the domestic courts, or the content of the domestic decision. It also does not set out any arguments made by the applicant or the Government before the European Court of Human Rights on the substance of the complaint, except that the applicant alleged that the civil proceedings had been excessively long and that the Government had been given notice of the application.

The appended table lists the applicant’s personal details, the representative’s name and location, the date of introduction of the application, the start date used for calculating the length of the domestic proceedings, the end date of those proceedings, the total duration, the number of jurisdictional levels, and the relevant domestic decision. It also records that the original applicant died during the proceedings and that her heirs continued the application.

The record contains no further concrete events, dates, or factual allegations relevant to the excessive-length complaint. In particular, it does not provide a chronology of hearings, adjournments, appeals, or other procedural developments within the domestic civil proceedings, nor does it identify the court or courts below the Supreme Court by name or the dates of their decisions. The only domestic decision specifically identified is the Supreme Court of Montenegro decision referred to above. Thus, the factual basis supplied is limited to the procedural history and duration data set out in the application and appended table.

case_name: CASE OF ȘCERBININA v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA AND RUSSIA
summary:
Application no. 76892/14 was lodged by Ms Irina Șcerbinina, a Moldovan national born in 1981 who lives in Tiraspol. She was represented before the European Court of Human Rights by Ms N. Hriplivîi, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The respondents are the Republic of Moldova and the Russian Federation. The Moldovan Government were represented by their Agent, Mr O. Rotari. The Russian Government were represented by Mr M. Galperin, the Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights. The application was lodged on 4 December 2014. Notice of the application was given to both Governments, and the parties submitted observations.

The factual background to the case, including the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991-1992 and subsequent events, is identified in the record as being set out in two earlier cases: Ilașcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia (GC, no. 48787/99, §§ 28-185, ECHR 2004-VII) and Catan and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (GC, nos. 43370/04, 8252/05 and 18454/06, §§ 8-42, ECHR 2012). The present record does not reproduce those background facts in detail.

As to the applicant’s domestic employment proceedings, in 2013 she was dismissed from employment. She initiated proceedings against her employer seeking reinstatement. Those proceedings were conducted before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The proceedings ended with the final judgment of the Supreme Court of the “MRT” dated 5 June 2014. By that judgment, the applicant’s action was dismissed. No further detail is given in the supplied record about the lower courts’ decisions, the grounds for dismissal, or the content of the reinstatement claim.

On an unspecified date, the applicant complained to the authorities of Moldova. A criminal investigation was initiated by the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office into her complaints. Later, those criminal proceedings were discontinued. The stated ground for discontinuation was that the facts complained about by the applicant did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence. The record does not give the date of the applicant’s complaint, the date the investigation began, or the date it was discontinued.

The record also notes a relevant legal framework section. It states that reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations, the relevant domestic law and practice of the Republic of Moldova, and other pertinent documents were summarised in Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (GC, no. 11138/10, §§ 61-77, 23 February 2016). That case is identified as earlier authority. Apart from the above, the supplied text does not set out additional concrete factual events, detailed allegations by the applicant, or detailed arguments by the respondent Governments concerning the merits. It identifies the parties, the domestic employment and criminal proceedings, the relevant dates that appear in the record, and the background references.

case_name: CASE OF VIEIRA GOMES BEZERRA v. PORTUGAL
summary:
The applicant, Ms Tomásia Vieira Gomes Bezerra, is a Portuguese national born in Silves, Portugal, and living in Bonn, Germany. On 4 October 2010 she lodged application no. 60786/10 against the Portuguese Republic with the European Court of Human Rights. The Portuguese Government were represented by their Agent, Ms M. F. Graça de Carvalho, Deputy-Attorney General. On 17 October 2012 the application was communicated to the Government.

The factual record concerns civil proceedings initiated by the applicant in Portugal. On 28 February 2007 she started proceedings against two companies before the Court of Vila Nova de Gaia. The proceedings concerned the occupation of land that the applicant claimed to be her own. They were registered as domestic proceedings no. 1908/07.8TBVNG. The defendants contested the proceedings, and the court ordered that the size of the land be analysed by an expertise. Those procedural steps ended on 18 December 2007.

In the first trimester of 2008, an attempt was made to conciliate the parties. On 18 July 2008, the court ordered suspension of the proceedings because the property was not registered in the applicant’s name before the Land Registry Office (Conservatória do Registo Predial). On 20 January 2010, the court ordered the interruption of the proceedings. On 18 July 2010, the applicant joined an additional supporting document to the proceedings and informed the court that the land had been registered. The judge then ordered the proceedings to be resumed. According to the last information received by the Court on 3 May 2013, the domestic proceedings were still pending.

The supplied record does not describe any further substantive arguments by the parties or identify a specific Convention complaint. It sets out only the above procedural and factual chronology: the applicant’s ownership claim concerning occupied land, the defendants’ contestation, the court-ordered expertise, the conciliation attempt, the suspension for lack of registration, the interruption of the proceedings, the later registration information submitted by the applicant, and the resumption of the proceedings. The record does not give details about the identities of the companies, the exact location or size of the land, the content of the defendants’ defence, the result of the conciliation attempt, or any domestic decision on the merits or appeal. It also does not specify the relief sought in the domestic proceedings or the precise basis of the application to the European Court of Human Rights. The concrete events and dates relevant to the domestic proceedings are therefore limited to: 28 February 2007, when the applicant commenced the civil action; 18 December 2007, when the procedural steps concerning the expertise ended; the first trimester of 2008, when conciliation was attempted; 18 July 2008, when suspension was ordered; 20 January 2010, when interruption was ordered; 18 July 2010, when the applicant submitted the registration document and the judge ordered resumption; and 3 May 2013, when the Court last received information indicating that the proceedings remained pending.

case_name: CASE OF ALIŠIĆ AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA, CROATIA, SERBIA, SLOVENIA AND "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
The application was lodged on 30 July 2005 by three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak and Sakib Šahdanović, against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The first applicant is also a German citizen; all live in Germany. Before the dissolution of the SFRY, Ališić and Sadžak deposited foreign currency with Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, and Šahdanović with the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30 and DEM 63,880.44; Šahdanović also had USD 73 and 4 Austrian schillings. They alleged that they could not withdraw their “old” foreign-currency savings from those accounts.

In the SFRY, banks were organised as basic and associated banks. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was a basic bank; in 1978 it and others founded Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. Foreign-currency deposits were State-guaranteed and largely “redeposited” with the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo shipped foreign currency to the National Bank of Slovenia; between 1984 and 1991 DEM 244,665,082 was shipped to Ljubljana and DEM 41,469,528 returned. In 1990, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which took over its rights, assets and liabilities. Investbanka became independent with headquarters in Serbia and branches in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Tuzla. From 1990/91, SFRY measures restricted withdrawals of foreign-currency savings, at times to DEM 500 at a time and DEM 1,000 per month.

After the SFRY dissolved in 1991/92, each successor State adopted measures. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State and Entities addressed “old” savings. The FBH assumed liability in 1997, but later legislation expressly excluded savings in branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. A 2006 State law excluded those branches but required the State to help clients recover from Slovenia and Serbia. Domestic Constitutional Court decisions, including AP 164/04 of 1 April 2006, AP 423/07 of 14 October 2008 and AP 14/08 of 21 December 2010, found neither Bosnia and Herzegovina nor its Entities liable and ordered help in recovering from Slovenia and Serbia. The Sarajevo branch had about DEM 250 million in savings at 31 December 1991. A domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was set up in 1993 and purported to assume liability; in November 2004 the Sarajevo Municipal Court held it was not the successor and deleted the 1993 register entry. Bankruptcy proceedings against it began in 2010 and remained pending. The Tuzla branch of Investbanka closed on 1 June 1992. A Serbian court made a bankruptcy order against Investbanka in 2002; bankruptcy remained pending, and in 2011 Serbia began a criminal investigation into transfer of the Tuzla archives in 2008.

Other States took measures. Croatia stated it repaid old savings in domestic banks and foreign branches, and repaid citizens’ savings transferred from Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana’s Zagreb branch; some remaining clients obtained payment from forced sale of branch assets in Croatia, while others sued in Croatian or Slovenian courts. Serbia in 1998 and 2002 agreed to repay certain domestic-bank savings, but left successor-State citizens’ and branch savings frozen pending succession; after Investbanka’s 2002 bankruptcy, 322 clients of Bosnian branches unsuccessfully sought payment, and 20 sued without success. Slovenia assumed the SFRY guarantee in 1991; after restructuring, old Ljubljanska Banka retained liability for branches in other successor States. In 1997 proceedings concerning those branches were stayed pending succession negotiations; in December 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the stay unconstitutional. Thereafter Ljubljana District Court judgments ordered the old bank to pay savings in the Sarajevo and Zagreb branches; one Sarajevo-branch judgment became final on 16 November 2010. Claims against Slovenia were rejected in three final cases. The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia repaid old savings in domestic banks and local branches of foreign banks regardless of citizenship. The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues, in force from 2 June 2004, provided for negotiations under BIS auspices on SFRY guarantees of hard-currency savings; after failed rounds, the BIS ended its role in 2002.

case_name: CASE OF M.O. v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The applicant, M.O., is an Eritrean national born in 1990. He grew up in Eritrea, entered Switzerland illegally on 23 June 2014 and applied for asylum the next day. He was heard by the Swiss asylum authorities on 1 July 2014, 11 March 2015 and 29 January 2016, with an interpreter and translated records; NGO witnesses attended the later hearings. He claimed he left school after eighth grade, was called up for military service, tried to avoid it, reported for duty, attempted to escape, was caught, beaten and imprisoned in Wi’a. In the first hearing he said he was detained from June 2012 to September 2013; in the second he said March to October 2013. He described limited military training, no weapon use, and no superior, unit or military number. He said he escaped from prison, stayed briefly in Eritrea, left illegally via Mereb on 3 October 2013, was picked up by Ethiopian soldiers and later registered in the Hitsas refugee camp. In the third hearing he said a smuggler, not a neighbour, had helped him; he left A. at about 6 p.m., lost his way and was apprehended around 3–4 a.m. He submitted a student card, church deacon card, Italian food-distribution card, marriage certificate from 2010, his son’s baptism certificate from 2012, a deacon attestation and a UNHCR letter confirming registration in Hitsas on 8 November 2013. He stated he was married and had a son born in October 2012.

On 8 March 2016 the State Secretariat for Migration rejected the asylum request and ordered his departure. It found his account not credible because of contradictions about the detention period, military training, schooling, departure and illegal exit. On 14 April 2016 the applicant appealed to the Federal Administrative Court. He argued that his deacon status had delayed conscription until the 2010 change in practice, that poor students were sent to Wi’a, that he tried to escape and was detained from March to September 2013, and that his family arranged a smuggler. He attributed date errors to poor education, stressed consistent elements, scars and fear, and relied on the UNHCR registration and the impossibility of legal exit. He claimed refugee status for fear of ill-treatment for desertion, alternatively temporary admission based on post-flight grounds and Article 3.

On 9 May 2016 the Federal Administrative Court rejected the appeal. It found the asylum claim not credibly demonstrated, citing irreconcilable school dates, a substance-poor military account, and fundamental contradictions on detention duration and dates. It found his departure account insufficient and said the UNHCR camp letter did not establish individual persecution risk. It held removal possible, permitted and reasonable under the Aliens Act, noting he was young, healthy and had a support network. The State Secretariat set a voluntary departure deadline that expired on 17 July 2016.

The record also contains country information describing Eritrea’s open-ended national service, forced labour, punishment of deserters and draft evaders, strict exit controls and risks for illegal exit and returnees, including detention and ill-treatment. The applicant alleged before the Court that expulsion to Eritrea would violate Articles 3 and 4 of the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF N.M.B. v. SWEDEN
summary:
The applicant, N.M.B., is an Iraqi national born in 1973 and originally from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden on 12 December 2007 and applied for asylum the following day. In his application against Sweden, lodged on 15 November 2010, he alleged that his deportation to Iraq would involve a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. He was represented by Mr T. Stilus; the Swedish Government were represented by Ms C. Hellner and Ms H. Lindquist.

In support of his asylum claim, the applicant stated that he was a Christian academic employed at a university in Baghdad. In April 2006 he began working for a committee established to develop research methods at the university. The committee was soon accused of cooperating with Americans. On 20 June 2006 the applicant wrote to the Minister of Education, accusing a university colleague, a member of the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP), of corruption and of counteracting the committee’s work. The colleague learned of the accusation and threatened the applicant.

On 27 June 2006 armed men attempted to kidnap the applicant’s daughter. Her mother called the police; after some shooting, the daughter was released. On 30 June 2006 the applicant received a letter calling him and his family Christian traitors and stating that they would be killed if he did not quit his job. On 8 July 2006 he reported the incidents to the police, and the family moved in with relatives. On 16 July 2006 the head of the committee was kidnapped and killed, after committee members had received threatening letters; the committee’s work then ended. On 3 October 2006 the applicant fled with his family to Syria.

On 15 January 2008 the applicant’s parents, who lived in Baghdad, were shot at; his father was kidnapped and tortured until he told the kidnappers the applicant’s whereabouts. In October and December 2008 the applicant received threatening messages on a website. In one, the Islamic Brigade, a militia within the IIP, warned him against returning to Iraq.

On 17 March 2009 the Migration Board rejected the asylum application. It did not question that the applicant was a Christian and had worked for the university committee, but did not find it likely that his work had made him a suspect of cooperating with Americans. It noted that he had quit the job three years earlier and that there was nothing to indicate a remaining work-related threat. It also found that he had not made plausible that his accusation against a former colleague had harmed that person or the IIP, and it questioned the credibility of the alleged attack on his parents. The Board further noted that the security situation in Baghdad and Iraq as a whole had improved.

The applicant appealed, claiming a risk of persecution as a Christian and an academic. He added that members of the IIP had asked for him and had written threatening messages on the wall of his old house in December 2009. He also stated that he had reported to the police his suspicion that high-profile members of the Ministry of Education were responsible for the kidnapping attempt against his daughter.

On 9 June 2010 the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It held that the incidents did not constitute persecution on religious grounds. It found that the applicant had exaggerated his story by adding the police report about his suspicions, that his work for the committee was limited in scope and had ended long ago, and that, absent political activity, his letter to the Ministry was unlikely to cause the alleged threat. It concluded that there was no individual threat against him.

On 3 November 2010 the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal. The applicant subsequently claimed impediments to enforcement, invoking the general situation for Christians in Baghdad and attacks in November 2010 in the residential area where he had lived. On 26 January 2011 the Migration Board declined to reconsider the case, finding no new circumstances justifying reconsideration. The record also referred to the earlier case M.Y.H. and Others v. Sweden for relevant domestic law and information about Iraq.

case_name: CASE OF VAN WESENBEECK v. BELGIUM
summary:
The case concerns two applications against Belgium brought by Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, a Dutch national born in 1961 and living in Beveren. He alleged that he had not received a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 and that his defence rights under Article 6 § 3 (d) were breached because he was unable to question the undercover agents involved.

On 10 May 2006, the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation against the applicant and others on suspicion of drug trafficking, involvement in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. It included infiltration; observation was authorised on 1 August 2006. A separate confidential file was established. The proactive investigation continued until 17 September 2008. Reports of 17 and 18 September 2008 summarised the evidence and the infiltration and observation operations and were added to the criminal file. On 18 September 2008 the public prosecutor confirmed the authorisations and requested that the investigating judge open a judicial investigation. A reactive investigation followed before the Hasselt investigating judge, also using phone-tapping and international mutual legal assistance. A report of 25 September 2008 referred to information on the criminal organisation and confirmations obtained through the special investigative measures. On 20 October 2008 the Federal Prosecutor’s Office took over the case, still under the Hasselt investigating judge.

The observation and infiltration operations ended on 14 June 2009, when several suspects, including the applicant, were arrested and placed in pre-trial detention. On 29 December 2009 the Federal Prosecutor asked the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal to verify the confidential file under Article 235ter of the Code of Criminal Procedure; the parties also sought a lawfulness review under Article 235bis. At a hearing on 2 March 2010, the Federal Prosecutor was heard separately in the absence of the parties, and the confidential file was made available to the Division. The defendants, including the applicant, then presented their case with their lawyers.

By interim judgment of 20 May 2010, the Indictments Division held that it had to verify information concerning both the reactive and proactive investigations, found that some evidence had still to be added to the criminal file, and reopened proceedings. The 18 September 2008 decisions and the 25 September 2008 report were then added. On 24 June 2010 the Indictments Division declared the criminal file complete and found no nullity, irregularity or violation of legal or Convention provisions. It also found no irregularities in the special investigative methods, stating that the proactive investigation had complied with conditions including reasonable suspicion, proportionality and subsidiarity; a debit indicator found on 15 August 2008 was decisive.

The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 21 September 2010. His complaint that the file lacked the report underlying the 10 May 2006 proactive investigation and related documents was rejected as requiring a factual assessment. On 29 September 2010 the Hasselt Court committed seventeen defendants, including the applicant, for trial.

On 16 March 2011 the Hasselt Court of First Instance sentenced the applicant to ten years’ imprisonment and fined him 137,500 euros for drug trafficking, involvement in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. The judgment relied partly on evidence obtained through the special investigative methods. The court refused the applicant’s request for a face-to-face meeting with the undercover agents, citing lack of necessity, the agents’ safety and anonymity, the long infiltration, friendships formed, alleged online exposure, unclear specific questions, and the Indictments Division’s verification. It also rejected claims of incitement, finding that the agent acted only in relation to an offence from January to June 2009, while the judicial investigation had begun on 18 September 2008, and that reports, messages and calls showed no incitement.

On 23 June 2011 the Antwerp Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment in absentia. On 13 October 2011, after adversarial proceedings, it confirmed the judgment. It again refused a face-to-face meeting, referring to the lower court’s reasoning, adding that it gave only relative evidentiary value to the agents’ statements and that other evidence established guilt; it also considered the request rather academic because the applicant had refused to appear. The applicant appealed on points of law, alleging breaches of fair-trial and defence rights, the adversarial principle, use of evidence from the undisclosed confidential file, and the refusal of a face-to-face meeting. On 20 March 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that lack of access to the confidential file did not in itself violate Article 6, that the restriction was justified by protection of investigative techniques and the safety and anonymity of those implementing them, and was counterbalanced by oversight by the Indictments Division and the ability to contest the methods. As to the face-to-face meeting, it held that Article 6 § 3 (d) did not prevent the judge from assessing the necessity and relevance of hearing a requested witness.

case_name: CASE OF SETA v. GREECE AND GERMANY
summary:
Application no. 30287/09 was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 April 2009 by Mr Selim Seta, a Kosovar national born in 1942 who lives in Besian. The application was lodged against the Hellenic Republic. The Greek Government were represented by their Agent, Mr F. P. Georgakopoulos, President of the Legal Council of the State. On 5 July 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. Although the case is named Seta v. Greece and Germany, the supplied factual record describes the application as having been brought against the Hellenic Republic; apart from the applicant’s allegation involving a German national and his prior residence in Germany, no factual events concerning Germany are set out.

The facts concern events beginning on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested by the Greek authorities at the Greek-Albanian borders. He was charged with drug trafficking after 25 kg of heroin was found in the car he was driving. On the same day, the Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor prosecuted him for illegal drug trafficking and ordered his detention on remand by order no. 25/2002. The applicant alleges that his arrest was a set-up by a German national with whom he had had disagreements in Germany, where the applicant had allegedly lived for an unspecified period, and that the drugs were placed in the car without his knowledge.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, on 20 May 2003 the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twenty years’ imprisonment by judgment no. 81/2003. On an unspecified date the applicant lodged an appeal. On 5 June 2007 the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment by judgment no. 58/2007. On 8 September 2007 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation challenging that decision. According to the record, in the grounds of appeal the applicant did not raise any complaint regarding interpretation service at the moment he was arrested or afterwards during the proceedings. The hearing before the Court of Cassation was originally set for 12 March 2008 but was adjourned to 19 November 2008. As it appears from the case file, those proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation.

case_name: CASE OF THUO v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, David William Thuo, a Kenyan national born in 1978, complained under Article 3 about his conditions of detention at Nicosia Central Prisons, his ill-treatment during deportation on 9 March 2007, and the absence of an effective investigation into that ill-treatment.

He entered Cyprus unlawfully on 4 April 2005 and was arrested at Larnaca Airport on 6 April 2005 attempting to travel on a forged passport. On 12 April 2005 the Larnaca District Court sentenced him to nine months’ imprisonment after a guilty plea. He was held in Wing 1B of Nicosia Central Prisons; his appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 4 July 2005. He applied for asylum on 21 April 2005. On 10 November 2005 detention and deportation orders were issued against him as a “prohibited immigrant,” but enforcement was suspended pending his asylum claim. Released on 14 November 2005 after serving his sentence, he was re-arrested the same day and placed in immigration detention in Block 10. His asylum application was rejected on 31 January 2006; an appeal was dismissed on 6 April 2006, and he brought a Supreme Court recourse on 3 May 2006. He also complained to the Ombudsman on 11 June 2006 and, through counsel, wrote to the Minister of the Interior in May and August 2006.

Deportation was initially impossible because he lacked a travel document and refused to cooperate. After the Kenyan Embassy issued a travel document on 20 February 2007 in the name David Kandiri Wanjiku, new orders were issued on 22 February 2007. He was deported on 9 March 2007 and placed on the authorities’ stop list. His Supreme Court recourse was withdrawn on 9 May 2007.

According to the applicant, early on 9 March 2007 prison guards and two immigration officers insulted him, refused his request to call a lawyer, pushed him, hit him, pinched his testicles and held his neck; he was later allowed to call his lawyer. At Larnaca Airport, three men in military uniform and two immigration officers allegedly beat and verbally abused him, forced him into a chair, held him by the neck, stuffed brown paper into his mouth, taped his mouth and neck with Cyprus Airways adhesive tape, and wrapped bandages around his head and neck. He was handcuffed on the aircraft and remained in pain until near Milan. He alleged four top teeth later became loose and said he could identify the officers.

He complained to the Ombudsman on 27 December 2007. Her report of 4 June 2009 found the allegations not substantiated, noting difficulties in gathering evidence after deportation. He complained to the IAIACAP on 23 February 2008. After a preliminary investigation, on 9 July 2008 the IAIACAP considered the complaint investigable but sought the Attorney General’s opinion; on 28 July 2008 counsel for the Attorney General said it could not be investigated because the applicant had left Cyprus. On 17 June 2009 the Attorney General ordered a formal investigation, which began on 14 July 2009. The investigator collected police records; airport CCTV had been destroyed, and the cabin crew report did not mention the incident. Five officers were treated as suspects. On 12 June 2010 the applicant returned and was medically examined: the maxillofacial surgeon could not attribute tooth damage with certainty after three years; the urologist found no issues; a forensic pathologist considered ill-treatment minimal to negligible. On 17 June 2010 an identity parade took place; N.S., Pa.P. and A.I. were absent, but the applicant identified them from photographs. T.C. and Po.P. denied ill-treatment but later said the applicant tried to harm himself and was wrapped in bandages to protect him, not gagged. N.S. and A.I. refused to answer questions. The investigator’s report of 22 July 2010 noted deficient records, possible exaggeration by the applicant, uniform discrepancies and the failure of some officers to attend the parade; he considered force may have exceeded permissible limits but favoured disciplinary action. The IAIACAP found only necessary force had been used and the applicant self-serving. On 2 September 2010 the Attorney General decided no criminal or disciplinary action was merited; the Chief of Police took no disciplinary action but issued recording instructions and held lectures.

As to detention conditions, the applicant alleged a shared 5.5 sq. m cell, no exercise, poor hygiene and overcrowding, including after a May 2006 fire and renovation work. The Government described a cell of about 2.73 by 2 m with hygiene facilities, air conditioning, communal areas and outdoor access, and renovation from October 2005 to October 2010. IAIACAP material recorded 36 cells of 5.4 sq. m, about one hour daily outdoor exercise, up to 58 detainees in February 2007, and isolation for refusing cleaning. The applicant told the investigator that treatment was good but conditions were not.

case_name: CASE OF SOLOMAKHIN v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Mr Sergey Dmitriyevich Solomakhin, was a Ukrainian national born in 1964 who lived in Donetsk. He died on 13 September 2010; his mother, Mrs Vera Petrovna Solomakhina, later expressed the wish to pursue the application. The applicant was represented by Ms I. Gavrilenko, and the Ukrainian Government by Mr Y. Zaytsev. On 22 July 2003 the applicant lodged an application alleging, in particular, that the court proceedings in his case were excessively lengthy and that his health had suffered as a result of medical malpractice.

On 23 November 1998 the applicant sought medical assistance from Donetsk City Hospital No. 16, where he was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease and prescribed out-patient treatment. On 27 November 1998 he was tested for reaction to a diphtheria vaccination; the test showed no susceptibility to diphtheria antigens. On 28 November 1998 he was vaccinated against diphtheria. According to the applicant, the vaccination was contraindicated for him. On 30 November 1998 a doctor indicated that his health had improved and diagnosed tracheobronchitis, confirmed at visits on 3, 4 and 7 December 1998. From 28 December 1998 the applicant spent more than half a year in various medical institutions receiving treatment for chronic diseases, including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis and colitis.

On 4 February 1999 the Chief Doctor of the Hospital reprimanded doctor Ya. and nurse Sh. for vaccinating the applicant although he had consistently objected and was being treated for an acute respiratory infection. The Chief Doctor considered that they had violated vaccination rules and ordered them to pass a test on those rules.

On 26 April 1999 the applicant instituted proceedings in the Budyonnovskiy District Court in Donetsk against the local department of public health and the Hospital, seeking compensation for damage to his health. He alleged that the 28 November 1998 vaccination had been conducted while he was ill and had caused a number of chronic diseases. He also complained that the vaccine had been of poor quality, uncertified, expired and stored in inappropriate conditions, and that doctors had tried to falsify medical records and conceal negative effects.

Between 30 May and 30 June 2000, 17 July 2000, 29 January 2001, 2 and 30 January 2002, 4 March 2002 and 17 February 2003, medical expert examinations were conducted. On 2 June 2003 the court found against the applicant. Referring to the expert conclusions, it established that his diseases had no causal link to the vaccination. It noted that he had not had an allergic reaction or other signs normally appearing within several days; the only disease possibly associated with vaccination was urticaria, suffered more than eight months later, which could not have a causal link. The court found that he had no acute symptoms upon vaccination and that no medical rules had been violated. It stated that the epidemic situation in the Donetsk region had called for diphtheria vaccination. No physical force had been applied, and, as an adult of sound mind, he could have refused, as he had done before. Although the vaccination was not performed in the vaccination room, it was conducted by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s office, in the doctor’s presence, after prior verification of his reaction, and caused no negative side-effects. His allegations about vaccine quality were speculative and unconfirmed. The court observed that none of his diseases had a causal link to the vaccination and that his hospital time was due to his attempts to obtain disabled status. His allegations about falsification of medical records were rejected as unsubstantiated.

On 19 March 2008 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and on 22 August 2008 the Supreme Court upheld the judgment. The applicant died of a heart attack on 13 September 2010. By letter of 26 September 2011 his mother informed the Court of her wish to pursue the application. Domestic law included the 1994 Health Care and Control of Diseases Act, under which preventive vaccinations against tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and measles were compulsory in Ukraine, with procedures set by the Ministry of Health. Guidelines approved on 25 January 1996 addressed vaccination organisation, contraindications, side-effects and notification. Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly Recommendation 1317 (1997) concerned vaccination in Europe and the diphtheria epidemic.

case_name: CASE OF TSATANI v. GREECE
summary:
The applicant, Georgia Tsatani, born in 1952, was a prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2016 V.T., President of the Court of Cassation, informed her that she had opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation against her. This followed letters dated 24 February 2016 from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General expressing concern about the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a media-covered fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. sent the applicant evidence and reports and invited written defence within ten days.

On 30 March 2016 the applicant wrote to the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation, arguing that he had exclusive competence and asking him to launch a preliminary investigation. She also complained that D.P., Deputy Minister of Justice, had referred in Parliament on 29 March 2016 to the confidential disciplinary proceedings. On 1 April she replied to V.T., complaining that she had not been offered an oral defence and that the alleged disciplinary acts were unclear. On 4 April V.T. provided a detailed statement and invited written and oral defence within a fresh ten-day period. The applicant submitted written defence and a recusal request against V.T., alleging bias: V.T. had served as interim prime minister in September 2015 and allegedly had special relations with D.P. and the Cypriot officials; V.T. had allegedly leaked confidential information, asked prejudicial questions and supplied an incomplete file.

On 12 April 2016 V.T. referred the case to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation to continue the preliminary investigation. She stated that the recusal request was an abuse of process and unfounded, that her relations with the Cypriot officials and D.P. were official, that she had not acted under Cypriot pressure, and that she had conducted the investigation herself because of high socioeconomic interest. On 21 April the applicant complained to the Vice-President that V.T. had issued a press release about the recusal request and asked that no further action be taken pending a decision on recusal. On 5 May the Vice-President concluded the investigation and proposed disciplinary action; she declared the applicant’s reiterated recusal request inadmissible for lack of standing.

On 24 June 2016 V.T. brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant before the seven-member disciplinary council of the Court of Cassation. She maintained that the recusal request was inadmissible because it had not been lodged with the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation and was, at most, an invitation to withdraw; she had not dismissed it but had delegated the investigation. On 10 October 2016 the seven-member council found the applicant guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary: she had terminated investigations within the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s exclusive competence and breached a Greece–Cyprus EUROJUST agreement. It imposed sixty days’ salary deprivation. It found the recusal request inadmissible and the delegation lawful. The applicant appealed. On 16 March 2017 the nine-member disciplinary council dismissed her appeal. It held that the recusal request had not been validly submitted and was in any event unfounded; V.T. had not dismissed it but had lawfully referred the investigation. On 22 March 2021 the nine-member council rejected a request to reopen.

The record also notes V.T.’s press release of 18 April 2016, reported in the press on 18–19 April, in which she called the recusal request unfounded and an abuse of process, and D.P.’s parliamentary statements of 29 March 2016 mentioning the pending disciplinary investigation. The applicant complained that she had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because V.T., who had opened the investigation and dealt with the recusal request, subsequently brought the disciplinary action against her.

case_name: CASE OF GRUPA ZASTAVA VOZILA, A.D. v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D., is a Serbian company. In 1996 it concluded a contract with PS ZA AVTO p.o. before a notary concerning joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO instituted proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of that contract and the notarial protocol. The applicant company was the defendant in those domestic proceedings.

On 14 July 1998, the District Court ordered the claim to be served on the applicant company in the Republic of Serbia with the assistance of the Ministry of Justice through diplomatic channels. On 29 October 1998 the court made an inquiry with the Ministry about service. On 12 November 1998 the Ministry informed the court that it was still waiting for a reply from the Serbian authorities. On 30 May 2000, ZASTAVA AVTO d.o.o. requested third-party intervention. On 6 June 2000 the court made another inquiry with the Ministry concerning service. On 29 June 2000 the applicant company’s representative sent an authority form and a request for joinder with another case. On 17 May 2001 the applicant company requested that a hearing be set. The first hearing, scheduled for 11 October 2001, was postponed. On 12 October 2001 the State Attorney’s Office submitted a request for third-party intervention. On 10 June 2002 the court allowed both third parties to participate in the proceedings.

On 12 September 2002 the applicant company lodged a counterclaim. Because of the counterclaim, the court postponed the hearing set for 19 September 2002. On 3 February 2003 the court held a settlement hearing, but the parties did not reach a settlement. On 14 April 2003 the court held the first hearing. On 23 April 2003 the applicant company requested an extension of the deadline for submitting documents; the deadline was extended by one month. On 10 November 2003 the court appointed a financial expert. On 23 February 2004 the court granted the expert’s request for an extension of the deadline for submitting the report. On 3 May 2004 the expert submitted the report. On 6 October 2004 the court held a hearing.

On 13 December 2004 the District Court rendered judgment in favour of the applicant company; the notarial protocol and the contract remained in force. The plaintiff appealed. On 7 November 2006 the Ljubljana Higher Court delivered judgment amending the first-instance judgment and ruling against the applicant company. The applicant company lodged an appeal on points of law. On 12 May 2008 the Supreme Court delivered judgment upholding the appeal court’s decision. The applicant company lodged a constitutional appeal. On 13 May 2010 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

The applicant company lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 November 2010. It was represented by Ms M. Kranjčevič, a lawyer practising in Ljubljana. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. The Serbian Government indicated that they did not intend to take part in the proceedings.
