case_name: CASE OF KOPRIVNIKAR v. SLOVENIA
summary:
Mr Boštjan Koprivnikar, born in 1979 and detained in Dob pri Mirni, lodged application no. 67503/13 against Slovenia. He alleged that the overall thirty-year prison sentence imposed on him breached Article 7 of the Convention. He was represented by M. Petek; the Government by A. Vran.

On 23 April 1999 the 1999 Amendment to the 1994 Criminal Code entered into force. It introduced a maximum thirty-year prison sentence for the most serious intentional offences. The then applicable rules on combining multiple sentences provided that if any offence carried a thirty-year sentence, only that sentence was to be imposed; otherwise, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years’ imprisonment.

On 17 September 2004 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of robbery and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. He served that sentence from 7 December 2007 to 7 December 2011.

On 1 November 2008 the 2008 Criminal Code entered into force. It set the general maximum term at thirty years and introduced life imprisonment for certain serious crimes. Its Article 53 provided that if two or more thirty-year sentences were imposed, an overall life sentence was to be imposed; if prison sentences were imposed for all multiple offences, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years. It contained no separate rule for the situation where only one of the combined sentences was thirty years.

On 16 June 2009 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of paying with a bad cheque and fraudulent use of a bank card between 19 January and 19 August 2005, sentencing him to five months’ imprisonment. That judgment became final on 7 October 2009, and he began serving the sentence on 7 December 2011.

In the meantime, on 9 April 2009 the Ljubljana District Court found the applicant guilty, with another person, of murder committed on 15 September 2002. It sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment, the maximum under the 1994 Criminal Code applicable at the time of the offence. The Ljubljana Higher Court upheld the conviction on 9 December 2009, and it became final that day.

On 28 November 2011 the applicant applied to the Ljubljana District Court to join the three prison terms into an overall sentence. On 13 January 2012 the District Court joined the three sentences—including the completed robbery sentence—and imposed an overall thirty-year sentence. Applying the 2008 Criminal Code before the 2011 Amendment, it noted that Article 53 conditions had been met but not previously applied. It acknowledged that Article 53 § 2(2) provided a maximum of twenty years, but held that the legislature had made an obvious error, later rectified by the 2011 Amendment, because the 1994 Code had provided that a thirty-year sentence combined with others would consist only of that term.

The applicant appealed, arguing lack of legal basis, breach of the rule of law and nullum crimen et nulla poena sine lege, and that semantic interpretation should prevail and ambiguities should not be construed to his detriment. On 29 May 2012 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal and upheld the judgment, reiterating the lower court’s reasoning. On 6 December 2012 the Supreme Court rejected his application for protection of legality, disagreeing that semantic interpretation had priority and relying on historical and systematic interpretation. On 24 April 2013 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint.

On 24 March 2015 the applicant was convicted of another murder committed between 30 June and 15 September 2002 and sentenced to thirty years; a new overall thirty-year sentence covered the prior overall sentence, another four-month sentence, and the new thirty-year sentence. His appeal and protection-of-legality application were dismissed, the latter by the Supreme Court on 2 June 2016.

case_name: CASE OF LIVANČIĆ AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA
summary:
The case concerns eight applications against Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants complained of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions. The relevant applicants and enforcement facts are as follows.

Jerko Livančić (application no. 15313/15, introduced 20 March 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža of Travnik, relied on a Novi Travnik Cantonal Court decision of 7 June 2012. The non-enforcement period began on 28 September 2012 and ended on 13 June 2016, lasting 3 years, 8 months and 17 days.

Tončo Livančić (no. 15315/15, introduced 20 March 2015), also represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on the same Novi Travnik Cantonal Court decision of 7 June 2012. The non-enforcement period began on 14 September 2012 and ended on 3 June 2016, lasting 3 years, 8 months and 21 days.

Kebir Šehić (no. 15321/15, introduced 20 March 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on numerous decisions of the Bugojno First Instance Court issued between 25 April 2003 and 29 May 2008. The record lists seventeen such decisions. The start dates of the non-enforcement periods ran from 2 July 2012 to 31 October 2012. The enforcement periods ended between 30 July 2015 and 13 April 2017, with lengths ranging from 2 years, 11 months and 2 days to 4 years, 7 months and 29 days.

Vahid Dervišić (no. 16853/15, introduced 23 March 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on a Sarajevo First Instance Court decision of 10 July 2008. The non-enforcement period began on 15 June 2012 and ended on 21 January 2016, lasting 3 years, 7 months and 7 days.

Jasminka Basara (no. 18752/15, introduced 3 April 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on a Bugojno First Instance Court decision of 30 September 2011. The non-enforcement period began on 2 April 2012 and ended on 25 April 2016, lasting 4 years and 24 days.

Fatima Čajdo (no. 18756/15, introduced 3 April 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on a Bugojno First Instance Court decision of 20 November 2006. The non-enforcement period began on 23 February 2012 and ended on 30 July 2015, lasting 3 years, 5 months and 8 days.

Nedim Nurkić (no. 18761/15, introduced 3 April 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža, relied on a Bugojno First Instance Court decision of 14 November 2006. The non-enforcement period began on 10 February 2012 and ended on 5 October 2015, lasting 3 years, 7 months and 26 days.

Hajrudin Bešić (no. 5488/17, introduced 6 January 2017), represented by Salkanović Husein of Živinice, relied on a Živinice First Instance Court decision of 16 November 2001. The non-enforcement period began on 15 February 2012 and ended on 4 October 2019, lasting 7 years, 7 months and 20 days.

The applicants accordingly complained to the European Court of Human Rights about the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of these domestic decisions.

case_name: CASE OF VAN COLLE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The applicants, Mr and Mrs Van Colle, are British nationals. Their son, Giles Van Colle, an optometrist born in 1975, was murdered on 22 November 2000 by Daniel Brougham. Brougham had worked for Giles under the alias Lee Jordan, concealing a criminal record. After a dispute over equipment and unpaid repairs, Brougham left in December 1999.

In February 2000 police arrested Brougham on suspicion of theft from “Southern Counties” and found optical equipment; Giles later identified some as his. On 23 April 2000 Brougham was charged with theft and obtaining property by deception concerning Giles, Southern Counties and Alpha Optical, and was bailed unconditionally.

During 2000 Brougham attempted to deter witnesses. In summer he offered Mr H £1,000 not to give evidence; this was not reported until after the murder. On 10 August he offered Mr P £650 for Alpha Optical material. On 13 October he telephoned Mr P and offered a bribe, which Mr P reported to DC Ridley. On the same day Brougham telephoned Giles and threatened that he knew where Giles lived, where his businesses were and where his parents lived, and that if Giles did not drop the charges he would be in danger. Giles reported this to DC Ridley between 16 and 18 October. On 19 October DC Ridley took statements from Giles and Mr P and sent them to the CPS.

On 28 and 29 October fires occurred at Mr P’s wife’s car and at Mr P’s business premises. They were initially considered possibly accidental; later, during the murder investigation, experts found they had been started deliberately. On 5 November DC Ridley was seconded to an unconnected murder investigation. On 9 November the CPS served additional evidence including the 19 October statements. That day Brougham telephoned Giles again, using aggressive language and telling him to get Alpha Optical to drop the charges. Giles left a message for DC Ridley and later provided a written account sent on 20 November. On 22 November DC Ridley arranged to take a statement the next day and intended to arrest Brougham for witness intimidation. That evening Brougham shot Giles dead. Brougham was convicted of murder in March 2002.

In domestic disciplinary proceedings, on 12 June 2003 a Police Disciplinary Panel found DC Ridley guilty of failing to perform his duties conscientiously and diligently regarding the intimidation of Giles and Mr P. It found an escalating situation of intimidation and that DC Ridley failed thoroughly to investigate, analyse links between events, or consider arrest. He was fined five days’ pay.

The applicants, the first as administrator of Giles’s estate, brought a claim against the Chief Constable of Hertfordshire under the Human Rights Act 1998, seeking damages for breaches of Articles 2 and 8. The Chief Constable accepted the Panel’s findings and that DC Ridley gave inadequate consideration to responses to the threats, but argued that the criticisms were made with hindsight, that Brougham’s drastic act could not reasonably have been predicted, and that the errors were not sufficiently exceptional to be unlawful.

On 10 March 2006 the High Court found violations of Articles 2 and 8 and awarded damages. On 24 April 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed the Chief Constable’s appeal, upholding findings that DC Ridley should have recognised a real and immediate risk and taken protective steps. On 30 July 2008 the House of Lords allowed the Chief Constable’s appeal, holding that the domestic courts had misdirected themselves and that the relevant risk test had not been met.

The applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 January 2009, complaining under Articles 2 and 8 that the police failed to protect their son’s life from Brougham, a criminal accused in proceedings in which Giles was a witness.

case_name: CASE OF TARASOV v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 and living in Makiyivka, alleged that police had ill-treated him and that his right to mount a defence had been violated.

On 13 January 2000 Makiyivka police arrested him and held him in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that he had no access to a lawyer and was forced to confess. He claimed repeated severe beatings during interrogation, suffocation with a plastic bag and gas mask, and electric shocks applied to his genitals. The Government stated that his rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination were explained and that he signed waivers; he was questioned about a car theft and confessed, and also confessed to involvement in a robbery. On 14 January 2000 an ambulance took him to hospital; medical reports recorded abdominal trauma and a bruise in the lumbar region. On 15 January 2000 criminal proceedings were instituted against him for garage theft, theft of non-ferrous metals and attempted robbery. On 16 January 2000 he was charged with car theft; he denied guilt and said his earlier confession had been made under duress. Further charges followed on 18 January 2000. On 25 January 2000 he was transferred to the SIZO. On 29 February 2000, at a confrontation with co-accused D., he denied guilt and refused to sign the report. On 2 March 2000, with lawyer M. present, he denied guilt and alleged duress. On 13 March 2000 his mother appointed lawyer I.

The trial began on 17 March 2000. During hearings the applicant claimed his confession had been extracted by beatings and ill-treatment and sought witnesses. On 2 June 2000 witnesses U.G. and U.A. testified that they had heard him screaming and had seen him after beatings. On 8 June 2000 the court refused to summon the ambulance doctor but ordered a forensic medical examination. Health issues affected proceedings: in August 2000 he was not brought to court due to renal colic; in September 2000 the SIZO said he was fit; in October 2000 it said his health was very poor; in August 2001 it said he could participate and recommended a stretcher. On 21 December 2001 he was transferred to court by ambulance and brought in on a stretcher, with a doctor present and lawyer N. representing him. He said he felt unwell and lost consciousness; the Government said his health was satisfactory and that he took part in final pleadings.

On 25 December 2001 the Gornyatskiy Local Court of Makiyivka convicted the applicant and others of theft and robbery and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It relied on his prior confessions plus co-defendants’ testimony, victims, witnesses, material evidence and stolen goods. It rejected his ill-treatment complaint and did not accept U.G. and U.A.’s testimony, citing lack of support and their relationship with him. Appeals in January and February 2002 were left without examination for procedural defects, with extensions granted. On 13 May 2002 he lodged a cassation appeal complaining of torture, lack of access to a lawyer, falsification of case-file documents, failure to question cellmates, and pronouncement of judgment in his absence because his lawyer had convinced him to waive his right to be present at the last hearing, depriving him of arguments and closing submissions. On 29 October 2002 a Supreme Court panel found the first-instance judgment well-founded, no procedural violations, and his ill-treatment allegations duly checked and rejected.

Separately, on 14 March 2000 he wrote to a human rights NGO. On 25 May 2000 the prosecutor refused criminal proceedings over the alleged ill-treatment. On 2 August 2000 the regional prosecutor quashed that refusal and ordered further investigation. On 7 September 2000 the Makiyivka prosecutor again refused for lack of proof. In November 2000 the court ordered another forensic examination; from November 2000 to May 2001 experts noted scars and pigmentations and found no link between the January 2000 injuries and later health problems. In August 2003 he challenged the 7 September 2000 decision; on 6 November 2003 the district court quashed it and remitted the case. On 20 May 2005 cellmates were re-questioned. On 15 June 2005 the prosecutor refused proceedings for lack of corpus delicti, citing police denials, conflicting cellmate statements, destroyed SIZO records and no evidence; the applicant did not challenge that decision. A CPT report on its September 2000 visit described similar allegations and visible marks; the applicant said the passage concerned him.

case_name: CASE OF STANDARD VERLAGS GMBH v. AUSTRIA (No. 3)
summary:
Standard Verlags GmbH, a Vienna-based limited liability company and owner of the daily newspaper Der Standard, lodged application no. 34702/07 against Austria on 3 August 2007, alleging a violation of the right to freedom of expression. In its issue of 4 April 2006, in the economics section, Der Standard published an article entitled “Haider’s Hypo now also facing criminal investigation”. The article concerned losses at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. It reported that the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had initiated an investigation into suspected embezzlement by Hypo senior managers, partly in light of a Financial Market Authority audit. It mentioned criticisms by Jörg Haider and Martin Strutz. It also named Christian Rauscher, described as the son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, as the person whom Wolfgang Kulterer and Jörg Haider had blamed for speculative losses of 328 million euros. The article stated that Rauscher had headed the bank’s treasury department in 2004 together with Andreas Zois, that he had not been dismissed but demoted and transferred, and that he had been relieved of his duties only after the losses became known.

On 16 June 2006 Rauscher brought proceedings against the applicant company under section 7a of the Media Act, seeking disclosure of his identity in breach of that provision. He submitted that he was not a public figure and that his position at the bank had not justified naming him. He asserted that he had acted in accordance with instructions and under supervision when authorising the transactions, and that publication of his name had harmed his professional advancement and had not been justified by public interest. The applicant company replied that the article had not portrayed Rauscher as responsible but rather as a “scapegoat”. It argued that the public interest in disclosing his name outweighed his private interests because he had held a leading position at the bank and because of his father’s political role. It also said the reporting had been neutral.

case_name: CASE OF CELA AND OTHERS v. GREECE
summary:
The application was lodged on 28 January 2014 by six Albanian and Greek nationals against Greece. They were represented by K. Tsitselikis and A. Spathis. The Greek Government was represented by State Legal Council delegates; the Albanian Government did not intervene. At the time of lodging, the applicants were detained in Korydallos Prison, Athens.

The first applicant was held in Korydallos from 7 March 2013 and remained there when observations were submitted, except for temporary transfers to Ioannina Prison (3–11 July 2013) and Komotini Prison (2–17 December 2013). The second applicant was detained in Korydallos from 22 March 2013 and the third from 21 August 2013; both remained detained when they submitted observations. The fourth applicant was in Korydallos from 26 June 2013 to 1 May 2014, except for periods in Chania Prison from 17 July to 3 September 2013, 27 November to 10 December 2013, and 6–17 February 2014. The fifth applicant was in Korydallos from 22 May 2013 to 19 June 2014, except 20–28 March 2013. The sixth was in Korydallos from 30 January 2013 to 15 August 2014.

The applicants alleged overcrowding: the prison held about 2,400 prisoners though designed for 700. They were detained in wings A and D in 9 sq m cells, including sanitary facilities, shared by three or four prisoners, leaving under 3 sq m each. Toilets were only partially separated; heating and hot water were insufficient; inmates used a washbasin to wash themselves, dishes and clothes. Cells were dirty and infested with cockroaches and pests, with no extermination. Rubbish was not properly collected and food remains stayed in cells and corridors for days. Prisoners were not adequately separated by health condition or drug use. Medical care was inadequate, especially psychological care. Inmates were confined to cells 16 hours daily, with no recreational or educational activities, and ate poor-quality meals in cells. The prison was understaffed and unsafe.

The Government submitted that the first to fifth applicants were held in wings A and D. Cells measured 9.60 sq m and held three, rarely four, detainees. The first applicant was also held in wing E: one cell of 10.44 sq m and another of 42.78 sq m holding 10–22 detainees, though 22 only briefly. All cells had windows with sufficient light and were furnished with washbasin, toilet, beds, table, chairs and usually shelves. Wings A–D had twelve communal showers each and wing E nine; each wing provided 2,000 litres of hot water daily. Sheets and blankets were provided unless detainees used their own. There was central heating and summer fans. Cells were disinfected and cleaned twice daily by detainee crews; rubbish bins existed. The infirmary was open 24 hours with eighteen doctors and three nurses; transfers to Korydallos Prison Hospital, Psychiatric Hospital or external hospitals were possible. Medical records showed treatment, and social services assisted. Menus were varied. Prisoners had four to five hours daily in the yard, sport, television, a lending library and book club, jobs, and “second chance” school. The Government made no observations on the sixth applicant.

The CPT’s report on its April 2013 visit, published 16 October 2014, stated that Korydallos Men’s Prison held more than 2,300 prisoners for an official capacity of 840. Cells designed for single occupancy, measuring 9.5 sq m, routinely held three or four inmates; some slept on mattresses on the floor or in toilet areas. Cell A-3 in wing E measured 36 sq m, had 16 beds but held 27 inmates, leaving under 1.5 sq m per person; nine slept on the concrete floor on filthy mattresses, two in the toilet area, and the cell was infested with cockroaches and bed bugs. Cell B-3 had 14 beds and held 19 prisoners, five on mattresses on the floor; there was no artificial light at night and the toilet was filthy. Garbage containers were full of food waste. Health-care resources had deteriorated: four GP posts were abolished, no full-time doctor worked there, visiting GPs provided only 15 hours weekly and sometimes failed to attend, and two-monthly rotations hindered continuity; the CPT considered at least four full-time GPs necessary. A wing of about 400 inmates usually had one or two officers by day; at night eight officers covered the entire prison.

The relevant domestic law and practice were described in the earlier judgment Kanakis v. Greece (no. 2).

case_name: CASE OF KYRIAN v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, David Kyrian, a Czech national born in 1982, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the mother that began in 2012. Because the mother was married, her husband became the child’s legal father by presumption; the child lived with the legal parents. The applicant’s biological paternity was confirmed by a DNA test he arranged in 2015. Until February 2016 he saw the child two to four times a month when the mother visited him.

In April 2016 the applicant applied to the Příbram District Court under Article 927 of the Civil Code for contact rights. On 18 May 2016 the court granted provisional contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer holidays. The Prague Regional Court upheld that decision on 9 November 2016, noting an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father. Conflicts during visits led to supervised visits in July and August 2016. From September 2016 to November 2017 contact mostly followed the judgment, but the child’s psychological condition worsened.

In September 2017 the applicant sought more contact; the mother sought prohibition, alleging verbal abuse and that the child refused visits, was anxious and seeing a psychologist. The legal father alleged the applicant had physically assaulted him. A judgment of 3 October 2017 dismissing both requests was quashed by the Regional Court for insufficient fact-finding; it noted a weakening bond and recommended counselling. After mediation in April 2018, contact continued until mid-July 2018. On 17 July 2018 the District Court approved a mediated agreement granting contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer. Later visits were missed because the child refused; an incident with the legal parents led to police being called. Two supervised visits in October 2018 ended in conflict. A psychologist report of 10 October 2018 described the child as strongly attached to his mother and legal father and stressed by imposed contact.

In December 2018 the legal parents requested prohibition. In 2020 the Český Krumlov District Court and České Budějovice Regional Court ruled that no contact regime should be set, finding no positive emotional bond or harm from lack of contact. An expert opinion cited the child’s developmental delay, attachment to his legal father, the applicant’s pressure and conflicts, and considered no contact in the child’s best interests at that time. A constitutional appeal was dismissed on 13 October 2022.

On 23 April 2021 the applicant lodged a new application seeking contact every Wednesday afternoon. At a hearing on 24 August 2021, the legal parents described the child’s anxiety; the guardian ad litem advised dismissal. An expert report of 18 March 2022 found previous conflicted visits traumatic and did not recommend contact, though future contact was not excluded. A psychologist report of 20 March 2022 noted anxiety attacks. At a hearing on 24 March 2022, the applicant alternatively sought written communication via the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, citing distress and alleging he lingered near the child’s kindergarten or their home, bordering on stalking. The guardian opposed all requests.

On 24 March 2022 the Příbram District Court dismissed the claim but warned the legal parents about non-cooperation and ordered respect for the applicant’s biological parenthood. It found contact contrary to the child’s best interests and no basis for information rights. On 12 September 2022 the Prague Regional Court upheld that judgment. On 24 January 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal.

Subsequently, the legal parents divorced in April 2022 but shared custody and continued living together. The mother later moved out and resumed a relationship with the applicant, who had occasional contact through her. In 2024 shared-custody proceedings, the child said he did not want to see the mother mainly because he feared the applicant; the court placed the child with the legal father, and the mother’s contact application was dismissed because she would not meet without the applicant.

case_name: CASE OF JEZNIK v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Ms Marija Jeznik, is a Slovenian national born in 1940 who lives in Vuzenica. The respondent is the Republic of Slovenia. The case originated in an application against Slovenia lodged on 1 July 2008. The applicant was represented by Odvetniška Družba Marčič in Ostali, O.P., D.N.O., a law firm from Slovenj Gradec. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. On 27 April 2012 the application was communicated to the Government and, under Protocol No. 14, assigned to a committee of three judges.

In 1994 the applicant began investing in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d. through the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. At the end of 1994 such trading was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but the applicant continued the activity until 1996. In 1996 she instituted enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor D.O.O. before the Maribor District Court. She sought payment of lost investments from Kompas Maribor for not informing her of the legislative amendments and for continuing with the trading of commercial papers. She further complained before the domestic courts that, because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could receive back only a small proportion of her investments in bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. On 12 November 1996, following an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings. On 4 February 1998 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment rejecting the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The second-instance court found that, because the applicant had clarified during the appeal phase that she was seeking compensation for damages only, this constituted a new fact that the first-instance court would have to deliberate upon.

On 24 October 2001 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment. The court found that, given the contractual arrangements, the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. could not be held responsible for the damages sustained. The applicant appealed. On 15 September 2004 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the first-instance judgment and rejected the appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected her appeal. She lodged a constitutional appeal. On 10 December 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected her appeal.

The record also states that relevant domestic law is set out in Tomažič v. Slovenia (no. 38350/02, 13 December 2007). The domestic proceedings therefore comprised two first-instance decisions, two decisions of the Maribor Higher Court, one Supreme Court decision, and one Constitutional Court decision. The applicant pursued her claim through the ordinary courts and then through constitutional review, and her domestic appeals were ultimately rejected at the final stages of those proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF KRISTIANSEN AND TYVIK AS v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicants are Arne Kristiansen (born 1931), a Norwegian national, and Tyvik A/S, a Norwegian limited liability company. On 30 November 1990 Kristiansen filed patent application no. 19905214 with NIPO, the Norwegian Industrial Property Office, for a method of propulsion of aircraft and sea vessels.

On 21 March 1991 NIPO preliminarily found the application not patentable because it lacked a concrete solution and questioned whether the invention had any effect. It required practical tests at an independent research institute. Kristiansen disputed the need, citing costs, but said prototypes were under construction. Between 1992 and 1994 there was correspondence about confidentiality; in 1993 the Military Supreme Command said secrecy was not needed. On 9 May 1994 Kristiansen supplied further information. On 24 February 1995 NIPO repeated its test request. On 23 May 1995 he submitted theoretical views and a 1965 report, arguing tests were superfluous. On 27 November 1996 he complained of delay; NIPO apologised on 9 December 1996 and prioritised the case. On 16 December 1996 NIPO maintained the test requirement; exchanges followed, including protests about NIPO’s technical competence and two academic statements in 1997. On 5 May 1999 NIPO maintained its position and set a 5 November 1999 deadline. Kristiansen’s registered letter of 26 October 1999, received 11 November 1999, complained again but made no new arguments. NIPO discontinued examination under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. On 18 February 2000 it maintained shelving because the substantive requirements had not been met.

On 8 March 2001 Kristiansen petitioned the Parliamentary Ombudsman. Following an inquiry, on 30 August 2001 NIPO annulled the discontinuation and allowed until 28 February 2002 to respond to its 5 May 1999 letter. He replied on 24 September 2001 without new arguments. On 2 October 2001 NIPO refused the application because the alleged technical effect was not made probable. On 23 January 2002 the Ombudsman found no grounds to continue.

On 27 November 2001 Kristiansen appealed to the Board of Appeals. Its first meeting was on 13 September 2004; the Board indicated a new claim formulation might lead to a patent, but only for sea vessels, communicated on 29 September 2004. A meeting followed on 2 February 2005. On 14 February 2005 NIPO learned that 50% ownership had been transferred to Tyvik AS. On 14 November 2005 the Board concluded the invention had technical effect but did not decide other patent requirements; the applicants had been advised how to amend the claims but were unwilling. The Board set aside NIPO’s decision and remitted the case.

case_name: CASE OF PUTISTIN v. UKRAINE
summary:
Mr Vladlen Mikhaylovich Putistin, born in 1934, lives in Kyiv. He is the son of Mr Mikhail Putistin, a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who played in the 1936 USSR championship, when Dynamo took second place. On 9 August 1942 his father took part in the “Death Match” between FC Start—mostly Dynamo Kyiv professionals then working in a Kyiv bakery—and Flakelf, a team of German Luftwaffe pilots, air-defence soldiers and airport technicians. FC Start won 5–3. The match allegedly involved Flakelf’s lack of sportsmanship, physical challenges, threats and unfair refereeing by an SS officer. The victory allegedly led to the players’ arrest and transfer to a local concentration camp, where four were eventually executed. In 2002 Kyiv authorities commemorated the 60th anniversary, with wide media coverage.

On 3 April 2001 Komsomolska Pravda published “The Truth about the Death Match,” by journalist O.M. It discussed a planned film about the 1942 events and included an interview with future director/producer A.S. and D.K., plus a picture of the 1942 match poster with the footballers’ names. The article named four executed Dynamo Kyiv players—Kuzmenko, Klimenko, Korotkikh and Trusevych—but did not name the applicant’s father; his name was not legible on the poster. D.K. stated that only four Dynamo players were in the Start team created by the local bread factory, that those four were executed, and that other players worked in the police and collaborated with the Gestapo.

In July 2001 the applicant sued Komsomolska Pravda and the journalist, alleging the article suggested his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo. He sought rectification of the untrue information and non-pecuniary damages. He supplied State Security Service documents showing no archive information about his father’s alleged collaboration and no criminal proceedings against him; the archives and Kyiv Regional State Archives confirmed his father had participated in the Death Match and had been detained at Syrets concentration camp. On 25 December 2001 the Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv rejected the claim. It found that the applicant was not directly affected, that the article concerned a film script, that it did not name his father or the applicant, and that it made no allegation that his father had collaborated with the Gestapo. On 13 March 2002 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, and on 15 November 2002 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s points-of-law appeal.

In other domestic proceedings, on 27 April 2000 the Moskovskyy District Court ordered Dzerkalo Tyzhnia to rectify information about the applicant’s father; on 29 April 2000 it published a correction that he played for Dynamo, was arrested in summer 1942 with other players and sent to Syrets, and escaped in October 1942. In May 2002 Argumenty i Fakty stated that only four Death Match players were arrested and sent to Syrets, without naming the applicant’s father. After his request, issue no. 27 named all eight arrested players, including his father. His subsequent suit ended on 28 December 2004 with a final Supreme Court ruling against him. On 12 May 2003 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court ordered Fakty i Komentari to publish a rectification concerning the applicant’s father; the order was upheld on appeal on 21 October 2003 and in cassation on 31 August 2005, while his damages claim was rejected.

case_name: CASE OF PROJECT-TRADE D.O.O. v. CROATIA
summary:
The applicant, Project-Trade d.o.o., is a Croatian limited liability company registered in Zagreb. It was a shareholder in Croatia Bank d.d. (the bank), holding 1,251 shares with a nominal value of HRK 200 each. On 23 February 1999 the Croatian National Bank (CNB) appointed a temporary administrator at the bank; the term was extended on 23 August 1999. On 18 June 1999, based on an expert report that the bank’s debts largely exceeded its share capital and threatened financial-market stability, the CNB proposed recovery and restructuring of the bank.

On 23 September 1999 the Croatian Government adopted the Decision on the recovery and restructuring of Croatia Bank, published on 27 September 1999. From publication, all existing shares of the bank were revoked and cancelled. New shares in the amount of HRK 204.6 million were to be issued to the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). The powers of the bank’s governing bodies and the rights of shareholders were extinguished. The recovery process was completed on 13 September 2000. The Decision was slightly amended on 25 May 2000, and the Constitutional Court later held that it was subordinate legislation rather than an individual legal act.

In 1999 and 2000, five shareholders of the bank, but not the applicant company, filed four petitions with the Constitutional Court challenging the Government Decision. They alleged violations of Croatian constitutional rights, argued that the bank had been in good standing and that the Decision was unnecessary. After obtaining expert opinions, on 30 January 2003 the Constitutional Court discontinued the proceedings because the 1994 Recovery and Restructuring of Banks Act had been repealed on 31 May 2000. It stated that the Decision’s effects interfered with individual rights of founders and former shareholders, but that judicial protection was available in civil proceedings under the Obligations Act and section 19(2) of the Courts Act, and ultimately by constitutional complaint. Two dissenting judges argued that the review could have continued, that the Decision was unconstitutional, and that no effective remedy, especially a judicial one, existed. One dissent contested that civil proceedings could succeed without a finding that the Government Decision was unconstitutional.

On 12 September 2003 the applicant company brought a civil action in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. It sought a declaration that it still held 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer corresponding shares to it, and an order that the bank register it as holder. The applicant argued that the Government Decision revoking and cancelling its shares was economically unjustified because the bank had been in good standing, that statutory requirements had not been met, and that the Decision violated Articles 48 § 1, 49 § 4 and 50 of the Croatian Constitution, as allegedly acknowledged by the High Commercial Court in a judgment of 21 December 2004 in another case.

On 21 February 2006 the Zagreb Commercial Court dismissed the action. On 18 June 2008 the High Commercial Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment, served on 16 September 2008. It reasoned that under point 7 of the Government Decision all existing shares had been extinguished and new shares issued to DAB, so the applicant’s shares no longer existed and could not be returned. The applicant had argued on appeal that the first-instance court misapplied substantive law, that the Government Decision was unconstitutional, and that the Government had to compensate the market value of the revoked shares under Article 50 § 1 of the Constitution. The applicant company lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 December 2013.

On 12 September 2003 the applicant company brought a civil action in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. On 21 February 2006 the Zagreb Commercial Court dismissed the action. On 18 June 2008 the High Commercial Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment, served on 16 September 2008. It reasoned that under point 7 of the Government Decision all existing shares had been extinguished and new shares issued to DAB, so the applicant’s shares no longer existed and could not be returned. The applicant had argued on appeal that the first-instance court misapplied substantive law, that the Government Decision was unconstitutional, and that the Government had to compensate the market value of the revoked shares under Article 50 § 1 of the Constitution. case_name: CASE OF LIEBSCHER v. AUSTRIA
summary:
The applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, born in 1957 and living in Vienna, is an Austrian national. On 21 May 2013 he and his wife divorced by mutual consent and concluded a divorce settlement under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act before the Döbling District Court, acting as family court. The settlement regulated division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

On 13 December 2015 the applicant asked the same court, acting as land register court, to enter into the land register the transfer of his share of the couple’s joint property to his former wife. He submitted a partial engrossment of the divorce settlement issued by the family court on 1 December 2015. It was designated an “excerpt from the … divorce settlement” and reproduced only the chapter concerning real estate. It also contained a family court note that it “contained … all agreements pertaining to the real estate property”. Under section 7(1) of the Land Register Act, the land register is public and can be consulted by anyone without restriction.

By decision of 25 February 2016, the land register court rejected the application. It found that submitting a partial engrossment rather than the “original” did not satisfy section 87 of the Land Register Act. A partial engrossment could not be an original; the complete document was required so the court could examine whether the settlement contained conditions or legally relevant facts affecting registration, as required by section 94(1).

The applicant appealed. He argued that refusal to transfer his property share infringed his right to dispose freely of his property. He maintained that the partial engrossment complied with section 87 because it had been issued by the same judge and stated that it reproduced the relevant part. He also complained that requiring the full divorce settlement breached data protection rules, because highly personal and sensitive data—such as names and places of abode of minor children and his former spouse, alimony amounts, and custody agreements—would become publicly accessible in the document archive. He relied on Article 8, section 1(2) of the Data Protection Act 2000, and Article 52 of the EU Charter, arguing that no legitimate aim or public interest outweighed his privacy.

On 25 April 2016 the Vienna Regional Civil Court rejected the appeal (47 R 108/16d). It confirmed that a partial engrossment was not an “original” under section 87(1) and that even the family court’s statement could not bind the land register court; the original full settlement was needed. It cited an earlier Supreme Court decision, no. 5 Ob 250/15y of 25 January 2016, requiring a complete document. It found a legal basis for the interference regarding Article 8 and the Data Protection Act.

On 24 June 2016 the applicant filed an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating that the lower courts’ interpretation was incompatible with Article 8 and other laws. He requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU and a constitutional review. On 11 July 2016 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal (5 Ob 125/16t). It relied on its earlier decision no. 5 Ob 250/15y that a partial engrossment was insufficient under section 87(1); the excerpt’s confirmation could not change that. Under section 94(1), the land register court had to examine the application and documents comprehensively, approving registration only if justified by their content and in the required form. The family court could not bind it on completeness. On Article 8, the Supreme Court found the data protection concerns unpersuasive: examination of the entire document was mandatory under sections 87(1) and 94(1) and served protection of registered property. It stated that inclusion of documents in the document archive was not the subject of the decision and saw no reason to initiate a preliminary ruling or constitutional review.

The applicant alleged violations concerning his personal data and the lack of an effective remedy, and that the refusal infringed his property rights.

case_name: CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, an Afghan national, alleged that Slovak authorities failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, returned him to Ukraine, where he was detained in inadequate conditions despite his alleged minor status and could not participate effectively in detention proceedings, and that he was later returned to Afghanistan without an adequate risk assessment. He also alleged that an NGO representative was denied access to him in Ukraine, preventing an interim-measure application to the Court. He claimed birth in 1993 or 1994; Slovak and Ukrainian authorities recorded 14 January 1992.

He came from Kunduz. His father, who worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department, was killed around 2005, possibly by Taliban-linked persons. In 2010 his maternal uncle received a threatening letter and arranged for him to leave. In May 2010 smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He stayed in Moscow for a month and entered Ukraine in early July 2010, remaining in Kyiv for three months. His brother-in-law later crossed into Slovakia, travelled to Spain and sought asylum.

On 23 September 2010 at 4.10 p.m. Slovak border police arrested him crossing illegally with three other Afghans; he had no identity papers. At 7.25 p.m. he was interviewed with Slovak-English and English-Pashto interpretation. His birth date was recorded as 14 January 1992. He said he wished to reach western Europe and did not request asylum in Slovakia. The record was signed by police and the Slovak-English interpreter, not by him or the Afghan interpreter. Slovakia said he refused to sign; two others signed similar records.

On 24 September 2010 an expulsion decision and five-year entry ban were issued. He received Pashto guidelines, though some case-specific details were in Slovak. At 2 p.m. he was handed to Ukrainian authorities. He alleged that in Slovakia he had no interpretation, asylum information or lawyer; tried to request asylum and said he was a minor; and received no written return decision or appeal information.

In Ukraine he was held at the Chop Border Guard facility, where he alleged overcrowding and lack of guaranteed daily exercise. He said he told a guard via other detainees and a Caritas representative that he was 14 and wished to apply for asylum, but no action was taken. The SBCS ordered voluntary departure and sought forcible expulsion and detention. On 1 October 2010, according to the court, the SBCS and applicant asked for written proceedings in their absence. On 13 October 2010 the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court ordered expulsion and detention pending expulsion, relying on his recorded 1992 birth date, illegal entry, lack of means or relatives in Ukraine, and a UNHCR publication indicating no risk in Afghanistan. The applicant alleged he was unaware of the proceedings, had no lawyer, did not understand his rights, signed a waiver without understanding, was not served the decision and missed the ten-day appeal deadline.

On 14 October 2010 he was moved to temporary accommodation in Volyn; he alleged he again said he was 14. On 20/22 February 2011 the Afghan Embassy interviewed him and issued a travel document recording his birth date as 14 January 1992. On 23 February 2011 he applied for asylum, saying he would be killed if returned. On 2 March 2011 he was interviewed. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the application as inadmissible, citing manifestly unfounded facts, failure to meet the refugee definition, his Afghan travel document, failure to seek asylum earlier and lack of identity documents. On 11 March 2011 he was transferred to Mukacheve and notified. On 12 March 2011 an NGO partner of UNHCR was allegedly denied access to provide legal advice, preventing an interim-measure application. On 14 March 2011 he was expelled to Kabul. He alleged that about three weeks later unknown people sought him at home and left a threatening letter, causing him to relocate frequently.

case_name: CASE OF WALCZAK v. POLAND
summary:
Damian Walczak, a Polish national born in 1971 living in Plewiska, was arrested on 16 December 2014 and charged with organised-crime and robbery-related offences. The Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Court ordered his detention on remand until 16 March 2015; the Poznań Regional Court later extended it until 16 June and then 16 September 2015. He was released on 4 February 2016. He alleged that during detention he was deprived of personal contact with his wife, M.W., for a significant period.

On 30 December 2014 M.W. applied to visit him. On 5 January 2015 the Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Prosecutor refused because she was a witness in the proceedings; no appeal was lodged. Applications of 26 February and 17 March 2015 were dismissed on 27 February and 24 March 2015 because evidence still needed to be heard from M.W.; again no appeals were lodged. On 3 April 2015 M.W. refused to testify at the investigation stage and applied again. On 7 April 2015 the prosecutor refused, saying she could still be asked to testify while the investigation was ongoing; no appeal was lodged. A 27 May application was dismissed on 5 June 2015, without interlocutory appeal. On 10 June 2015 M.W. applied again; on 15 June 2015 the prosecutor dismissed it, saying a visit could impede proceedings because she knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. On 28 August 2015 the Poznań Regional Prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s interlocutory appeal against that decision. Applications of 15 June and 15 July 2015 were dismissed on 25 June and 24 July 2015; the applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015 was dismissed on 6 July 2015.

On 27 August 2015 the prosecutor allowed M.W. to visit; the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment. On 10 September 2015 the Poznań Regional Court dismissed M.W.’s application to visit because she was a witness, served on her on 14 September 2015. On 24 September 2015 the Regional Court dismissed her interlocutory appeal. It held that her statement that she would not testify against her husband was irrelevant because court proceedings had not begun and she could change her mind when summoned. It also held that investigation-stage visits allowed by the prosecutor were irrelevant because those decisions could not be assessed by the court. A further request of 15 September 2015 was marked “examined” on 17 September 2015. On 1 October 2015 M.W. requested a visit and stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify. On 2 October 2015 the Regional Court allowed the visit, which took place on 11 October 2015. Her later requests were granted. There were no significant subsequent developments, and M.W. was not asked to testify at later hearings.

Under Article 217 of the 1997 Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences, visits required permission from the investigating prosecutor or, once trial had begun, the trial court; interlocutory appeals were available under Article 217 § 1c, but § 1d restricted further appeals if a refusal was upheld within three months.

case_name: CASE OF FERNÁNDEZ MARTÍNEZ v. SPAIN
summary:
José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937 and living in Cieza, was ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; receiving no immediate reply, he married in a civil ceremony in 1985 and later had five children. From October 1991 he worked as a teacher of Catholic religion and ethics in a State-run secondary school in the Region of Murcia under a renewable one-year contract. Under the 1979 Agreement between Spain and the Holy See and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed annually from candidates proposed by the diocesan Ordinary; appointment was renewed automatically unless the Ordinary objected before the school year or the public authority annulled it for serious academic or disciplinary reasons.

In November 1996 the Murcian newspaper La Verdad published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). It named Fernández Martínez as a former seminary director among married priests gathered at La Luz to advocate optional celibacy and related reforms. On 20 August 1997 the Pope granted his long-pending request for dispensation from celibacy; the rescript stated that he lost clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise for lower-level schools, provided there was no scandal. He was notified on 15 September 1997. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that his service as a teacher was terminated. On 9 October 1997 the Ministry told him his employment had ended with effect from 29 September 1997. In a memorandum of 11 November 1997, the Diocese explained that once his situation became publicly known, the bishop could no longer authorise him to teach Catholic religion and ethics; it also referred to avoiding scandal, respecting parents’ sensitivities, and his entitlement to unemployment benefit. The school board expressed support for him and satisfaction with his teaching.

His administrative complaint was unsuccessful, and an administrative court dismissed his appeal on 30 June 2000, holding that termination was the only course once the Diocese did not propose him. He then brought unfair-dismissal proceedings before Murcia Employment Tribunal no. 3. By judgment of 28 September 2000, the tribunal found he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, with his appearance in the press having caused his dismissal. It declared the dismissal null, ordered the Region of Murcia to reinstate him, and ordered the State to pay outstanding salary; it dismissed his claim against the Diocese. The Ministry, the Region, and the Diocese appealed.

On 26 February 2001 the Murcia High Court of Justice allowed the appeal. It described the link between the Catholic religion teacher and the bishop as based on trust, held that the bishop had acted within his prerogatives, found no violation of the Spanish Constitution, and considered the contract a temporary one that had expired rather than a dismissal.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court relying on Articles 14, 18 and 20 of the Spanish Constitution. The public prosecutor supported him, noting that his public appearance preceded the rescript and that Church authorities knew of his MOCEOP membership. In a judgment of 4 June 2007, served on 18 June 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo appeal. It rejected the discrimination and private-life complaints and found the religious reasons for non-renewal justified by the Catholic Church’s religious freedom and parents’ rights. Two judges dissented. On 23 July 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected his request to declare the judgment null.

On 11 December 2007 the applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. Relying on Article 8, separately and with Article 14, he alleged that the non-renewal of his contract was an unjustified interference with his private life. He alleged that publicity given to his family and personal situation as a married priest caused the non-renewal and was incompatible with his rights under Articles 9 and 10.

case_name: CASE OF YELNIK v. UKRAINE
summary:
The factual record in *Yelnik v. Ukraine*, application no. 10444/13, is limited to the application, the parties, the applicant’s complaints, and a table of detention periods. The applicant, Andrey Aleksandrovich Yelnik, born on 6 April 1987, lodged the application against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on 29 January 2013. The Ukrainian Government were the respondent party and were given notice of the application. The applicant complained of the excessive length of his pre-trial detention. He also raised another complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The supplied record does not otherwise describe the domestic proceedings, the authorities involved, the charges, the procedural stages, the legal basis for detention, or the reasons given by domestic courts.

The appended table provides the principal concrete facts. It lists two periods of detention: from 24 September 2008 to 21 May 2010, and from 29 March 2012 to 12 March 2013. case_name: CASE OF JESTCOV v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA AND RUSSIA
summary:
Application no. 33567/15 was lodged by Mr Petru Jestcov, a Moldovan national born in 1950 who lives in Chișinău, against the Republic of Moldova and Russia. He was represented by A. Tighinean, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The Governments were represented by their Agents. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Moldova and Russia were responsible for the impunity of the perpetrator of his wife’s murder, whom he alleged was hiding in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (MRT). The case concerned the failure to enforce a custodial sentence after the perpetrator fled.

On 9 November 2010 the applicant’s wife was robbed and murdered in Chișinău, Moldova. An investigation was initiated against several suspected perpetrators, including N.C., a Russian national. N.C. was held in pre-trial detention during the proceedings. On 2 December 2011 the Botanica District Court convicted N.C. of being an accomplice in armed robbery and murder and sentenced her to 13 years’ imprisonment. On 11 April 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld N.C.’s appeal, reheard the case, acquitted her of all charges, and released her from detention in the courtroom. On 29 January 2013, in N.C.’s absence, the Supreme Court of Justice finally quashed the appellate judgment and upheld the first-instance judgment against N.C.

On 20 March 2013 the Botanica District Court sent all materials of the criminal file to the Dubăsari Police to enforce the sentence in respect of N.C. On 2 July 2013 the General Police Inspectorate informed the applicant that N.C. had not yet been declared wanted. Following a request from the Dubăsari Police, on 6 May 2015 the Dubăsari District Court declared N.C. wanted.

Following a search notice issued by Moldovan authorities, on 11 September 2015 the Russian authorities traced N.C. to Surgut, Russia, and interviewed her about the circumstances of the case. She claimed to be unaware of her conviction in Moldova, saying that she had moved back to Russia after her acquittal by the appellate court in 2012. On 17 September 2015 the Russian authorities informed the Moldovan authorities of N.C.’s location. On 19 October 2015 they confirmed that she was a Russian national and therefore could not be extradited pursuant to Article 57 of the 1993 Minsk Convention on mutual legal assistance in civil, family and criminal matters.

After communication of the case, on 15 October 2019 the Chișinău District Court requested transfer of the enforcement of N.C.’s custodial sentence to the Russian Federation, relying on Article 2 of the 1997 Additional Protocol to the Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons. On 25 October 2019 the Moldovan Minister of Justice forwarded the request to the Russian Ministry of Justice. On 4 February 2020 the Russian Ministry of Justice directed the Moldovan transfer request to the Surgut City Court. On 10 April 2020 the Surgut City Court granted recognition and enforcement on the territory of the Russian Federation of the custodial sentence in respect of N.C. and ordered her arrest.

The Additional Protocol to the Council of Europe Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons was ratified by Moldova in 2004 and by Russia in 2007. Article 2 of that Protocol concerns persons who have fled from the sentencing State. It provides that where a national of a Party who is the subject of a sentence imposed in another Party seeks to avoid execution or further execution of the sentence by fleeing to the former Party before having served it, the sentencing State may request the other Party to take over execution. At the request of the sentencing State, the administering State may arrest the sentenced person or take other measures pending a decision on the request. The consent of the sentenced person is not required for the transfer.

case_name: CASE OF STRØBYE AND ROSENLIND v. DENMARK
summary:
The applicants are Tomas Strøbye (born 1966, living in Frederiksberg) and Martin Rosenlind (born 1987, living in Greve), both Danish nationals. In earlier domestic proceedings, the first applicant was declared legally incompetent to manage his financial and personal affairs by the Copenhagen City Court on 20 March 1984. The second applicant was placed under financial guardianship and deprived of his legal capacity by the District Court of Roskilde on 23 March 2009; that court found he could not manage his financial affairs because of mental disability and needed protection from further debt.

Under section 29 of the Danish Constitution and section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, persons who were legally incompetent did not have the right to vote in general elections. Consequently, both applicants were not entitled to vote in the parliamentary elections held on 18 June 2015. By Act no. 391 of 27 April 2016, persons who were legally incompetent were later given the right to vote in European Parliament elections and in local and regional elections, but not in national parliamentary elections.

The applicants, joined by two other persons, brought proceedings before the Danish courts against the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Interior. They claimed they had been wrongfully denied the right to vote in the 18 June 2015 parliamentary elections and relied, among other things, on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Ministry contested the claims.

Before the High Court of Eastern Denmark, a written statement by the first applicant was read out. It stated that he had suffered brain damage after being immunised during his first year of life and lived at Egmont folk high school. For many years he had had to share a single vote with his mother, who was his guardian, and he found it humiliating not to cast his own vote. The second applicant stated that he lived in his own flat in a group home, had a mentor who helped him, worked at the Glad Foundation reception desk, felt sad and excluded when not allowed to vote in June 2015, read newspapers and watched news, and was interested in politics. He said he had requested a guardian himself because it was difficult for him to manage his financial affairs.

On 29 June 2017, the High Court dismissed the claim. It considered that the Constitution had continuously been construed as excluding persons deprived of legal capacity under section 6 of the Guardianship Act from voting in general elections, and that Denmark’s international obligations did not imply an absolute right to vote for that limited group. The applicants appealed. On 18 January 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s decision. It found that persons deprived of legal capacity under section 6 were legally incompetent and disenfranchised, and that, notwithstanding Denmark’s international obligations, section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act applied and no compensation was due.

After the Supreme Court judgment, political focus led to a private members’ bill and a Ministry of Justice analysis. On 3 October 2018, the Ministry concluded that section 29 of the Constitution did not bar changes allowing some persons deprived of legal capacity to manage their assets. An amendment was passed on 20 December 2018 and entered into force on 1 January 2019. It introduced the possibility of partial deprivation of legal capacity; only persons fully deprived remained disenfranchised, while partially deprived persons remained legally competent and retained the right to vote in general elections.

Following the amendment, the first applicant applied to change his guardianship status. On 20 May 2019, his legal incapacitation order was quashed entirely, and he gained the right to vote. The second applicant also applied; by a district court order of 9 November 2019, he was only partially deprived of legal capacity under section 6(2)(2) of the Guardianship Act and consequently was granted the right to vote in general elections. The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights of a breach of their right to vote under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, taken alone or read in conjunction with Article 14.

case_name: CASE OF MOGYLA AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
The case concerns three applications lodged against Ukraine: no. 1129/18 by Vadym Mykolayovych Mogyla, born in 1986 and introduced on 21 December 2017; no. 50410/18 by Petro Ivanovych Stetsenko, born in 1974 and introduced on 9 January 2019; and no. 34853/24 by Firma Svitlana, TOV, a company registered in 1996 and represented by Pleskach Vyacheslav Yuriyovych of Gozhuly, introduced on 8 November 2024. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention that their access to a court had been restricted. In application no. 1129/18, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention.

Mogyla filed an administrative claim on 24 November 2008 challenging a local council’s refusal to allocate him a plot of land. The claim was reconsidered several times. On 26 January 2011 the Higher Administrative Court confirmed that it should be examined within administrative proceedings. On 30 September 2014, in the second round of consideration, the Higher Administrative Court remitted the case to the first-instance administrative court for a new consideration. On 21 June 2017, however, the Higher Administrative Court ruled that the claim fell to be examined in civil proceedings and terminated the case. Consequently, Mogyla’s claim was not determined on the merits.

Stetsenko’s complaint arose from proceedings concerning his claim about a local court’s refusal to grant him access to a case file relating to his property. On 21 June 2018 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal ruled on his request for full or partial exemption from, or deferral of, payment of court fees of approximately EUR 34. He relied on an alleged lack of funds and submitted official tax certificates showing his family’s monthly income of approximately EUR 139, which was significantly lower than the applicable minimum family subsistence level. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the request, holding that he had “failed to provide relevant evidence to prove his allegedly difficult financial situation,” without further explanation. The Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 17 September 2018.

Firma Svitlana’s complaint concerned commercial proceedings relating to registration of property. On 26 July 2024 the Poltava Regional Commercial Court dismissed the company’s request for exemption from or deferral of a court fee of UAH 27,252 (approximately EUR 650), based on its alleged lack of funds, income or assets. In support, the company provided copies of financial reports and bank statements. The court reasoned that under Article 8 of the Court Fee Act only individuals, not legal entities, could be released from the obligation to pay court fees. On 31 July 2024 the court returned the claim for failure to pay the court fee. On 12 August 2024 the Eastern Commercial Court of Appeal dismissed the company’s request for deferral of the appellate court fee of UAH 2,422 (approximately EUR 60), applying the same reasoning. On 11 September 2024 the appellate court returned the company’s appeal against the 26 July 2024 decision for failure to pay the appellate court fee. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court refused to open cassation proceedings, essentially upholding the appellate court’s reasoning.

case_name: CASE OF HUMPERT AND OTHERS v. GERMANY
summary:
The applicants are four German nationals—Karin Humpert, Kerstin Wienrank, Eberhard Grabs and Monika Dahl—who were State school teachers with civil servant status employed by different German Länder. They were members of the Trade Union for Education and Science and participated, during working hours, in strikes and a demonstration organised by that union to protest worsening working conditions for teachers. They were subsequently reprimanded or fined in disciplinary proceedings for breaching their duties as civil servants. On 10 December 2018 they lodged applications against Germany, complaining in particular about those disciplinary measures and about the prohibition on strikes by civil servants, which they considered incompatible with their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention.

The individual measures were as follows. Ms Humpert, a primary school teacher, was reprimanded by the Schleswig-Holstein Ministry for Education and Culture on 5 July 2011 for participating in a strike on 3 June 2010 and not teaching one lesson; it was later found she had missed two classes. Ms Wienrank, a vocational school teacher, and Mr Grabs, a secondary school teacher, were each fined EUR 100 by the Lower Saxony School Authority on 10 and 11 January 2011 respectively for unauthorised absence during a strike on 25 February 2009, when they did not give about five lessons each. The strike aimed, among other things, at securing a collective agreement for contractual State employees in the public educational sector and transferring its results to civil servants. Ms Dahl, a secondary school teacher, was fined EUR 1,500 by the Cologne District Government on 10 May 2010 for unauthorised absence during 12 lessons because of her participation in strikes on 28 January and 5 and 10 February 2009; those strikes had the same aims.

The applicants’ actions in the administrative courts were unsuccessful. The administrative courts found that they had breached their professional duties by participating in strikes. They considered that the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5 of the Basic Law restricted civil servants’ freedom of association under Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law through a prohibition on strike action. At first instance, the Schleswig-Holstein, Stade and Osnabrück Administrative Courts upheld the decisions against the first, second and third applicants by judgments of 8 August 2012, 6 December 2012 and 19 August 2011 respectively. The Düsseldorf Administrative Court, by judgment of 15 December 2010, initially considered that the employing State entity had to avoid a breach of Article 11 by discontinuing proceedings against the fourth applicant. On appeal, the Lower Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal, in a judgment of 12 June 2012 in the third applicant’s case, found the prohibition on strikes by civil servants part of the essence of Article 33 §§ 4 and 5 of the Basic Law and not alterable by interpretation in line with Article 11. On 16 May 2013 it rejected the second applicant’s request for leave to appeal by reference to that judgment. In the fourth applicant’s case, the North Rhine-Westphalia Court of Appeal overturned the first-instance judgment on 7 March 2012. On 27 February 2014 the Federal Administrative Court found the disciplinary decision against her lawful, though the fine should have been EUR 300; it considered that Article 33 § 5 could not be interpreted in a Convention-compliant manner and that the legislature had to resolve the conflict. The Schleswig-Holstein Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s appeal on 29 September 2014, and on 26 February 2015 the Federal Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicants lodged separate constitutional complaints, arguing that the decisions breached Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and that the administrative courts had failed to interpret national law in line with public international law, because the prohibition on strikes by teachers with civil servant status who did not exercise core public authority violated Article 11. On 12 June 2018 the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints (file nos. 2 BvR 1738/12 and others). It found no violation of Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and considered the prohibition on strikes by civil servants compatible with Article 11, based on the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5, and serving a functioning public administration and the State’s educational mandate.

They considered that the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5 of the Basic Law restricted civil servants’ freedom of association under Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law through a prohibition on strike action. At first instance, the Schleswig-Holstein, Stade and Osnabrück Administrative Courts upheld the decisions against the first, second and third applicants by judgments of 8 August 2012, 6 December 2012 and 19 August 2011 respectively. The Düsseldorf Administrative Court, by judgment of 15 December 2010, initially considered that the employing State entity had to avoid a breach of Article 11 by discontinuing proceedings against the fourth applicant. On appeal, the Lower Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal, in a judgment of 12 June 2012 in the third applicant’s case, found the prohibition on strikes by civil servants part of the essence of Article 33 §§ 4 and 5 of the Basic Law and not alterable by interpretation in line with Article 11. On 16 May 2013 it rejected the second applicant’s request for leave to appeal by reference to that judgment. In the fourth applicant’s case, the North Rhine-Westphalia Court of Appeal overturned the first-instance judgment on 7 March 2012. On 27 February 2014 the Federal Administrative Court found the disciplinary decision against her lawful, though the fine should have been EUR 300; it considered that Article 33 § 5 could not be interpreted in a Convention-compliant manner and that the legislature had to resolve the conflict. The Schleswig-Holstein Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s appeal on 29 September 2014, and on 26 February 2015 the Federal Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicants lodged separate constitutional complaints, arguing that the decisions breached Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and that the administrative courts had failed to interpret national law in line with public international law, because the prohibition on strikes by teachers with civil servant status who did not exercise core public authority violated Article 11.
