It found no violation of Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and considered the prohibition on strikes by civil servants compatible with Article 11, based on the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5, and serving a functioning public administration and the State’s educational mandate.

case_name: CASE OF DOYLE v. IRELAND
summary:
The applicant, Barry Doyle, an Irish national born in 1985 and serving a life sentence for murder, lodged an application against Ireland on 12 July 2017. He complained that, after his arrest, he was not entitled to have a solicitor present during police interrogation, representing an alleged failure by the State to vindicate his fair-trial right under Article 6 § 3 (c).

On 9 November 2008, the applicant killed S.G., aged 28, in Limerick. It was a case of mistaken identity: the applicant had set out to kill another man at the behest of a criminal figure during a gang feud. He shot and wounded S.G. in the street, pursued him into a back garden and shot him several times, inflicting five wounds including a fatal head wound.

On 24 February 2009, police searched the applicant’s residence and arrested him at 7.15 a.m.; he was brought to a police station shortly before 8.00 a.m. He was informed of his rights, including access to a solicitor, and requested a particular solicitor, who was notified. At 9.55 a.m. the solicitor spoke to him by telephone for two minutes. The first interview began at 10.12 a.m. and lasted fifty minutes. All interviews were video-recorded and conducted without the solicitor physically present. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor requested the solicitor’s presence; it was later confirmed that, under police practice at the time, such a request would have been denied.

Another solicitor, Mr O’D., arrived at 11.00 a.m. and represented the applicant. Further interviews took place that day, but the applicant made no admissions. On 25 February, three interviews took place, lasting almost five hours in total. The District Court extended his detention by 72 hours, with his solicitor present. In a tenth interview that night, police told him that his former girlfriend, G, the mother of his child, had been arrested in Dublin on suspicion of withholding information and was being detained and interviewed; they gave him details of her replies. He requested no further consultations and made no admissions.

On 26 February, during interviews, police stressed G’s detention and separation from her child and the victim’s innocence. In the thirteenth interview, the applicant asked to consult his solicitor; questioning stopped and a telephone consultation of about two minutes took place. In the fourteenth interview, he again asked to speak to his solicitor, saying the earlier call had been inadequate; later he repeated the request. The interview was briefly suspended, then officers asked background questions until 6.35 p.m. The solicitor arrived at 6.52 p.m. and spoke with him for about ten minutes. A police memo later recorded that the solicitor said, off the record, that the applicant would admit to the murder if G were released. Police replied that they wanted the truth; the solicitor said there would be no admissions before release, and police replied that an induced confession would not be accepted. The solicitor left. In the fifteenth interview, beginning at 7.42 p.m., the applicant first refused questions, then said he had been present at the scene. An officer said the solicitor had telephoned; the interview was suspended for a four-minute consultation. On resuming at 7.51 p.m., the applicant admitted shooting the victim and gave details and a map; the interview ended at 9.05 p.m. G was released at 9.00 p.m. In the sixteenth interview, he refused to answer questions. Further interviews followed on 27 and 28 February. On 28 February at 3.15 p.m., he was charged with murder.

The applicant pleaded not guilty in the Central Criminal Court. The first trial in 2011 was inconclusive. The second trial began on 16 January 2012 and lasted 22 days. He sought to exclude his admissions. The trial judge held a ten-day voir dire, viewed over twenty hours of recordings, heard evidence and submissions on threat, inducement, oppression, fairness and legal access, and ruled on the eleventh day. The judge found the prosecution had to prove admissibility beyond reasonable doubt. On legal access, he noted two consultations before the admissions and the solicitor’s presence in court for the detention extension; he found no breach of the constitutional right to legal advice and held police could continue interview 14 when the applicant complained the short telephone call was inadequate and the solicitor was expected within an hour. On oppression, he found the applicant physically and mentally strong, in control, and the interviews careful, patient, professional and not oppressive. Promptings about the truth, G and the child might objectively amount to inducement, but were not immediately acted on and were dissipated by the solicitor consultation and interaction, breaking any causative link; the admissions in interview 15 were voluntary and not caused by oppression, threat or inducement. He considered fundamental fairness in the round.

case_name: CASE OF OMDAHL v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicant, Olav Omdahl, a Norwegian national born in 1951, lives in Oslo. His grandfather, O.A. Knutsen, died on 24 April 1993. The estate included extensive property, shares, securities and moveable property worth approximately NOK 100 million, with debts of about NOK 10 million. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren; two children, including the applicant’s mother, died before final distribution.

On 5 May 1993 public administration of the estate began before the Probate Court, later the District Court, and an advocate was appointed administrator. Early on, some small properties were sold, but litigation over heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind under the will and a codicil tied up proceeds until the turn of 2005/06. Probate Court decisions to convert further assets were quashed or amended on appeal by the High Court, so no assets could be distributed.

A trust established by the deceased in the Bahamas and managed by a London bank emerged after the applicant’s mother died in 2002. In December 2005 each of the deceased’s children and grandchildren received NOK 5.5 million from it. The trust led to disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and to tax questions, clarified with the tax authorities from 2006 and finally during winter 2010.

An interim distribution on 1 July 2010 gave each branch of the lineal descendants NOK 10 million. The heirs appealed; the High Court dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2011 and the Supreme Court refused leave on 1 November 2011. Disputes over the sale of shares led to a District Court decision on 11 June 2010, finally settled on 25 March 2011. Other disputes, a recusal motion, and disputes over the sale of shares in a property company and a fish oil factory ended during 2012. Share sales were mostly completed in the first half of 2013, and remaining limited liability companies were wound up in December 2013.

The Probate Court decided final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Final distribution was disbursed on 16 April 2015, each branch receiving about NOK 18.9 million. A further distribution decided on 10 August 2015 entailed no payments and became final in September 2015. The administration thus lasted twenty-two years and four months.

In domestic proceedings, on 9 March 2016 the applicant sued the Norwegian Government before Oslo City Court, seeking a declaratory judgment that Article 6 § 1 had been violated because the administration exceeded a reasonable time, and claiming compensation. In its judgment of 15 September 2016, the City Court found that the length alone indicated a violation but considered the estate complex, the applicant not particularly litigious, and many actions brought by other heirs; it found no proven inactivity and no violation, and no compensation. The applicant appealed. After a hearing on 6–7 March 2018, the High Court on 22 March 2018 found no inactivity and considered the administration extraordinary, citing the large number of disputes, codicil-related blockage, sale difficulties, the 2008 financial crisis, and trust and tax complications. It noted that the applicant had argued a High Court ruling of 23 October 1997 was erroneous and blocked progress, but that ruling had become binding and was not appealed. The High Court concluded that there had been sufficient progress and no violation, and no liability. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 21 June 2018. The applicant lodged application no. 46371/18 on 21 September 2018.

case_name: CASE OF SHIPS WASTE OIL COLLECTOR B.V. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
The applicants are six Dutch limited liability companies. They complained about the transmission of intercept data obtained in criminal investigations to competition authorities and about the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

**First group.** Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. were engaged in collecting waste liquids from ships in Rotterdam. In late 2006, the VROM-IOD began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company, a subsidiary of Port Invest, for forgery and environmental offences. With an investigating judge’s authorisation, telephone calls were intercepted, including calls between I. company employees and Ships Waste Oil Collector employees. Some calls indicated price-fixing. On 21 April 2008 an official record with transcripts was drawn up. On 21 October 2008 a public prosecutor approved transmission to the NMA under section 39f WJSG; transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further material was authorised on 23 October 2009 and transmitted in 2010 after contact between the NMA and VROM-IOD. NMA inspectors visited premises on 29 and 30 June 2010. The I. company and an employee settled criminal charges on 11 March 2010; on 5 July 2010 the Regional Court declared the prosecution inadmissible.

On 16 November 2011 the NMA found competition-law infringements and imposed fines: EUR 834,000 on Ships Waste Oil Collector; EUR 1,861,000 jointly and severally on the I. company, Port Invest and Burando, with Burando’s liability capped at EUR 621,000. Objections argued that the transmissions lacked a proper basis, that there had been no prior judicial review, that the NMA had no power to intercept, and that no ex post criminal review occurred after settlement. On 11 July 2013 the Regional Court quashed the NMA decisions, finding the data were “criminal data” but that there was no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment. It found the data were criminal data, the transmissions had a statutory basis, judicial review safeguards existed, there was a compelling general interest in competition enforcement, less intrusive means were unlikely, and the criminal case ended on 19 July 2010 so the destruction period had not passed. Later, on 20 October 2016 and 30 October 2018, domestic courts upheld the competition infringements and fines.

**Second group.** Janssen de Jong Groep B.V., Janssen de Jong Infrastructuur Nederland B.V. and Janssen de Jong Infra B.V. were construction companies. Around 2007, the Public Prosecution Service and Rijksrecherche investigated “Cleveland” into bribery of local officials. With an investigating judge’s authorisation, telephone and internet communications of Janssen employees were intercepted. Some conversations indicated price-fixing. From July 2008 police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts on police premises. On 19 August 2008 the prosecutor provided a CD of about thirty audio recordings for information only. On 9 December 2008 the NMA opened an investigation; on 16 December 2008 the prosecutor permitted use of “Cleveland” information. On 22 December 2008 the NMA provided search terms; transcripts were transmitted on 24 December 2008. The Janssen companies sought civil provisional measures, arguing the transmission was not “in accordance with the law” and not foreseeable. On 26 June 2009 the provisional-measures judge dismissed the request, finding a compelling general interest and no less intrusive means. The Janssen companies did not appeal.

On 29 October 2010 the NMA imposed a EUR 3,000,000 joint and several fine. Objection was dismissed on 8 March 2012. On 13 June 2013 the Regional Court quashed the NMA decision, finding the data qualified as criminal data but that there was no identifiable, reviewable weighing of interests before use as evidence. The ACM appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry, advancing similar arguments; the Board of Prosecutors-General joined. The supplied record ends there.

case_name: CASE OF HORNCASTLE AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The application was brought by four British nationals—Michael Horncastle, David Blackmore, Abijah Marquis and Joseph Graham—against the United Kingdom. They alleged that admitting witness statements at their trials made the proceedings unfair.

Horncastle and Blackmore were charged, with D., with causing P.R. grievous bodily harm with intent. On 7 May 2005 P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat, suffered extensive injuries and was hospitalised for a month. On 3 June 2005 he made a police statement naming “Horncastle” and describing two other attackers, but said his memory was vague and he had drunk heavily. He died on 23 July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. The prosecution alleged that B. and M. had burgled another flat, stored stolen goods in P.R.’s flat, and that Horncastle and Blackmore went with D. to recover the property. The defence accepted they went to help recover D.’s property but denied attacking P.R.; they argued M. was responsible. Because P.R. was dead, the prosecution applied under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 to read his statement. The applicants opposed this under section 78 PACE, arguing it was the only admissible evidence against them, could not be cross-examined and was unreliable due to P.R.’s alcoholism, vague memory and description of Blackmore. On 24 January 2007 the judge admitted it as not unfair. After earlier juries were discharged, Horncastle and Blackmore were convicted in November 2007. The judge told the jury the prosecution depended on P.R.’s evidence and gave directions about the lack of cross-examination. On appeal, the applicants argued the statement was sole or decisive evidence. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. It found substantial independent evidence but accepted the statement was decisive; it relied on statutory safeguards, no section 125 application, full directions and material to attack credibility. On 9 December 2009 the Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal.

Marquis and Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. On 1 November 2007 six men entered her home, stole property, threatened her with a knife, kidnapped her and took her partner G.P.’s BMW. H.M. gave a statement but identified no one; G.P. described ransom demands. Graham was arrested on 2 November 2007 in G.P.’s car, where a knife was found; H.M. later confirmed it was the knife used. On 4 November 2007 a police officer told H.M. and G.P. the suspects were dangerous and cited relocated witnesses being murdered. On 22 November 2007 they retracted their statements, saying they feared for their families. H.M. later failed to attend court, was arrested, bailed and warned; she then made video statements saying her retraction was due to fear. G.P. said he was not scared but did not want reprisals. Neither attended the May 2008 trial. The prosecution applied to read their statements under section 116(2)(e) on grounds of fear. The applicants argued the fear was not caused by them but by police advice. On 13 May 2008 the judge admitted H.M.’s statement as a witness in fear, finding no police bad faith and no unfairness, but refused G.P.’s statement because fear was not established; a later defence application to admit part of it was refused. Marquis and Graham were convicted on 12 May 2008. They appealed, arguing H.M.’s statement should not have been admitted because the fear was not caused by them and because her evidence was decisive. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, finding the convictions not decisively based on H.M.’s statement. The Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal on 9 December 2009.

On 24 January 2007 the judge admitted it as not unfair. After earlier juries were discharged, Horncastle and Blackmore were convicted in November 2007. The judge told the jury the prosecution depended on P.R.’s evidence and gave directions about the lack of cross-examination. On appeal, the applicants argued the statement was sole or decisive evidence. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. It found substantial independent evidence but accepted the statement was decisive; it relied on statutory safeguards, no section 125 application, full directions and material to attack credibility. On 9 December 2009 the Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal.

Marquis and Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. On 1 November 2007 six men entered her home, stole property, threatened her with a knife, kidnapped her and took her partner G.P.’s BMW. H.M. gave a statement but identified no one; G.P. described ransom demands. Graham was arrested on 2 November 2007 in G.P.’s car, where a knife was found; H.M. later confirmed it was the knife used. On 4 November 2007 a police officer told H.M. and G.P. the suspects were dangerous and cited relocated witnesses being murdered. On 22 November 2007 they retracted their statements, saying they feared for their families. H.M. later failed to attend court, was arrested, bailed and warned; she then made video statements saying her retraction was due to fear. G.P. said he was not scared but did not want reprisals. Neither attended the May 2008 trial. The prosecution applied to read their statements under section 116(2)(e) on grounds of fear. The applicants argued the fear was not caused by them but by police advice. On 13 May 2008 the judge admitted H.M.’s statement as a witness in fear, finding no police bad faith and no unfairness, but refused G.P.’s statement because fear was not established; a later defence application to admit part of it was refused. Marquis and Graham were convicted on 12 May 2008. They appealed, arguing H.M.’s statement should not have been admitted because the fear was not caused by them and because her evidence was decisive. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, finding the convictions not decisively based on H.M.’s statement. The Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal on 9 December 2009.

case_name: CASE OF KOROŠEC v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Tadej Korošec, a Slovenian national born in 1980, lives in Ljubljana. He suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires twenty-four-hour assistance with daily activities. He alleged under Article 6 of the Convention that court proceedings to which he had been a party were unfair.

In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of the Republic of Slovenia awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance set at 70% of the reference amount. On 28 May 2009 his general practitioner applied for an increase, citing worsening condition, particularly respiratory function, and stating that the applicant needed twenty-four-hour assistance from a family member or lay care assistant, together with permanent professional assistance. At that time the applicant organised care through students and relied significantly on family members.

On 9 July 2009 the Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of an internal medicine specialist and an occupational medicine specialist, examined medical documentation from an internal medicine doctor, a pulmonologist and a clinical neurologist, and examined the applicant. It reported that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. On 20 July 2009 the Ljubljana unit of the Institute dismissed his request based on that opinion. The applicant appealed on 28 July 2009.

On 23 September 2009 the second-instance disability commission, composed of an occupational medicine specialist and a specialist neuropsychiatrist, examined the file and again reported that the applicant did not need permanent professional assistance and could be cared for by a combination of care assistants without specific medical knowledge and by family members. On 24 September 2009 the Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the second-instance commission and on the 1998 Decision on Assistance and Attendance Allowance for Beneficiaries Suffering from a Severe Disability, under which a higher allowance required twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance.

On 22 October 2009 the applicant brought court proceedings against the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent expert. On 30 September 2010 the court heard his testimony, reviewed the file, dismissed his claim, and rejected the independent expert request, finding the first- and second-instance commission opinions together with other evidence sufficient to establish that he did not need professional assistance. On 2 November 2010 he appealed, challenging that conclusion and the failure to appoint an independent medical expert, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise to assess his care needs. On 24 January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance court had relied on commission opinions given by experts and that both commissions had considered the medical records.

On 9 March 2011 the applicant sought leave to appeal on points of law. He argued that the lower courts’ refusal to appoint an independent expert was contrary to Supreme Court case-law, under which the Institute’s Disability Commissions could not be considered independent in proceedings against the Institute and should not be used as evidence. On 17 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the challenged decisions had not departed from established case-law. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (the record gives the date as 28 July 2007), and on 11 June 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed it with reference to section 55.b of the Constitutional Court Act.

The record also notes that social courts carry out judicial review of the Institute’s decisions; under the Civil Procedure Act, a court should obtain an expert opinion if it lacks the necessary expertise. A domestic Supreme Court decision of 7 November 2006 (no. VIII Ips 3/2006) held that the opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could only be expert opinions in pre-judicial proceedings within the Institute, not in judicial proceedings, because they were opinions of representatives of one of the parties.

case_name: CASE OF FILOZOFENKO v. UKRAINE

attempts.text:
The applicant, Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938 who lives in the Odessa Region. The respondent is Ukraine. In the domestic proceedings, she claimed against the State Pension Fund. She has the special status of a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006 (“the 2006 Act”), meaning a person who on 2 September 1945 was no more than 18 years old. Section 6 of that Act entitled her to a special supplement to her pension amounting to 30% of the minimum pension. She complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the State had failed to pay that supplement. On 18 November 2011 she lodged application no. 72954/11 against Ukraine. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.

On 11 December 2008 the applicant lodged a claim against the State Pension Fund with the domestic courts. She asked them to recalculate her pension in accordance with section 6 of the 2006 Act for 2006–2008 and to pay her the outstanding debt.

On 10 June 2009 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the claim. It held that in 2006 section 6 of the 2006 Act had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Amendments to the latter Act, which entered into force on 1 April 2006, had empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to set up a mechanism for a pension increase. However, no such mechanism had been set up in 2006, so the applicant’s claims relating to 2006 were rejected. As to 2007 and 2008, the court noted that section 6 had been suspended and modified respectively by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. On 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008 the Constitutional Court had found that suspension and modification unconstitutional. The court therefore held that the State Pension Fund should recalculate the applicant’s pension, but only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010 the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the lower court’s findings as regards the applicant’s claims for 2006. As to her claims for 2007 and 2008, it also upheld her right to a pension increase for the period from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008. However, it held that since she had missed a one-year statutory period for lodging a claim, the claim for 2007 had to be allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007.

On 18 May 2011 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the latter judgment. The record states that the relevant domestic law and practice are set out in the earlier case of Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine (nos. 68385/10 and 71378/10, §§ 17–25, 26 June 2014).

case_name: CASE OF ABDI v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The applicant, Mustafa Abdi, a Somali national, arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. His claim was refused, but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to make a deportation order; on 27 May 2002 detention was authorised. He appealed and made a fresh asylum claim; appeal rights were exhausted on 4 December 2003. He was assessed as high risk of sexual offending and medium risk of general offending. His release became automatic on 3 September 2003, but he remained detained. On 5 April 2004 a deportation order including detention authority was issued and served on 19 April 2004.

He claimed Isaaq clan membership from Somaliland, with parents born in Hargeisa, although he was born in Mogadishu. Authorities initially sought removal to Somaliland but required clan-history bio-data; he did not cooperate. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew; only voluntary returns with a disclaimer were possible. In November 2004 he refused to sign a disclaimer. Bail was refused in December 2004; further asylum representations in March 2005 were refused as a fresh claim in September 2005; bail was again refused on 11 October 2005, when an immigration judge was wrongly told enforced removal would soon be possible. In July 2006 an agreement with African Express Airlines made enforced removals possible; the first took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 he obtained permission to seek judicial review of his detention, but interim release was refused. Removal directions for 29 November 2006 were cancelled pending judicial review.

In domestic proceedings, the Administrative Court on 7 December 2006 applied the Hardial Singh principles. It held detention lawful up to August 2004; unlawful from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 because of length, impossibility of removal, and misleading statements; and lawful after 30 June 2006 because immediate removal was again possible. Both sides appealed. On 30 July 2007 the Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal and dismissed the applicant’s, holding the disputed period lawful because he could have returned voluntarily and posed a high reoffending risk. Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 13 December 2007.

In the separate deportation-order challenge, revocation was refused on 1 February 2007. An Immigration Judge allowed his appeal; the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal ordered reconsideration on 10 May 2007. After a reconsideration hearing on 26 February 2008, a rehearing was ordered. On 18 December 2008 the Tribunal reheard the case and dismissed the appeal by determination of 1 July 2009. The Court of Appeal allowed his appeal on 23 April 2010, but the Supreme Court allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal on 24 November 2010. Removal directions were issued on 6 December 2010 for 8 December 2010; on 7 December 2010 an interim measure prevented removal. He remained in immigration detention. He had been released on bail after 13 April 2007 but was re-detained on 3 April 2008 after breaching bail. The application concerns only the first period of detention, ending shortly after 13 April 2007.

Monthly reviews occurred during 3 September 2003–13 April 2007. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced an unpublished policy presuming detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending deportation; it was not disclosed until mid-2008 or published until September 2008, while published policy stated a presumption of release.

case_name: CASE OF LEVINTA v. MOLDOVA (No. 2)
summary:
The applicants, Pavel and Vitalie Levinţa, Moldovan nationals, were arrested in Russia in October 2000 and extradited to Moldova. They were allegedly ill-treated to compel self-incriminatory statements and convicted by Moldovan courts relying in part on those confessions. In an earlier case (Levinţa v. Moldova, no. 17332/03, 16 December 2008), the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3 and 6. On 3 April 2009 the applicants lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions. On 8 September 2009 they applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging in particular detention without legal basis and without reasons, inability to present their case fully, and failure to decide on detention pending trial within a reasonable time.

On 8 February 2010 the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice accepted the extraordinary appeal, quashed all previous judgments, ordered re-hearing and verification of the ill-treatment complaint, and stated that the applicants were to continue to be detained, with the trial court to decide the preventive measure. On 10 February their lawyer complained to the Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General, seeking immediate release because no valid detention order existed. The Prosecutor General’s Office referred to the 8 February judgment; the Ministry of Justice said it had not been informed of any judgment concerning the applicants after 16 April 2002.

On 15 March 2010 the Supreme Court sent the case to the Chişinău Court of Appeal. On 13 April the applicants’ lawyer asked that court for immediate release, while the prosecution requested 30 days’ detention pending trial; the applicants said no supporting evidence was submitted. After hearings were postponed on 14 and 16 April, on 19 April the Court of Appeal found continued detention necessary to ensure proper conduct, citing reasonable grounds to suspect exceptionally serious crimes and risks of absconding or obstruction. It rejected release and ordered 30 days’ detention from 2 p.m. on 14 April, then relinquished jurisdiction to the Supreme Court.

On 22 April the lawyer appealed, arguing absence of a valid court decision or warrant, breach of presumption of innocence, detention beyond the statutory 12-month maximum, lack of evidence of risk, and procedural delay. On 13 May the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

Later on 13 May, the lawyer was allegedly called at short notice about a 4 p.m. Court of Appeal hearing on a prosecution request, submitted 7 May, to extend detention by 60 days. He was in Anenii Noi on another case. The applicants were absent; a State-appointed lawyer represented them and objected. The court granted the extension for reasons similar to 19 April. A dissenting judge noted the request reached the Supreme Court on 11 May, criticised the lack of specific risk evidence and absence of the chosen lawyer, and concluded defence rights were breached.

On appeal, the lawyer repeated his arguments and added that the applicants had been held two hours after the previous order expired and had not agreed to the State-appointed lawyer. On 3 June 2010 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal, finding no breach because the applicants refused to appear and the lawyer had been informed; it also found the earlier order ran until 14 May. It held post-quashing detention could be exceptional and based on a prosecution request, citing risks of obstruction or absconding, prior absconding, international wanted status, extradition, and lack of social ties, income or employment. Later, release requests were made monthly and rejected; on 28 December 2010 detention was replaced by house arrest, and on 4 February 2011 by an undertaking not to leave the country during investigation.

case_name: CASE OF HUSAYN (ABU ZUBAYDAH) v. POLAND
summary:
Husayn (Abu Zubaydah), a stateless Palestinian born in 1971 and detained at the US Guantánamo Bay facility, lodged application no. 7511/13 against Poland on 28 January 2013. He alleged that Poland had enabled the CIA to detain him secretly on Polish territory, allowing torture, incommunicado detention, mental and physical abuse, and deprivation of contact with family or the outside world. He further alleged that Poland enabled his transfer from its territory, exposing him to further torture, ill-treatment, secret and arbitrary detention, and denial of justice by the US authorities. He also complained that Poland failed to conduct an effective investigation into these allegations. A related case, Al Nashiri v. Poland, was examined simultaneously.

After 11 September 2001 the US Government began a special interrogation and detention programme. On 17 September 2001 President Bush signed a classified Presidential Finding granting the CIA extended covert-action powers, including authority to detain terrorist suspects and establish secret detention facilities outside the United States in cooperation with host governments. The CIA later established the High-Value Detainees Programme. Abu Zubaydah was the first High-Value Detainee in CIA custody. According to the 2004 CIA Inspector General report, he was captured in Faisalabad, Pakistan, in late March 2002 and transported to a secret CIA “black site,” where he was treated for gunshot wounds.

In August 2002 the US Department of Justice provided an opinion that ten specific Enhanced Interrogation Techniques would not violate the prohibition of torture. These included attention grasp, walling, facial hold, insult slap, cramped confinement, use of harmless insects, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation not exceeding 11 days, and waterboarding. CIA psychologists later proposed twelve such techniques for Abu Zubaydah. From November 2002 the techniques were applied to other suspects in CIA custody, including Al Nashiri. A 2004 CIA background paper described routine capture, rendition, and reception: the detainee was flown to a black site, shackled and deprived of sight and sound, with no interaction except medical assessments; on arrival he was medically assessed and placed under complete American control through “precise, quiet, and almost clinical” procedures.

An investigation had been opened in Poland on 11 March 2008. In the related case, the Chamber sought materials showing the grounds for injured-person status in that investigation and whether detention in Poland had been established. In the present case, the Polish Government stated that a criminal investigation was pending and that they could not address the Court’s questions in detail or produce requested documentary evidence. They offered classified or ex parte access to a document prepared by the Appellate Prosecutor’s Office in Kraków and to case files Ap. V Ds. 12/12/S. The Court requested a comprehensive extract from the non-confidential part of those files by 30 October 2013. The Government did not submit it by that deadline. At the 2 December 2013 fact-finding hearing, they brought a classified document but proposed that it be reviewed in situ only by judges, interpreters, and Polish representatives. After the Chamber directed production of a redacted version, the Government did not produce it.

The Court held a fact-finding and in camera hearing on 2 December 2013 and a public hearing on 3 December 2013. It heard evidence from Giovanni Claudio Fava, Senator Dick Marty, J.G.S., and Senator Józef Pinior. Senator Marty and J.G.S. presented flight-data material concerning Poland and the cases of Al Nashiri and Abu Zubaydah. Documentary evidence came mainly from the applicant, partly supplemented by the Government, and from public-domain material.

case_name: CASE OF BUZADJI v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
summary:
The applicant, Petru Buzadji, a Moldovan national born in 1947 and living in Comrat, was director of State company B-G. In March 2006 he acknowledged in court that B-G owed a private company USD 594,067 plus penalties (total USD 842,404). He was dismissed on 26 May 2006. From July 2006 he was summoned over alleged defrauding of B-G and appeared whenever summoned. Thirteen criminal investigations were opened against him and his two sons, most on 5 April 2007, and joined on 25 May 2007; his sons were questioned as suspects in May 2007 but not arrested. On 26 October 2006 bankruptcy proceedings were initiated against B-G. On 21 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed lower judgments, finding the debt fictitious; retrial remained pending.

On 2 May 2007 the applicant was arrested. On 5 May 2007 he was charged with defrauding B-G. The same day the Buiucani District Court ordered 15 days’ pre-trial detention, citing the exceptionally serious charge, complexity, and reasonable grounds to believe he could collude with his sons, not yet interviewed; other prosecution fears were unsubstantiated. The applicant appealed, relying on pending civil debt proceedings, confirmation of the debt by a court-appointed administrator, absence of material showing risk of absconding or interference, his age and health problems needing unavailable in-patient care, family, residence and job, compliance with summonses from July 2006 to May 2007, and the fact that the detention court lacked the investigation file. On 8 May 2007 the Chişinău Court of Appeal upheld the detention, repeating the lower court’s reasons.

On 16 May 2007 the district court extended detention by 20 days, finding grounds valid, most investigative actions done, further measures requiring his participation necessary, and house arrest premature given seriousness, complexity and public interest. On 22 May 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld this, adding a continuing risk of evidence destruction because not all financial documents had been seized. On 5 June 2007 detention was extended another 20 days for the same reasons; on 11 June 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld it, citing the serious offence, alleged damage of almost MDL 9 million (about EUR 553,000), possible 10–25 year sentence, thirteen charges, ongoing investigation, and risks of absconding or influencing B-G staff witnesses.

On 26 June 2007 the district court rejected further extension and placed him under house arrest for 30 days. It noted 55 days’ detention, his participation in investigative actions, weakening grounds over time, the prosecutor’s burden to prove risk, and that severity alone did not justify detention; it found it improbable he would abscond, influence witnesses, or destroy evidence. Conditions barred leaving home, phone calls and discussing the case. On 29 June 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed this and ordered 20 days’ detention, citing complexity, seriousness, possible communication with his unarrested sons, flight to Transdniestria, influencing former staff witnesses, and available prison medical care.

On 16 July 2007 the district court extended detention 20 days, referring to the prosecutor’s position that the investigation was finalised and the file ready to be presented. On 20 July 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed that and changed the measure to house arrest, finding no evidence of continued need, no additional materials on witness influence, his promise to appear, and no specific risk of absconding. House arrest was maintained on 14 September and 14 December 2007. On 12 March 2008 he was released on bail after over ten months of detention/house arrest without breaching restrictions.

The applicant alleged unlawful arrest and that the courts had not given relevant and sufficient reasons for his detention pending trial.

case_name: CASE OF GUÐMUNDUR GUNNARSSON AND MAGNÚS DAVÍÐ NORÐDAHL v. ICELAND
summary:
Mr Guðmundur Gunnarsson (born 1976, Kópavogur) and Mr Magnús Davíð Norðdahl (born 1982, Reykjavík) lodged applications against Iceland on 6 and 20 May 2022. The case arose from the 25 September 2021 elections to Althingi. In the Northwest constituency, the smallest in Iceland, Gunnarsson stood as the top candidate for the Liberal Reform Party (Viðreisn), and Norðdahl as the top candidate for the Pirate Party (Píratar).

According to the Northwest constituency’s senior electoral commission, the initial vote count was finalised in the early morning of 26 September 2021. The reported result was that Liberal Reform received 1,072 of 17,666 votes, meaning Gunnarsson qualified for a levelling seat, while the Pirate Party received 1,082 votes, leaving Norðdahl a few votes short of a constituency seat.

At around noon that day, the National Electoral Commission telephoned the Northwest senior electoral commission, noting a very narrow margin of two votes in the Northwest and South constituencies that could affect levelling-seat allocation, and suggested a recount. A recount of Liberal Reform’s votes in the Northwest reduced its tally to 1,063, nine votes fewer. A full recount followed in the early afternoon: six parties lost between one and nine votes and four gained between one and ten; Liberal Reform ended with 1,063 votes and the Pirate Party with 1,081, one vote less than initially. A recount in the South constituency produced no changes. The Northwest recount led to a national reallocation of levelling seats. Gunnarsson lost his levelling seat, and the Northwest levelling seat went from Liberal Reform to the Centre Party.

The applicants lodged separate complaints on 1 and 5 October 2021, along with fifteen other complaints. Gunnarsson alleged that the recount lacked a legal basis; that ballots had been improperly stored and handled between counts; that party agents were not informed of the recount and could not observe it; and that changes in votes, blank ballots and invalid ballots were inconsistent and unexplained. He also disputed Althingi’s role in deciding electoral disputes and argued the defects could have influenced the outcome. Norðdahl alleged improper storage and handling of ballots and failure to inform him, as his party’s list agent, about the recount, depriving him of the chance to observe it. He argued it was sufficient that the defects could have influenced the result.

The Preparatory Credentials Committee, composed of nine members none elected in the Northwest, adopted procedural rules on 8 October 2021. It conducted an extensive inquiry over less than two months, obtaining documents, comments and information, questioning witnesses and experts, holding thirty-four meetings and making field visits to the count facility. The applicants appeared before it on 22 October 2021 and were invited to comment on draft descriptions in November. Most material was published on Althingi’s website, except confidential material and closed-hearing material. Gunnarsson’s lawyer requested access to various items, including material from a pending criminal investigation; Althingi provided some materials but refused others as confidential, and later refused a repeated request.

On 23 November 2021 the Preparatory Credentials Committee issued a ninety-page report identifying irregularities in the Northwest recount. It found that ballots had not been sealed and were left unattended in open boxes in a closed but unsupervised hotel room; one entrance could not be locked, hotel staff had keys, cameras did not cover the area, and the commission chairman had been alone there for about half an hour. It also found defects concerning the absence or insufficient notification of agents, changed numbers of valid ballots, and failure to secure agents’ participation in validity rulings. Other deviations concerned verification, mixing and counting procedures, and incomplete minutes.

On 25 November 2021 the Credentials Committee issued recommendations. Its majority found no indication of tampering and no effect on results, recommending confirmation of all sixty-three newly elected members. Minority members recommended annulling the Northwest or nationwide results and holding re-elections. Althingi debated the recommendations for over five hours and rejected the minority proposals. By forty-two votes to five, with sixteen abstentions, it confirmed the credentials. Under domestic law, Article 46 of the Constitution leaves Althingi to decide whether members are legally elected; the Act on Parliamentary Elections and Standing Orders govern complaints and credentials scrutiny.

case_name: CASE OF SOUSA GOUCHA v. PORTUGAL
summary:
The applicant, Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, is a Portuguese national born in 1954 who lives in Fontanelas. He is a well-known television host and publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008. The events at issue concerned a live talk show, *Five Minutes to Midnight* (*5 Para a Meia-Noite*), broadcast on RTP2 between midnight and 1 a.m. on 28 December 2009. The programme was presented by F.C. and featured two well-known media guests. During a quiz, F.C. asked, as the most important question, “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The possible answers included three female television hosts and the applicant; the applicant was the “correct” answer. In the transcript, guest J.M. first chose another guest, referred to as “the pregnant one” (option B, C.V.), and F.C. then revealed that the answer was Manuel Luís Goucha. F.C. described J.M.’s earlier answer as dishonest and contrary to his beliefs, while J.M. said he had known the answer and had been about to say it.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint for defamation and “insult” (*injúria*) with the Lisbon Criminal Department for Investigation and Prosecution. The defendants were the State-owned television company RTP, the production company, the television presenter F.C., and the directors of programming and content. The applicant complained that including his name among the possible answers had damaged his reputation and dignity. On 2 March 2011 a public prosecutor discontinued the proceedings, stating that the defendants had not intended to offend him.

The applicant sought to intervene in the proceedings as an assistant to the public prosecutor (*assistente*) and lodged private prosecution submissions with the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court against the defendants. The defendants challenged those submissions by requesting that a judicial investigation be opened. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge dismissed the case (*despacho de não pronúncia*). As regards the individual defendants, the judge found insufficient evidence of defamation or insult, so the case could not proceed to trial. The judge stated that the defendants had not intended to attack the applicant’s honour, nor had they anticipated doing so; the subjective element of the offence was therefore unverified. The judge noted that the applicant was a public figure and must be used to having his characteristics captured by comedians for humour. The judge referred to public knowledge that the applicant’s characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, such as his way of expressing himself, his colourful feminine clothes, and the fact that he had always lived in a world of women. The judge also noted that the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public and that the defendants never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. As regards the two defendant companies, the proceedings were discontinued under Article 11 of the Criminal Code, which excludes legal persons from liability for defamation and insult.

The applicant appealed against the decision not to indict the natural defendants before the Lisbon Court of Appeal. He argued in particular that the reason his name had been included in the list of possible answers was his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012 the appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal upheld the Criminal Investigation Court’s decision, finding insufficient evidence of defamation. It stated that not everything the complainant considers offensive should be so regarded, but rather what the majority of reasonable people would consider an offence to social and individual values of respect. It cited the context of a comedy show and treated the question as one of the many jokes typical of such shows. It repeated that the applicant was a public figure, that his characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, and that the defendants had never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. It considered that the expression, used in a playful and irreverent context and in the show’s normal style, even if in bad taste, did not reach the legal threshold for protection of honour and consideration. The applicant alleged that the unfavourable outcome of his defamation case before the Portuguese courts was discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, citing Article 14 of the Convention.

The Court of Appeal upheld the Criminal Investigation Court’s decision, finding insufficient evidence of defamation. It stated that not everything the complainant considers offensive should be so regarded, but rather what the majority of reasonable people would consider an offence to social and individual values of respect. It cited the context of a comedy show and treated the question as one of the many jokes typical of such shows. It repeated that the applicant was a public figure, that his characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, and that the defendants had never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. It considered that the expression, used in a playful and irreverent context and in the show’s normal style, even if in bad taste, did not reach the legal threshold for protection of honour and consideration. The applicant alleged that the unfavourable outcome of his defamation case before the Portuguese courts was discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, citing Article 14 of the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF SINKO AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applications were lodged against Ukraine by Anatoliy Leonidovych Sinko (born 1959), Oleg Petrovych Karpenko (born 1974), and Yuriy Yakovych Pushkar (born 1950) on 18 December 2020, 12 March 2021, and 27 August 2021 respectively.

In Sinko’s case, his mother was admitted to hospital on 26 August 2011 for planned examination and treatment of knee osteoarthrosis. After examination by doctor S., further health problems were found, and she agreed to surgery to remove an abdominal hernia, performed on 6 September 2011. Her condition deteriorated the next day, and she died on 9 September 2011 from exacerbation of cardiovascular disease. Internal and regional health examinations found significant shortcomings in the preoperative examination, surgery, and postoperative care leading to death. Criminal proceedings began on 25 December 2011. Forensic examination no. 171 identified shortcomings by doctor S. On 5 July 2012 Sinko was granted victim status; on 3 August 2012 doctor S. was charged with medical negligence causing death. The prosecutor returned the case for additional investigation due to procedural defects and violation of doctor S.’s defence rights, ordering another forensic examination. The second examination, by the same experts, confirmed the first. An indictment was drawn up on 29 April 2013. On 11 December 2013 doctor S. was convicted; the appellate court changed the sanction. On 20 November 2014 the Higher Specialised Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 31 March 2015 the appellate court ordered forensic examination no. 81/к, which found no specific contraindications for surgery and no direct causal link between doctor S.’s actions and the death, despite shortcomings. On 24 September 2015 the case was returned to the trial court. The indictment was returned twice, and the case was remitted several times. On 10 January 2019 the trial court acquitted doctor S., relying mainly on examination no. 81/к and dismissing earlier expert examinations as inadmissible. On 17 June 2020 the Supreme Court, in Sinko’s absence, upheld the acquittal. The courts noted that the 2012 and 2013 examinations involved surgeon B., who was also a member of internal medical commissions; the additional examination used the same experts, so both examinations and the questioning of those experts were inadmissible. No direct causal link was established because other doctors involved in postoperative treatment had not been assessed.

In Karpenko’s case, his 79-year-old father had chronic kidney and urinary diseases. On 28 March 2015 he felt unwell; on 2 April 2015 he was taken by ambulance to a district hospital in Sumy. On 7 April 2015 he was transported to a regional hospital with a urinary department and underwent urgent surgery. Two hours later he was transported back to the district hospital; on arrival his condition worsened and he died that day. Karpenko refused a post-mortem, alleging death due to inappropriate treatment and transportation. Criminal proceedings began on 21 December 2015. A forensic examination on 14 June 2016 found no signs of negligence, could not establish the exact cause without a post-mortem, and found no contraindications to transportation. Further examinations on 15 February 2018 and 10 February 2021 reached the same conclusions. On 6 April 2021 proceedings were discontinued for lack of evidence. On 19 January 2023 the investigating judge quashed that decision for failure to carry out necessary investigative actions, assess evidence, and substantiate termination; the investigation resumed.

In Pushkar’s case, his 27-year-old son was admitted on 29 September 2009 with acute pancreatitis and died on 13 October 2009 of severe complications. Pushkar alleged the death resulted from an unconsented blood purification procedure, failure to test tolerance to medications, and errors in diagnosis and treatment. In December 2009 an investigator began pre-investigative inquiries but repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings. A post-mortem began on 14 October 2009 and ended on 14 January 2010. Pushkar alleged medical staff forged documentation, changed records, and forged his son’s signature; investigators never examined those allegations. Experts concluded death resulted from intoxication and pancreatitis complications. On 21 March 2011 a Ministry of Health commission found several errors that had aggravated his son’s condition but generally adequate treatment. On 16 December 2012 criminal proceedings were instituted under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code (medical negligence). On 30 January 2013 the investigator terminated proceedings for lack of evidence; that decision was later quashed. Pushkar repeatedly complained of inactivity, and another investigator was appointed. A supervising police department and a prosecutor confirmed the inactivity of both investigators. The investigator did not reply to requests, and no medical personnel were questioned. On 20 June 2018 a forensic examination confirmed adequate treatment. Pushkar disagreed and requested an additional examination. On 25 June 2020 a new examination was ordered but never performed. On 27 January 2025 the investigation was closed for lack of evidence.

case_name: CASE OF NIKOLIĆ v. CROATIA
summary:
Ms Nada Nikolić, a Croatian national born in 1964 living in Vukovar, lodged application no. 5096/12 against Croatia on 9 December 2011. She alleged that national authorities had not adequately responded to the killing of her husband, Lj.N.

Vukovar was heavily attacked by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian paramilitary forces from August to November 1991 and occupied at the end of November 1991. It was part of the UN Protected Area from 1992 to 1996. In 1996 UNTAES was established; its mandate ceased on 15 January 1998 and transfer to Croatian authorities began.

On 2 October 1991, between 4 and 5 p.m., during a general alert, two unknown uniformed, armed men apprehended Lj.N. in the basement or courtyard of a building in Kudeljarska Street, Vukovar, and drove him away. On 24 November 1991 his body was found in the River Danube at Novi Sad, Serbia. A 25 November 1991 autopsy found death was caused by a hand-gun gunshot wound.

In 2004 the applicant sued the State for damages in the Vukovar Municipal Court. In connection, the Vukovar Municipality State Attorney’s Office asked police for information. The police thereby first learned of the death and opened an enquiry. On 24 January 2005 police interviewed the applicant; she said her husband had been abducted from the basement by two Croatian soldiers. She named B.Š., K.Š., J.T., S.P., M.P. and J.M. as present; K.Š., S.P. and M.P. had died. That day J.T. said two uniformed, armed, masked men had taken Lj.N. On 3 February 2005 B.Š. said he had joined the Croatian Army in August 1991 and was visiting his wife K.Š. and children in the same basement; he denied being present. On 15 February 2005 Vukovar police lodged a criminal complaint with the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office against an unknown perpetrator, classifying the offence as a war crime against the civilian population.

On 5 May 2009 the applicant told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office that B.Š. had been present. She said that after K.Š. died around 10 November 1991, one abductor came to take J.M.; B.Š. whispered, “This is the man who took Lj.[N.]”. She said B.Š. lived in Zagreb. On 9 July 2009 Zagreb police interviewed B.Š., who denied being present or knowing the abductors. On 21 July 2009 Vukovar police interviewed J.M., who said she was present but did not see the men. On 24 March 2011 a Zagreb County Court investigating judge heard B.Š., who repeated his statement. On 3 May 2011 a Vukovar County Court investigating judge interviewed the applicant, who repeated her statement. On 12 November 2011 Vukovar police told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office they had found no new information.

The applicant’s civil claim was dismissed on 18 September 2008. The Vukovar County Court upheld that decision on 21 April 2009 and the Supreme Court on 16 February 2011, finding the claim time-barred. Her constitutional complaint was dismissed on 12 July 2011.

case_name: CASE OF BERLAND v. FRANCE
summary:
The applicant, Daniel Berland, a French national born in 1987 and in the specialised hospital centre of Sevrey, lodged application no. 42875/10 against France on 21 July 2010, alleging a violation of Article 7 §1.

On 12 September 2007, aged 20, he went to the workplace of C.G., his former girlfriend, who after threats and violence had told him she no longer wanted to see him. He inflicted several stab wounds on C.G., who died from a massive haemorrhage from throat and thorax wounds, and wounded two other people. On 14 September 2007 he was placed under judicial investigation for premeditated murder and intentional wounding, remanded in custody, and the Prefect ordered his compulsory admission to Sevrey CHS. Expert psychiatric boards found that at the material time he had a mental disorder impairing his discernment and ability to control his actions under Article 122-1 of the Criminal Code.

On 8 September 2008 the public prosecutor asked the Dijon investigating judge to refer the case to the Investigation Division for a ruling on lack of criminal liability under Article 706-20 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, derived from the 25 February 2008 Act. On 30 September 2008 the judge found sufficient evidence to commit the offences and plausible reasons to apply Article 122-1, and ordered transmission to the Principal Public Prosecutor. On 18 November 2008 the Principal Public Prosecutor called for referral under new Article 706-122. On 25 November the President noted the applicant could not appear for medical reasons. At the 27 November hearing, his representative argued that applying the new procedure breached the non-retroactivity of harsher criminal legislation: it required the Investigation Division to rule on commission of the offences when imposing indefinite compulsory psychiatric treatment, tantamount to conviction and sentence not applicable in 2007.

case_name: CASE OF SULEJMANI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
The application (no. 74681/11) was lodged against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia by Mr Osman Sulejmani, a Macedonian national born in 1958 and living in Tetovo. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the confiscation of his vehicle in criminal proceedings against a third person.

On 12 April 2006 the applicant concluded a sales contract with Sh.A. to purchase a concrete mixing and transport lorry (“the vehicle”) for the equivalent of EUR 5,000 in Macedonian denars. On 15 May 2007 he lent the vehicle to his company. On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate from him to examine the chassis; a record of temporarily seized objects was issued.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted Sh.A. of forgery of a document concerning the vehicle’s chassis number and rejected an indictment against I.S. It found that it had not been established that Sh.A. had altered the chassis. Under section 102(3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act, it advised the applicant, who had claimed compensation in the criminal proceedings, to pursue that claim in a separate civil action. That judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 16 November 2010 the applicant asked the first-instance court to return the vehicle. On 3 December 2010 the court heard him; he said he had bought the vehicle from Sh.A. for EUR 25,000 and could not have known at the time that its chassis number had been forged. On 6 December 2010 the court, relying on Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, found no grounds to confiscate his vehicle: he had not known and could not have known that it had been used to commit a crime. It also ordered return of the registration certificate.

On the public prosecutor’s appeal, on 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed that decision. Relying on Article 100-a(2), it found that the chassis had been forged and that the vehicle, in the interest of public safety, could not be declared roadworthy. It referred to Article 100-a(3) and instructed the first-instance court to assess whether continued use of the vehicle would constitute the offence of using a forged document.

On 22 February 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s application and ordered confiscation of the vehicle and registration certificate. Referring to Article 100-a(2) and (3), it found the chassis number had been forged and the vehicle could be used to commit an offence; for that reason and for road safety, confiscation was necessary. It referred to section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act and found that, although there were no proceedings against the applicant and he was not an offender, confiscation was necessary for general safety.

On 11 March 2011 the applicant appealed, arguing wrong application of Article 100-a(2) and (3) and that he had not known the vehicle had been used to commit a crime. On 19 May 2011 the appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It stated that it was true the applicant did not know the chassis had been forged, that he had registered the vehicle as last buyer, obtained a driving licence and paid a large amount. However, it considered that under Article 100-a(2) objects used to commit an offence are confiscated regardless of ownership if general safety, public health or ethics require it; the applicant’s lack of knowledge did not satisfy Article 100-a(3). The first-instance court had correctly found that use of the vehicle with forged identification numbers would affect road-user safety and general safety. The decision appears to have been served on the applicant on 2 June 2011.

case_name: CASE OF MIHHAILOV v. ESTONIA
summary:
Aleksandr Mihhailov, a stateless person born in 1976 living in Narva, lodged an application with the European Court on 28 October 2010, alleging that police had used unwarranted violence during his arrest and later detention at a police station.

On 29 April 2009, shortly before 6 p.m., Narva police received a call about two men near Kreenholmi and Kerese streets; one was reportedly carrying a knife, while the other was drunk and had difficulty walking. Officers S.B. and E.V. found the applicant and M.Z. at a public playground. The applicant alleged that, although drunk, he was not aggressive or abusive; S.B. punched him in the jaw, he fell and briefly lost consciousness, was handcuffed, and was then punched and kicked until he lost consciousness, waking at the police station. The Government, relying on the criminal investigation, stated that the applicant behaved aggressively, swore, waved his hands, and disobeyed orders. E.V. forced him to the ground; Officers S.J. and N.S. helped handcuff him. He resisted, kicked the police car, and was restrained on the ground. While being placed in the van, he hit his left temple against the door. He remained aggressive during transport.

At the police station, the applicant alleged that S.B. kneed him near the left ear, repeatedly punched and kicked him, at one point put his head under a running tap, and beat him again after E.V. returned; he lost consciousness and later had blood on his face. The Government said he remained aggressive and was restrained; he fell off a chair twice, and officers later left him on the floor. At 7.45 p.m. a report was drafted stating he had been taken to sober up and noting a dirty face and abrasions on his head.

At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009 an ambulance was called. The applicant complained of head and wrist pain, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss in his left ear. He was found to have haematomas on the left cranium and a swollen right wrist, and was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and a fracture of the right hand/wrist. He was taken to hospital, where he was diagnosed with concussion. A CT scan at 6.26 a.m. showed no haemorrhage or intracranial pathology, and he was released. At 2.15 a.m. police took a statement from him at the hospital, and at 2.40 a.m. drafted a misdemeanour report alleging drunkenness and breach of the peace. On 1 May 2009 an ambulance was again called; he was diagnosed with concussion and had a haematoma around the left ear, oedema around the left eye, and bruises on the neck and upper limbs.

On 30 April 2009 the applicant complained to police of ill-treatment. After initial difficulties, a criminal investigation was opened on 5 May 2009. Investigators took statements from the applicant, M.Z., detainees A.P., M.S., and R.L., police officers, children who witnessed the arrest, and ambulance staff. A.P. and R.L. said they heard or saw the applicant being beaten at the station; M.S. heard shouting but saw no beating. M.Z. said he saw the applicant beaten at the station, but later, during photo identification, said there had been no beating at the playground. The children said officers used force but did not punch or kick the applicant during the arrest. A forensic medical expert concluded on 13 August 2009 that the injuries had been caused by blunt force, likely shortly before the applicant saw a doctor, possibly on 29 April 2009, but the exact cause could not be established.

On 20 January 2010 the police investigator discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no evidence that officers had committed abuse of authority and that the force used had been lawful and not excessive. The prosecutor approved this on 15 February 2010. The applicant appealed on 15 March 2010, but the State Prosecutor’s Office rejected the appeal as out of time on 23 March 2010, and the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 30 April 2010.

Separately, on 25 May 2009 the East Police Prefecture fined the applicant for breach of the peace. On 17 November 2010 the Viru County Court acquitted him, finding no evidence of the misdemeanour, setting aside unlawfully obtained hospital statements, finding M.Z. reliable that police had unduly influenced him by letting him hear the applicant being beaten, and concluding that evidence had been collected unlawfully, infringing the applicant’s honour and dignity and endangering his health.

case_name: CASE OF ROHLENA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966 living in Brno, lodged application no. 59552/08 against the Czech Republic on 4 December 2008. Relying on Article 7, he alleged that the domestic courts, by convicting him of a continuous criminal offence, had applied criminal law retroactively to his detriment.

On 29 May 2006 the Brno municipal prosecutor indicted him for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. The alleged conduct included verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping, holding her throat, attempting to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or to the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling away household money and smashing crockery. His wife sustained haematomas, bruising and a fractured nose, seeking medical assistance on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003 and 8 February 2006 after assaults on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003 and 8 February 2006. The prosecutor classified the conduct as the “continuing” offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code, noting that conduct before that offence was introduced on 1 June 2004 had amounted to violence against an individual or group under Article 197a and assault occasioning bodily harm under Article 221.

On 18 April 2007 the Brno Municipal Court found him guilty of that offence, committed at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006 as indicted. It sentenced him to a suspended two-and-a-half-year prison term, five years’ probation, supervision and alcohol-dependency treatment. It relied on statements by the applicant, the victim and witnesses, including the couple’s children, who reported ten verbal insults, four instances of grabbing and strangling, and monthly verbal and/or physical assaults, as well as documentary and expert evidence. The applicant admitted quarrels and physical violence, including sometimes slapping his wife or hitting her with his fist. The court applied Article 215a as in force since 1 June 2004, treating it as extending to pre-1 June 2004 acts because they were punishable at the time and at least amounted to Article 197a. It found the duration gave relatively high danger and imposed a suspended sentence at the lower end of the range.

On 6 September 2007 the Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal contesting the facts and evidence assessment, finding no defects and that the classification conformed to the Criminal Code. On 21 February 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded his appeal on points of law complaining that Article 215a had been applied to conduct before 1 June 2004. Referring to its earlier decision Tzn 12/93 of 8 December 1993, it stated that a continuation of a criminal offence constituted a single act and was to be classified under the law in force when the last occurrence was completed, provided earlier acts had been criminal under previous law. It found the pre-amendment conduct amounted at least to Article 197a or Article 221 § 1, and that the facts disclosed all elements of Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b), including continuation over several years. On 10 June 2008 the Constitutional Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded the applicant’s constitutional appeal alleging unfair proceedings and retroactive detrimental application of the Criminal Code; it held the domestic decisions logical and coherent and without prohibited retroactive effect.

Because the applicant later committed another offence while on probation and did not undergo alcohol treatment, he had to serve the prison sentence from the 18 April 2007 judgment. He began serving it on 3 January 2011; according to the Government, he was conditionally released on 17 May 2012.

summary:
The application was lodged on 15 October 2010 by Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and serving a life sentence. He alleged in particular that, in sentencing him, the domestic courts had not applied the most lenient criminal provisions, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention.

On 13 August 1996 the Voznesensk local prosecutor’s office began investigating the murder of four persons on 12 August 1996. On 18 October 1999 the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office began investigating the murder of A., and on 10 November 1999 the Slavyansk Police Department began investigating hooliganism concerning R. case_name: CASE OF MASLÁK AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
summary:
The applicants are three Slovak nationals, Miroslav Maslák, Tomáš Ďuriš and Vladimír Haviar, all residing in Pružina. They lodged an application against Slovakia, represented by R. Toman; the Government were represented by Ms M. Pirošíková. They alleged under Article 5 §§4 and 5 that they had been denied a speedy procedure for review of the lawfulness of their pre-trial detention and an enforceable right to compensation for the alleged breach of the speediness requirement in relation to release requests of 2 and 10 May 2010 and December 2010 (amended in January 2011), and their interlocutory appeal against the detention order of 4 April 2011.

Since 2007 the applicants had faced multiple charges, mainly violent offences linked to organised crime. They were repeatedly arrested, remanded, released, re-arrested and re-remanded. The relevant events began after their arrest on 1 April 2010 on a perjury charge. Their detention then ended on 1 April 2011, when they were released but immediately re-arrested and later remanded on an extortion charge.

The first applicant requested release on 2 May 2010; the request reached the Považská Bystrica District Court on 11 May and was amended on 19 May. On 21 May he challenged the judge for bias, alleging that the case had not been assigned to the lawful judge. The challenge was dismissed the same day. His appeal was dismissed by the Trenčín Regional Court on 10 June, served on 21 June. His release request was dismissed by the District Court on 25 June and, on appeal, by the Regional Court on 20 July, served on 26 July. On 27 September 2010 he complained to the Constitutional Court that the review was not speedy, the dismissal arbitrary, and the judge not lawful. On 4 October 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible; on length it found no violation at either court level, and other complaints were partly out of time or manifestly ill-founded. The decision was served on 23 November 2011.

The second and third applicants requested release on 10 May 2010, filing with the District Prosecution Office and offering a pledge under Article 80 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecution sent the request to the District Court on 17 May; the file was received on 21 May. The District Court found the file incomplete, requested a complete version on 27 May, and received it on 2 June. The applicants waived a personal hearing on 27 May. The District Court dismissed the request on 3 June; the Regional Court dismissed their appeal on 15 July. The District Court decision was served on 9 June. On 8 July the court learned that one lawyer had stopped representing them but had failed to inform it, citing a holiday. The Regional Court decision was served on 2 and 9 August. On 30 September 2010 they complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of Article 5 §§3 and 4 to speedy review and release. On 9 November 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible; it noted delays by the authorities and by the lawyer, but found the length compatible with the speediness requirement. The decision was served on 19 December 2011.

On 22 December 2010 the applicants made a fresh release request. The District Court replied on 3 January 2011 that, absent new relevant information, a new request could be made at the earliest thirty days after the final determination of the previous request; the previous request had become final on 16 December 2010, so the request could not be entertained. The first applicant amended on 20 January 2011; the second and third amended on 31 January. The District Court dismissed the request on 7 February; the Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 23 February, served on 2 March. On 31 March 2011 the applicants complained to the Constitutional Court under Article 5 §§3 and 4. On 14 June 2011 that court declared the complaint inadmissible; it held that the courts had been legally prevented from examining the original request, so the relevant periods began on the amendment dates, and the length was acceptable. The decision was served on 18 August 2011.

Following their arrest on 1 April 2011, the District Court remanded the applicants on 4 April 2011 on an extortion charge. On 14 April they appealed; the Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 21 April, served on 19 May. On 15 June 2011 they complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of Article 5 §§1 and 4, including lack of speedy review of the appeal. On 13 December 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, served on 16 January 2012. On 27 September 2011 the applicants were indicted and on 15 November 2011 they were released; the merits proceedings appeared still pending.
