case_name: CASE OF GLOVELI v. GEORGIA
summary:
The applicant, Marina Gloveli, a Georgian national born in 1958 and living in Tbilisi, is a practising lawyer with over twenty years’ experience. She also served as a judge in the Tbilisi Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2005. She participated in competitions for vacant judicial positions six times, most recently in October 2017. The present case concerns her latest attempt to obtain a judicial appointment.

In earlier domestic proceedings, on 9 February 2016 the applicant and two other unsuccessful candidates lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court. They alleged that sections 36(4), 49(1)(a) and 50(4) of the Act of 13 June 1997 on Courts of Ordinary Jurisdiction did not comply with Articles 29 and 42 of the Constitution, arguing in particular that no court had jurisdiction to examine disputes concerning judicial appointments. On 10 March 2017 amendments to the Courts Act entered into force, making decisions of the High Council of Justice (HCJ) on judicial appointments appealable to the Supreme Court. On 7 April 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, concluding that the amendments had created a new judicial remedy through the Qualifications Chamber of the Supreme Court, which had jurisdiction to examine appeals concerning allegedly arbitrary refusals of judicial appointments.

On 18 October 2017 the HCJ announced a new judicial competition. The applicant applied for a vacant position as a judge in a court of appeal and submitted documents confirming her professional and academic achievements. On 25 November 2017 the HCJ announced that she had been admitted to the competition. On 29 December 2017 HCJ members interviewed her and individually assessed her using score sheets. On 20 January 2018 she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the score sheets completed by the HCJ members who had interviewed and assessed her.

On 2 February 2018 the applicant lodged an appeal with the Qualifications Chamber seeking invalidation of the HCJ decision under section 354(3)(b) of the Courts Act. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that during the competition several HCJ members had had “protégé” candidates and had arbitrarily lowered the assessment scores of other judicial candidates. She also argued that the very low scores assigned to her by several HCJ members indicated bias.

On 6 February 2018 the Qualifications Chamber declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had not achieved the minimum pass score in the competency component, her candidacy had not been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the precondition in section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met; the HCJ had not examined her application for appointment and had not issued a decision refusing appointment that could be challenged before the Qualifications Chamber. The Qualifications Chamber further held, referring to earlier European Court cases Beaumartin v. France and Sigma Radio Television Ltd v. Cyprus, that it did not satisfy the requirement of a court or tribunal with “full jurisdiction” to review the facts of the case, and that its decision followed its established practice (case no. სსპ-2-17). The decision stated that it was final and not amenable to appeal.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court on 3 April 2018.

case_name: CASE OF COMMUNAUTÉ GENEVOISE D'ACTION SYNDICALE (CGAS) v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The applicant, Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS), is a Swiss-law association established in 1962 and based in Geneva. Its statutory aim is to defend workers and its member organisations, particularly in trade-union and democratic freedoms; it states that it organises or participates in dozens of gatherings each year in the Canton of Geneva. The respondent is Switzerland.

The case arose during the COVID-19 pandemic. The first cases were reported in Wuhan, China, on 31 December 2019. The new coronavirus was first detected in Switzerland on 25 February 2020, in the Canton of Ticino. On 28 February 2020 the Federal Council declared a “special situation” under section 6(1)(b) of the Epidemics Act and adopted an ordinance prohibiting public or private events involving more than 1,000 persons. On 11 March 2020 the WHO described the situation as a pandemic. On 13 March 2020 the Federal Council replaced that ordinance with Ordinance 2 on measures to tackle coronavirus (O.2 COVID-19), closing schools, universities and training establishments and prohibiting public or private gatherings of more than 100 persons; cantonal authorities could grant exemptions for gatherings exercising political or training rights. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council announced an “extraordinary situation” under section 7 of the Epidemics Act and amended O.2 COVID-19. From 17 March 2020, all public and private gatherings were prohibited, the exemption for political rights was removed, and Article 10(d)(1) made intentionally organising or conducting a prohibited gathering punishable by up to three years’ custody or a fine. On 20 March 2020 gatherings of more than five persons in public places were prohibited. On 8 April 2020 the measures were extended until 26 April 2020. On 29 April 2020 a relaxation from 11 May 2020 was announced, and on 20 May 2020 religious worship was allowed to resume from 28 May 2020.

CGAS lodged its application with the Court on 26 May 2020. Relying on Article 11 of the Convention, it alleged that, following O.2 COVID-19, it had been obliged to cancel a gathering planned for 1 May 2020 and had withdrawn its authorisation request. More generally, it claimed that it had been deprived of the possibility of organising or participating in public meetings. It submitted that the Federal Council’s ordinances were generally applicable measures and that no appeal lay against them to a domestic court; it said this was why it had not applied to national courts.

On 27 May 2020 the Federal Council announced further reopening: from 30 May 2020 the ban on gatherings was relaxed to a maximum of 30 persons; from 6 June 2020 private and public gatherings of up to 300 persons, including political gatherings, were authorised again; events of more than 1,000 persons remained prohibited until the end of August; and on 20 June 2020 the prohibition on gatherings was lifted, although masks remained compulsory. On 19 June 2020 the Federal Council declared a return to the “special situation” as of 22 June 2020.

Domestically, Federal Council ordinances cannot be challenged by abstract review before the Federal Supreme Court under Article 189(4) of the Constitution and section 82(c) of the Federal Supreme Court Act; implementing acts may be appealed, and the ordinance’s conformity with higher-ranking law may be examined in a preliminary ruling. In Geneva, gatherings on public land require authorisation; decisions can be appealed to cantonal courts and then to the Federal Supreme Court. On 18 August 2020 the Administrative Division of the Geneva Court of Justice examined Article 6 of O.2 COVID-19 in a preliminary ruling and found it had a sufficient legal basis, with public health interests prevailing over the party’s interest in demonstrating. On 12 August 2021 the Federal Supreme Court declared an appeal inadmissible for lack of current purpose because the requested demonstration date had passed and the five-person gathering ban had been lifted on 30 May 2020.

case_name: CASE OF R.B.A.B. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
The applicants are five Sudanese nationals—R.B.A.B., her husband H.S., their daughters X and Y, and son Z—who entered the Netherlands on 28 April 2001. The parents sought asylum separately, and R.B.A.B. also applied for the children. They claimed to be from Dilling, South Kordofan, and said H.S. had attracted Sudanese authorities’ attention through opposition movement M. After interviews in May, August and November 2001, the Deputy Minister intended to reject the claims due to contradictions and lack of knowledge about tribes, topography and movement M. On 17 January 2002 their asylum requests were rejected. Appeals were declared inadmissible for failure to submit grounds; an objection was dismissed on 10 September 2002.

On 12 April 2003 they filed a second asylum request on essentially the same grounds. On 14 April 2003 the Minister rejected it, finding no new facts or altered circumstances; no appeal was lodged.

case_name: CASE OF DELECOLLE v. FRANCE
summary:
Mr Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937 and living in Paris, lodged an application against France on 5 June 2013. He alleged a violation of Article 12, complaining that he had been denied the right to marry because his marriage was subject to the authorisation of his supervisor or the guardianship judge.

On 23 June 2009, when he was seventy-two, the guardianship judge of the Paris District Court of the 15th Administrative District placed him under enhanced protective supervision (curatelle renforcée) for five years, following an initial request by his adoptive daughter. The judge relied on medical certificates from Dr M.F. (25 November 2008) and Dr J.-P.B. (14 March 2009), and appointed M.-C.M. as supervisor. The applicant sought lifting of the measure, or ordinary supervision, or reduction to twenty-four months. On 18 December 2009 the Paris Regional Court dismissed those requests. It noted that Dr R. had excluded dementia but found slight cognitive impairment and psychological fragility and vulnerability, and that the applicant lacked capacity to manage or dispose of his property, though he could hold a bank account and cash card.

The applicant asked his supervisor to authorise his marriage to M.S., a friend since 1996 and his partner since 2008. The supervisor interviewed them separately and together and refused on 17 December 2009, stating that she had known the applicant only a few months. On 21 December 2009 the guardianship judge ordered a social inquiry by the UDAF into the applicant’s living conditions, lifestyle, social status and circle of friends. The applicant appealed against that order. That same day the judge also commissioned a medical opinion on his capacity to marry. On 18 January 2010 the psychiatrist reported that the applicant suffered from intellectual disorders; while able to consent to marriage, he was considered incapable of dealing with its property and financial consequences. The psychiatrist also gave personal opinions and described some of the applicant’s arguments as bordering on absurd.

On 1 March 2010 the Paris Court of Appeal declared the appeal against the inquiry order inadmissible. It held that a vulnerable adult’s interests allowed the guardianship judge to order such inquiries, and that a supervisee could marry only with the supervisor’s authorisation or, failing that, the judge’s. On 1 June 2010 the UDAF reported a financial stake at the heart of a major family conflict; the applicant’s daughter and M.S. accused each other of being interested in his fortune, and it was unclear whether he was being influenced. The applicant was deeply affected and appeared to see marriage as ensuring assistance and companionship.

On 24 June 2010 the guardianship judge, after hearing the applicant and his daughter, dismissed the marriage request. The judge found his attachment to M.S. insufficient, noted that both were former alcoholics and that the applicant apparently still drank, and considered that he sought safety against a break-up and loneliness. Financial implications were unclear because he was torn between his daughter and M.S. The applicant appealed.

On 6 September 2011 the Paris Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. It cited serious disorders and the medical certificates, stating that anosognosia prevented him from planning joint life and understanding marriage’s financial and legal implications. It noted unreasonable management since living with M.S., 250,000 euros of work after his wife’s death, questionable storage of furniture, a draft handwritten will of 14 August 2009 in M.S.’s favour, assets of about 6,000,000 euros, and deteriorated relations with his daughter M.D. It concluded that mutual affection existed but that his psychopathological condition and failing grasp of finances prevented informed consent.

The applicant appealed on points of law and raised a QPC on Article 460(1) of the Civil Code. On 29 June 2012 the Constitutional Council declared that provision constitutional. On 5 December 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that the Court of Appeal had lawfully reasoned from the medical certificates and file that he could not give informed consent. The applicant died on 4 February 2016; M.S. later indicated an intention to pursue the application.

case_name: CASE OF KIIVERI v. FINLAND
summary:
The applicant, Timo Veikko Kiiveri, is a Finnish national born in 1960 who lives in Tampere. He owns 90% of the shares in a limited liability construction and decoration company and is its managing director and a board member. In 2005 the tax authorities inspected the company and concluded that it had failed to declare and pay considerable taxes, paid salaries off the books, and engaged in other fraudulent activity. On 8 September 2008 the tax authorities imposed additional income tax and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant for tax years 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2006. He apparently did not appeal, and the bailiff seized the imposed sums. The tax years 2002, 2003 and 2005 became final on 31 December 2008, 31 December 2009 and 31 December 2011 respectively; the appeal period for 2006 elapsed on 31 December 2012.

In June 2007 the police started a criminal investigation into the applicant’s activities. On 6 March 2009 the prosecutor charged him with accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned tax years 2000–2006 and his role as managing director and board member: he was accused of deducting fabricated receipts, failing to declare the company’s real income, paying salaries off the books, and causing the company’s tax to be too low. The second count concerned tax years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006: he was accused of failing to declare his own income and causing his personal tax to be too low. The tax authorities joined the charges and sought compensation for approximately the avoided taxes.

On 9 September 2009 Tampere District Court convicted him as charged of two counts of aggravated tax fraud and accounting offence. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay EUR 685,080.66 plus interest compensation, with sums already seized in the administrative proceedings deductible, and banned from business activities for six years.

On 9 October 2009 he appealed to Turku Court of Appeal, seeking to quash the judgment and dismiss the charges, relying also on ne bis in idem and relevant case-law. On 15 September 2010, after an oral hearing, the Court of Appeal largely upheld the judgment, found part of the accounting offence aggravated, and ordered EUR 20,000 more compensation. On ne bis in idem, it reasoned that for tax years 2003, 2005 and 2006 the appeal period had not elapsed when charges were brought in 2009, so no issue arose; for 2002, taxation became final on 31 December 2008 before charges, but because another kind of tax appeal remained available, ne bis in idem did not prevent examination.

On 12 October 2010 he appealed to the Supreme Court, repeating his grounds and seeking a stay. On 27 February 2012 the Supreme Court dismissed without examining the merits the part concerning tax year 2002 because the tax surcharges had become final in 2008, before the March 2009 charges, preventing examination. It otherwise upheld the lower judgment, finding no ne bis in idem issue for the other years because the appeal periods had not elapsed when charges were brought; the sentence was reduced to 2 years 10 months. On 21 August 2012 he lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking reopening based on incorrect application of law and the prohibition on self-incrimination; it was apparently refused in March 2013. On 22 August 2012 he lodged an application with the ECtHR alleging, in particular, a violation of the ne bis in idem principle.

case_name: CASE OF HRNČIĆ v. CROATIA
summary:
The application was lodged against Croatia with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 September 2016 (application no. 53563/16). The applicant is Dalibor Hrnčić, born in 1977. He was represented by Ms L. Horvat (Lidija Horvat), a lawyer practising in Zagreb. The Croatian Government were given notice of the application. The applicant complained of the inadequate conditions of his detention. The supplied record does not describe any domestic proceedings, earlier domestic decisions, or domestic remedies.

The appended factual table describes three successive periods of detention in two Croatian prisons. From 20 April 2010 to 22 March 2011, the applicant was held in Varaždin Prison for 11 months and 3 days. The table records 2.43 m² of space per inmate for that period. From 23 March 2011 to 13 April 2011, he was held in Zagreb Prison for 22 days, with 2.79 m² per inmate. From 14 April 2011 to 23 January 2012, he was again held in Varaždin Prison for 9 months and 10 days; for this later Varaždin period, the recorded space per inmate was between 2.21 and 2.62 m². The listed periods run continuously from 20 April 2010 to 23 January 2012, with a transfer to Zagreb Prison between 23 March and 13 April 2011.

The table sets out the specific grievances concerning those conditions. They include overcrowding; lack of fresh air; inadequate temperature; no or restricted access to a shower; lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air; lack or inadequate furniture; insufficient number of sleeping places; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of privacy for the toilet; and lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen. The list repeats several of these grievances across the periods, including overcrowding, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, no or restricted access to a shower, lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, lack or inadequate furniture, insufficient number of sleeping places, no or restricted access to warm water, and lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities.

In substance, the applicant alleged that the material conditions of his detention were inadequate. He relied on the recorded amount of space per inmate and on the alleged deficiencies in facilities, hygiene, ventilation, heating, bedding, sleeping arrangements, privacy for the toilet, and opportunities for physical exercise in fresh air. The record does not contain any further concrete events, domestic proceedings, or arguments by the parties. It identifies only the applicant, his representative, the respondent Government, the date of introduction, the complaint about detention conditions, and the tabulated detention periods, space per inmate, and specific grievances. No other facts beyond those in the application and appended table are supplied.

case_name: CASE OF RAZGON AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA
summary:

The applicants complained of a lack of impartiality of the tribunal because the prosecuting party was absent in administrative-offence proceedings. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applications were introduced between 10 January 2020 and 2 March 2020. The final domestic decisions identified were given between 30 July 2019 and 12 November 2019, all by the Moscow City Court. In every case, the penalty was a fine of RUB 10,000, imposed on each applicant where an application was brought by two applicants. The supplied record does not describe the underlying administrative-offence events, the first-instance decisions, or the domestic courts’ reasoning.

Each applicant was fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the Moscow City Court on 12 November 2019.

case_name: CASE OF BOKAL v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Lidija Bokal, a Slovenian national born in 1955 and living in Ljubljana, lodged application no. 34386/10 against Slovenia on 26 May 2010. The Government were represented by their Agent.

On 21 July 1997 the applicant began civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a determination of the validity of a sale contract between the defendants concerning an apartment in a building partially owned by her, and proposed that a note on dispute be entered in the Land Register. She stated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (about EUR 2,100).

On 20 August 1997 the Local Court rejected her proposal to enter the note on dispute. She appealed. On 18 February 1998, after several unsuccessful attempts to serve her appeal on the first defendant, the court posted the appeal on its notice board. On 4 March 1998 the Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed her appeal against the 20 August 1997 decision. Following a supervisory appeal to the Ministry of Justice, the court reported on 18 February 1998 that the case could not be given priority. On 21 April 1998 the applicant asked the court to schedule a hearing. On 27 March 2000 she requested priority for her claims; the court dismissed that request on 5 April 2000.

On 16 June 2000 a third-party intervener, D.S., who had in the meantime bought the apartment from the first defendant, joined the proceedings. On 1 March 2002 the intervener lodged a supervisory appeal, submitting among other things that because the proceedings were still pending she could not dispose of the apartment.

The first hearing was scheduled for 13 February 2004 but was postponed to 26 March 2004. On 18 March 2004 the applicant filed written submissions raising the claim value to SIT 1,100,000 (about EUR 4,600). At the first main hearing on 26 March 2004 the court modified the value of the claim as requested. On 11 May 2004 the applicant requested an interim order. Between 9 April and 4 June 2004 three further main hearings were held. On 4 June 2004 the court issued a judgment partially upholding her claim. It was served personally on the applicant and the second defendant, and on the first defendant and the third party by posting on the court notice board.

On 27 September 2004 the applicant appealed. On 7 December 2005 the Ljubljana Higher Court returned the file to the first-instance court, instructing it that the first defendant should be served the appeal-related documents under Section 145 of the Civil Procedure Act and that it should decide on the interim-order request. On 6 January 2006 the Local Court asked the applicant to pay court fees and supplement her interim-order proposal. On 3 March 2006 the 4 June 2004 judgment and her appeal were served on the first defendant by posting on the notice board. On 20 March 2006 the Local Court dismissed the interim-order request. The applicant appealed. On 21 June 2006 the Higher Court dismissed her appeals against the 4 June 2004 judgment and the 20 March 2006 decision.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 23 October 2008 the Supreme Court rejected it on procedural grounds. It held that the Local Court had wrongly applied the Civil Procedure Act by allowing a modification of the disputed value at a later stage, took the value indicated in the original claim, and concluded that the threshold for an appeal on points of law had not been reached. The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal. On 26 November 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed it; the decision was served on the applicant on 1 December 2009.

case_name: CASE OF MARCINKEVIČIUS v. LITHUANIA
summary:
Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, born in 1971, lives in Vilnius and is a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba. In 2015 he lodged a complaint with law-enforcement authorities alleging that Vilniaus Prekyba had, through financial deals, avoided taxes, damaged the State and unjustly enriched N.N., another founder and major shareholder. A pre-trial investigation opened in August 2015. On 19 August 2016 the prosecutor discontinued it, finding no grounds that the deals were unlawful; the senior prosecutor upheld that decision on 21 November 2016. On 23 November 2016 the applicant asked to reopen the investigation, citing new facts. On 1 December 2016 he answered written questions from a Delfi journalist for an article about his conflict with N.N. and the proceedings. On 21 December 2016 the prosecutor dismissed the reopening request and forwarded the material to the tax authorities. On 2 January 2017 a pre-trial investigation judge upheld the discontinuation; the same day Delfi published the article quoting the applicant. On 10 January 2017 the applicant sent his allegations to the tax authorities. On 17 February 2017 the Vilnius Regional Court finally upheld the discontinuation. On 1 March 2017 the senior prosecutor dismissed his complaint, and on 9 March 2017 the tax authorities opened an inquiry into N.N.’s tax compliance; it was still pending as of December 2021.

In the article, the applicant said documents showed that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba had allegedly been used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoiding Lithuanian taxes and appropriating other shareholders’ funds; that one company, T., had allegedly laundered more than EUR 20 million and hidden at least EUR 3 million in taxes; and that the main goal had been to appropriate profit without paying taxes in Lithuania. He also said: “It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.” N.N. sued, alleging false and defamatory statements of fact. He complained of three statements but not the following sentence about contacting the company, shareholders’ meetings and the prosecutor. He argued the statements were unsupported and formulated as facts, and asked for a public retraction. The applicant argued they were value judgments, based on documents submitted to authorities, not insulting, and that N.N., as a public figure, had to tolerate criticism.

On 22 December 2017 the Vilnius District Court partly allowed N.N.’s claim. It found the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments with sufficient factual basis and not insulting. It found the second sentence of the third statement (“It is obvious…”) a verifiable statement of fact, false and insulting: the applicant knew prosecutors had twice declined to confirm his allegations and had not proved damage. It ordered retraction. The applicant appealed. On 18 February 2019 the Vilnius Regional Court quashed that finding, treating the phrase in context as subjective, abstract and exaggerated opinion; it dismissed N.N.’s appeal. N.N. appealed on points of law. On 2 October 2019 the Supreme Court quashed the Regional Court decision because it had admitted new documents without allowing N.N. time to respond, and remitted the case.

In fresh proceedings, the applicant submitted additional financial reports. On 25 February 2020 the Vilnius Regional Court refused the new evidence and upheld the District Court: the sentence was affirming, lacked concrete facts and denigrated N.N. On 4 March 2020 Delfi published a retraction. The applicant’s appeals on points of law were refused by the Supreme Court on 12 March, 29 April and 27 May 2020 as raising no important legal issues. The applicant complained that the statement was a value judgment and that the retraction order violated his freedom of expression.

case_name: CASE OF E.M. AND OTHERS v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicants are E.M., a Czech national born in 1976, and her two sons, B (born 2005) and C (born 2008). E.M. moved to Norway in 2005 to live with A, a Czech national resident in Norway since 1986. Both children were born in Norway. On 20 May 2011 they were placed in emergency care because of concerns about sexual abuse and violence. The parents later lived apart; E.M. initially had weekly contact, later twice-weekly, until contact stopped at the end of August 2011 after further statements and a police investigation. E.M. filed for separation in autumn 2011.

In domestic proceedings, on 8 February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took B and C into public care and placed them in foster homes. It found serious neglect and physical abuse, did not further assess possible sexual abuse, and considered that returning them to E.M. would likely lead to serious neglect. E.M. was granted supervised contact of two hours four times a year; A was granted none. On 4 July 2012 the District Court upheld the care order but withdrew E.M.’s contact rights. It found serious care deficiencies, physical punishment, probable sexual abuse by A, and E.M.’s awareness/failure to stop it; it did not decide whether she actively participated. Contact was withdrawn due to E.M.’s conduct, the children’s stress reactions and their association of her with violence and abuse. On 4 March 2013 the High Court restored supervised contact of two hours twice a year. It found insufficient grounds to believe E.M. sexually abused the children or knew of A’s abuse, but found she failed to shield them, slapped them, caused significant fear and was jointly responsible for neglect. It relied on expert psychological assessments and noted likely long-term fostering. The Supreme Court Appeals Committee refused leave on 21 May 2013.

On 10 December 2014 E.M. applied to lift the care order. The child welfare services sought continuation, removal of E.M.’s parental responsibilities for both children, refusal of contact for her and A regarding B, and authorisation of C’s adoption. After a hearing on 15–17 September 2015, the Board decided on 24 September 2015 not to lift the care orders, to withdraw E.M.’s parental responsibilities for B and C, to refuse her contact with B, and to authorise C’s adoption. For B, it cited E.M.’s repeated media exposure of the children, including photos and texts about sexual violations, causing strain and risks through future access to information.

E.M. appealed to the District Court. After hearings on 25–27 May 2016 with 18 witnesses, a Czech Republic submission and the children’s representative, the District Court gave judgment on 30 June 2016. It found E.M.’s caring abilities had improved, but B had PTSD from complex continued neglect and needed secure care not provided by those who caused the trauma; C had less extensive needs and strong foster attachment. B did not want to return, citing painful experiences and violence; C said he did not want anything to do with his parents and wanted to stay where nobody was mean. Sensitive material, including B’s health and sexual-abuse information, was found online. The court found E.M. could not provide needed care. It upheld refusal of contact with B for special and compelling reasons: B feared being alone with E.M., showed severe physical anxiety, and on 9 March 2015 staff considered forced contact an immediate health risk. For C, despite partly positive contact reports, he showed adverse reactions including agitation, anxiety, trouble sleeping and defecating in his pants; contact was not in his best interests at that time. The District Court refused C’s adoption because it would sever biological family ties, especially with B.

E.M. appealed; A made an ancillary appeal. The High Court refused leave on 28 November 2016. On 24 January 2017 the Supreme Court Appeals Committee dismissed E.M.’s further appeal as having no prospects. E.M. lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2017 on behalf of herself and the children, complaining under Article 8 about the decisions not to lift the care order, to withdraw parental responsibilities and to refuse contact.

case_name: CASE OF PEJŘILOVÁ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, Hana Pejřilová, a Czech national born in 1983, lodged application no. 14889/19 against the Czech Republic on 12 March 2019. She married in 2012. Because the couple could not conceive naturally and her husband had a serious disease, they approached an assisted reproduction centre. On 26 June 2014 the husband’s sperm was cryopreserved; he signed a consent form for preservation for infertility treatment. The form stated further written consent was required before each thawing and that, unless clearly determined otherwise, storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death. On 15 December 2014 the applicant and her husband signed informed consent forms for IVF, thawing his sperm and ICSI; they agreed to notify the centre of relationship changes that could cause treatment to end. The husband died on 16 June 2015 before further steps; the record does not show the applicant had begun hormone treatment or had ova collected.

On 7 September 2015 the applicant asked the centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm. The centre refused, saying this was contrary to law, and suggested court proceedings for a settlement. On 26 October 2015 she sued the centre, seeking an order to perform the treatment in accordance with his wishes as shown by the consent forms. At a 4 April 2016 hearing both parties were ready to settle, but the Plzeň-City District Court did not approve the settlement because it contravened section 6 of the SHS Act, which required consent less than six months old.

On 22 July 2016 the Plzeň Regional Court upheld that decision. It said the SHS Act allowed infertility treatment only for a couple, not a single woman without a partner; the aim was to give a child an initial chance to grow up with both parents. The applicant and her husband ceased to be a couple upon his death. His later wishes could not be prejudged or replaced by a court, and his earlier consent was not a binding “previously expressed wish” because it was not in the required form. On 28 November 2016 the district court dismissed her action: she was no longer part of a couple and there was no valid informed consent from her late husband.

On 30 May 2017 the regional court upheld the dismissal. It found the request contrary to sections 6 and 8 of the SHS Act: assisted reproduction could be performed only on the application and written consent of the infertile couple, with consent less than six months old. Even the initial consent did not mean the husband would not have changed his mind, and further consent could not be replaced by a court decision. On 21 February 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on points of law. It considered family life required an actual family and a mere wish to found one was not protected; the failure to complete the procedure could interfere with private life. It referred to comparative legislation and the explanatory report. It found it in the child’s best interests to be born to a complete family with both parents at least at conception; after the man’s death the infertile couple no longer existed. The six-month consent rule protected the sperm provider and allowed revocation. It was unclear whether the husband would have wished fatherhood after death, as he had signed a form containing an explicit destruction-on-death provision. The centre was not obliged to perform the procedure. The applicant was not deprived of all opportunities to become a mother; she could conceive naturally or with another partner.

On 8 November 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal. It held the lower courts had adequately examined her arguments and reasoned their findings; the Supreme Court had considered the constitutional dimension and Court case-law; the conclusions were compliant with the Constitution; there was no European consensus. Legislation on assisted reproduction was based on moral, cultural, religious and ethical values, primarily for the legislature. A dissenting judge considered the law should only prevent a child being born against a man’s will; in his view the legislation had been misused and the courts should have determined the husband’s wishes.

The form stated further written consent was required before each thawing and that, unless clearly determined otherwise, storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death. On 15 December 2014 the applicant and her husband signed informed consent forms for IVF, thawing his sperm and ICSI; they agreed to notify the centre of relationship changes that could cause treatment to end. The husband died on 16 June 2015 before further steps; the record does not show the applicant had begun hormone treatment or had ova collected.

On 7 September 2015 the applicant asked the centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm. The centre refused, saying this was contrary to law, and suggested court proceedings for a settlement. On 26 October 2015 she sued the centre, seeking an order to perform the treatment in accordance with his wishes as shown by the consent forms. At a 4 April 2016 hearing both parties were ready to settle, but the Plzeň-City District Court did not approve the settlement because it contravened section 6 of the SHS Act, which required consent less than six months old.

On 22 July 2016 the Plzeň Regional Court upheld that decision. It said the SHS Act allowed infertility treatment only for a couple, not a single woman without a partner; the aim was to give a child an initial chance to grow up with both parents. The applicant and her husband ceased to be a couple upon his death. His later wishes could not be prejudged or replaced by a court, and his earlier consent was not a binding “previously expressed wish” because it was not in the required form. On 28 November 2016 the district court dismissed her action: she was no longer part of a couple and there was no valid informed consent from her late husband.

On 30 May 2017 the regional court upheld the dismissal. It found the request contrary to sections 6 and 8 of the SHS Act: assisted reproduction could be performed only on the application and written consent of the infertile couple, with consent less than six months old. Even the initial consent did not mean the husband would not have changed his mind, and further consent could not be replaced by a court decision. On 21 February 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on points of law. It considered family life required an actual family and a mere wish to found one was not protected; the failure to complete the procedure could interfere with private life. It referred to comparative legislation and the explanatory report. It found it in the child’s best interests to be born to a complete family with both parents at least at conception; after the man’s death the infertile couple no longer existed. The six-month consent rule protected the sperm provider and allowed revocation. It was unclear whether the husband would have wished fatherhood after death, as he had signed a form containing an explicit destruction-on-death provision. The centre was not obliged to perform the procedure. The applicant was not deprived of all opportunities to become a mother; she could conceive naturally or with another partner.

On 8 November 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal. It held the lower courts had adequately examined her arguments and reasoned their findings; the Supreme Court had considered the constitutional dimension and Court case-law; the conclusions were compliant with the Constitution; there was no European consensus. Legislation on assisted reproduction was based on moral, cultural, religious and ethical values, primarily for the legislature. A dissenting judge considered the law should only prevent a child being born against a man’s will; in his view the legislation had been misused and the courts should have determined the husband’s wishes.

case_name: CASE OF DANILCZUK v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, Robert Tadeusz Danilczuk, a Polish national born in 1965 and currently detained in Czarne Prison, Poland, brought an application against Cyprus concerning conditions at Nicosia Central Prisons.

On 14 September 2010 he was placed in detention on remand at Nicosia Central Prisons pending criminal proceedings before the Limassol District Court (case no. 25536/10). On 11 January 2011 he was convicted of offences including burglary, theft, road traffic offences and unlawful residence. On 24 January 2011 the court imposed four concurrent sentences ranging from six months to two years, running from 5 September 2010. He was released on 18 May 2012 after his sentence was suspended by presidential decree.

The applicant alleged that he had been held in overcrowded cells with only 0.5 to 1.7 sq. m of personal space. He said the cells were cold and lacked adequate light; there were no toilets in the cells; he sometimes waited two to three hours to use a toilet; and when the cells were locked he had to urinate into a bottle and defecate into a waste bag. He did not specify the exact periods.

The Government stated that he had been detained from 14 September 2010 to 18 May 2012 in three parts of the prison. From 14 September 2010 to 24 January 2011 he was in Block 5, which held remand prisoners; after conviction he was transferred to Block 2B, where he remained until 5 October 2011; and from 5 October 2011 until his release he was in Block 2A. Block 5 had up to 68 remand prisoners, 34 double cells of 6.21 sq. m, eight toilets and eight showers; it was almost certain he shared a cell, giving him 3.10 sq. m. Block 2B, then unrenovated, had 26 double cells of 9.98 sq. m, two large cells of 19.55 sq. m accommodating five to seven detainees, and a 90 sq. m dormitory for 20 to 50 inmates; daily occupancy varied from 80 to 124. Depending on placement, his personal space could have been 4.99 sq. m in a double cell, about 2.8–3.9 sq. m in a larger cell, or 1.8–4.5 sq. m in the dormitory; in spring or winter, with 94–110 inmates, it would have been 2.04–3.2 sq. m. Block 2A, renovated, had 41 double cells of 9.80 sq. m for 82 prisoners, giving 4.9 sq. m, and six toilets, six showers and three urinals. General conditions included central heating, corridor air conditioning, cell fans, insulated windows, and movement outside cells from 6 a.m. to 5/6 p.m. and within blocks until 9/10 p.m. Following the CPT’s 2012 report, the prison discontinued switching off cell bells at night; order no. 32/2008 provided for toilet access, though no records were kept of night openings; detainees could leave up to three times between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m.

The CPT’s 2012 report on its 2008 visit found severe overcrowding, prisoners lacking night toilet access, and degrading use of makeshift receptacles. Its 2014 report on a 2013 visit welcomed renovation of Block 2 but found continuing overcrowding and difficulty accessing toilets at night. The Ombudsman’s 6 September 2011 report similarly described crowded, unsuitable detention areas, insufficient hygiene facilities, and complaints that deactivated night cell bells forced detainees to use bottles and waste bags. Domestic law provided for damages for violations of detainees’ rights, and the Ombudsman served as national preventive mechanism under the Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture.

case_name: CASE OF MORTIER v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicant, Tom Mortier, a Belgian national born in 1976 living in Rotselaar, is the son of G.T., who had chronic depression for about forty years and had been treated by psychiatrist B. The respondent is Belgium. In 2011 G.T. considered euthanasia; her general practitioner Dr W. did not wish to act as main doctor and referred her to Professor D. On 29 September 2011 Prof D saw her and agreed to become her main doctor, referring her to psychiatrist Dr V. On 17 November 2011 Dr V considered the request premature and referred her to Dr V.D. On 12 January 2012 Prof D referred her to psychiatrist Dr T, who met her on 17 January. On 20 January G.T. agreed to be assisted by Dr V.D.; it was suggested she inform her children. On 31 January she emailed the applicant and her daughter about her euthanasia request and suffering; her daughter respected her wishes, while the applicant did not reply. On 7 February Prof D contacted Dr B, who saw no chance of improvement; on 10 February Dr B wrote to Dr T describing serious chronic conditions and a bleak outlook. On 14 February G.T. lodged a handwritten euthanasia request; Prof D formally became main doctor, and Dr T reported G.T. was rational, informed, under no third-party pressure, and could be assisted. On 17 February Dr V.D. examined her and on 20 February reported she could be assisted. Prof D saw her again on 22 February and 8/12 March. On 27 February she drafted a body-donation statement. On 29 February she donated EUR 2,500 to LEIF, run by Prof D, whose members included Dr T and Dr V.D. On 12 March Dr B concluded there was no point contacting her children. On 20 March P.D. became a person of trust. On 3 April a meeting set euthanasia for 19 April. On 10 April Prof D assured her that her wishes would be respected. On 19 April 2012 Prof D performed euthanasia; G.T. died at 11:15 a.m. in a public hospital in the presence of friends. The hospital informed the applicant on 20 April 2012.

On 20 June 2012 the Federal Euthanasia Board received Prof D’s registration document. On 26 June 2012 the Board, co-chaired by Prof D, found the euthanasia complied with the Euthanasia Act. Dr C later examined G.T.’s medical file on 2 August 2013 and noted the euthanasia declaration was not in it. The applicant requested a copy of the registration document from the Board on 23 October 2013 and 4 March 2014; on 19 March 2014 the Board refused, citing legal confidentiality. On 16 February 2014 he complained to the Medical Association; he says the outcome was not communicated because of confidentiality. On 4 April 2014 he lodged a criminal complaint against persons unknown. On 8 May 2017 the Crown Prosecutor discontinued for insufficient evidence. On 2 May 2019 the investigation was reopened. An expert report of 5 May 2020 concluded G.T. had intolerable, incurable mental suffering, requested euthanasia freely and constantly, the statutory waiting period was respected, and two psychiatrists were consulted; it noted the applicant learned of the death unfortunately and the file lacked the Board declaration and assessment. Prof D was interviewed by police on 16 June 2020. The Crown Prosecutor found compliance and sought closure; the applicant declined to have Prof D summoned. On 11 December 2020 the Pre-Trial Division found no grounds for prosecution and closed the investigation; no appeal was lodged. The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 13.

case_name: CASE OF KEŠELJ AND OTHERS v. MONTENEGRO
summary:
The case originated in an application against Montenegro lodged on 24 May 2011 by ten nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants were represented by Mr I. Darmanović, a lawyer practising in Podgorica. The Montenegrin Government were represented by their Agent, Ms V. Pavličić. The applicants’ complaints concerned the non-enforcement of a final court settlement concluded in their favour.

On 28 February 1996, the applicants and the debtor, JSP “Tara” Cetinje, reached a court-approved settlement before the Cetinje Municipal Court. Under the settlement, the debtor undertook to pay the applicants specified amounts in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The settlement became final on the same date. The debtor ultimately paid only part of the amounts determined in the settlement.

On 26 May 1997, the Podgorica Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 19 August 1997, the applicants submitted their respective claims based on the settlement. In the course of the insolvency proceedings, the Podgorica Commercial Court acknowledged the applicants’ claims.

On 23 December 2009, the Podgorica Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor, but continued the proceedings against the debtor’s estate. That decision was upheld by the Appellate Court on 9 April 2010. The proceedings are still pending.

On 14 October 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds.

The court settlement in question remains partly unenforced to the present day.

As to the debtor’s legal status, it appears from the case file that, at the time the court settlement was concluded and became final, the debtor was a company predominantly comprised of State-controlled capital. The Government neither contested this nor provided any evidence to the contrary.

case_name: CASE OF THEO NATIONAL CONSTRUCT S.R.L. v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
summary:
The applicant, Theo National Construct S.R.L., is a Romanian road-construction company. It alleged a “raider attack”, namely the illegal seizure of its goods with the assistance of presumedly corrupt courts and law-enforcement agencies. In 2007 it agreed with Moldovan businessman and political-party leader Mr Ș. to enter Moldova. Under a 4 April 2007 agreement, the applicant was to become a 50% partner in company Q, contributing 23 pieces of road-construction equipment worth over EUR 1 million. The remaining capital was controlled by company S., controlled by Mr Ș. (49.77%), and another company (0.23%). On 5 April 2007 company Q admitted the applicant as a 50% partner.

On 25 April 2007 the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) valued the equipment at EUR 1,031,965, based on documents and pictures. On 3 May 2007 the State Registration Chamber registered charter amendments; company Q’s statutory capital rose from MDL 236,621 to MDL 17,540,179. On 8 May 2007 the applicant imported the equipment; at customs’ request, the MCC physically examined it and confirmed the earlier valuation. In October 2007 company Q signed a MDL 393 million road-renovation contract with the State Road Administration. It took bank loans exceeding EUR 1.5 million, pledging the equipment; the applicant’s CEO also pledged his Chișinău house. By 2010 delays were generally caused by delayed State payments. In early 2010 the applicant learned that company Q’s CEO had given interest-free loans of about MDL 4.5 million to company S. without consultation, in breach of the charter. Relations deteriorated; the CEO was changed and recovery proceedings began. By early 2011 company Q had no financial difficulties.

On 25 May 2010 company S. brought administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal against the MCC, seeking annulment of the 25 April 2007 valuation. It did not name the applicant as a defendant. The court later involved the State Registration Chamber, company Q and the applicant. The applicant alleged procedural irregularities. Although a 21 December 2010 request postponed a hearing to 20 January 2011, the file contained minutes of a 22 December 2010 hearing with the plaintiff present and an impossible case number. Those minutes recorded new claims to annul the 8 May 2007 valuation and the 3 May 2007 registration, to reinstate the parties, and to enforce immediately. At the 20 January 2011 hearing—the applicant’s first and last—the applicant said no such supplement was in the file. Minutes stated the next hearing would be 2 February 2011; summons and confirmation forms allegedly showed handwritten corrections from 2 March to 2 February.

On 2 February 2011 the applicant was absent. The Chișinău Court of Appeal annulled the MCC valuation reports and the State Registration Chamber’s decision of 3 May 2007, reinstated the parties as before 3 May 2007, and excluded the applicant from company Q. Transactions after 3 May 2007 were unaffected. Immediate enforcement was ordered without stated reasons. On 3–4 February 2011 the State Registration Chamber enforced the judgment; officer A.B., later found to be the wife of the deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party, signed the decision. Company Q’s capital fell to MDL 236,662. The applicant’s action against the Chamber was dismissed. On 3 March 2011 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, complaining of late involvement, manipulated documents, unanswered arguments, wrong administrative jurisdiction and time-bar. On 20 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without addressing those arguments.

After 4 February 2011 company Q’s management changed; the recovery actions were withdrawn. The equipment continued to be used by company Q. A bank later sought possession of the pledged equipment. In 2013 the Supreme Court ordered its transfer to the bank; the CEO’s house was also taken, and in 2014 bankruptcy proceedings began against company Q.

case_name: CASE OF NICHOLAS v. CYPRUS
summary:
Mr Charalambos Nicholas, born in 1951 and living in Larnaca, is a Cypriot and British national. After his dismissal from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot, on 26 June 1998 he brought a civil action before the District Court of Nicosia for wrongful dismissal and defamation (no. 7562/98). The defendant company was represented by a law firm. On 29 December 2006 the District Court dismissed the action. On 9 February 2007 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 43/07); a bench of three judges heard the appeal. At the hearing on 11 March 2007, Mr P.G.P., managing partner of the defendant’s law firm, appeared for the defendant company and addressed the Supreme Court. Other lawyers from the same firm had previously appeared before the appeal bench for the defendant. On 21 April 2010 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal unanimously.

The applicant alleged that after the Supreme Court judgment he discovered that the son of one of the judges on the bench, Judge A.K., and the daughter of Mr P.G.P. were married and both worked at Mr P.G.P.’s law firm. His domestic lawyer had not requested the judge’s exemption because he lacked sufficient knowledge of the relevant facts at the time. The applicant had not instructed him to do so because he found out only after the appeal ended. The applicant complained of a lack of impartiality, under the objective test, concerning Judge A.K.

Under the code of judicial practice adopted on 17 March 1988 and amended on 21 July 1989, 18 September 2003, 30 November 2006 and 4 October 2011, the version applicable when the applicant’s case was heard—after the 30 November 2006 amendment—provided that a judge did not sit alone or on a bench at any level in cases in which lawyers appearing before him or her were close relatives. Close relatives were parents, spouses, children, children’s spouses, siblings, siblings’ children and siblings’ spouses. The practice did not apply to minor matters. case_name: CASE OF KHANI KABBARA v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, Hani Abdul Khani Kabbara, a Canadian national born in 1984 and living in Canada, lodged an application against Cyprus on 29 March 2012. He alleged ill-treatment by police officers during detention at Limassol central police station and the absence of an effective investigation into his complaint.

On 27 February 2011, police were informed of illegal ATM withdrawals with a fake credit card in Limassol. The applicant alleged that, while in front of the ATM, he was attacked from behind by a police officer, arrested without a warrant, and taken to the police station, where he was detained for six hours with his hands handcuffed behind his back. He said officers tortured him to confess to theft using a forged credit card, repeatedly beat him with a wooden stick and a metal chair, punched and kicked him, broke a tooth, threatened to kill him, refused him asthma medicine and hospital care until his lawyer, C.H., intervened. He was taken to hospital around 3.30 p.m. He alleged that police told the doctor he had fallen, that no painkillers were given until the Canadian Consul visited, and that the doctor gave no proper explanation.

The Government’s account, based on investigation files, was that Special Constable G.S., in uniform, approached the applicant at the ATM, identified himself as police, and asked for identification. The applicant allegedly struck him and fled; during the chase he fell and hit his head. A struggle followed. He was arrested for assaulting a police officer and resisting lawful arrest. He was taken to the police station around 9.30 a.m., searched, and handed to the Economic Crime Investigations Office. An interview took place between 1 p.m. and 1.30 p.m. with an interpreter. At about 1.35 p.m., a body search recorded abrasions on his left forehead and left shoulder blade. His lawyer visited from 3.05 p.m. to 3.30 p.m. and complained that the applicant had been ill-treated. He was taken to Limassol General Hospital around 3.50 p.m. A District Court arrest warrant was issued at 3.30 p.m. He was discharged at 11.20 p.m. On 28 February and 8 March 2011, the District Court ordered and extended his detention on remand; on 16 March 2011, it ordered detention pending trial.

Medical examinations at Limassol General Hospital recorded a cephalohaematoma, abrasions, nasal oedema, a bruised lip, a broken upper incisor, chest bruising, wrist abrasions/oedema, knee abrasions and spinal sensitivity. CT scans showed no fractures. A private practitioner, Dr S.J., examined the applicant on 7 March 2011 and noted restricted movement, cervical tension, a 10 x 5 cm chest bruise and loss of half an upper incisor. G.S. was also examined and diagnosed with lumbar strain, and was given nine days’ sick leave.

On 2 March 2011, police appointed Chief Inspector M.M. to conduct an administrative investigation. M.M.’s report of 26 April 2011 found the ill-treatment allegations unproven and recommended closing the case. In July 2011, the Attorney General referred the complaint to the Independent Authority for the Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police. Investigator A.S. reported on 10 October 2011, singling out four officers as suspects. He found the applicant’s testimony unconvincing and concluded that no criminal or disciplinary charges were justified. The IAIACAP president adopted the findings on 16 November 2011, although he rejected evidence that the applicant had no external injuries. On 13 February 2012, the Attorney General concluded that some force had been used but that it was necessary and proportionate to prevent the applicant from fleeing, and closed the file.

In separate criminal proceedings, the applicant was charged with 439 offences, later reduced to theft, assault occasioning actual bodily harm to G.S., and resisting lawful arrest. On 14 September 2012, the District Court convicted him on all counts; on 19 September 2012, it imposed concurrent sentences. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 19 February 2013. He was then deported and placed on a stop list.

On 9 April 2013, after gaps and inconsistencies were identified, the Attorney General appointed two new investigators. They treated nine officers as suspects, took statements from forty-nine people, including the Canadian Consul, and gathered CCTV, photographs, police diaries and court records. The Canadian Consul’s statement of 22 April 2013 described the applicant at the hospital as being in a wheelchair and on a drip.

case_name: CASE OF LUNEV v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Andrey Lunev, a Ukrainian national, lodged an application against Ukraine on 17 January 2013. He alleged inadequate medical assistance in detention, ill-treatment intended to discourage him from applying to the European Court, and failure to investigate that ill-treatment.

**Medical assistance.** In January 2012 he was arrested for suspected drug trafficking and on 30 January placed in Starobilsk SIZO. On arrival he was diagnosed with HIV stage 3, chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy/neuropathy from drug use, and tuberculosis residual changes. The Government said he refused a CD4+ count and a blood test in February 2012 and sought no medical help until 8 January 2013, although records show a September 2012 tuberculosis examination and X-ray and November 2012 bronchitis and kidney pain in another facility. On 8 January 2013 he was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis and treated. On 9 January he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked a court to expedite proceedings or release him for urgent treatment. On 10 January the court kept him in detention but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. He was hospitalised from 9 to 11 January with acute serose meningoencephalitis and was soporose; on 11 January he returned to the SIZO medical unit until 15 February and was also held at least once in Alchevsk ITT. On 17 January he requested hospital placement, citing need for psychiatric examination for ART, correct tuberculosis staging, epilepsy treatment and adequate care. At the end of January his lawyer received a call from an unknown man posing as a prosecutor’s employee, asking whether she represented the applicant and whether he had applied to the European Court; she confirmed. On 4 February the medical unit reported HIV since 2010, chronic bronchitis and toxic encephalopathy; his CD4+ count had been 374 in October 2010 and he had refused treatment. On 19 February a domestic court sentenced him to six and a half years for drug trafficking. On 26 February his CD4+ count was 119. On 7 March the Government said hospitalisation was unnecessary. On 12 March ART was recommended; on 14 March admission to Lugansk Temporary Detention Centre No. 17 Hospital was approved. He was hospitalised from 20 to 25 March and later from 29 March to 5 April and 12 April to 12 May; ART was prescribed on 16 April. On 24 May the Lugansk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction and remitted the case. On 19 June the Bryankovskyy Town Court released him under house arrest, noting he needed treatment unavailable in detention.

**Ill-treatment and investigation.** On 25 January 2013 he was placed in Alchevsk ITT. On 30 January, after acute liver pain, an ambulance was called and he was taken to hospital, returning about 4 p.m. He alleged that at about 5.25 p.m. two policemen from the regional police office beat him and told him to write that the SIZO provided adequate treatment; one hit his liver six or seven times, the other his kidneys four times, after which he wrote the statement. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court; he was diagnosed with possible blunt abdominal trauma, but a surgeon found no acute surgical pathology. He and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor, alleging pressure to withdraw his medical complaint and confess. On 14 February a forensic expert found no injuries. On 25 February the Alchevsk Town Prosecutor terminated proceedings for lack of evidence. On 26 March the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the investigation not thorough and cellmates not questioned. On 24 April an ambulance station reported the blunt abdominal trauma diagnosis and beating complaint. On 25 April proceedings were again terminated. Cellmate K. said the applicant was absent 40–60 minutes and returned claiming two unknown policemen beat him to force him to refuse treatment, with a red cheek and swollen liver. Officer So. denied involvement; surveillance was not working from 26 January to 4 February. On 3 June the prosecutor quashed the 25 April decision as premature and unsubstantiated. On 27 June proceedings were terminated again. On 4 November the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the lawyer’s complaint inadequately investigated and no explanation why a confrontation with officer So. was impossible.

case_name: CASE OF FILOZOFENKO v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938 who lives in the Odessa Region. She holds the special status of a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006 (“the 2006 Act”). A “child of war” is defined there as a person who on 2 September 1945 was no more than 18 years of age. Under section 6 of the 2006 Act, the applicant was entitled to a special supplement to her pension amounting to 30% of the minimum pension. She complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the State’s failure to pay that supplement. The application (no. 72954/11) against Ukraine was lodged on 18 November 2011.

On 11 December 2008 the applicant lodged a claim with the domestic courts against the State Pension Fund. She asked the courts to recalculate her pension in accordance with section 6 of the 2006 Act for 2006–2008 and to pay her the outstanding debt.

On 10 June 2009 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the claim. It found that, in 2006, section 6 of the 2006 Act had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Amendments to the latter Act, which entered into force on 1 April 2006, had empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to set up a mechanism for a pension increase. However, no such mechanism had been set up in 2006, so the applicant’s claims relating to 2006 were rejected. As to 2007 and 2008, the court noted that section 6 had been suspended and modified, respectively, by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. On 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008, however, the Constitutional Court had found that suspension and modification unconstitutional. The court therefore held that the State Pension Fund should recalculate the applicant’s pension only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010 the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the lower court’s findings as regards the applicant’s 2006 claims. It also upheld her right to a pension increase for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008. However, it held that because she had missed a one-year statutory period for lodging a claim, the 2007 claim could be allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007. On 18 May 2011 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the appellate judgment.

case_name: CASE OF STANDARD VERLAGS GMBH v. AUSTRIA (No. 3)
summary:
Standard Verlags GmbH, a Vienna-based limited liability company and owner of the daily newspaper Der Standard, lodged application no. 34702/07 against Austria on 3 August 2007, alleging a violation of the right to freedom of expression. In its issue of 4 April 2006, in the economics section, Der Standard published an article entitled “Haider’s Hypo now also facing criminal investigation”. The article concerned losses at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. It reported that the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had initiated an investigation into suspected embezzlement by Hypo senior managers, partly in light of a Financial Market Authority audit. It mentioned criticisms by Jörg Haider and Martin Strutz. It also named Christian Rauscher, described as the son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, as the person whom Wolfgang Kulterer and Jörg Haider had blamed for speculative losses of 328 million euros. The article stated that Rauscher had headed the bank’s treasury department in 2004 together with Andreas Zois, that he had not been dismissed but demoted and transferred, and that he had been relieved of his duties only after the losses became known.

On 16 June 2006 Rauscher brought proceedings against the applicant company under section 7a of the Media Act, seeking disclosure of his identity in breach of that provision. He submitted that he was not a public figure and that his position at the bank had not justified naming him. He asserted that he had acted in accordance with instructions and under supervision when authorising the transactions, and that publication of his name had harmed his professional advancement and had not been justified by public interest. The applicant company replied that the article had not portrayed Rauscher as responsible but rather as a “scapegoat”. It argued that the public interest in disclosing his name outweighed his private interests because he had held a leading position at the bank and because of his father’s political role. It also said the reporting had been neutral.

By judgment of 18 July 2006, the Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed Rauscher’s action. It found that the article contained information that Rauscher was suspected of a criminal offence and that naming him could damage his professional advancement. It found that he had been head of the treasury department from 1996 to 2006, that he had been responsible for authorising or refusing foreign currency transactions, and that he had been answerable only to the bank’s executive board. It found that 45% of the bank was owned by the Land of Carinthia, that losses of 288 to 328 million euros had been incurred in 2004, and that Rauscher’s father had been a regional government member responsible for finance until 1996 and had sat on the bank’s supervisory board while Rauscher headed the treasury. The Regional Court accepted that Rauscher was not a public figure and that his father’s position did not justify naming him. However, it found a connection between his professional activity and public life because the Land, and thus taxpayers, bore a considerable share of the losses, and because Rauscher had led the department that caused them. It held that the public had an overriding interest in identifying those responsible, so Der Standard had been entitled to name him.

On 14 February 2007, the Vienna Court of Appeal granted Rauscher’s appeal and ordered the applicant company to pay EUR 5,000 compensation and reimburse his procedural costs. It agreed that Rauscher had been presented as suspected of embezzling a large sum. It held that the Regional Court had wrongly weighed the interests. It reasoned that the public interest had to be assessed objectively and with reference to the person’s identity; mere interest in reporting a crime was insufficient. It applied a strict standard, noting that the public generally has no legal right to know the identity of persons concerned. At the time of publication, the investigation was at an early stage; no proceedings had been brought against Rauscher, and the article concerned rumours of accusations by two senior bank officials. case_name: CASE OF LEVINTA v. MOLDOVA (No. 2)
summary:
The applicants, Pavel and Vitalie Levinţa, Moldovan nationals, were arrested in Russia in October 2000 and extradited to Moldova. They were allegedly ill-treated to compel self-incriminatory statements and convicted by Moldovan courts relying in part on those confessions. In an earlier case (Levinţa v. Moldova, no. 17332/03, 16 December 2008), the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3 and 6. On 3 April 2009 the applicants lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions. On 8 September 2009 they applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging in particular detention without legal basis and without reasons, inability to present their case fully, and failure to decide on detention pending trial within a reasonable time.

On 8 February 2010 the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice accepted the extraordinary appeal, quashed all previous judgments, ordered re-hearing and verification of the ill-treatment complaint, and stated that the applicants were to continue to be detained, with the trial court to decide the preventive measure. On 10 February their lawyer complained to the Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General, seeking immediate release because no valid detention order existed. The Prosecutor General’s Office referred to the 8 February judgment; the Ministry of Justice said it had not been informed of any judgment concerning the applicants after 16 April 2002.

On 15 March 2010 the Supreme Court sent the case to the Chişinău Court of Appeal. On 13 April the applicants’ lawyer asked that court for immediate release, while the prosecution requested 30 days’ detention pending trial; the applicants said no supporting evidence was submitted. After hearings were postponed on 14 and 16 April, on 19 April the Court of Appeal found continued detention necessary to ensure proper conduct, citing reasonable grounds to suspect exceptionally serious crimes and risks of absconding or obstruction. It rejected release and ordered 30 days’ detention from 2 p.m. on 14 April, then relinquished jurisdiction to the Supreme Court.

On 22 April the lawyer appealed, arguing absence of a valid court decision or warrant, breach of presumption of innocence, detention beyond the statutory 12-month maximum, lack of evidence of risk, and procedural delay. On 13 May the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

Later on 13 May, the lawyer was allegedly called at short notice about a 4 p.m. Court of Appeal hearing on a prosecution request, submitted 7 May, to extend detention by 60 days. He was in Anenii Noi on another case. The applicants were absent; a State-appointed lawyer represented them and objected. The court granted the extension for reasons similar to 19 April. A dissenting judge noted the request reached the Supreme Court on 11 May, criticised the lack of specific risk evidence and absence of the chosen lawyer, and concluded defence rights were breached.

On appeal, the lawyer repeated his arguments and added that the applicants had been held two hours after the previous order expired and had not agreed to the State-appointed lawyer. On 3 June 2010 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal, finding no breach because the applicants refused to appear and the lawyer had been informed; it also found the earlier order ran until 14 May. It held post-quashing detention could be exceptional and based on a prosecution request, citing risks of obstruction or absconding, prior absconding, international wanted status, extradition, and lack of social ties, income or employment. Later, release requests were made monthly and rejected; on 28 December 2010 detention was replaced by house arrest, and on 4 February 2011 by an undertaking not to leave the country during investigation.

case_name: CASE OF SOLOMAKHIN v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Mr Sergey Dmitriyevich Solomakhin, was a Ukrainian national born in 1964 who lived in Donetsk. He died on 13 September 2010; his mother, Mrs Vera Petrovna Solomakhina, later expressed the wish to pursue the application. The applicant was represented by Ms I. Gavrilenko, and the Ukrainian Government by Mr Y. Zaytsev. On 22 July 2003 the applicant lodged an application alleging, in particular, that the court proceedings in his case were excessively lengthy and that his health had suffered as a result of medical malpractice.

On 23 November 1998 the applicant sought medical assistance from Donetsk City Hospital No. 16, where he was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease and prescribed out-patient treatment. On 27 November 1998 he was tested for reaction to a diphtheria vaccination; the test showed no susceptibility to diphtheria antigens. On 28 November 1998 he was vaccinated against diphtheria. According to the applicant, the vaccination was contraindicated for him. On 30 November 1998 a doctor indicated that his health had improved and diagnosed tracheobronchitis, confirmed at visits on 3, 4 and 7 December 1998. From 28 December 1998 the applicant spent more than half a year in various medical institutions receiving treatment for chronic diseases, including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis and colitis.

On 4 February 1999 the Chief Doctor of the Hospital reprimanded doctor Ya. and nurse Sh. for vaccinating the applicant although he had consistently objected and was being treated for an acute respiratory infection. The Chief Doctor considered that they had violated vaccination rules and ordered them to pass a test on those rules.

On 26 April 1999 the applicant instituted proceedings in the Budyonnovskiy District Court in Donetsk against the local department of public health and the Hospital, seeking compensation for damage to his health. He alleged that the 28 November 1998 vaccination had been conducted while he was ill and had caused a number of chronic diseases. He also complained that the vaccine had been of poor quality, uncertified, expired and stored in inappropriate conditions, and that doctors had tried to falsify medical records and conceal negative effects.

Between 30 May and 30 June 2000, 17 July 2000, 29 January 2001, 2 and 30 January 2002, 4 March 2002 and 17 February 2003, medical expert examinations were conducted. On 2 June 2003 the court found against the applicant. Referring to the expert conclusions, it established that his diseases had no causal link to the vaccination. It noted that he had not had an allergic reaction or other signs normally appearing within several days; the only disease possibly associated with vaccination was urticaria, suffered more than eight months later, which could not have a causal link. The court found that he had no acute symptoms upon vaccination and that no medical rules had been violated. It stated that the epidemic situation in the Donetsk region had called for diphtheria vaccination. No physical force had been applied, and, as an adult of sound mind, he could have refused, as he had done before. Although the vaccination was not performed in the vaccination room, it was conducted by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s office, in the doctor’s presence, after prior verification of his reaction, and caused no negative side-effects. His allegations about vaccine quality were speculative and unconfirmed. The court observed that none of his diseases had a causal link to the vaccination and that his hospital time was due to his attempts to obtain disabled status. His allegations about falsification of medical records were rejected as unsubstantiated.

On 19 March 2008 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and on 22 August 2008 the Supreme Court upheld the judgment. The applicant died of a heart attack on 13 September 2010. By letter of 26 September 2011 his mother informed the Court of her wish to pursue the application. Domestic law included the 1994 Health Care and Control of Diseases Act, under which preventive vaccinations against tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and measles were compulsory in Ukraine, with procedures set by the Ministry of Health. Guidelines approved on 25 January 1996 addressed vaccination organisation, contraindications, side-effects and notification. Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly Recommendation 1317 (1997) concerned vaccination in Europe and the diphtheria epidemic.
