case_name: CASE OF SETA v. GREECE AND GERMANY
summary:
Application no. 30287/09 was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 April 2009 by Mr Selim Seta, a Kosovar national born in 1942 who lives in Besian. The application was lodged against the Hellenic Republic. The Greek Government were represented by their Agent, Mr F. P. Georgakopoulos, President of the Legal Council of the State. On 5 July 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. Although the case is named Seta v. Greece and Germany, the supplied factual record describes the application as having been brought against the Hellenic Republic; apart from the applicant’s allegation involving a German national and his prior residence in Germany, no factual events concerning Germany are set out.

The facts concern events beginning on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested by the Greek authorities at the Greek-Albanian borders. He was charged with drug trafficking after 25 kg of heroin was found in the car he was driving. On the same day, the Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor prosecuted him for illegal drug trafficking and ordered his detention on remand by order no. 25/2002. The applicant alleges that his arrest was a set-up by a German national with whom he had had disagreements in Germany, where the applicant had allegedly lived for an unspecified period, and that the drugs were placed in the car without his knowledge.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, on 20 May 2003 the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twenty years’ imprisonment by judgment no. 81/2003. On an unspecified date the applicant lodged an appeal. On 5 June 2007 the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment by judgment no. 58/2007. On 8 September 2007 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation challenging that decision. According to the record, in the grounds of appeal the applicant did not raise any complaint regarding interpretation service at the moment he was arrested or afterwards during the proceedings. The hearing before the Court of Cassation was originally set for 12 March 2008 but was adjourned to 19 November 2008. As it appears from the case file, those proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation.

The supplied record contains no further concrete events, dates, domestic decisions, or allegations. It does not describe any other domestic proceedings, evidence, or steps taken by the applicant beyond those set out above. The factual account is therefore limited to the applicant’s arrest, prosecution, conviction, appeal, cassation proceedings, and his allegation about how the drugs came to be in the car.

case_name: CASE OF ALIŠIĆ AND OTHERS v. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA, CROATIA, SERBIA, SLOVENIA AND "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
The application was lodged on 30 July 2005 by three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak and Sakib Šahdanović, against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The first applicant is also a German citizen; all live in Germany. Before the dissolution of the SFRY, Ališić and Sadžak deposited foreign currency with Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, and Šahdanović with the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30 and DEM 63,880.44; Šahdanović also had USD 73 and 4 Austrian schillings. They alleged that they could not withdraw their “old” foreign-currency savings from those accounts.

In the SFRY, banks were organised as basic and associated banks. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was a basic bank; in 1978 it and others founded Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. Foreign-currency deposits were State-guaranteed and largely “redeposited” with the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo shipped foreign currency to the National Bank of Slovenia; between 1984 and 1991 DEM 244,665,082 was shipped to Ljubljana and DEM 41,469,528 returned. In 1990, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which took over its rights, assets and liabilities. Investbanka became independent with headquarters in Serbia and branches in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Tuzla. From 1990/91, SFRY measures restricted withdrawals of foreign-currency savings, at times to DEM 500 at a time and DEM 1,000 per month.

After the SFRY dissolved in 1991/92, each successor State adopted measures. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State and Entities addressed “old” savings. The FBH assumed liability in 1997, but later legislation expressly excluded savings in branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. A 2006 State law excluded those branches but required the State to help clients recover from Slovenia and Serbia. Domestic Constitutional Court decisions, including AP 164/04 of 1 April 2006, AP 423/07 of 14 October 2008 and AP 14/08 of 21 December 2010, found neither Bosnia and Herzegovina nor its Entities liable and ordered help in recovering from Slovenia and Serbia. The Sarajevo branch had about DEM 250 million in savings at 31 December 1991. A domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was set up in 1993 and purported to assume liability; in November 2004 the Sarajevo Municipal Court held it was not the successor and deleted the 1993 register entry. Bankruptcy proceedings against it began in 2010 and remained pending. The Tuzla branch of Investbanka closed on 1 June 1992. A Serbian court made a bankruptcy order against Investbanka in 2002; bankruptcy remained pending, and in 2011 Serbia began a criminal investigation into transfer of the Tuzla archives in 2008.

Other States took measures. Croatia stated it repaid old savings in domestic banks and foreign branches, and repaid citizens’ savings transferred from Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana’s Zagreb branch; some remaining clients obtained payment from forced sale of branch assets in Croatia, while others sued in Croatian or Slovenian courts. Serbia in 1998 and 2002 agreed to repay certain domestic-bank savings, but left successor-State citizens’ and branch savings frozen pending succession; after Investbanka’s 2002 bankruptcy, 322 clients of Bosnian branches unsuccessfully sought payment, and 20 sued without success. Slovenia assumed the SFRY guarantee in 1991; after restructuring, old Ljubljanska Banka retained liability for branches in other successor States. In 1997 proceedings concerning those branches were stayed pending succession negotiations; in December 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the stay unconstitutional. Thereafter Ljubljana District Court judgments ordered the old bank to pay savings in the Sarajevo and Zagreb branches; one Sarajevo-branch judgment became final on 16 November 2010. Claims against Slovenia were rejected in three final cases. The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia repaid old savings in domestic banks and local branches of foreign banks regardless of citizenship. The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues, in force from 2 June 2004, provided for negotiations under BIS auspices on SFRY guarantees of hard-currency savings; after failed rounds, the BIS ended its role in 2002.

case_name: CASE OF VAN COLLE v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The applicants, Mr and Mrs Van Colle, are British nationals. Their son, Giles Van Colle, an optometrist born in 1975, was murdered on 22 November 2000 by Daniel Brougham. Brougham had worked for Giles under the alias Lee Jordan, concealing a criminal record. After a dispute over equipment and unpaid repairs, Brougham left in December 1999.

In February 2000 police arrested Brougham on suspicion of theft from “Southern Counties” and found optical equipment; Giles later identified some as his. On 10 August he offered Mr P £650 for Alpha Optical material. On 13 October he telephoned Mr P and offered a bribe, which Mr P reported to DC Ridley. On the same day Brougham telephoned Giles and threatened that he knew where Giles lived, where his businesses were and where his parents lived, and that if Giles did not drop the charges he would be in danger. Giles reported this to DC Ridley between 16 and 18 October. On 19 October DC Ridley took statements from Giles and Mr P and sent them to the CPS.

On 28 and 29 October fires occurred at Mr P’s wife’s car and at Mr P’s business premises. They were initially considered possibly accidental; later, during the murder investigation, experts found they had been started deliberately. On 5 November DC Ridley was seconded to an unconnected murder investigation. On 9 November the CPS served additional evidence including the 19 October statements. That day Brougham telephoned Giles again, using aggressive language and telling him to get Alpha Optical to drop the charges. Giles left a message for DC Ridley and later provided a written account sent on 20 November. On 22 November DC Ridley arranged to take a statement the next day and intended to arrest Brougham for witness intimidation. That evening Brougham shot Giles dead. Brougham was convicted of murder in March 2002.

In domestic disciplinary proceedings, on 12 June 2003 a Police Disciplinary Panel found DC Ridley guilty of failing to perform his duties conscientiously and diligently regarding the intimidation of Giles and Mr P. It found an escalating situation of intimidation and that DC Ridley failed thoroughly to investigate, analyse links between events, or consider arrest. He was fined five days’ pay.

The applicants, the first as administrator of Giles’s estate, brought a claim against the Chief Constable of Hertfordshire under the Human Rights Act 1998, seeking damages for breaches of Articles 2 and 8. The Chief Constable accepted the Panel’s findings and that DC Ridley gave inadequate consideration to responses to the threats, but argued that the criticisms were made with hindsight, that Brougham’s drastic act could not reasonably have been predicted, and that the errors were not sufficiently exceptional to be unlawful.

On 10 March 2006 the High Court found violations of Articles 2 and 8 and awarded damages. On 24 April 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed the Chief Constable’s appeal, upholding findings that DC Ridley should have recognised a real and immediate risk and taken protective steps. On 30 July 2008 the House of Lords allowed the Chief Constable’s appeal, holding that the domestic courts had misdirected themselves and that the relevant risk test had not been met.

The applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 January 2009, complaining under Articles 2 and 8 that the police failed to protect their son’s life from Brougham, a criminal accused in proceedings in which Giles was a witness.

case_name: CASE OF ABDI v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The applicant, Mustafa Abdi, a Somali national, arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. His claim was refused, but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to make a deportation order; on 27 May 2002 detention was authorised. He appealed and made a fresh asylum claim; appeal rights were exhausted on 4 December 2003. He was assessed as high risk of sexual offending and medium risk of general offending. His release became automatic on 3 September 2003, but he remained detained. On 5 April 2004 a deportation order including detention authority was issued and served on 19 April 2004.

He claimed Isaaq clan membership from Somaliland, with parents born in Hargeisa, although he was born in Mogadishu. Authorities initially sought removal to Somaliland but required clan-history bio-data; he did not cooperate. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew; only voluntary returns with a disclaimer were possible. In November 2004 he refused to sign a disclaimer. Bail was refused in December 2004; further asylum representations in March 2005 were refused as a fresh claim in September 2005; bail was again refused on 11 October 2005, when an immigration judge was wrongly told enforced removal would soon be possible. In July 2006 an agreement with African Express Airlines made enforced removals possible; the first took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 he obtained permission to seek judicial review of his detention, but interim release was refused. Removal directions for 29 November 2006 were cancelled pending judicial review.

In domestic proceedings, the Administrative Court on 7 December 2006 applied the Hardial Singh principles. It held detention lawful up to August 2004; unlawful from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 because of length, impossibility of removal, and misleading statements; and lawful after 30 June 2006 because immediate removal was again possible. Both sides appealed. On 30 July 2007 the Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal and dismissed the applicant’s, holding the disputed period lawful because he could have returned voluntarily and posed a high reoffending risk. Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 13 December 2007.

In the separate deportation-order challenge, revocation was refused on 1 February 2007. An Immigration Judge allowed his appeal; the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal ordered reconsideration on 10 May 2007. After a reconsideration hearing on 26 February 2008, a rehearing was ordered. On 18 December 2008 the Tribunal reheard the case and dismissed the appeal by determination of 1 July 2009. The Court of Appeal allowed his appeal on 23 April 2010, but the Supreme Court allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal on 24 November 2010. Removal directions were issued on 6 December 2010 for 8 December 2010; on 7 December 2010 an interim measure prevented removal. He remained in immigration detention. He had been released on bail after 13 April 2007 but was re-detained on 3 April 2008 after breaching bail. The application concerns only the first period of detention, ending shortly after 13 April 2007.

Monthly reviews occurred during 3 September 2003–13 April 2007. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced an unpublished policy presuming detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending deportation; it was not disclosed until mid-2008 or published until September 2008, while published policy stated a presumption of release.

case_name: CASE OF GRUPA ZASTAVA VOZILA, A.D. v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D., is a Serbian company. In 1996 it concluded a contract with PS ZA AVTO p.o. before a notary concerning joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO instituted proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of that contract and the notarial protocol. The applicant company was the defendant in those domestic proceedings.

On 14 July 1998, the District Court ordered the claim to be served on the applicant company in the Republic of Serbia with the assistance of the Ministry of Justice through diplomatic channels. On 29 October 1998 the court made an inquiry with the Ministry about service. On 12 November 1998 the Ministry informed the court that it was still waiting for a reply from the Serbian authorities. On 30 May 2000, ZASTAVA AVTO d.o.o. requested third-party intervention. On 6 June 2000 the court made another inquiry with the Ministry concerning service. On 29 June 2000 the applicant company’s representative sent an authority form and a request for joinder with another case. On 17 May 2001 the applicant company requested that a hearing be set. The first hearing, scheduled for 11 October 2001, was postponed. On 12 October 2001 the State Attorney’s Office submitted a request for third-party intervention. On 10 June 2002 the court allowed both third parties to participate in the proceedings.

On 12 September 2002 the applicant company lodged a counterclaim. Because of the counterclaim, the court postponed the hearing set for 19 September 2002. On 3 February 2003 the court held a settlement hearing, but the parties did not reach a settlement. On 14 April 2003 the court held the first hearing. On 23 April 2003 the applicant company requested an extension of the deadline for submitting documents; the deadline was extended by one month. On 10 November 2003 the court appointed a financial expert. On 23 February 2004 the court granted the expert’s request for an extension of the deadline for submitting the report. On 3 May 2004 the expert submitted the report. On 6 October 2004 the court held a hearing.

On 13 December 2004 the District Court rendered judgment in favour of the applicant company; the notarial protocol and the contract remained in force. The plaintiff appealed. On 7 November 2006 the Ljubljana Higher Court delivered judgment amending the first-instance judgment and ruling against the applicant company. The applicant company lodged an appeal on points of law. On 12 May 2008 the Supreme Court delivered judgment upholding the appeal court’s decision. The applicant company lodged a constitutional appeal. On 13 May 2010 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

The applicant company lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 November 2010. It was represented by Ms M. Kranjčevič, a lawyer practising in Ljubljana. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. The Serbian Government indicated that they did not intend to take part in the proceedings.

case_name: CASE OF KRISTIANSEN AND TYVIK AS v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicants are Arne Kristiansen (born 1931), a Norwegian national, and Tyvik A/S, a Norwegian limited liability company. On 30 November 1990 Kristiansen filed patent application no. 19905214 with NIPO, the Norwegian Industrial Property Office, for a method of propulsion of aircraft and sea vessels.

On 21 March 1991 NIPO preliminarily found the application not patentable because it lacked a concrete solution and questioned whether the invention had any effect. It required practical tests at an independent research institute. Kristiansen disputed the need, citing costs, but said prototypes were under construction. Between 1992 and 1994 there was correspondence about confidentiality; in 1993 the Military Supreme Command said secrecy was not needed. On 9 May 1994 Kristiansen supplied further information. On 24 February 1995 NIPO repeated its test request. On 23 May 1995 he submitted theoretical views and a 1965 report, arguing tests were superfluous. On 27 November 1996 he complained of delay; NIPO apologised on 9 December 1996 and prioritised the case. On 16 December 1996 NIPO maintained the test requirement; exchanges followed, including protests about NIPO’s technical competence and two academic statements in 1997. On 5 May 1999 NIPO maintained its position and set a 5 November 1999 deadline. Kristiansen’s registered letter of 26 October 1999, received 11 November 1999, complained again but made no new arguments. NIPO discontinued examination under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. On 18 February 2000 it maintained shelving because the substantive requirements had not been met.

On 8 March 2001 Kristiansen petitioned the Parliamentary Ombudsman. Following an inquiry, on 30 August 2001 NIPO annulled the discontinuation and allowed until 28 February 2002 to respond to its 5 May 1999 letter. He replied on 24 September 2001 without new arguments. On 2 October 2001 NIPO refused the application because the alleged technical effect was not made probable. On 23 January 2002 the Ombudsman found no grounds to continue.

On 27 November 2001 Kristiansen appealed to the Board of Appeals. Its first meeting was on 13 September 2004; the Board indicated a new claim formulation might lead to a patent, but only for sea vessels, communicated on 29 September 2004. A meeting followed on 2 February 2005. On 14 February 2005 NIPO learned that 50% ownership had been transferred to Tyvik AS. On 14 November 2005 the Board concluded the invention had technical effect but did not decide other patent requirements; the applicants had been advised how to amend the claims but were unwilling. The Board set aside NIPO’s decision and remitted the case.

On 29 November 2005 NIPO found the subject-matter not novel. On 13 March 2006 the applicants complained to the Ombudsman, alleging prejudice by a NIPO officer; the Ombudsman said it could not decide until processing ended but assumed due diligence. Exchanges continued between 31 May and 11 June 2006; NIPO suggested changes and the applicants disagreed. On 20 June 2007 NIPO formally refused the application for lack of novelty. On 20 August 2007 the applicants appealed. On 29 November 2007 the Board, having examined the case on 12 November 2007, found conditions unmet for aircraft but possible for limited sea vessels; it warned refusal might be confirmed if claims were not redefined, and discussed splitting the aircraft and sea-vessel parts, with the aircraft part likely rejected. The applicants commented on 28 January 2008 and altered the claims. On 22 September 2008 the Board confirmed refusal on different reasoning: it found the results industrially achievable and no novelty for aviation, but unlike NIPO found the application could have succeeded for limited sea transport; applicants had been advised to exclude aviation but were unwilling. They apparently did not challenge that decision before the Norwegian courts.

The applicants later said 2003 applications based on no. 19905214 were granted in the United States, Russia, China, Singapore and through the EPO. The Government said Espacenet showed no priority claimed from no. 19905214; the EPO patent claimed priority from separate no. 20015844, based on knowledge from no. 19905214, with additional features. Under the Patents Act 1967, section 1 requires industrial application and technical effect; section 2 requires novelty; section 15 allows shelving; section 27 sets appeal and court time limits; section 40 sets a twenty-year term, so a granted patent would have expired on 30 November 2010.

case_name: CASE OF JEZNIK v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Ms Marija Jeznik, is a Slovenian national born in 1940 who lives in Vuzenica. The respondent is the Republic of Slovenia. The case originated in an application against Slovenia lodged on 1 July 2008. The applicant was represented by Odvetniška Družba Marčič in Ostali, O.P., D.N.O., a law firm from Slovenj Gradec. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. On 27 April 2012 the application was communicated to the Government and, under Protocol No. 14, assigned to a committee of three judges.

In 1994 the applicant began investing in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d. through the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. At the end of 1994 such trading was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but the applicant continued the activity until 1996. In 1996 she instituted enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor D.O.O. before the Maribor District Court. She sought payment of lost investments from Kompas Maribor for not informing her of the legislative amendments and for continuing with the trading of commercial papers. She further complained before the domestic courts that, because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could receive back only a small proportion of her investments in bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. On 12 November 1996, following an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings. On 4 February 1998 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment rejecting the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The second-instance court found that, because the applicant had clarified during the appeal phase that she was seeking compensation for damages only, this constituted a new fact that the first-instance court would have to deliberate upon.

On 24 October 2001 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment. The court found that, given the contractual arrangements, the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. could not be held responsible for the damages sustained. The applicant appealed. On 15 September 2004 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the first-instance judgment and rejected the appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected her appeal. She lodged a constitutional appeal. On 10 December 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected her appeal.

The record also states that relevant domestic law is set out in Tomažič v. Slovenia (no. 38350/02, 13 December 2007). The domestic proceedings therefore comprised two first-instance decisions, two decisions of the Maribor Higher Court, one Supreme Court decision, and one Constitutional Court decision. The applicant pursued her claim through the ordinary courts and then through constitutional review, and her domestic appeals were ultimately rejected at the final stages of those proceedings.

On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected her appeal. She lodged a constitutional appeal. On 10 December 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected her appeal.

The domestic proceedings therefore comprised two first-instance decisions, two decisions of the Maribor Higher Court, one Supreme Court decision, and one Constitutional Court decision. case_name: CASE OF N.M.B. v. SWEDEN
summary:
The applicant, N.M.B., is an Iraqi national born in 1973 and originally from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden on 12 December 2007 and applied for asylum the following day. In his application against Sweden, lodged on 15 November 2010, he alleged that his deportation to Iraq would involve a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. He was represented by Mr T. Stilus; the Swedish Government were represented by Ms C. Hellner and Ms H. Lindquist.

In support of his asylum claim, the applicant stated that he was a Christian academic employed at a university in Baghdad. In April 2006 he began working for a committee established to develop research methods at the university. The committee was soon accused of cooperating with Americans. On 20 June 2006 the applicant wrote to the Minister of Education, accusing a university colleague, a member of the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP), of corruption and of counteracting the committee’s work. The colleague learned of the accusation and threatened the applicant.

On 27 June 2006 armed men attempted to kidnap the applicant’s daughter. Her mother called the police; after some shooting, the daughter was released. On 30 June 2006 the applicant received a letter calling him and his family Christian traitors and stating that they would be killed if he did not quit his job. On 8 July 2006 he reported the incidents to the police, and the family moved in with relatives. On 16 July 2006 the head of the committee was kidnapped and killed, after committee members had received threatening letters; the committee’s work then ended. On 3 October 2006 the applicant fled with his family to Syria.

On 15 January 2008 the applicant’s parents, who lived in Baghdad, were shot at; his father was kidnapped and tortured until he told the kidnappers the applicant’s whereabouts. In October and December 2008 the applicant received threatening messages on a website. In one, the Islamic Brigade, a militia within the IIP, warned him against returning to Iraq.

On 17 March 2009 the Migration Board rejected the asylum application. It did not question that the applicant was a Christian and had worked for the university committee, but did not find it likely that his work had made him a suspect of cooperating with Americans. It noted that he had quit the job three years earlier and that there was nothing to indicate a remaining work-related threat. It also found that he had not made plausible that his accusation against a former colleague had harmed that person or the IIP, and it questioned the credibility of the alleged attack on his parents. The Board further noted that the security situation in Baghdad and Iraq as a whole had improved.

The applicant appealed, claiming a risk of persecution as a Christian and an academic. He added that members of the IIP had asked for him and had written threatening messages on the wall of his old house in December 2009. He also stated that he had reported to the police his suspicion that high-profile members of the Ministry of Education were responsible for the kidnapping attempt against his daughter.

On 9 June 2010 the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It held that the incidents did not constitute persecution on religious grounds. It found that the applicant had exaggerated his story by adding the police report about his suspicions, that his work for the committee was limited in scope and had ended long ago, and that, absent political activity, his letter to the Ministry was unlikely to cause the alleged threat. It concluded that there was no individual threat against him.

On 3 November 2010 the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal. The applicant subsequently claimed impediments to enforcement, invoking the general situation for Christians in Baghdad and attacks in November 2010 in the residential area where he had lived. On 26 January 2011 the Migration Board declined to reconsider the case, finding no new circumstances justifying reconsideration. The record also referred to the earlier case M.Y.H. and Others v. Sweden for relevant domestic law and information about Iraq.

case_name: CASE OF TARASOV v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 and living in Makiyivka, alleged that police had ill-treated him and that his right to mount a defence had been violated.

On 13 January 2000 Makiyivka police arrested him and held him in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that he had no access to a lawyer and was forced to confess. He claimed repeated severe beatings during interrogation, suffocation with a plastic bag and gas mask, and electric shocks applied to his genitals. The Government stated that his rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination were explained and that he signed waivers; he was questioned about a car theft and confessed, and also confessed to involvement in a robbery. On 14 January 2000 an ambulance took him to hospital; medical reports recorded abdominal trauma and a bruise in the lumbar region. On 15 January 2000 criminal proceedings were instituted against him for garage theft, theft of non-ferrous metals and attempted robbery. On 16 January 2000 he was charged with car theft; he denied guilt and said his earlier confession had been made under duress. Further charges followed on 18 January 2000. On 25 January 2000 he was transferred to the SIZO. On 29 February 2000, at a confrontation with co-accused D., he denied guilt and refused to sign the report. On 2 March 2000, with lawyer M. present, he denied guilt and alleged duress. On 13 March 2000 his mother appointed lawyer I.

The trial began on 17 March 2000. During hearings the applicant claimed his confession had been extracted by beatings and ill-treatment and sought witnesses. On 2 June 2000 witnesses U.G. and U.A. testified that they had heard him screaming and had seen him after beatings. On 8 June 2000 the court refused to summon the ambulance doctor but ordered a forensic medical examination. Health issues affected proceedings: in August 2000 he was not brought to court due to renal colic; in September 2000 the SIZO said he was fit; in October 2000 it said his health was very poor; in August 2001 it said he could participate and recommended a stretcher. On 21 December 2001 he was transferred to court by ambulance and brought in on a stretcher, with a doctor present and lawyer N. representing him. He said he felt unwell and lost consciousness; the Government said his health was satisfactory and that he took part in final pleadings.

On 25 December 2001 the Gornyatskiy Local Court of Makiyivka convicted the applicant and others of theft and robbery and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It relied on his prior confessions plus co-defendants’ testimony, victims, witnesses, material evidence and stolen goods. It rejected his ill-treatment complaint and did not accept U.G. and U.A.’s testimony, citing lack of support and their relationship with him. Appeals in January and February 2002 were left without examination for procedural defects, with extensions granted. On 13 May 2002 he lodged a cassation appeal complaining of torture, lack of access to a lawyer, falsification of case-file documents, failure to question cellmates, and pronouncement of judgment in his absence because his lawyer had convinced him to waive his right to be present at the last hearing, depriving him of arguments and closing submissions. On 29 October 2002 a Supreme Court panel found the first-instance judgment well-founded, no procedural violations, and his ill-treatment allegations duly checked and rejected.

Separately, on 14 March 2000 he wrote to a human rights NGO. On 25 May 2000 the prosecutor refused criminal proceedings over the alleged ill-treatment. On 2 August 2000 the regional prosecutor quashed that refusal and ordered further investigation. On 7 September 2000 the Makiyivka prosecutor again refused for lack of proof. In November 2000 the court ordered another forensic examination; from November 2000 to May 2001 experts noted scars and pigmentations and found no link between the January 2000 injuries and later health problems. In August 2003 he challenged the 7 September 2000 decision; on 6 November 2003 the district court quashed it and remitted the case. On 20 May 2005 cellmates were re-questioned. On 15 June 2005 the prosecutor refused proceedings for lack of corpus delicti, citing police denials, conflicting cellmate statements, destroyed SIZO records and no evidence; the applicant did not challenge that decision. A CPT report on its September 2000 visit described similar allegations and visible marks; the applicant said the passage concerned him.

case_name: CASE OF PUTISTIN v. UKRAINE
summary:
Mr Vladlen Mikhaylovich Putistin, born in 1934, lives in Kyiv. He is the son of Mr Mikhail Putistin, a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who played in the 1936 USSR championship, when Dynamo took second place. On 9 August 1942 his father took part in the “Death Match” between FC Start—mostly Dynamo Kyiv professionals then working in a Kyiv bakery—and Flakelf, a team of German Luftwaffe pilots, air-defence soldiers and airport technicians. FC Start won 5–3. The match allegedly involved Flakelf’s lack of sportsmanship, physical challenges, threats and unfair refereeing by an SS officer. The victory allegedly led to the players’ arrest and transfer to a local concentration camp, where four were eventually executed. In 2002 Kyiv authorities commemorated the 60th anniversary, with wide media coverage.

On 3 April 2001 Komsomolska Pravda published “The Truth about the Death Match,” by journalist O.M. It discussed a planned film about the 1942 events and included an interview with future director/producer A.S. and D.K., plus a picture of the 1942 match poster with the footballers’ names. The article named four executed Dynamo Kyiv players—Kuzmenko, Klimenko, Korotkikh and Trusevych—but did not name the applicant’s father; his name was not legible on the poster. D.K. stated that only four Dynamo players were in the Start team created by the local bread factory, that those four were executed, and that other players worked in the police and collaborated with the Gestapo.

In July 2001 the applicant sued Komsomolska Pravda and the journalist, alleging the article suggested his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo. He sought rectification of the untrue information and non-pecuniary damages. He supplied State Security Service documents showing no archive information about his father’s alleged collaboration and no criminal proceedings against him; the archives and Kyiv Regional State Archives confirmed his father had participated in the Death Match and had been detained at Syrets concentration camp. On 25 December 2001 the Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv rejected the claim. It found that the applicant was not directly affected, that the article concerned a film script, that it did not name his father or the applicant, and that it made no allegation that his father had collaborated with the Gestapo. On 13 March 2002 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, and on 15 November 2002 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s points-of-law appeal.

In other domestic proceedings, on 27 April 2000 the Moskovskyy District Court ordered Dzerkalo Tyzhnia to rectify information about the applicant’s father; on 29 April 2000 it published a correction that he played for Dynamo, was arrested in summer 1942 with other players and sent to Syrets, and escaped in October 1942. In May 2002 Argumenty i Fakty stated that only four Death Match players were arrested and sent to Syrets, without naming the applicant’s father. After his request, issue no. 27 named all eight arrested players, including his father. His subsequent suit ended on 28 December 2004 with a final Supreme Court ruling against him. On 12 May 2003 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court ordered Fakty i Komentari to publish a rectification concerning the applicant’s father; the order was upheld on appeal on 21 October 2003 and in cassation on 31 August 2005, while his damages claim was rejected.

case_name: CASE OF VIEIRA GOMES BEZERRA v. PORTUGAL
summary:
The applicant, Ms Tomásia Vieira Gomes Bezerra, is a Portuguese national born in Silves, Portugal, and living in Bonn, Germany. On 4 October 2010 she lodged application no. 60786/10 against the Portuguese Republic with the European Court of Human Rights. The Portuguese Government were represented by their Agent, Ms M. F. Graça de Carvalho, Deputy-Attorney General. On 17 October 2012 the application was communicated to the Government.

The factual record concerns civil proceedings initiated by the applicant in Portugal. On 28 February 2007 she started proceedings against two companies before the Court of Vila Nova de Gaia. The proceedings concerned the occupation of land that the applicant claimed to be her own. They were registered as domestic proceedings no. 1908/07.8TBVNG. The defendants contested the proceedings, and the court ordered that the size of the land be analysed by an expertise. Those procedural steps ended on 18 December 2007.

In the first trimester of 2008, an attempt was made to conciliate the parties. On 18 July 2008, the court ordered suspension of the proceedings because the property was not registered in the applicant’s name before the Land Registry Office (Conservatória do Registo Predial). On 20 January 2010, the court ordered the interruption of the proceedings. On 18 July 2010, the applicant joined an additional supporting document to the proceedings and informed the court that the land had been registered. The judge then ordered the proceedings to be resumed. According to the last information received by the Court on 3 May 2013, the domestic proceedings were still pending.

The supplied record does not describe any further substantive arguments by the parties or identify a specific Convention complaint. It sets out only the above procedural and factual chronology: the applicant’s ownership claim concerning occupied land, the defendants’ contestation, the court-ordered expertise, the conciliation attempt, the suspension for lack of registration, the interruption of the proceedings, the later registration information submitted by the applicant, and the resumption of the proceedings. The record does not give details about the identities of the companies, the exact location or size of the land, the content of the defendants’ defence, the result of the conciliation attempt, or any domestic decision on the merits or appeal. It also does not specify the relief sought in the domestic proceedings or the precise basis of the application to the European Court of Human Rights. The concrete events and dates relevant to the domestic proceedings are therefore limited to: 28 February 2007, when the applicant commenced the civil action; 18 December 2007, when the procedural steps concerning the expertise ended; the first trimester of 2008, when conciliation was attempted; 18 July 2008, when suspension was ordered; 20 January 2010, when interruption was ordered; 18 July 2010, when the applicant submitted the registration document and the judge ordered resumption; and 3 May 2013, when the Court last received information indicating that the proceedings remained pending.

case_name: CASE OF BOKAL v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Lidija Bokal, a Slovenian national born in 1955 and living in Ljubljana, lodged application no. 34386/10 against Slovenia on 26 May 2010. The Government were represented by their Agent.

On 21 July 1997 the applicant began civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a determination of the validity of a sale contract between the defendants concerning an apartment in a building partially owned by her, and proposed that a note on dispute be entered in the Land Register. She stated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (about EUR 2,100).

On 20 August 1997 the Local Court rejected her proposal to enter the note on dispute. She appealed. On 18 February 1998, after several unsuccessful attempts to serve her appeal on the first defendant, the court posted the appeal on its notice board. On 4 March 1998 the Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed her appeal against the 20 August 1997 decision. Following a supervisory appeal to the Ministry of Justice, the court reported on 18 February 1998 that the case could not be given priority. On 21 April 1998 the applicant asked the court to schedule a hearing. On 27 March 2000 she requested priority for her claims; the court dismissed that request on 5 April 2000.

On 16 June 2000 a third-party intervener, D.S., who had in the meantime bought the apartment from the first defendant, joined the proceedings. On 1 March 2002 the intervener lodged a supervisory appeal, submitting among other things that because the proceedings were still pending she could not dispose of the apartment.

The first hearing was scheduled for 13 February 2004 but was postponed to 26 March 2004. On 18 March 2004 the applicant filed written submissions raising the claim value to SIT 1,100,000 (about EUR 4,600). At the first main hearing on 26 March 2004 the court modified the value of the claim as requested. On 11 May 2004 the applicant requested an interim order. Between 9 April and 4 June 2004 three further main hearings were held. On 4 June 2004 the court issued a judgment partially upholding her claim. It was served personally on the applicant and the second defendant, and on the first defendant and the third party by posting on the court notice board.

On 27 September 2004 the applicant appealed. On 7 December 2005 the Ljubljana Higher Court returned the file to the first-instance court, instructing it that the first defendant should be served the appeal-related documents under Section 145 of the Civil Procedure Act and that it should decide on the interim-order request. On 6 January 2006 the Local Court asked the applicant to pay court fees and supplement her interim-order proposal. On 3 March 2006 the 4 June 2004 judgment and her appeal were served on the first defendant by posting on the notice board. On 20 March 2006 the Local Court dismissed the interim-order request. The applicant appealed. On 21 June 2006 the Higher Court dismissed her appeals against the 4 June 2004 judgment and the 20 March 2006 decision.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 23 October 2008 the Supreme Court rejected it on procedural grounds. It held that the Local Court had wrongly applied the Civil Procedure Act by allowing a modification of the disputed value at a later stage, took the value indicated in the original claim, and concluded that the threshold for an appeal on points of law had not been reached. The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal. On 26 November 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed it; the decision was served on the applicant on 1 December 2009.

case_name: CASE OF FERNÁNDEZ MARTÍNEZ v. SPAIN
summary:
José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937 and living in Cieza, was ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; receiving no immediate reply, he married in a civil ceremony in 1985 and later had five children. From October 1991 he worked as a teacher of Catholic religion and ethics in a State-run secondary school in the Region of Murcia under a renewable one-year contract. Under the 1979 Agreement between Spain and the Holy See and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed annually from candidates proposed by the diocesan Ordinary; appointment was renewed automatically unless the Ordinary objected before the school year or the public authority annulled it for serious academic or disciplinary reasons.

In November 1996 the Murcian newspaper La Verdad published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). It named Fernández Martínez as a former seminary director among married priests gathered at La Luz to advocate optional celibacy and related reforms. On 20 August 1997 the Pope granted his long-pending request for dispensation from celibacy; the rescript stated that he lost clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise for lower-level schools, provided there was no scandal. He was notified on 15 September 1997. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that his service as a teacher was terminated. On 9 October 1997 the Ministry told him his employment had ended with effect from 29 September 1997. In a memorandum of 11 November 1997, the Diocese explained that once his situation became publicly known, the bishop could no longer authorise him to teach Catholic religion and ethics; it also referred to avoiding scandal, respecting parents’ sensitivities, and his entitlement to unemployment benefit. The school board expressed support for him and satisfaction with his teaching.

His administrative complaint was unsuccessful, and an administrative court dismissed his appeal on 30 June 2000, holding that termination was the only course once the Diocese did not propose him. He then brought unfair-dismissal proceedings before Murcia Employment Tribunal no. 3. By judgment of 28 September 2000, the tribunal found he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, with his appearance in the press having caused his dismissal. It declared the dismissal null, ordered the Region of Murcia to reinstate him, and ordered the State to pay outstanding salary; it dismissed his claim against the Diocese. The Ministry, the Region, and the Diocese appealed.

On 26 February 2001 the Murcia High Court of Justice allowed the appeal. It described the link between the Catholic religion teacher and the bishop as based on trust, held that the bishop had acted within his prerogatives, found no violation of the Spanish Constitution, and considered the contract a temporary one that had expired rather than a dismissal.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court relying on Articles 14, 18 and 20 of the Spanish Constitution. The public prosecutor supported him, noting that his public appearance preceded the rescript and that Church authorities knew of his MOCEOP membership. In a judgment of 4 June 2007, served on 18 June 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo appeal. It rejected the discrimination and private-life complaints and found the religious reasons for non-renewal justified by the Catholic Church’s religious freedom and parents’ rights. Two judges dissented. On 23 July 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected his request to declare the judgment null.

On 11 December 2007 the applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. Relying on Article 8, separately and with Article 14, he alleged that the non-renewal of his contract was an unjustified interference with his private life. He alleged that publicity given to his family and personal situation as a married priest caused the non-renewal and was incompatible with his rights under Articles 9 and 10.

case_name: CASE OF HUSAYN (ABU ZUBAYDAH) v. POLAND
summary:
Husayn (Abu Zubaydah), a stateless Palestinian born in 1971 and detained at the US Guantánamo Bay facility, lodged application no. 7511/13 against Poland on 28 January 2013. He alleged that Poland had enabled the CIA to detain him secretly on Polish territory, allowing torture, incommunicado detention, mental and physical abuse, and deprivation of contact with family or the outside world. He further alleged that Poland enabled his transfer from its territory, exposing him to further torture, ill-treatment, secret and arbitrary detention, and denial of justice by the US authorities. He also complained that Poland failed to conduct an effective investigation into these allegations. A related case, Al Nashiri v. Poland, was examined simultaneously.

After 11 September 2001 the US Government began a special interrogation and detention programme. On 17 September 2001 President Bush signed a classified Presidential Finding granting the CIA extended covert-action powers, including authority to detain terrorist suspects and establish secret detention facilities outside the United States in cooperation with host governments. The CIA later established the High-Value Detainees Programme. Abu Zubaydah was the first High-Value Detainee in CIA custody. According to the 2004 CIA Inspector General report, he was captured in Faisalabad, Pakistan, in late March 2002 and transported to a secret CIA “black site,” where he was treated for gunshot wounds.

In August 2002 the US Department of Justice provided an opinion that ten specific Enhanced Interrogation Techniques would not violate the prohibition of torture. These included attention grasp, walling, facial hold, insult slap, cramped confinement, use of harmless insects, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation not exceeding 11 days, and waterboarding. CIA psychologists later proposed twelve such techniques for Abu Zubaydah. From November 2002 the techniques were applied to other suspects in CIA custody, including Al Nashiri. A 2004 CIA background paper described routine capture, rendition, and reception: the detainee was flown to a black site, shackled and deprived of sight and sound, with no interaction except medical assessments; on arrival he was medically assessed and placed under complete American control through “precise, quiet, and almost clinical” procedures.

An investigation had been opened in Poland on 11 March 2008. In the related case, the Chamber sought materials showing the grounds for injured-person status in that investigation and whether detention in Poland had been established. In the present case, the Polish Government stated that a criminal investigation was pending and that they could not address the Court’s questions in detail or produce requested documentary evidence. They offered classified or ex parte access to a document prepared by the Appellate Prosecutor’s Office in Kraków and to case files Ap. V Ds. 12/12/S. The Court requested a comprehensive extract from the non-confidential part of those files by 30 October 2013. The Government did not submit it by that deadline. At the 2 December 2013 fact-finding hearing, they brought a classified document but proposed that it be reviewed in situ only by judges, interpreters, and Polish representatives. After the Chamber directed production of a redacted version, the Government did not produce it.

The Court held a fact-finding and in camera hearing on 2 December 2013 and a public hearing on 3 December 2013. It heard evidence from Giovanni Claudio Fava, Senator Dick Marty, J.G.S., and Senator Józef Pinior. Senator Marty and J.G.S. presented flight-data material concerning Poland and the cases of Al Nashiri and Abu Zubaydah. Documentary evidence came mainly from the applicant, partly supplemented by the Government, and from public-domain material.

case_name: CASE OF BUZADJI v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
summary:
The applicant, Petru Buzadji, a Moldovan national born in 1947 and living in Comrat, was director of State company B-G. In March 2006 he acknowledged in court that B-G owed a private company USD 594,067 plus penalties (total USD 842,404). He was dismissed on 26 May 2006. From July 2006 he was summoned over alleged defrauding of B-G and appeared whenever summoned. Thirteen criminal investigations were opened against him and his two sons, most on 5 April 2007, and joined on 25 May 2007; his sons were questioned as suspects in May 2007 but not arrested. On 26 October 2006 bankruptcy proceedings were initiated against B-G. On 21 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed lower judgments, finding the debt fictitious; retrial remained pending.

On 2 May 2007 the applicant was arrested. On 5 May 2007 he was charged with defrauding B-G. The same day the Buiucani District Court ordered 15 days’ pre-trial detention, citing the exceptionally serious charge, complexity, and reasonable grounds to believe he could collude with his sons, not yet interviewed; other prosecution fears were unsubstantiated. The applicant appealed, relying on pending civil debt proceedings, confirmation of the debt by a court-appointed administrator, absence of material showing risk of absconding or interference, his age and health problems needing unavailable in-patient care, family, residence and job, compliance with summonses from July 2006 to May 2007, and the fact that the detention court lacked the investigation file. On 8 May 2007 the Chişinău Court of Appeal upheld the detention, repeating the lower court’s reasons.

On 16 May 2007 the district court extended detention by 20 days, finding grounds valid, most investigative actions done, further measures requiring his participation necessary, and house arrest premature given seriousness, complexity and public interest. On 22 May 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld this, adding a continuing risk of evidence destruction because not all financial documents had been seized. On 5 June 2007 detention was extended another 20 days for the same reasons; on 11 June 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld it, citing the serious offence, alleged damage of almost MDL 9 million (about EUR 553,000), possible 10–25 year sentence, thirteen charges, ongoing investigation, and risks of absconding or influencing B-G staff witnesses.

On 26 June 2007 the district court rejected further extension and placed him under house arrest for 30 days. It noted 55 days’ detention, his participation in investigative actions, weakening grounds over time, the prosecutor’s burden to prove risk, and that severity alone did not justify detention; it found it improbable he would abscond, influence witnesses, or destroy evidence. Conditions barred leaving home, phone calls and discussing the case. On 29 June 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed this and ordered 20 days’ detention, citing complexity, seriousness, possible communication with his unarrested sons, flight to Transdniestria, influencing former staff witnesses, and available prison medical care.

On 16 July 2007 the district court extended detention 20 days, referring to the prosecutor’s position that the investigation was finalised and the file ready to be presented. On 20 July 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed that and changed the measure to house arrest, finding no evidence of continued need, no additional materials on witness influence, his promise to appear, and no specific risk of absconding. House arrest was maintained on 14 September and 14 December 2007. On 12 March 2008 he was released on bail after over ten months of detention/house arrest without breaching restrictions.

The applicant alleged unlawful arrest and that the courts had not given relevant and sufficient reasons for his detention pending trial.

case_name: CASE OF HORNCASTLE AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The application was brought by four British nationals—Michael Horncastle, David Blackmore, Abijah Marquis and Joseph Graham—against the United Kingdom. They alleged that admitting witness statements at their trials made the proceedings unfair.

Horncastle and Blackmore were charged, with D., with causing P.R. grievous bodily harm with intent. On 7 May 2005 P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat, suffered extensive injuries and was hospitalised for a month. On 3 June 2005 he made a police statement naming “Horncastle” and describing two other attackers, but said his memory was vague and he had drunk heavily. He died on 23 July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. The prosecution alleged that B. and M. had burgled another flat, stored stolen goods in P.R.’s flat, and that Horncastle and Blackmore went with D. to recover the property. The defence accepted they went to help recover D.’s property but denied attacking P.R.; they argued M. was responsible. Because P.R. was dead, the prosecution applied under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 to read his statement. The applicants opposed this under section 78 PACE, arguing it was the only admissible evidence against them, could not be cross-examined and was unreliable due to P.R.’s alcoholism, vague memory and description of Blackmore. case_name: CASE OF NIKOLIĆ v. CROATIA
summary:
Ms Nada Nikolić, a Croatian national born in 1964 living in Vukovar, lodged application no. 5096/12 against Croatia on 9 December 2011. She alleged that national authorities had not adequately responded to the killing of her husband, Lj.N.

Vukovar was heavily attacked by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian paramilitary forces from August to November 1991 and occupied at the end of November 1991. It was part of the UN Protected Area from 1992 to 1996. In 1996 UNTAES was established; its mandate ceased on 15 January 1998 and transfer to Croatian authorities began.

On 2 October 1991, between 4 and 5 p.m., during a general alert, two unknown uniformed, armed men apprehended Lj.N. in the basement or courtyard of a building in Kudeljarska Street, Vukovar, and drove him away. On 24 November 1991 his body was found in the River Danube at Novi Sad, Serbia. A 25 November 1991 autopsy found death was caused by a hand-gun gunshot wound.

In 2004 the applicant sued the State for damages in the Vukovar Municipal Court. In connection, the Vukovar Municipality State Attorney’s Office asked police for information. The police thereby first learned of the death and opened an enquiry. On 24 January 2005 police interviewed the applicant; she said her husband had been abducted from the basement by two Croatian soldiers. She named B.Š., K.Š., J.T., S.P., M.P. and J.M. as present; K.Š., S.P. and M.P. had died. That day J.T. said two uniformed, armed, masked men had taken Lj.N. On 3 February 2005 B.Š. said he had joined the Croatian Army in August 1991 and was visiting his wife K.Š. and children in the same basement; he denied being present. On 15 February 2005 Vukovar police lodged a criminal complaint with the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office against an unknown perpetrator, classifying the offence as a war crime against the civilian population.

On 5 May 2009 the applicant told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office that B.Š. had been present. She said that after K.Š. died around 10 November 1991, one abductor came to take J.M.; B.Š. whispered, “This is the man who took Lj.[N.]”. She said B.Š. lived in Zagreb. On 9 July 2009 Zagreb police interviewed B.Š., who denied being present or knowing the abductors. On 21 July 2009 Vukovar police interviewed J.M., who said she was present but did not see the men. On 24 March 2011 a Zagreb County Court investigating judge heard B.Š., who repeated his statement. On 3 May 2011 a Vukovar County Court investigating judge interviewed the applicant, who repeated her statement. On 12 November 2011 Vukovar police told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office they had found no new information.

The applicant’s civil claim was dismissed on 18 September 2008. The Vukovar County Court upheld that decision on 21 April 2009 and the Supreme Court on 16 February 2011, finding the claim time-barred. Her constitutional complaint was dismissed on 12 July 2011.

case_name: CASE OF KIIVERI v. FINLAND
summary:
The applicant, Timo Veikko Kiiveri, is a Finnish national born in 1960 who lives in Tampere. He owns 90% of the shares in a limited liability construction and decoration company and is its managing director and a board member. In 2005 the tax authorities inspected the company and concluded that it had failed to declare and pay considerable taxes, paid salaries off the books, and engaged in other fraudulent activity. On 8 September 2008 the tax authorities imposed additional income tax and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant for tax years 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2006. He apparently did not appeal, and the bailiff seized the imposed sums. The tax years 2002, 2003 and 2005 became final on 31 December 2008, 31 December 2009 and 31 December 2011 respectively; the appeal period for 2006 elapsed on 31 December 2012.

In June 2007 the police started a criminal investigation into the applicant’s activities. On 6 March 2009 the prosecutor charged him with accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned tax years 2000–2006 and his role as managing director and board member: he was accused of deducting fabricated receipts, failing to declare the company’s real income, paying salaries off the books, and causing the company’s tax to be too low. The second count concerned tax years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006: he was accused of failing to declare his own income and causing his personal tax to be too low. The tax authorities joined the charges and sought compensation for approximately the avoided taxes.

On 9 September 2009 Tampere District Court convicted him as charged of two counts of aggravated tax fraud and accounting offence. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay EUR 685,080.66 plus interest compensation, with sums already seized in the administrative proceedings deductible, and banned from business activities for six years.

On 9 October 2009 he appealed to Turku Court of Appeal, seeking to quash the judgment and dismiss the charges, relying also on ne bis in idem and relevant case-law. On 15 September 2010, after an oral hearing, the Court of Appeal largely upheld the judgment, found part of the accounting offence aggravated, and ordered EUR 20,000 more compensation. On ne bis in idem, it reasoned that for tax years 2003, 2005 and 2006 the appeal period had not elapsed when charges were brought in 2009, so no issue arose; for 2002, taxation became final on 31 December 2008 before charges, but because another kind of tax appeal remained available, ne bis in idem did not prevent examination.

On 12 October 2010 he appealed to the Supreme Court, repeating his grounds and seeking a stay. On 27 February 2012 the Supreme Court dismissed without examining the merits the part concerning tax year 2002 because the tax surcharges had become final in 2008, before the March 2009 charges, preventing examination. It otherwise upheld the lower judgment, finding no ne bis in idem issue for the other years because the appeal periods had not elapsed when charges were brought; the sentence was reduced to 2 years 10 months. On 21 August 2012 he lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking reopening based on incorrect application of law and the prohibition on self-incrimination; it was apparently refused in March 2013. On 22 August 2012 he lodged an application with the ECtHR alleging, in particular, a violation of the ne bis in idem principle.

case_name: CASE OF ROHLENA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966 living in Brno, lodged application no. 59552/08 against the Czech Republic on 4 December 2008. Relying on Article 7, he alleged that the domestic courts, by convicting him of a continuous criminal offence, had applied criminal law retroactively to his detriment.

On 29 May 2006 the Brno municipal prosecutor indicted him for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. The alleged conduct included verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping, holding her throat, attempting to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or to the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling away household money and smashing crockery. His wife sustained haematomas, bruising and a fractured nose, seeking medical assistance on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003 and 8 February 2006 after assaults on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003 and 8 February 2006. The prosecutor classified the conduct as the “continuing” offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code, noting that conduct before that offence was introduced on 1 June 2004 had amounted to violence against an individual or group under Article 197a and assault occasioning bodily harm under Article 221.

On 18 April 2007 the Brno Municipal Court found him guilty of that offence, committed at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006 as indicted. It sentenced him to a suspended two-and-a-half-year prison term, five years’ probation, supervision and alcohol-dependency treatment. It relied on statements by the applicant, the victim and witnesses, including the couple’s children, who reported ten verbal insults, four instances of grabbing and strangling, and monthly verbal and/or physical assaults, as well as documentary and expert evidence. The applicant admitted quarrels and physical violence, including sometimes slapping his wife or hitting her with his fist. The court applied Article 215a as in force since 1 June 2004, treating it as extending to pre-1 June 2004 acts because they were punishable at the time and at least amounted to Article 197a. It found the duration gave relatively high danger and imposed a suspended sentence at the lower end of the range.

On 6 September 2007 the Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal contesting the facts and evidence assessment, finding no defects and that the classification conformed to the Criminal Code. On 21 February 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded his appeal on points of law complaining that Article 215a had been applied to conduct before 1 June 2004. Referring to its earlier decision Tzn 12/93 of 8 December 1993, it stated that a continuation of a criminal offence constituted a single act and was to be classified under the law in force when the last occurrence was completed, provided earlier acts had been criminal under previous law. It found the pre-amendment conduct amounted at least to Article 197a or Article 221 § 1, and that the facts disclosed all elements of Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b), including continuation over several years. On 10 June 2008 the Constitutional Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded the applicant’s constitutional appeal alleging unfair proceedings and retroactive detrimental application of the Criminal Code; it held the domestic decisions logical and coherent and without prohibited retroactive effect.

Because the applicant later committed another offence while on probation and did not undergo alcohol treatment, he had to serve the prison sentence from the 18 April 2007 judgment. He began serving it on 3 January 2011; according to the Government, he was conditionally released on 17 May 2012.

case_name: CASE OF MASLÁK AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
summary:
The applicants are three Slovak nationals, Miroslav Maslák, Tomáš Ďuriš and Vladimír Haviar, all residing in Pružina. They lodged an application against Slovakia, represented by R. Toman; the Government were represented by Ms M. Pirošíková. They alleged under Article 5 §§4 and 5 that they had been denied a speedy procedure for review of the lawfulness of their pre-trial detention and an enforceable right to compensation for the alleged breach of the speediness requirement in relation to release requests of 2 and 10 May 2010 and December 2010 (amended in January 2011), and their interlocutory appeal against the detention order of 4 April 2011.

Since 2007 the applicants had faced multiple charges, mainly violent offences linked to organised crime. They were repeatedly arrested, remanded, released, re-arrested and re-remanded. case_name: CASE OF BERLAND v. FRANCE
summary:
The applicant, Daniel Berland, a French national born in 1987 and in the specialised hospital centre of Sevrey, lodged application no. 42875/10 against France on 21 July 2010, alleging a violation of Article 7 §1.

On 12 September 2007, aged 20, he went to the workplace of C.G., his former girlfriend, who after threats and violence had told him she no longer wanted to see him. He inflicted several stab wounds on C.G., who died from a massive haemorrhage from throat and thorax wounds, and wounded two other people. On 14 September 2007 he was placed under judicial investigation for premeditated murder and intentional wounding, remanded in custody, and the Prefect ordered his compulsory admission to Sevrey CHS. Expert psychiatric boards found that at the material time he had a mental disorder impairing his discernment and ability to control his actions under Article 122-1 of the Criminal Code.

On 8 September 2008 the public prosecutor asked the Dijon investigating judge to refer the case to the Investigation Division for a ruling on lack of criminal liability under Article 706-20 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, derived from the 25 February 2008 Act. On 30 September 2008 the judge found sufficient evidence to commit the offences and plausible reasons to apply Article 122-1, and ordered transmission to the Principal Public Prosecutor. On 18 November 2008 the Principal Public Prosecutor called for referral under new Article 706-122. On 25 November the President noted the applicant could not appear for medical reasons. At the 27 November hearing, his representative argued that applying the new procedure breached the non-retroactivity of harsher criminal legislation: it required the Investigation Division to rule on commission of the offences when imposing indefinite compulsory psychiatric treatment, tantamount to conviction and sentence not applicable in 2007.

On 18 February 2009 the Investigation Division found sufficient evidence that he had “intentionally killed C.G.” and lacked criminal liability because of mental disorder impairing discernment and control. It ordered compulsory hospitalisation under Article 706-135, finding his disorder risked the safety of others and required long-term hospital care. It also imposed a 20-year prohibition on contact with the complainants and on possessing or carrying weapons, as preventive measures under new Article 706-136, and sent the case back to Dijon Criminal Court for civil liability and damages. It rejected objections based on immediate application and Article 7, characterising the finding as not a conviction but a factual situation with legal consequences; the hospitalisation as preventive, not a penalty, under medical and administrative authority; and the 25 February 2008 Act and 16 April 2008 Decree as applicable.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 6 §1 and 7, arguing that no punishment without law precluded immediate application of a procedure exposing him to measures not entailed under former legislation. Before the Court of Cassation, the public prosecutor considered it impossible to find sufficient evidence that he acted “intentionally”, since criminal insanity precluded ruling on the mental element, and called for deletion of “intentionally”. On 14 April 2010 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, holding that Article 112-1 of the Criminal Code did not apply to preventive measures for criminal insanity under Articles 706-135 and 706-136.

On 23 February 2011 the Prefect of Saône-et-Loire denied requests for unescorted leave. Assessments indicated his health allowed possible unescorted leave, but after contacting the Dijon public prosecutor about the 18 February 2009 prohibitions, the Prefect considered it impossible to guarantee he would not contact the complainants, and allowed future leave only if escorted.

case_name: CASE OF KOROŠEC v. SLOVENIA
summary:
The applicant, Tadej Korošec, a Slovenian national born in 1980, lives in Ljubljana. He suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires twenty-four-hour assistance with daily activities. He alleged under Article 6 of the Convention that court proceedings to which he had been a party were unfair.

In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of the Republic of Slovenia awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance set at 70% of the reference amount. On 28 May 2009 his general practitioner applied for an increase, citing worsening condition, particularly respiratory function, and stating that the applicant needed twenty-four-hour assistance from a family member or lay care assistant, together with permanent professional assistance. At that time the applicant organised care through students and relied significantly on family members.

On 9 July 2009 the Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of an internal medicine specialist and an occupational medicine specialist, examined medical documentation from an internal medicine doctor, a pulmonologist and a clinical neurologist, and examined the applicant. It reported that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. On 20 July 2009 the Ljubljana unit of the Institute dismissed his request based on that opinion. The applicant appealed on 28 July 2009.

On 23 September 2009 the second-instance disability commission, composed of an occupational medicine specialist and a specialist neuropsychiatrist, examined the file and again reported that the applicant did not need permanent professional assistance and could be cared for by a combination of care assistants without specific medical knowledge and by family members. On 24 September 2009 the Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the second-instance commission and on the 1998 Decision on Assistance and Attendance Allowance for Beneficiaries Suffering from a Severe Disability, under which a higher allowance required twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance.

On 22 October 2009 the applicant brought court proceedings against the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent expert. On 30 September 2010 the court heard his testimony, reviewed the file, dismissed his claim, and rejected the independent expert request, finding the first- and second-instance commission opinions together with other evidence sufficient to establish that he did not need professional assistance. On 2 November 2010 he appealed, challenging that conclusion and the failure to appoint an independent medical expert, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise to assess his care needs. On 24 January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance court had relied on commission opinions given by experts and that both commissions had considered the medical records.

On 9 March 2011 the applicant sought leave to appeal on points of law. He argued that the lower courts’ refusal to appoint an independent expert was contrary to Supreme Court case-law, under which the Institute’s Disability Commissions could not be considered independent in proceedings against the Institute and should not be used as evidence. On 17 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the challenged decisions had not departed from established case-law. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (the record gives the date as 28 July 2007), and on 11 June 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed it with reference to section 55.b of the Constitutional Court Act.

The record also notes that social courts carry out judicial review of the Institute’s decisions; under the Civil Procedure Act, a court should obtain an expert opinion if it lacks the necessary expertise. A domestic Supreme Court decision of 7 November 2006 (no. VIII Ips 3/2006) held that the opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could only be expert opinions in pre-judicial proceedings within the Institute, not in judicial proceedings, because they were opinions of representatives of one of the parties.
