case_name: CASE OF LUNEV v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Andrey Lunev, a Ukrainian national, lodged an application against Ukraine on 17 January 2013. He alleged inadequate medical assistance in detention, ill-treatment intended to discourage him from applying to the European Court, and failure to investigate that ill-treatment.

**Medical assistance.** In January 2012 he was arrested for suspected drug trafficking and on 30 January placed in Starobilsk SIZO. On arrival he was diagnosed with HIV stage 3, chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy/neuropathy from drug use, and tuberculosis residual changes. The Government said he refused a CD4+ count and a blood test in February 2012 and sought no medical help until 8 January 2013, although records show a September 2012 tuberculosis examination and X-ray and November 2012 bronchitis and kidney pain in another facility. On 8 January 2013 he was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis and treated. On 9 January he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked a court to expedite proceedings or release him for urgent treatment. On 10 January the court kept him in detention but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. He was hospitalised from 9 to 11 January with acute serose meningoencephalitis and was soporose; on 11 January he returned to the SIZO medical unit until 15 February and was also held at least once in Alchevsk ITT. On 17 January he requested hospital placement, citing need for psychiatric examination for ART, correct tuberculosis staging, epilepsy treatment and adequate care. At the end of January his lawyer received a call from an unknown man posing as a prosecutor’s employee, asking whether she represented the applicant and whether he had applied to the European Court; she confirmed. On 4 February the medical unit reported HIV since 2010, chronic bronchitis and toxic encephalopathy; his CD4+ count had been 374 in October 2010 and he had refused treatment. On 19 February a domestic court sentenced him to six and a half years for drug trafficking. On 26 February his CD4+ count was 119. On 7 March the Government said hospitalisation was unnecessary. On 12 March ART was recommended; on 14 March admission to Lugansk Temporary Detention Centre No. 17 Hospital was approved. He was hospitalised from 20 to 25 March and later from 29 March to 5 April and 12 April to 12 May; ART was prescribed on 16 April. On 24 May the Lugansk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction and remitted the case. On 19 June the Bryankovskyy Town Court released him under house arrest, noting he needed treatment unavailable in detention.

**Ill-treatment and investigation.** On 25 January 2013 he was placed in Alchevsk ITT. On 30 January, after acute liver pain, an ambulance was called and he was taken to hospital, returning about 4 p.m. He alleged that at about 5.25 p.m. two policemen from the regional police office beat him and told him to write that the SIZO provided adequate treatment; one hit his liver six or seven times, the other his kidneys four times, after which he wrote the statement. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court; he was diagnosed with possible blunt abdominal trauma, but a surgeon found no acute surgical pathology. He and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor, alleging pressure to withdraw his medical complaint and confess. On 14 February a forensic expert found no injuries. On 25 February the Alchevsk Town Prosecutor terminated proceedings for lack of evidence. On 26 March the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the investigation not thorough and cellmates not questioned. On 24 April an ambulance station reported the blunt abdominal trauma diagnosis and beating complaint. On 25 April proceedings were again terminated. Cellmate K. said the applicant was absent 40–60 minutes and returned claiming two unknown policemen beat him to force him to refuse treatment, with a red cheek and swollen liver. Officer So. denied involvement; surveillance was not working from 26 January to 4 February. On 3 June the prosecutor quashed the 25 April decision as premature and unsubstantiated. On 27 June proceedings were terminated again. On 4 November the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the lawyer’s complaint inadequately investigated and no explanation why a confrontation with officer So. was impossible.

case_name: CASE OF SOUSA GOUCHA v. PORTUGAL
summary:
The applicant, Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, is a Portuguese national born in 1954 who lives in Fontanelas. He is a well-known television host and publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008. The events at issue concerned a live talk show, *Five Minutes to Midnight* (*5 Para a Meia-Noite*), broadcast on RTP2 between midnight and 1 a.m. on 28 December 2009. The programme was presented by F.C. and featured two well-known media guests. During a quiz, F.C. asked, as the most important question, “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The possible answers included three female television hosts and the applicant; the applicant was the “correct” answer. In the transcript, guest J.M. first chose another guest, referred to as “the pregnant one” (option B, C.V.), and F.C. then revealed that the answer was Manuel Luís Goucha. F.C. described J.M.’s earlier answer as dishonest and contrary to his beliefs, while J.M. said he had known the answer and had been about to say it.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint for defamation and “insult” (*injúria*) with the Lisbon Criminal Department for Investigation and Prosecution. The defendants were the State-owned television company RTP, the production company, the television presenter F.C., and the directors of programming and content. On 2 March 2011 a public prosecutor discontinued the proceedings, stating that the defendants had not intended to offend him.

The applicant sought to intervene in the proceedings as an assistant to the public prosecutor (*assistente*) and lodged private prosecution submissions with the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court against the defendants. The defendants challenged those submissions by requesting that a judicial investigation be opened. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge dismissed the case (*despacho de não pronúncia*). As regards the individual defendants, the judge found insufficient evidence of defamation or insult, so the case could not proceed to trial. The judge stated that the defendants had not intended to attack the applicant’s honour, nor had they anticipated doing so; the subjective element of the offence was therefore unverified. The judge noted that the applicant was a public figure and must be used to having his characteristics captured by comedians for humour. The judge referred to public knowledge that the applicant’s characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, such as his way of expressing himself, his colourful feminine clothes, and the fact that he had always lived in a world of women. The judge also noted that the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public and that the defendants never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. case_name: CASE OF SULEJMANI v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
The application (no. 74681/11) was lodged against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia by Mr Osman Sulejmani, a Macedonian national born in 1958 and living in Tetovo. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the confiscation of his vehicle in criminal proceedings against a third person.

On 12 April 2006 the applicant concluded a sales contract with Sh.A. to purchase a concrete mixing and transport lorry (“the vehicle”) for the equivalent of EUR 5,000 in Macedonian denars. On 15 May 2007 he lent the vehicle to his company. On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate from him to examine the chassis; a record of temporarily seized objects was issued.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted Sh.A. of forgery of a document concerning the vehicle’s chassis number and rejected an indictment against I.S. It found that it had not been established that Sh.A. had altered the chassis. Under section 102(3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act, it advised the applicant, who had claimed compensation in the criminal proceedings, to pursue that claim in a separate civil action. That judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 16 November 2010 the applicant asked the first-instance court to return the vehicle. On 3 December 2010 the court heard him; he said he had bought the vehicle from Sh.A. for EUR 25,000 and could not have known at the time that its chassis number had been forged. On 6 December 2010 the court, relying on Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, found no grounds to confiscate his vehicle: he had not known and could not have known that it had been used to commit a crime. It also ordered return of the registration certificate.

On the public prosecutor’s appeal, on 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed that decision. Relying on Article 100-a(2), it found that the chassis had been forged and that the vehicle, in the interest of public safety, could not be declared roadworthy. It referred to Article 100-a(3) and instructed the first-instance court to assess whether continued use of the vehicle would constitute the offence of using a forged document.

On 22 February 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s application and ordered confiscation of the vehicle and registration certificate. Referring to Article 100-a(2) and (3), it found the chassis number had been forged and the vehicle could be used to commit an offence; for that reason and for road safety, confiscation was necessary. It referred to section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act and found that, although there were no proceedings against the applicant and he was not an offender, confiscation was necessary for general safety.

On 11 March 2011 the applicant appealed, arguing wrong application of Article 100-a(2) and (3) and that he had not known the vehicle had been used to commit a crime. On 19 May 2011 the appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It stated that it was true the applicant did not know the chassis had been forged, that he had registered the vehicle as last buyer, obtained a driving licence and paid a large amount. However, it considered that under Article 100-a(2) objects used to commit an offence are confiscated regardless of ownership if general safety, public health or ethics require it; the applicant’s lack of knowledge did not satisfy Article 100-a(3). The first-instance court had correctly found that use of the vehicle with forged identification numbers would affect road-user safety and general safety. The decision appears to have been served on the applicant on 2 June 2011.

case_name: CASE OF R.B.A.B. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
The applicants are five Sudanese nationals—R.B.A.B., her husband H.S., their daughters X and Y, and son Z—who entered the Netherlands on 28 April 2001. The parents sought asylum separately, and R.B.A.B. also applied for the children. They claimed to be from Dilling, South Kordofan, and said H.S. had attracted Sudanese authorities’ attention through opposition movement M. After interviews in May, August and November 2001, the Deputy Minister intended to reject the claims due to contradictions and lack of knowledge about tribes, topography and movement M. On 17 January 2002 their asylum requests were rejected. Appeals were declared inadmissible for failure to submit grounds; an objection was dismissed on 10 September 2002.

On 12 April 2003 they filed a second asylum request on essentially the same grounds. On 14 April 2003 the Minister rejected it, finding no new facts or altered circumstances; no appeal was lodged.

On 14 June 2005 they filed a third asylum request, alleging that if returned to Sudan their daughters X and Y would be subjected to FGM due to tribal and social pressure. In interviews on 16 June 2005 the parents said they opposed FGM but could not protect the daughters. They submitted a Sudanese Embassy document of 26 April 2005 stating they were Sudanese citizens but lacked documents for a laissez-passer. On 17 June 2005 the Minister intended to reject the request, doubting its sincerity because FGM had not been raised earlier. Citing WBV 2004/36 and a 3 February 2004 Ministry report, she considered that higher-educated women in larger cities could avoid FGM, while rural/low-educated women had little choice. Because identity, origin and asylum statements were not credible, the applicants had not shown they fell outside the educated group. She also noted H.S. had accepted a negotiated penalty for shoplifting. In comments of 20 June 2005 the applicants said R.B.A.B. had only primary education and offered an IQ test. On 20 June 2005 the Minister rejected the request, stating it was for the applicants to prove identity and background.

A domestic provisional-measures judge ruled in the applicants’ favour, quashed the decisions and remitted the case, noting the daughters were uncircumcised, FGM was widespread, legal protection ineffective, and the earlier credibility finding concerned the parents, not the daughters’ protection. The Minister appealed. On 25 August 2005 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division quashed that ruling and rejected the appeal. It held the applicants bore the burden under section 31 of the Aliens Act 2000 and, given the final 17 January 2002 credibility decision, the Minister could reasonably find they had not shown compliance with policy conditions, lack of protection, or absence of an internal relocation alternative.

Later, X gave birth in 2011 and 2013; in 2015 she received a Netherlands residence permit and said she no longer wished to maintain the application insofar as it concerned her. In 2012 Y’s residence request was rejected; her objection was rejected on 29 December 2015, the Minister finding her parents opposed FGM and that she had not substantiated identity or Dilling origin. Z applied in 2013 under the long-term children regulation, seeking family permits; this was rejected and later again on objection. In September 2014 the Deputy Minister declined discretionary admission; related proceedings ended without further information.

Country material described FGM as widespread in Sudan, generally not prosecuted, prevalent in North Sudan, with urban educated families increasingly refusing it and no evidence of internal relocation to avoid it.

case_name: CASE OF RUBAN v. UKRAINE
summary:
The application was lodged on 15 October 2010 by Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and serving a life sentence. He alleged in particular that, in sentencing him, the domestic courts had not applied the most lenient criminal provisions, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention.

On 13 August 1996 the Voznesensk local prosecutor’s office began investigating the murder of four persons on 12 August 1996. On 18 October 1999 the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office began investigating the murder of A., and on 10 November 1999 the Slavyansk Police Department began investigating hooliganism concerning R. On 22 November 1999 the three investigations were joined. Several persons, including the applicant, were suspected of committing the crimes as a group. On 14 December 1999 the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office charged the applicant in absentia and placed him on the wanted list; the investigation concerning him was suspended until his apprehension, while proceedings continued against other suspects.

On 23 December 2002 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal convicted and sentenced G., P. and F. for those crimes. On 2 February 2004 the Slavyansk Local Court ordered the applicant’s detention. On 28 June 2007 he was apprehended in the Smolensk region, Russia. On 31 March 2008, after extradition to Ukraine, the investigation was resumed. He was charged with participation in an organised criminal group together with G., P., F. and two deceased persons. He was accused of strangling A., killing four persons with G. in 1996, and inflicting grievous bodily harm on R. in a murder attempt linked to extortion of R.’s brother; all allegedly as a group. On 22 May 2008 the investigation was completed, and on 26 June 2008 the case was transferred to the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal.

On 10 July 2009 that court, as a first-instance court, found the applicant guilty of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant and his lawyer appealed, saying guilt had not been proved. On 15 July 2010 the Supreme Court upheld the judgment. The same day his lawyer submitted an additional appeal arguing that the Court of Appeal should have applied the most favourable wording of the Criminal Code, in force between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000, when the death penalty had already been abolished but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. The Supreme Court stated that the sentence had been correct.

Under the 1960 Criminal Code, before 29 December 1999, aggravated murder under Article 93 was punishable by eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment or death. On 29 December 1999 the Constitutional Court declared the death penalty unconstitutional and void from that date. Law no. 1483 of 22 February 2000 replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment; it entered into force on 29 March 2000. The 2001 Criminal Code provided for ten to fifteen years’ imprisonment or life imprisonment for aggravated murder under Article 115 § 2. A 2008 Amendment Act on Humanisation established retroactive application of laws mitigating criminal liability. On 26 January 2011 the Constitutional Court held that after 29 December 1999 the 1960 Code had not become a new law mitigating liability for particularly serious crimes and that the interim period did not mean the sanction provided only a maximum fifteen-year term. It concluded that the amendments introduced by Law no. 1483 replacing the death penalty with life imprisonment should be understood as a new act mitigating liability with retroactive effect.

case_name: CASE OF MIHHAILOV v. ESTONIA
summary:
Aleksandr Mihhailov, a stateless person born in 1976 living in Narva, lodged an application with the European Court on 28 October 2010, alleging that police had used unwarranted violence during his arrest and later detention at a police station.

On 29 April 2009, shortly before 6 p.m., Narva police received a call about two men near Kreenholmi and Kerese streets; one was reportedly carrying a knife, while the other was drunk and had difficulty walking. Officers S.B. and E.V. found the applicant and M.Z. at a public playground. The applicant alleged that, although drunk, he was not aggressive or abusive; S.B. punched him in the jaw, he fell and briefly lost consciousness, was handcuffed, and was then punched and kicked until he lost consciousness, waking at the police station. The Government, relying on the criminal investigation, stated that the applicant behaved aggressively, swore, waved his hands, and disobeyed orders. E.V. forced him to the ground; Officers S.J. and N.S. helped handcuff him. He resisted, kicked the police car, and was restrained on the ground. While being placed in the van, he hit his left temple against the door. He remained aggressive during transport.

At the police station, the applicant alleged that S.B. kneed him near the left ear, repeatedly punched and kicked him, at one point put his head under a running tap, and beat him again after E.V. returned; he lost consciousness and later had blood on his face. The Government said he remained aggressive and was restrained; he fell off a chair twice, and officers later left him on the floor. At 7.45 p.m. a report was drafted stating he had been taken to sober up and noting a dirty face and abrasions on his head.

At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009 an ambulance was called. The applicant complained of head and wrist pain, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss in his left ear. He was found to have haematomas on the left cranium and a swollen right wrist, and was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and a fracture of the right hand/wrist. He was taken to hospital, where he was diagnosed with concussion. A CT scan at 6.26 a.m. showed no haemorrhage or intracranial pathology, and he was released. At 2.15 a.m. police took a statement from him at the hospital, and at 2.40 a.m. drafted a misdemeanour report alleging drunkenness and breach of the peace. On 1 May 2009 an ambulance was again called; he was diagnosed with concussion and had a haematoma around the left ear, oedema around the left eye, and bruises on the neck and upper limbs.

On 30 April 2009 the applicant complained to police of ill-treatment. After initial difficulties, a criminal investigation was opened on 5 May 2009. Investigators took statements from the applicant, M.Z., detainees A.P., M.S., and R.L., police officers, children who witnessed the arrest, and ambulance staff. A.P. and R.L. said they heard or saw the applicant being beaten at the station; M.S. heard shouting but saw no beating. M.Z. said he saw the applicant beaten at the station, but later, during photo identification, said there had been no beating at the playground. The children said officers used force but did not punch or kick the applicant during the arrest. A forensic medical expert concluded on 13 August 2009 that the injuries had been caused by blunt force, likely shortly before the applicant saw a doctor, possibly on 29 April 2009, but the exact cause could not be established.

On 20 January 2010 the police investigator discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no evidence that officers had committed abuse of authority and that the force used had been lawful and not excessive. The prosecutor approved this on 15 February 2010. The applicant appealed on 15 March 2010, but the State Prosecutor’s Office rejected the appeal as out of time on 23 March 2010, and the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 30 April 2010.

Separately, on 25 May 2009 the East Police Prefecture fined the applicant for breach of the peace. On 17 November 2010 the Viru County Court acquitted him, finding no evidence of the misdemeanour, setting aside unlawfully obtained hospital statements, finding M.Z. reliable that police had unduly influenced him by letting him hear the applicant being beaten, and concluding that evidence had been collected unlawfully, infringing the applicant’s honour and dignity and endangering his health.

Aleksandr Mihhailov, a stateless person born in 1976 living in Narva, lodged an application with the European Court on 28 October 2010, alleging that police had used unwarranted violence during his arrest and later detention at a police station.

Officers S.B. and E.V. found the applicant and M.Z. at a public playground. At the police station, the applicant alleged that S.B. kneed him near the left ear, repeatedly punched and kicked him, at one point put his head under a running tap, and beat him again after E.V. returned; he lost consciousness and later had blood on his face. At 7.45 p.m. a report was drafted stating he had been taken to sober up and noting a dirty face and abrasions on his head.

He was found to have haematomas on the left cranium and a swollen right wrist, and was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and a fracture of the right hand/wrist. At 2.15 a.m. police took a statement from him at the hospital, and at 2.40 a.m. drafted a misdemeanour report alleging drunkenness and breach of the peace. case_name: CASE OF KOPRIVNIKAR v. SLOVENIA
summary:
Mr Boštjan Koprivnikar, born in 1979 and detained in Dob pri Mirni, lodged application no. 67503/13 against Slovenia. He alleged that the overall thirty-year prison sentence imposed on him breached Article 7 of the Convention. He was represented by M. Petek; the Government by A. Vran.

On 23 April 1999 the 1999 Amendment to the 1994 Criminal Code entered into force. It introduced a maximum thirty-year prison sentence for the most serious intentional offences. The then applicable rules on combining multiple sentences provided that if any offence carried a thirty-year sentence, only that sentence was to be imposed; otherwise, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years’ imprisonment.

On 17 September 2004 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of robbery and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. He served that sentence from 7 December 2007 to 7 December 2011.

On 1 November 2008 the 2008 Criminal Code entered into force. It set the general maximum term at thirty years and introduced life imprisonment for certain serious crimes. Its Article 53 provided that if two or more thirty-year sentences were imposed, an overall life sentence was to be imposed; if prison sentences were imposed for all multiple offences, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years. It contained no separate rule for the situation where only one of the combined sentences was thirty years.

On 16 June 2009 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of paying with a bad cheque and fraudulent use of a bank card between 19 January and 19 August 2005, sentencing him to five months’ imprisonment. That judgment became final on 7 October 2009, and he began serving the sentence on 7 December 2011.

In the meantime, on 9 April 2009 the Ljubljana District Court found the applicant guilty, with another person, of murder committed on 15 September 2002. It sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment, the maximum under the 1994 Criminal Code applicable at the time of the offence. The Ljubljana Higher Court upheld the conviction on 9 December 2009, and it became final that day.

On 28 November 2011 the applicant applied to the Ljubljana District Court to join the three prison terms into an overall sentence. On 13 January 2012 the District Court joined the three sentences—including the completed robbery sentence—and imposed an overall thirty-year sentence. Applying the 2008 Criminal Code before the 2011 Amendment, it noted that Article 53 conditions had been met but not previously applied. It acknowledged that Article 53 § 2(2) provided a maximum of twenty years, but held that the legislature had made an obvious error, later rectified by the 2011 Amendment, because the 1994 Code had provided that a thirty-year sentence combined with others would consist only of that term.

The applicant appealed, arguing lack of legal basis, breach of the rule of law and nullum crimen et nulla poena sine lege, and that semantic interpretation should prevail and ambiguities should not be construed to his detriment. On 29 May 2012 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal and upheld the judgment, reiterating the lower court’s reasoning. On 6 December 2012 the Supreme Court rejected his application for protection of legality, disagreeing that semantic interpretation had priority and relying on historical and systematic interpretation. On 24 April 2013 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint.

On 24 March 2015 the applicant was convicted of another murder committed between 30 June and 15 September 2002 and sentenced to thirty years; a new overall thirty-year sentence covered the prior overall sentence, another four-month sentence, and the new thirty-year sentence. His appeal and protection-of-legality application were dismissed, the latter by the Supreme Court on 2 June 2016.

case_name: CASE OF THUO v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, David William Thuo, a Kenyan national born in 1978, complained under Article 3 about his conditions of detention at Nicosia Central Prisons, his ill-treatment during deportation on 9 March 2007, and the absence of an effective investigation into that ill-treatment.

He entered Cyprus unlawfully on 4 April 2005 and was arrested at Larnaca Airport on 6 April 2005 attempting to travel on a forged passport. On 12 April 2005 the Larnaca District Court sentenced him to nine months’ imprisonment after a guilty plea. He was held in Wing 1B of Nicosia Central Prisons; his appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 4 July 2005. He applied for asylum on 21 April 2005. On 10 November 2005 detention and deportation orders were issued against him as a “prohibited immigrant,” but enforcement was suspended pending his asylum claim. Released on 14 November 2005 after serving his sentence, he was re-arrested the same day and placed in immigration detention in Block 10. His asylum application was rejected on 31 January 2006; an appeal was dismissed on 6 April 2006, and he brought a Supreme Court recourse on 3 May 2006. He also complained to the Ombudsman on 11 June 2006 and, through counsel, wrote to the Minister of the Interior in May and August 2006.

Deportation was initially impossible because he lacked a travel document and refused to cooperate. After the Kenyan Embassy issued a travel document on 20 February 2007 in the name David Kandiri Wanjiku, new orders were issued on 22 February 2007. He was deported on 9 March 2007 and placed on the authorities’ stop list. His Supreme Court recourse was withdrawn on 9 May 2007.

According to the applicant, early on 9 March 2007 prison guards and two immigration officers insulted him, refused his request to call a lawyer, pushed him, hit him, pinched his testicles and held his neck; he was later allowed to call his lawyer. At Larnaca Airport, three men in military uniform and two immigration officers allegedly beat and verbally abused him, forced him into a chair, held him by the neck, stuffed brown paper into his mouth, taped his mouth and neck with Cyprus Airways adhesive tape, and wrapped bandages around his head and neck. He was handcuffed on the aircraft and remained in pain until near Milan. He alleged four top teeth later became loose and said he could identify the officers.

He complained to the Ombudsman on 27 December 2007. Her report of 4 June 2009 found the allegations not substantiated, noting difficulties in gathering evidence after deportation. He complained to the IAIACAP on 23 February 2008. After a preliminary investigation, on 9 July 2008 the IAIACAP considered the complaint investigable but sought the Attorney General’s opinion; on 28 July 2008 counsel for the Attorney General said it could not be investigated because the applicant had left Cyprus. On 17 June 2009 the Attorney General ordered a formal investigation, which began on 14 July 2009. The investigator collected police records; airport CCTV had been destroyed, and the cabin crew report did not mention the incident. Five officers were treated as suspects. On 12 June 2010 the applicant returned and was medically examined: the maxillofacial surgeon could not attribute tooth damage with certainty after three years; the urologist found no issues; a forensic pathologist considered ill-treatment minimal to negligible. On 17 June 2010 an identity parade took place; N.S., Pa.P. and A.I. were absent, but the applicant identified them from photographs. T.C. and Po.P. denied ill-treatment but later said the applicant tried to harm himself and was wrapped in bandages to protect him, not gagged. N.S. and A.I. refused to answer questions. The investigator’s report of 22 July 2010 noted deficient records, possible exaggeration by the applicant, uniform discrepancies and the failure of some officers to attend the parade; he considered force may have exceeded permissible limits but favoured disciplinary action. The IAIACAP found only necessary force had been used and the applicant self-serving. On 2 September 2010 the Attorney General decided no criminal or disciplinary action was merited; the Chief of Police took no disciplinary action but issued recording instructions and held lectures.

As to detention conditions, the applicant alleged a shared 5.5 sq. m cell, no exercise, poor hygiene and overcrowding, including after a May 2006 fire and renovation work. The Government described a cell of about 2.73 by 2 m with hygiene facilities, air conditioning, communal areas and outdoor access, and renovation from October 2005 to October 2010. IAIACAP material recorded 36 cells of 5.4 sq. m, about one hour daily outdoor exercise, up to 58 detainees in February 2007, and isolation for refusing cleaning. The applicant told the investigator that treatment was good but conditions were not.

case_name: CASE OF CELA AND OTHERS v. GREECE
summary:
The application was lodged on 28 January 2014 by six Albanian and Greek nationals against Greece. They were represented by K. Tsitselikis and A. Spathis. The Greek Government was represented by State Legal Council delegates; the Albanian Government did not intervene. At the time of lodging, the applicants were detained in Korydallos Prison, Athens.

The first applicant was held in Korydallos from 7 March 2013 and remained there when observations were submitted, except for temporary transfers to Ioannina Prison (3–11 July 2013) and Komotini Prison (2–17 December 2013). The second applicant was detained in Korydallos from 22 March 2013 and the third from 21 August 2013; both remained detained when they submitted observations. The fourth applicant was in Korydallos from 26 June 2013 to 1 May 2014, except for periods in Chania Prison from 17 July to 3 September 2013, 27 November to 10 December 2013, and 6–17 February 2014. The fifth applicant was in Korydallos from 22 May 2013 to 19 June 2014, except 20–28 March 2013. The sixth was in Korydallos from 30 January 2013 to 15 August 2014.

The applicants alleged overcrowding: the prison held about 2,400 prisoners though designed for 700. They were detained in wings A and D in 9 sq m cells, including sanitary facilities, shared by three or four prisoners, leaving under 3 sq m each. Toilets were only partially separated; heating and hot water were insufficient; inmates used a washbasin to wash themselves, dishes and clothes. Cells were dirty and infested with cockroaches and pests, with no extermination. Rubbish was not properly collected and food remains stayed in cells and corridors for days. Prisoners were not adequately separated by health condition or drug use. Medical care was inadequate, especially psychological care. Inmates were confined to cells 16 hours daily, with no recreational or educational activities, and ate poor-quality meals in cells. The prison was understaffed and unsafe.

The Government submitted that the first to fifth applicants were held in wings A and D. Cells measured 9.60 sq m and held three, rarely four, detainees. The first applicant was also held in wing E: one cell of 10.44 sq m and another of 42.78 sq m holding 10–22 detainees, though 22 only briefly. All cells had windows with sufficient light and were furnished with washbasin, toilet, beds, table, chairs and usually shelves. Wings A–D had twelve communal showers each and wing E nine; each wing provided 2,000 litres of hot water daily. Sheets and blankets were provided unless detainees used their own. There was central heating and summer fans. Cells were disinfected and cleaned twice daily by detainee crews; rubbish bins existed. The infirmary was open 24 hours with eighteen doctors and three nurses; transfers to Korydallos Prison Hospital, Psychiatric Hospital or external hospitals were possible. Medical records showed treatment, and social services assisted. Menus were varied. Prisoners had four to five hours daily in the yard, sport, television, a lending library and book club, jobs, and “second chance” school. The Government made no observations on the sixth applicant.

The CPT’s report on its April 2013 visit, published 16 October 2014, stated that Korydallos Men’s Prison held more than 2,300 prisoners for an official capacity of 840. Cells designed for single occupancy, measuring 9.5 sq m, routinely held three or four inmates; some slept on mattresses on the floor or in toilet areas. Cell A-3 in wing E measured 36 sq m, had 16 beds but held 27 inmates, leaving under 1.5 sq m per person; nine slept on the concrete floor on filthy mattresses, two in the toilet area, and the cell was infested with cockroaches and bed bugs. Cell B-3 had 14 beds and held 19 prisoners, five on mattresses on the floor; there was no artificial light at night and the toilet was filthy. Garbage containers were full of food waste. Health-care resources had deteriorated: four GP posts were abolished, no full-time doctor worked there, visiting GPs provided only 15 hours weekly and sometimes failed to attend, and two-monthly rotations hindered continuity; the CPT considered at least four full-time GPs necessary. A wing of about 400 inmates usually had one or two officers by day; at night eight officers covered the entire prison.

The relevant domestic law and practice were described in the earlier judgment Kanakis v. Greece (no. 2).

Cells designed for single occupancy, measuring 9.5 sq m, routinely held three or four inmates; some slept on mattresses on the floor or in toilet areas. Cell A-3 in wing E measured 36 sq m, had 16 beds but held 27 inmates, leaving under 1.5 sq m per person; nine slept on the concrete floor on filthy mattresses, two in the toilet area, and the cell was infested with cockroaches and bed bugs. Cell B-3 had 14 beds and held 19 prisoners, five on mattresses on the floor; there was no artificial light at night and the toilet was filthy. Garbage containers were full of food waste. case_name: CASE OF VAN WESENBEECK v. BELGIUM
summary:
The case concerns two applications against Belgium brought by Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, a Dutch national born in 1961 and living in Beveren. He alleged that he had not received a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 and that his defence rights under Article 6 § 3 (d) were breached because he was unable to question the undercover agents involved.

On 10 May 2006, the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation against the applicant and others on suspicion of drug trafficking, involvement in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. It included infiltration; observation was authorised on 1 August 2006. A separate confidential file was established. The proactive investigation continued until 17 September 2008. Reports of 17 and 18 September 2008 summarised the evidence and the infiltration and observation operations and were added to the criminal file. On 18 September 2008 the public prosecutor confirmed the authorisations and requested that the investigating judge open a judicial investigation. A reactive investigation followed before the Hasselt investigating judge, also using phone-tapping and international mutual legal assistance. A report of 25 September 2008 referred to information on the criminal organisation and confirmations obtained through the special investigative measures. On 20 October 2008 the Federal Prosecutor’s Office took over the case, still under the Hasselt investigating judge.

The observation and infiltration operations ended on 14 June 2009, when several suspects, including the applicant, were arrested and placed in pre-trial detention. On 29 December 2009 the Federal Prosecutor asked the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal to verify the confidential file under Article 235ter of the Code of Criminal Procedure; the parties also sought a lawfulness review under Article 235bis. At a hearing on 2 March 2010, the Federal Prosecutor was heard separately in the absence of the parties, and the confidential file was made available to the Division. The defendants, including the applicant, then presented their case with their lawyers.

By interim judgment of 20 May 2010, the Indictments Division held that it had to verify information concerning both the reactive and proactive investigations, found that some evidence had still to be added to the criminal file, and reopened proceedings. The 18 September 2008 decisions and the 25 September 2008 report were then added. On 24 June 2010 the Indictments Division declared the criminal file complete and found no nullity, irregularity or violation of legal or Convention provisions. It also found no irregularities in the special investigative methods, stating that the proactive investigation had complied with conditions including reasonable suspicion, proportionality and subsidiarity; a debit indicator found on 15 August 2008 was decisive.

The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 21 September 2010. His complaint that the file lacked the report underlying the 10 May 2006 proactive investigation and related documents was rejected as requiring a factual assessment. On 29 September 2010 the Hasselt Court committed seventeen defendants, including the applicant, for trial.

On 16 March 2011 the Hasselt Court of First Instance sentenced the applicant to ten years’ imprisonment and fined him 137,500 euros for drug trafficking, involvement in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. The judgment relied partly on evidence obtained through the special investigative methods. The court refused the applicant’s request for a face-to-face meeting with the undercover agents, citing lack of necessity, the agents’ safety and anonymity, the long infiltration, friendships formed, alleged online exposure, unclear specific questions, and the Indictments Division’s verification. It also rejected claims of incitement, finding that the agent acted only in relation to an offence from January to June 2009, while the judicial investigation had begun on 18 September 2008, and that reports, messages and calls showed no incitement.

On 23 June 2011 the Antwerp Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment in absentia. On 13 October 2011, after adversarial proceedings, it confirmed the judgment. It again refused a face-to-face meeting, referring to the lower court’s reasoning, adding that it gave only relative evidentiary value to the agents’ statements and that other evidence established guilt; it also considered the request rather academic because the applicant had refused to appear. The applicant appealed on points of law, alleging breaches of fair-trial and defence rights, the adversarial principle, use of evidence from the undisclosed confidential file, and the refusal of a face-to-face meeting. On 20 March 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that lack of access to the confidential file did not in itself violate Article 6, that the restriction was justified by protection of investigative techniques and the safety and anonymity of those implementing them, and was counterbalanced by oversight by the Indictments Division and the ability to contest the methods. As to the face-to-face meeting, it held that Article 6 § 3 (d) did not prevent the judge from assessing the necessity and relevance of hearing a requested witness.

case_name: CASE OF M.O. v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The applicant, M.O., is an Eritrean national born in 1990. He grew up in Eritrea, entered Switzerland illegally on 23 June 2014 and applied for asylum the next day. He was heard by the Swiss asylum authorities on 1 July 2014, 11 March 2015 and 29 January 2016, with an interpreter and translated records; NGO witnesses attended the later hearings. He claimed he left school after eighth grade, was called up for military service, tried to avoid it, reported for duty, attempted to escape, was caught, beaten and imprisoned in Wi’a. In the first hearing he said he was detained from June 2012 to September 2013; in the second he said March to October 2013. He described limited military training, no weapon use, and no superior, unit or military number. He said he escaped from prison, stayed briefly in Eritrea, left illegally via Mereb on 3 October 2013, was picked up by Ethiopian soldiers and later registered in the Hitsas refugee camp. In the third hearing he said a smuggler, not a neighbour, had helped him; he left A. at about 6 p.m., lost his way and was apprehended around 3–4 a.m. He submitted a student card, church deacon card, Italian food-distribution card, marriage certificate from 2010, his son’s baptism certificate from 2012, a deacon attestation and a UNHCR letter confirming registration in Hitsas on 8 November 2013. He stated he was married and had a son born in October 2012.

On 8 March 2016 the State Secretariat for Migration rejected the asylum request and ordered his departure. It found his account not credible because of contradictions about the detention period, military training, schooling, departure and illegal exit. On 14 April 2016 the applicant appealed to the Federal Administrative Court. He argued that his deacon status had delayed conscription until the 2010 change in practice, that poor students were sent to Wi’a, that he tried to escape and was detained from March to September 2013, and that his family arranged a smuggler. He attributed date errors to poor education, stressed consistent elements, scars and fear, and relied on the UNHCR registration and the impossibility of legal exit. He claimed refugee status for fear of ill-treatment for desertion, alternatively temporary admission based on post-flight grounds and Article 3.

On 9 May 2016 the Federal Administrative Court rejected the appeal. It found the asylum claim not credibly demonstrated, citing irreconcilable school dates, a substance-poor military account, and fundamental contradictions on detention duration and dates. It found his departure account insufficient and said the UNHCR camp letter did not establish individual persecution risk. It held removal possible, permitted and reasonable under the Aliens Act, noting he was young, healthy and had a support network. The State Secretariat set a voluntary departure deadline that expired on 17 July 2016.

The record also contains country information describing Eritrea’s open-ended national service, forced labour, punishment of deserters and draft evaders, strict exit controls and risks for illegal exit and returnees, including detention and ill-treatment. The applicant alleged before the Court that expulsion to Eritrea would violate Articles 3 and 4 of the Convention.

case_name: CASE OF NICHOLAS v. CYPRUS
summary:
Mr Charalambos Nicholas, born in 1951 and living in Larnaca, is a Cypriot and British national. After his dismissal from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot, on 26 June 1998 he brought a civil action before the District Court of Nicosia for wrongful dismissal and defamation (no. 7562/98). The defendant company was represented by a law firm. On 29 December 2006 the District Court dismissed the action. On 9 February 2007 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 43/07); a bench of three judges heard the appeal. At the hearing on 11 March 2007, Mr P.G.P., managing partner of the defendant’s law firm, appeared for the defendant company and addressed the Supreme Court. Other lawyers from the same firm had previously appeared before the appeal bench for the defendant. On 21 April 2010 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal unanimously.

The applicant alleged that after the Supreme Court judgment he discovered that the son of one of the judges on the bench, Judge A.K., and the daughter of Mr P.G.P. were married and both worked at Mr P.G.P.’s law firm. His domestic lawyer had not requested the judge’s exemption because he lacked sufficient knowledge of the relevant facts at the time. The applicant had not instructed him to do so because he found out only after the appeal ended. The applicant complained of a lack of impartiality, under the objective test, concerning Judge A.K.

Under the code of judicial practice adopted on 17 March 1988 and amended on 21 July 1989, 18 September 2003, 30 November 2006 and 4 October 2011, the version applicable when the applicant’s case was heard—after the 30 November 2006 amendment—provided that a judge did not sit alone or on a bench at any level in cases in which lawyers appearing before him or her were close relatives. Close relatives were parents, spouses, children, children’s spouses, siblings, siblings’ children and siblings’ spouses. The practice did not apply to minor matters. The earlier version, as amended on 21 July 1989, had also excluded cases where lawyers appearing were partners or employers of a judge’s close relatives; the 30 November 2006 amendment removed that stipulation. A later amendment of 4 October 2011 added spiritual relationships, father-in-law/son-in-law relationships and relationships between fathers-in-law. Judges precluded from sitting, or who for personal reasons considered it inadvisable to sit, were exempted. The Supreme Court examined the composition of its bench only when a party raised the issue; recusal for personal reasons was at the judge’s exclusive discretion.

Domestic law on finality provided that once a judgment was delivered, signed and filed, the court could not rehear arguments or change or set it aside, except in limited circumstances: under Order 25, Rule 6 for clerical mistakes or accidental slips or omissions; under Order 35, Rule 13 where an appeal dismissed for non-appearance could be reinstated; and under the Supreme Court’s exceptional inherent jurisdiction to correct errors or omissions, set aside an order or judgment on appeal, or reopen an appeal. That inherent power was limited, including to errors or omissions reflecting the court’s manifest intention or to facts arising after judgment was reserved, and did not permit reopening to raise new arguments. In Educational Service Commission v. Zena Poulli (19 November 2001), the full bench set aside an appeal judgment because interested parties had not been notified of the appeal or counter-appeal and ordered a rehearing. In Ioannis Adamou and others (15 October 2015), the Supreme Court reopened a case because it had not examined a preliminary objection and corresponding grounds of appeal.

case_name: CASE OF KEŠELJ AND OTHERS v. MONTENEGRO
summary:
The case originated in an application against Montenegro lodged on 24 May 2011 by ten nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants were represented by Mr I. Darmanović, a lawyer practising in Podgorica. The Montenegrin Government were represented by their Agent, Ms V. Pavličić. The applicants’ complaints concerned the non-enforcement of a final court settlement concluded in their favour.

On 28 February 1996, the applicants and the debtor, JSP “Tara” Cetinje, reached a court-approved settlement before the Cetinje Municipal Court. Under the settlement, the debtor undertook to pay the applicants specified amounts in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The settlement became final on the same date. The debtor ultimately paid only part of the amounts determined in the settlement.

On 26 May 1997, the Podgorica Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 19 August 1997, the applicants submitted their respective claims based on the settlement. In the course of the insolvency proceedings, the Podgorica Commercial Court acknowledged the applicants’ claims.

On 23 December 2009, the Podgorica Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor, but continued the proceedings against the debtor’s estate. That decision was upheld by the Appellate Court on 9 April 2010. The proceedings are still pending.

On 14 October 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds.

The court settlement in question remains partly unenforced to the present day.

As to the debtor’s legal status, it appears from the case file that, at the time the court settlement was concluded and became final, the debtor was a company predominantly comprised of State-controlled capital. The Government neither contested this nor provided any evidence to the contrary.

case_name: CASE OF DANILCZUK v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, Robert Tadeusz Danilczuk, a Polish national born in 1965 and currently detained in Czarne Prison, Poland, brought an application against Cyprus concerning conditions at Nicosia Central Prisons.

On 14 September 2010 he was placed in detention on remand at Nicosia Central Prisons pending criminal proceedings before the Limassol District Court (case no. 25536/10). On 11 January 2011 he was convicted of offences including burglary, theft, road traffic offences and unlawful residence. On 24 January 2011 the court imposed four concurrent sentences ranging from six months to two years, running from 5 September 2010. He was released on 18 May 2012 after his sentence was suspended by presidential decree.

The applicant alleged that he had been held in overcrowded cells with only 0.5 to 1.7 sq. m of personal space. He said the cells were cold and lacked adequate light; there were no toilets in the cells; he sometimes waited two to three hours to use a toilet; and when the cells were locked he had to urinate into a bottle and defecate into a waste bag. He did not specify the exact periods.

The Government stated that he had been detained from 14 September 2010 to 18 May 2012 in three parts of the prison. From 14 September 2010 to 24 January 2011 he was in Block 5, which held remand prisoners; after conviction he was transferred to Block 2B, where he remained until 5 October 2011; and from 5 October 2011 until his release he was in Block 2A. Block 5 had up to 68 remand prisoners, 34 double cells of 6.21 sq. m, eight toilets and eight showers; it was almost certain he shared a cell, giving him 3.10 sq. m. Block 2B, then unrenovated, had 26 double cells of 9.98 sq. m, two large cells of 19.55 sq. m accommodating five to seven detainees, and a 90 sq. m dormitory for 20 to 50 inmates; daily occupancy varied from 80 to 124. Depending on placement, his personal space could have been 4.99 sq. m in a double cell, about 2.8–3.9 sq. m in a larger cell, or 1.8–4.5 sq. m in the dormitory; in spring or winter, with 94–110 inmates, it would have been 2.04–3.2 sq. m. Block 2A, renovated, had 41 double cells of 9.80 sq. m for 82 prisoners, giving 4.9 sq. m, and six toilets, six showers and three urinals. General conditions included central heating, corridor air conditioning, cell fans, insulated windows, and movement outside cells from 6 a.m. to 5/6 p.m. and within blocks until 9/10 p.m. Following the CPT’s 2012 report, the prison discontinued switching off cell bells at night; order no. 32/2008 provided for toilet access, though no records were kept of night openings; detainees could leave up to three times between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m.

The CPT’s 2012 report on its 2008 visit found severe overcrowding, prisoners lacking night toilet access, and degrading use of makeshift receptacles. Its 2014 report on a 2013 visit welcomed renovation of Block 2 but found continuing overcrowding and difficulty accessing toilets at night. The Ombudsman’s 6 September 2011 report similarly described crowded, unsuitable detention areas, insufficient hygiene facilities, and complaints that deactivated night cell bells forced detainees to use bottles and waste bags. Domestic law provided for damages for violations of detainees’ rights, and the Ombudsman served as national preventive mechanism under the Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture.

case_name: CASE OF KHANI KABBARA v. CYPRUS
summary:
The applicant, Hani Abdul Khani Kabbara, a Canadian national born in 1984 and living in Canada, lodged an application against Cyprus on 29 March 2012. He alleged ill-treatment by police officers during detention at Limassol central police station and the absence of an effective investigation into his complaint.

On 27 February 2011, police were informed of illegal ATM withdrawals with a fake credit card in Limassol. The applicant alleged that, while in front of the ATM, he was attacked from behind by a police officer, arrested without a warrant, and taken to the police station, where he was detained for six hours with his hands handcuffed behind his back. He said officers tortured him to confess to theft using a forged credit card, repeatedly beat him with a wooden stick and a metal chair, punched and kicked him, broke a tooth, threatened to kill him, refused him asthma medicine and hospital care until his lawyer, C.H., intervened. He was taken to hospital around 3.30 p.m. He alleged that police told the doctor he had fallen, that no painkillers were given until the Canadian Consul visited, and that the doctor gave no proper explanation.

The Government’s account, based on investigation files, was that Special Constable G.S., in uniform, approached the applicant at the ATM, identified himself as police, and asked for identification. The applicant allegedly struck him and fled; during the chase he fell and hit his head. A struggle followed. He was arrested for assaulting a police officer and resisting lawful arrest. He was taken to the police station around 9.30 a.m., searched, and handed to the Economic Crime Investigations Office. An interview took place between 1 p.m. and 1.30 p.m. with an interpreter. At about 1.35 p.m., a body search recorded abrasions on his left forehead and left shoulder blade. His lawyer visited from 3.05 p.m. to 3.30 p.m. and complained that the applicant had been ill-treated. He was taken to Limassol General Hospital around 3.50 p.m. A District Court arrest warrant was issued at 3.30 p.m. He was discharged at 11.20 p.m. On 28 February and 8 March 2011, the District Court ordered and extended his detention on remand; on 16 March 2011, it ordered detention pending trial.

Medical examinations at Limassol General Hospital recorded a cephalohaematoma, abrasions, nasal oedema, a bruised lip, a broken upper incisor, chest bruising, wrist abrasions/oedema, knee abrasions and spinal sensitivity. CT scans showed no fractures. A private practitioner, Dr S.J., examined the applicant on 7 March 2011 and noted restricted movement, cervical tension, a 10 x 5 cm chest bruise and loss of half an upper incisor. G.S. was also examined and diagnosed with lumbar strain, and was given nine days’ sick leave.

On 2 March 2011, police appointed Chief Inspector M.M. to conduct an administrative investigation. M.M.’s report of 26 April 2011 found the ill-treatment allegations unproven and recommended closing the case. In July 2011, the Attorney General referred the complaint to the Independent Authority for the Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police. Investigator A.S. reported on 10 October 2011, singling out four officers as suspects. He found the applicant’s testimony unconvincing and concluded that no criminal or disciplinary charges were justified. The IAIACAP president adopted the findings on 16 November 2011, although he rejected evidence that the applicant had no external injuries. On 13 February 2012, the Attorney General concluded that some force had been used but that it was necessary and proportionate to prevent the applicant from fleeing, and closed the file.

In separate criminal proceedings, the applicant was charged with 439 offences, later reduced to theft, assault occasioning actual bodily harm to G.S., and resisting lawful arrest. On 14 September 2012, the District Court convicted him on all counts; on 19 September 2012, it imposed concurrent sentences. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 19 February 2013. He was then deported and placed on a stop list.

On 9 April 2013, after gaps and inconsistencies were identified, the Attorney General appointed two new investigators. They treated nine officers as suspects, took statements from forty-nine people, including the Canadian Consul, and gathered CCTV, photographs, police diaries and court records. The Canadian Consul’s statement of 22 April 2013 described the applicant at the hospital as being in a wheelchair and on a drip.

case_name: CASE OF DELECOLLE v. FRANCE
summary:
Mr Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937 and living in Paris, lodged an application against France on 5 June 2013. He alleged a violation of Article 12, complaining that he had been denied the right to marry because his marriage was subject to the authorisation of his supervisor or the guardianship judge.

On 23 June 2009, when he was seventy-two, the guardianship judge of the Paris District Court of the 15th Administrative District placed him under enhanced protective supervision (curatelle renforcée) for five years, following an initial request by his adoptive daughter. The judge relied on medical certificates from Dr M.F. (25 November 2008) and Dr J.-P.B. (14 March 2009), and appointed M.-C.M. as supervisor. The applicant sought lifting of the measure, or ordinary supervision, or reduction to twenty-four months. On 18 December 2009 the Paris Regional Court dismissed those requests. It noted that Dr R. had excluded dementia but found slight cognitive impairment and psychological fragility and vulnerability, and that the applicant lacked capacity to manage or dispose of his property, though he could hold a bank account and cash card.

The applicant asked his supervisor to authorise his marriage to M.S., a friend since 1996 and his partner since 2008. The supervisor interviewed them separately and together and refused on 17 December 2009, stating that she had known the applicant only a few months. On 21 December 2009 the guardianship judge ordered a social inquiry by the UDAF into the applicant’s living conditions, lifestyle, social status and circle of friends. The applicant appealed against that order. That same day the judge also commissioned a medical opinion on his capacity to marry. On 18 January 2010 the psychiatrist reported that the applicant suffered from intellectual disorders; while able to consent to marriage, he was considered incapable of dealing with its property and financial consequences. The psychiatrist also gave personal opinions and described some of the applicant’s arguments as bordering on absurd.

On 1 March 2010 the Paris Court of Appeal declared the appeal against the inquiry order inadmissible. It held that a vulnerable adult’s interests allowed the guardianship judge to order such inquiries, and that a supervisee could marry only with the supervisor’s authorisation or, failing that, the judge’s. On 1 June 2010 the UDAF reported a financial stake at the heart of a major family conflict; the applicant’s daughter and M.S. accused each other of being interested in his fortune, and it was unclear whether he was being influenced. The applicant was deeply affected and appeared to see marriage as ensuring assistance and companionship.

On 24 June 2010 the guardianship judge, after hearing the applicant and his daughter, dismissed the marriage request. The judge found his attachment to M.S. insufficient, noted that both were former alcoholics and that the applicant apparently still drank, and considered that he sought safety against a break-up and loneliness. Financial implications were unclear because he was torn between his daughter and M.S. The applicant appealed.

On 6 September 2011 the Paris Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. It cited serious disorders and the medical certificates, stating that anosognosia prevented him from planning joint life and understanding marriage’s financial and legal implications. It noted unreasonable management since living with M.S., 250,000 euros of work after his wife’s death, questionable storage of furniture, a draft handwritten will of 14 August 2009 in M.S.’s favour, assets of about 6,000,000 euros, and deteriorated relations with his daughter M.D. It concluded that mutual affection existed but that his psychopathological condition and failing grasp of finances prevented informed consent.

The applicant appealed on points of law and raised a QPC on Article 460(1) of the Civil Code. On 29 June 2012 the Constitutional Council declared that provision constitutional. On 5 December 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that the Court of Appeal had lawfully reasoned from the medical certificates and file that he could not give informed consent. The applicant died on 4 February 2016; M.S. later indicated an intention to pursue the application.

case_name: CASE OF DOYLE v. IRELAND
summary:
The applicant, Barry Doyle, an Irish national born in 1985 and serving a life sentence for murder, lodged an application against Ireland on 12 July 2017. He complained that, after his arrest, he was not entitled to have a solicitor present during police interrogation, representing an alleged failure by the State to vindicate his fair-trial right under Article 6 § 3 (c).

On 9 November 2008, the applicant killed S.G., aged 28, in Limerick. It was a case of mistaken identity: the applicant had set out to kill another man at the behest of a criminal figure during a gang feud. He shot and wounded S.G. in the street, pursued him into a back garden and shot him several times, inflicting five wounds including a fatal head wound.

On 24 February 2009, police searched the applicant’s residence and arrested him at 7.15 a.m.; he was brought to a police station shortly before 8.00 a.m. He was informed of his rights, including access to a solicitor, and requested a particular solicitor, who was notified. case_name: CASE OF FILOZOFENKO v. UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938 who lives in the Odessa Region. She holds the special status of a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006 (“the 2006 Act”). A “child of war” is defined there as a person who on 2 September 1945 was no more than 18 years of age. Under section 6 of the 2006 Act, the applicant was entitled to a special supplement to her pension amounting to 30% of the minimum pension. She complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the State’s failure to pay that supplement. The application (no. 72954/11) against Ukraine was lodged on 18 November 2011.

On 11 December 2008 the applicant lodged a claim with the domestic courts against the State Pension Fund. She asked the courts to recalculate her pension in accordance with section 6 of the 2006 Act for 2006–2008 and to pay her the outstanding debt.

On 10 June 2009 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the claim. It found that, in 2006, section 6 of the 2006 Act had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Amendments to the latter Act, which entered into force on 1 April 2006, had empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to set up a mechanism for a pension increase. However, no such mechanism had been set up in 2006, so the applicant’s claims relating to 2006 were rejected. As to 2007 and 2008, the court noted that section 6 had been suspended and modified, respectively, by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. On 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008, however, the Constitutional Court had found that suspension and modification unconstitutional. The court therefore held that the State Pension Fund should recalculate the applicant’s pension only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010 the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the lower court’s findings as regards the applicant’s 2006 claims. It also upheld her right to a pension increase for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008. However, it held that because she had missed a one-year statutory period for lodging a claim, the 2007 claim could be allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007. On 18 May 2011 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the appellate judgment.

case_name: CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE
summary:
The applicant, an Afghan national, alleged that Slovak authorities failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, returned him to Ukraine, where he was detained in inadequate conditions despite his alleged minor status and could not participate effectively in detention proceedings, and that he was later returned to Afghanistan without an adequate risk assessment. He also alleged that an NGO representative was denied access to him in Ukraine, preventing an interim-measure application to the Court. He claimed birth in 1993 or 1994; Slovak and Ukrainian authorities recorded 14 January 1992.

He came from Kunduz. His father, who worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department, was killed around 2005, possibly by Taliban-linked persons. In 2010 his maternal uncle received a threatening letter and arranged for him to leave. In May 2010 smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He stayed in Moscow for a month and entered Ukraine in early July 2010, remaining in Kyiv for three months. His brother-in-law later crossed into Slovakia, travelled to Spain and sought asylum.

On 23 September 2010 at 4.10 p.m. Slovak border police arrested him crossing illegally with three other Afghans; he had no identity papers. At 7.25 p.m. he was interviewed with Slovak-English and English-Pashto interpretation. His birth date was recorded as 14 January 1992. He said he wished to reach western Europe and did not request asylum in Slovakia. The record was signed by police and the Slovak-English interpreter, not by him or the Afghan interpreter. Slovakia said he refused to sign; two others signed similar records.

On 24 September 2010 an expulsion decision and five-year entry ban were issued. He received Pashto guidelines, though some case-specific details were in Slovak. At 2 p.m. he was handed to Ukrainian authorities. He alleged that in Slovakia he had no interpretation, asylum information or lawyer; tried to request asylum and said he was a minor; and received no written return decision or appeal information.

In Ukraine he was held at the Chop Border Guard facility, where he alleged overcrowding and lack of guaranteed daily exercise. He said he told a guard via other detainees and a Caritas representative that he was 14 and wished to apply for asylum, but no action was taken. The SBCS ordered voluntary departure and sought forcible expulsion and detention. On 1 October 2010, according to the court, the SBCS and applicant asked for written proceedings in their absence. On 13 October 2010 the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court ordered expulsion and detention pending expulsion, relying on his recorded 1992 birth date, illegal entry, lack of means or relatives in Ukraine, and a UNHCR publication indicating no risk in Afghanistan. The applicant alleged he was unaware of the proceedings, had no lawyer, did not understand his rights, signed a waiver without understanding, was not served the decision and missed the ten-day appeal deadline.

On 14 October 2010 he was moved to temporary accommodation in Volyn; he alleged he again said he was 14. On 20/22 February 2011 the Afghan Embassy interviewed him and issued a travel document recording his birth date as 14 January 1992. On 23 February 2011 he applied for asylum, saying he would be killed if returned. On 2 March 2011 he was interviewed. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the application as inadmissible, citing manifestly unfounded facts, failure to meet the refugee definition, his Afghan travel document, failure to seek asylum earlier and lack of identity documents. On 11 March 2011 he was transferred to Mukacheve and notified. On 12 March 2011 an NGO partner of UNHCR was allegedly denied access to provide legal advice, preventing an interim-measure application. case_name: CASE OF WALCZAK v. POLAND
summary:
Damian Walczak, a Polish national born in 1971 living in Plewiska, was arrested on 16 December 2014 and charged with organised-crime and robbery-related offences. The Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Court ordered his detention on remand until 16 March 2015; the Poznań Regional Court later extended it until 16 June and then 16 September 2015. He was released on 4 February 2016. He alleged that during detention he was deprived of personal contact with his wife, M.W., for a significant period.

On 30 December 2014 M.W. applied to visit him. On 5 January 2015 the Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Prosecutor refused because she was a witness in the proceedings; no appeal was lodged. Applications of 26 February and 17 March 2015 were dismissed on 27 February and 24 March 2015 because evidence still needed to be heard from M.W.; again no appeals were lodged. On 3 April 2015 M.W. refused to testify at the investigation stage and applied again. On 7 April 2015 the prosecutor refused, saying she could still be asked to testify while the investigation was ongoing; no appeal was lodged. A 27 May application was dismissed on 5 June 2015, without interlocutory appeal. On 10 June 2015 M.W. applied again; on 15 June 2015 the prosecutor dismissed it, saying a visit could impede proceedings because she knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. On 28 August 2015 the Poznań Regional Prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s interlocutory appeal against that decision. Applications of 15 June and 15 July 2015 were dismissed on 25 June and 24 July 2015; the applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015 was dismissed on 6 July 2015.

On 27 August 2015 the prosecutor allowed M.W. to visit; the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment. On 10 September 2015 the Poznań Regional Court dismissed M.W.’s application to visit because she was a witness, served on her on 14 September 2015. On 24 September 2015 the Regional Court dismissed her interlocutory appeal. It held that her statement that she would not testify against her husband was irrelevant because court proceedings had not begun and she could change her mind when summoned. It also held that investigation-stage visits allowed by the prosecutor were irrelevant because those decisions could not be assessed by the court. A further request of 15 September 2015 was marked “examined” on 17 September 2015. On 1 October 2015 M.W. requested a visit and stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify. On 2 October 2015 the Regional Court allowed the visit, which took place on 11 October 2015. Her later requests were granted. There were no significant subsequent developments, and M.W. was not asked to testify at later hearings.

Under Article 217 of the 1997 Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences, visits required permission from the investigating prosecutor or, once trial had begun, the trial court; interlocutory appeals were available under Article 217 § 1c, but § 1d restricted further appeals if a refusal was upheld within three months.

case_name: CASE OF PROJECT-TRADE D.O.O. v. CROATIA
summary:
The applicant, Project-Trade d.o.o., is a Croatian limited liability company registered in Zagreb. It was a shareholder in Croatia Bank d.d. (the bank), holding 1,251 shares with a nominal value of HRK 200 each. On 23 February 1999 the Croatian National Bank (CNB) appointed a temporary administrator at the bank; the term was extended on 23 August 1999. On 18 June 1999, based on an expert report that the bank’s debts largely exceeded its share capital and threatened financial-market stability, the CNB proposed recovery and restructuring of the bank.

On 23 September 1999 the Croatian Government adopted the Decision on the recovery and restructuring of Croatia Bank, published on 27 September 1999. From publication, all existing shares of the bank were revoked and cancelled. New shares in the amount of HRK 204.6 million were to be issued to the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). The powers of the bank’s governing bodies and the rights of shareholders were extinguished. The recovery process was completed on 13 September 2000. The Decision was slightly amended on 25 May 2000, and the Constitutional Court later held that it was subordinate legislation rather than an individual legal act.

In 1999 and 2000, five shareholders of the bank, but not the applicant company, filed four petitions with the Constitutional Court challenging the Government Decision. They alleged violations of Croatian constitutional rights, argued that the bank had been in good standing and that the Decision was unnecessary. After obtaining expert opinions, on 30 January 2003 the Constitutional Court discontinued the proceedings because the 1994 Recovery and Restructuring of Banks Act had been repealed on 31 May 2000. It stated that the Decision’s effects interfered with individual rights of founders and former shareholders, but that judicial protection was available in civil proceedings under the Obligations Act and section 19(2) of the Courts Act, and ultimately by constitutional complaint. Two dissenting judges argued that the review could have continued, that the Decision was unconstitutional, and that no effective remedy, especially a judicial one, existed. One dissent contested that civil proceedings could succeed without a finding that the Government Decision was unconstitutional.

On 12 September 2003 the applicant company brought a civil action in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. It sought a declaration that it still held 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer corresponding shares to it, and an order that the bank register it as holder. The applicant argued that the Government Decision revoking and cancelling its shares was economically unjustified because the bank had been in good standing, that statutory requirements had not been met, and that the Decision violated Articles 48 § 1, 49 § 4 and 50 of the Croatian Constitution, as allegedly acknowledged by the High Commercial Court in a judgment of 21 December 2004 in another case.

On 21 February 2006 the Zagreb Commercial Court dismissed the action. On 18 June 2008 the High Commercial Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment, served on 16 September 2008. It reasoned that under point 7 of the Government Decision all existing shares had been extinguished and new shares issued to DAB, so the applicant’s shares no longer existed and could not be returned. The applicant had argued on appeal that the first-instance court misapplied substantive law, that the Government Decision was unconstitutional, and that the Government had to compensate the market value of the revoked shares under Article 50 § 1 of the Constitution. The applicant company lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 December 2013.
