case_name: CASE OF STRØBYE AND ROSENLIND v. DENMARK
summary:
The applicants are Tomas Strøbye (born 1966, living in Frederiksberg) and Martin Rosenlind (born 1987, living in Greve), both Danish nationals. In earlier domestic proceedings, the first applicant was declared legally incompetent to manage his financial and personal affairs by the Copenhagen City Court on 20 March 1984. The second applicant was placed under financial guardianship and deprived of his legal capacity by the District Court of Roskilde on 23 March 2009; that court found he could not manage his financial affairs because of mental disability and needed protection from further debt.

Under section 29 of the Danish Constitution and section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, persons who were legally incompetent did not have the right to vote in general elections. Consequently, both applicants were not entitled to vote in the parliamentary elections held on 18 June 2015. By Act no. 391 of 27 April 2016, persons who were legally incompetent were later given the right to vote in European Parliament elections and in local and regional elections, but not in national parliamentary elections.

The applicants, joined by two other persons, brought proceedings before the Danish courts against the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Interior. They claimed they had been wrongfully denied the right to vote in the 18 June 2015 parliamentary elections and relied, among other things, on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Ministry contested the claims.

Before the High Court of Eastern Denmark, a written statement by the first applicant was read out. It stated that he had suffered brain damage after being immunised during his first year of life and lived at Egmont folk high school. For many years he had had to share a single vote with his mother, who was his guardian, and he found it humiliating not to cast his own vote. The second applicant stated that he lived in his own flat in a group home, had a mentor who helped him, worked at the Glad Foundation reception desk, felt sad and excluded when not allowed to vote in June 2015, read newspapers and watched news, and was interested in politics. He said he had requested a guardian himself because it was difficult for him to manage his financial affairs.

On 29 June 2017, the High Court dismissed the claim. It considered that the Constitution had continuously been construed as excluding persons deprived of legal capacity under section 6 of the Guardianship Act from voting in general elections, and that Denmark’s international obligations did not imply an absolute right to vote for that limited group. The applicants appealed. On 18 January 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s decision. case_name: CASE OF LIEBSCHER v. AUSTRIA
summary:
The applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, born in 1957 and living in Vienna, is an Austrian national. On 21 May 2013 he and his wife divorced by mutual consent and concluded a divorce settlement under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act before the Döbling District Court, acting as family court. The settlement regulated division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

On 13 December 2015 the applicant asked the same court, acting as land register court, to enter into the land register the transfer of his share of the couple’s joint property to his former wife. He submitted a partial engrossment of the divorce settlement issued by the family court on 1 December 2015. It was designated an “excerpt from the … divorce settlement” and reproduced only the chapter concerning real estate. It also contained a family court note that it “contained … all agreements pertaining to the real estate property”. Under section 7(1) of the Land Register Act, the land register is public and can be consulted by anyone without restriction.

By decision of 25 February 2016, the land register court rejected the application. It found that submitting a partial engrossment rather than the “original” did not satisfy section 87 of the Land Register Act. A partial engrossment could not be an original; the complete document was required so the court could examine whether the settlement contained conditions or legally relevant facts affecting registration, as required by section 94(1).

The applicant appealed. He argued that refusal to transfer his property share infringed his right to dispose freely of his property. He maintained that the partial engrossment complied with section 87 because it had been issued by the same judge and stated that it reproduced the relevant part. He also complained that requiring the full divorce settlement breached data protection rules, because highly personal and sensitive data—such as names and places of abode of minor children and his former spouse, alimony amounts, and custody agreements—would become publicly accessible in the document archive. He relied on Article 8, section 1(2) of the Data Protection Act 2000, and Article 52 of the EU Charter, arguing that no legitimate aim or public interest outweighed his privacy.

On 25 April 2016 the Vienna Regional Civil Court rejected the appeal (47 R 108/16d). It confirmed that a partial engrossment was not an “original” under section 87(1) and that even the family court’s statement could not bind the land register court; the original full settlement was needed. It cited an earlier Supreme Court decision, no. 5 Ob 250/15y of 25 January 2016, requiring a complete document. It found a legal basis for the interference regarding Article 8 and the Data Protection Act.

On 24 June 2016 the applicant filed an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating that the lower courts’ interpretation was incompatible with Article 8 and other laws. He requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU and a constitutional review. On 11 July 2016 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal (5 Ob 125/16t). It relied on its earlier decision no. 5 Ob 250/15y that a partial engrossment was insufficient under section 87(1); the excerpt’s confirmation could not change that. Under section 94(1), the land register court had to examine the application and documents comprehensively, approving registration only if justified by their content and in the required form. The family court could not bind it on completeness. On Article 8, the Supreme Court found the data protection concerns unpersuasive: examination of the entire document was mandatory under sections 87(1) and 94(1) and served protection of registered property. It stated that inclusion of documents in the document archive was not the subject of the decision and saw no reason to initiate a preliminary ruling or constitutional review.

The applicant alleged violations concerning his personal data and the lack of an effective remedy, and that the refusal infringed his property rights.

case_name: CASE OF OMDAHL v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicant, Olav Omdahl, a Norwegian national born in 1951, lives in Oslo. His grandfather, O.A. Knutsen, died on 24 April 1993. The estate included extensive property, shares, securities and moveable property worth approximately NOK 100 million, with debts of about NOK 10 million. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren; two children, including the applicant’s mother, died before final distribution.

On 5 May 1993 public administration of the estate began before the Probate Court, later the District Court, and an advocate was appointed administrator. Early on, some small properties were sold, but litigation over heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind under the will and a codicil tied up proceeds until the turn of 2005/06. Probate Court decisions to convert further assets were quashed or amended on appeal by the High Court, so no assets could be distributed.

A trust established by the deceased in the Bahamas and managed by a London bank emerged after the applicant’s mother died in 2002. In December 2005 each of the deceased’s children and grandchildren received NOK 5.5 million from it. The trust led to disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and to tax questions, clarified with the tax authorities from 2006 and finally during winter 2010.

An interim distribution on 1 July 2010 gave each branch of the lineal descendants NOK 10 million. The heirs appealed; the High Court dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2011 and the Supreme Court refused leave on 1 November 2011. Disputes over the sale of shares led to a District Court decision on 11 June 2010, finally settled on 25 March 2011. Other disputes, a recusal motion, and disputes over the sale of shares in a property company and a fish oil factory ended during 2012. Share sales were mostly completed in the first half of 2013, and remaining limited liability companies were wound up in December 2013.

The Probate Court decided final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Final distribution was disbursed on 16 April 2015, each branch receiving about NOK 18.9 million. A further distribution decided on 10 August 2015 entailed no payments and became final in September 2015. The administration thus lasted twenty-two years and four months.

In domestic proceedings, on 9 March 2016 the applicant sued the Norwegian Government before Oslo City Court, seeking a declaratory judgment that Article 6 § 1 had been violated because the administration exceeded a reasonable time, and claiming compensation. In its judgment of 15 September 2016, the City Court found that the length alone indicated a violation but considered the estate complex, the applicant not particularly litigious, and many actions brought by other heirs; it found no proven inactivity and no violation, and no compensation. The applicant appealed. After a hearing on 6–7 March 2018, the High Court on 22 March 2018 found no inactivity and considered the administration extraordinary, citing the large number of disputes, codicil-related blockage, sale difficulties, the 2008 financial crisis, and trust and tax complications. It noted that the applicant had argued a High Court ruling of 23 October 1997 was erroneous and blocked progress, but that ruling had become binding and was not appealed. The High Court concluded that there had been sufficient progress and no violation, and no liability. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 21 June 2018. The applicant lodged application no. 46371/18 on 21 September 2018.

Share sales were mostly completed in the first half of 2013, and remaining limited liability companies were wound up in December 2013.

The Probate Court decided final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Final distribution was disbursed on 16 April 2015, each branch receiving about NOK 18.9 million. A further distribution decided on 10 August 2015 entailed no payments and became final in September 2015. The administration thus lasted twenty-two years and four months.

In domestic proceedings, on 9 March 2016 the applicant sued the Norwegian Government before Oslo City Court, seeking a declaratory judgment that Article 6 § 1 had been violated because the administration exceeded a reasonable time, and claiming compensation. In its judgment of 15 September 2016, the City Court found that the length alone indicated a violation but considered the estate complex, the applicant not particularly litigious, and many actions brought by other heirs; it found no proven inactivity and no violation, and no compensation. The applicant appealed. After a hearing on 6–7 March 2018, the High Court on 22 March 2018 found no inactivity and considered the administration extraordinary, citing the large number of disputes, codicil-related blockage, sale difficulties, the 2008 financial crisis, and trust and tax complications. It noted that the applicant had argued a High Court ruling of 23 October 1997 was erroneous and blocked progress, but that ruling had become binding and was not appealed. The High Court concluded that there had been sufficient progress and no violation, and no liability. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 21 June 2018. The applicant lodged application no. 46371/18 on 21 September 2018.

The present record does not reproduce those background facts in detail.

As to the applicant’s domestic employment proceedings, in 2013 she was dismissed from employment. She initiated proceedings against her employer seeking reinstatement. Those proceedings were conducted before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The proceedings ended with the final judgment of the Supreme Court of the “MRT” dated 5 June 2014. By that judgment, the applicant’s action was dismissed. No further detail is given in the supplied record about the lower courts’ decisions, the grounds for dismissal, or the content of the reinstatement claim.

On an unspecified date, the applicant complained to the authorities of Moldova. A criminal investigation was initiated by the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office into her complaints. Later, those criminal proceedings were discontinued. The stated ground for discontinuation was that the facts complained about by the applicant did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence. The record does not give the date of the applicant’s complaint, the date the investigation began, or the date it was discontinued.

It states that reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations, the relevant domestic law and practice of the Republic of Moldova, and other pertinent documents were summarised in Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (GC, no. 11138/10, §§ 61-77, 23 February 2016). That case is identified as earlier authority. Apart from the above, the supplied text does not set out additional concrete factual events, detailed allegations by the applicant, or detailed arguments by the respondent Governments concerning the merits. It identifies the parties, the domestic employment and criminal proceedings, the relevant dates that appear in the record, and the background references.

case_name: CASE OF JESTCOV v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA AND RUSSIA
summary:
Application no. 33567/15 was lodged by Mr Petru Jestcov, a Moldovan national born in 1950 who lives in Chișinău, against the Republic of Moldova and Russia. He was represented by A. Tighinean, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The Governments were represented by their Agents. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Moldova and Russia were responsible for the impunity of the perpetrator of his wife’s murder, whom he alleged was hiding in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (MRT). The case concerned the failure to enforce a custodial sentence after the perpetrator fled.

On 9 November 2010 the applicant’s wife was robbed and murdered in Chișinău, Moldova. An investigation was initiated against several suspected perpetrators, including N.C., a Russian national. N.C. was held in pre-trial detention during the proceedings. On 2 December 2011 the Botanica District Court convicted N.C. of being an accomplice in armed robbery and murder and sentenced her to 13 years’ imprisonment. On 11 April 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld N.C.’s appeal, reheard the case, acquitted her of all charges, and released her from detention in the courtroom. On 29 January 2013, in N.C.’s absence, the Supreme Court of Justice finally quashed the appellate judgment and upheld the first-instance judgment against N.C.

On 20 March 2013 the Botanica District Court sent all materials of the criminal file to the Dubăsari Police to enforce the sentence in respect of N.C. On 2 July 2013 the General Police Inspectorate informed the applicant that N.C. had not yet been declared wanted. Following a request from the Dubăsari Police, on 6 May 2015 the Dubăsari District Court declared N.C. wanted.

Following a search notice issued by Moldovan authorities, on 11 September 2015 the Russian authorities traced N.C. to Surgut, Russia, and interviewed her about the circumstances of the case. She claimed to be unaware of her conviction in Moldova, saying that she had moved back to Russia after her acquittal by the appellate court in 2012. On 17 September 2015 the Russian authorities informed the Moldovan authorities of N.C.’s location. On 19 October 2015 they confirmed that she was a Russian national and therefore could not be extradited pursuant to Article 57 of the 1993 Minsk Convention on mutual legal assistance in civil, family and criminal matters.

After communication of the case, on 15 October 2019 the Chișinău District Court requested transfer of the enforcement of N.C.’s custodial sentence to the Russian Federation, relying on Article 2 of the 1997 Additional Protocol to the Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons. On 25 October 2019 the Moldovan Minister of Justice forwarded the request to the Russian Ministry of Justice. On 4 February 2020 the Russian Ministry of Justice directed the Moldovan transfer request to the Surgut City Court. On 10 April 2020 the Surgut City Court granted recognition and enforcement on the territory of the Russian Federation of the custodial sentence in respect of N.C. and ordered her arrest.

The Additional Protocol to the Council of Europe Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons was ratified by Moldova in 2004 and by Russia in 2007. Article 2 of that Protocol concerns persons who have fled from the sentencing State. It provides that where a national of a Party who is the subject of a sentence imposed in another Party seeks to avoid execution or further execution of the sentence by fleeing to the former Party before having served it, the sentencing State may request the other Party to take over execution. At the request of the sentencing State, the administering State may arrest the sentenced person or take other measures pending a decision on the request. The consent of the sentenced person is not required for the transfer.

summary:
The case concerns six applications against Romania, all alleging inadequate conditions of detention. The applicants and the factual details recorded are as follows.

**Ivanciu Radu** (born 1978), application no. 50868/16, introduced the application on 19 September 2016. He was detained in Gherla Prison from 1 to 15 September 2016 (15 days). He alleged infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, insufficient sleeping places, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack or insufficiency of natural light, poor bedding and bed linen, restricted leisure or educational activities, lack of toilet privacy, inadequate furniture, lack of toiletries, a mouldy or dirty cell, poor food, poor potable water, and constant electric light. The domestic compensation table records 504 days’ compensation for a total period of detention in inadequate conditions from 24 July 2012 to 23 December 2019, except for the period mentioned in Column no. 5.

**Laurențiu-Victor Popa** (born 1989), application no. 10817/17, introduced on 13 January 2017 and represented by Cândea Claudia Nadina Daciana, Timişoara. He was held in Arad Prison from 10 July 2014 to 16 January 2015 (6 months and 7 days) and from 20 August 2015 to 1 September 2016 (1 year and 13 days). He alleged constant electric light, deterioration of detention conditions through cumulative factors, inadequate temperature, infestation, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack or insufficiency of natural light, lack or insufficiency of outdoor exercise, poor bedding, lack of toiletries, inadequate furniture, insufficient quantity of food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted access to shower or warm water, and poor food. Domestic compensation: 258 days for the total period from 23 January 2013 to 28 February 2018, except the periods in Column no. 5.

**Dorel Popescu** (born 1979), application no. 13244/17, introduced on 6 March 2017. He was held in Giurgiu Prison from 27 July 2016 to 10 January 2017 (5 months and 15 days), and in Jilava and Rahova Prisons from 24 December 2019, pending, for more than 1 year, 8 months and 17 days. The space per inmate was 2.85 m². He alleged overcrowding, infestation, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack or insufficiency of natural light, poor bedding, restricted leisure or educational activities, lack of toilet privacy, inadequate furniture, insufficient food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted access to shower and warm water, and poor food. Domestic compensation: 354 days for the total period from 4 November 2014 to 23 December 2019, except the period in Column no. 5.

**Valentin Pricop** (born 1961), application no. 14363/17, introduced on 14 February 2017 and represented by Biro Vasile Rareş, Satu Mare. He was held in Arad Prison from 7 October to 14 November 2016 (1 month and 8 days). He alleged infestation, inadequate hygienic facilities, poor bedding, insufficient quantity of food, a mouldy or dirty cell, and poor food. Domestic compensation: 126 days for the total period from 7 October 2016 to 21 August 2018, except the period in Column no. 5.

**Ioan Mezin** (born 1969), application no. 17301/17, introduced on 21 February 2017 and represented by Nichita-Costescu Cezara-Maria, Timişoara. He was held in Arad Prison from 15 April 2013 to 25 February 2016 (2 years, 10 months and 11 days). The space per inmate was 3.48 m². He alleged overcrowding for the period 24 February to 20 April 2015, constant electric light, inadequate temperature, infestation, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack or insufficiency of natural light, lack or insufficiency of outdoor exercise, poor bedding, lack of toiletries, inadequate furniture, insufficient food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted access to shower and warm water, and poor food. Domestic compensation: 252 days for the total period from 16 August 2012 to 11 December 2018, except the period in Column no. 5.

**Teodor Crișan** (born 1988), application no. 18066/17, introduced on 1 March 2017 and represented by Biro Vasile Rareş, Satu Mare. He was held in Sălaj County Police Station from 6 to 23 December 2014 (18 days); in Arad Prison from 23 July to 11 December 2015 (4 months and 19 days), from 14 March to 1 April 2016 (19 days), and from 7 July 2016 to 5 January 2017 (5 months and 30 days). The space per inmate was 1.5–2.33 m². He alleged overcrowding, bunk beds, inadequate temperature, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack or insufficiency of natural light, poor bedding, lack of toilet privacy, inadequate furniture, insufficient food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted access to shower and warm water, poor food, infestation, and lack or insufficiency of outdoor exercise. case_name: CASE OF E.M. AND OTHERS v. NORWAY
summary:
The applicants are E.M., a Czech national born in 1976, and her two sons, B (born 2005) and C (born 2008). E.M. moved to Norway in 2005 to live with A, a Czech national resident in Norway since 1986. Both children were born in Norway. On 20 May 2011 they were placed in emergency care because of concerns about sexual abuse and violence. The parents later lived apart; E.M. initially had weekly contact, later twice-weekly, until contact stopped at the end of August 2011 after further statements and a police investigation. E.M. filed for separation in autumn 2011.

In domestic proceedings, on 8 February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took B and C into public care and placed them in foster homes. It found serious neglect and physical abuse, did not further assess possible sexual abuse, and considered that returning them to E.M. would likely lead to serious neglect. E.M. was granted supervised contact of two hours four times a year; A was granted none. On 4 July 2012 the District Court upheld the care order but withdrew E.M.’s contact rights. It found serious care deficiencies, physical punishment, probable sexual abuse by A, and E.M.’s awareness/failure to stop it; it did not decide whether she actively participated. Contact was withdrawn due to E.M.’s conduct, the children’s stress reactions and their association of her with violence and abuse. On 4 March 2013 the High Court restored supervised contact of two hours twice a year. It found insufficient grounds to believe E.M. sexually abused the children or knew of A’s abuse, but found she failed to shield them, slapped them, caused significant fear and was jointly responsible for neglect. It relied on expert psychological assessments and noted likely long-term fostering. The Supreme Court Appeals Committee refused leave on 21 May 2013.

On 10 December 2014 E.M. applied to lift the care order. The child welfare services sought continuation, removal of E.M.’s parental responsibilities for both children, refusal of contact for her and A regarding B, and authorisation of C’s adoption. After a hearing on 15–17 September 2015, the Board decided on 24 September 2015 not to lift the care orders, to withdraw E.M.’s parental responsibilities for B and C, to refuse her contact with B, and to authorise C’s adoption. For B, it cited E.M.’s repeated media exposure of the children, including photos and texts about sexual violations, causing strain and risks through future access to information.

E.M. appealed to the District Court. After hearings on 25–27 May 2016 with 18 witnesses, a Czech Republic submission and the children’s representative, the District Court gave judgment on 30 June 2016. It found E.M.’s caring abilities had improved, but B had PTSD from complex continued neglect and needed secure care not provided by those who caused the trauma; C had less extensive needs and strong foster attachment. B did not want to return, citing painful experiences and violence; C said he did not want anything to do with his parents and wanted to stay where nobody was mean. Sensitive material, including B’s health and sexual-abuse information, was found online. The court found E.M. could not provide needed care. It upheld refusal of contact with B for special and compelling reasons: B feared being alone with E.M., showed severe physical anxiety, and on 9 March 2015 staff considered forced contact an immediate health risk. For C, despite partly positive contact reports, he showed adverse reactions including agitation, anxiety, trouble sleeping and defecating in his pants; contact was not in his best interests at that time. The District Court refused C’s adoption because it would sever biological family ties, especially with B.

E.M. appealed; A made an ancillary appeal. The High Court refused leave on 28 November 2016. On 24 January 2017 the Supreme Court Appeals Committee dismissed E.M.’s further appeal as having no prospects. E.M. lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2017 on behalf of herself and the children, complaining under Article 8 about the decisions not to lift the care order, to withdraw parental responsibilities and to refuse contact.

case_name: CASE OF COMMUNAUTÉ GENEVOISE D'ACTION SYNDICALE (CGAS) v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The applicant, Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS), is a Swiss-law association established in 1962 and based in Geneva. Its statutory aim is to defend workers and its member organisations, particularly in trade-union and democratic freedoms; it states that it organises or participates in dozens of gatherings each year in the Canton of Geneva. The respondent is Switzerland.

The case arose during the COVID-19 pandemic. The first cases were reported in Wuhan, China, on 31 December 2019. The new coronavirus was first detected in Switzerland on 25 February 2020, in the Canton of Ticino. On 28 February 2020 the Federal Council declared a “special situation” under section 6(1)(b) of the Epidemics Act and adopted an ordinance prohibiting public or private events involving more than 1,000 persons. On 11 March 2020 the WHO described the situation as a pandemic. On 13 March 2020 the Federal Council replaced that ordinance with Ordinance 2 on measures to tackle coronavirus (O.2 COVID-19), closing schools, universities and training establishments and prohibiting public or private gatherings of more than 100 persons; cantonal authorities could grant exemptions for gatherings exercising political or training rights. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council announced an “extraordinary situation” under section 7 of the Epidemics Act and amended O.2 COVID-19. From 17 March 2020, all public and private gatherings were prohibited, the exemption for political rights was removed, and Article 10(d)(1) made intentionally organising or conducting a prohibited gathering punishable by up to three years’ custody or a fine. On 20 March 2020 gatherings of more than five persons in public places were prohibited. On 8 April 2020 the measures were extended until 26 April 2020. On 29 April 2020 a relaxation from 11 May 2020 was announced, and on 20 May 2020 religious worship was allowed to resume from 28 May 2020.

CGAS lodged its application with the Court on 26 May 2020. Relying on Article 11 of the Convention, it alleged that, following O.2 COVID-19, it had been obliged to cancel a gathering planned for 1 May 2020 and had withdrawn its authorisation request. More generally, it claimed that it had been deprived of the possibility of organising or participating in public meetings. It submitted that the Federal Council’s ordinances were generally applicable measures and that no appeal lay against them to a domestic court; it said this was why it had not applied to national courts.

On 27 May 2020 the Federal Council announced further reopening: from 30 May 2020 the ban on gatherings was relaxed to a maximum of 30 persons; from 6 June 2020 private and public gatherings of up to 300 persons, including political gatherings, were authorised again; events of more than 1,000 persons remained prohibited until the end of August; and on 20 June 2020 the prohibition on gatherings was lifted, although masks remained compulsory. On 19 June 2020 the Federal Council declared a return to the “special situation” as of 22 June 2020.

Domestically, Federal Council ordinances cannot be challenged by abstract review before the Federal Supreme Court under Article 189(4) of the Constitution and section 82(c) of the Federal Supreme Court Act; implementing acts may be appealed, and the ordinance’s conformity with higher-ranking law may be examined in a preliminary ruling. In Geneva, gatherings on public land require authorisation; decisions can be appealed to cantonal courts and then to the Federal Supreme Court. On 18 August 2020 the Administrative Division of the Geneva Court of Justice examined Article 6 of O.2 COVID-19 in a preliminary ruling and found it had a sufficient legal basis, with public health interests prevailing over the party’s interest in demonstrating. On 12 August 2021 the Federal Supreme Court declared an appeal inadmissible for lack of current purpose because the requested demonstration date had passed and the five-person gathering ban had been lifted on 30 May 2020.

case_name: CASE OF GLOVELI v. GEORGIA
summary:
The applicant, Marina Gloveli, a Georgian national born in 1958 and living in Tbilisi, is a practising lawyer with over twenty years’ experience. She also served as a judge in the Tbilisi Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2005. She participated in competitions for vacant judicial positions six times, most recently in October 2017. The present case concerns her latest attempt to obtain a judicial appointment.

In earlier domestic proceedings, on 9 February 2016 the applicant and two other unsuccessful candidates lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court. They alleged that sections 36(4), 49(1)(a) and 50(4) of the Act of 13 June 1997 on Courts of Ordinary Jurisdiction did not comply with Articles 29 and 42 of the Constitution, arguing in particular that no court had jurisdiction to examine disputes concerning judicial appointments. On 10 March 2017 amendments to the Courts Act entered into force, making decisions of the High Council of Justice (HCJ) on judicial appointments appealable to the Supreme Court. On 7 April 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, concluding that the amendments had created a new judicial remedy through the Qualifications Chamber of the Supreme Court, which had jurisdiction to examine appeals concerning allegedly arbitrary refusals of judicial appointments.

On 18 October 2017 the HCJ announced a new judicial competition. The applicant applied for a vacant position as a judge in a court of appeal and submitted documents confirming her professional and academic achievements. On 25 November 2017 the HCJ announced that she had been admitted to the competition. On 29 December 2017 HCJ members interviewed her and individually assessed her using score sheets. On 20 January 2018 she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the score sheets completed by the HCJ members who had interviewed and assessed her.

On 2 February 2018 the applicant lodged an appeal with the Qualifications Chamber seeking invalidation of the HCJ decision under section 354(3)(b) of the Courts Act. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that during the competition several HCJ members had had “protégé” candidates and had arbitrarily lowered the assessment scores of other judicial candidates. She also argued that the very low scores assigned to her by several HCJ members indicated bias.

On 6 February 2018 the Qualifications Chamber declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had not achieved the minimum pass score in the competency component, her candidacy had not been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the precondition in section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met; the HCJ had not examined her application for appointment and had not issued a decision refusing appointment that could be challenged before the Qualifications Chamber. The Qualifications Chamber further held, referring to earlier European Court cases Beaumartin v. France and Sigma Radio Television Ltd v. Cyprus, that it did not satisfy the requirement of a court or tribunal with “full jurisdiction” to review the facts of the case, and that its decision followed its established practice (case no. სსპ-2-17). The decision stated that it was final and not amenable to appeal.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court on 3 April 2018.

case_name: CASE OF THEO NATIONAL CONSTRUCT S.R.L. v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
summary:
The applicant, Theo National Construct S.R.L., is a Romanian road-construction company. It alleged a “raider attack”, namely the illegal seizure of its goods with the assistance of presumedly corrupt courts and law-enforcement agencies. In 2007 it agreed with Moldovan businessman and political-party leader Mr Ș. to enter Moldova. Under a 4 April 2007 agreement, the applicant was to become a 50% partner in company Q, contributing 23 pieces of road-construction equipment worth over EUR 1 million. The remaining capital was controlled by company S., controlled by Mr Ș. (49.77%), and another company (0.23%). On 5 April 2007 company Q admitted the applicant as a 50% partner.

On 25 April 2007 the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) valued the equipment at EUR 1,031,965, based on documents and pictures. On 3 May 2007 the State Registration Chamber registered charter amendments; company Q’s statutory capital rose from MDL 236,621 to MDL 17,540,179. On 8 May 2007 the applicant imported the equipment; at customs’ request, the MCC physically examined it and confirmed the earlier valuation. In October 2007 company Q signed a MDL 393 million road-renovation contract with the State Road Administration. It took bank loans exceeding EUR 1.5 million, pledging the equipment; the applicant’s CEO also pledged his Chișinău house. By 2010 delays were generally caused by delayed State payments. In early 2010 the applicant learned that company Q’s CEO had given interest-free loans of about MDL 4.5 million to company S. without consultation, in breach of the charter. Relations deteriorated; the CEO was changed and recovery proceedings began. By early 2011 company Q had no financial difficulties.

On 25 May 2010 company S. brought administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal against the MCC, seeking annulment of the 25 April 2007 valuation. It did not name the applicant as a defendant. The court later involved the State Registration Chamber, company Q and the applicant. The applicant alleged procedural irregularities. Although a 21 December 2010 request postponed a hearing to 20 January 2011, the file contained minutes of a 22 December 2010 hearing with the plaintiff present and an impossible case number. Those minutes recorded new claims to annul the 8 May 2007 valuation and the 3 May 2007 registration, to reinstate the parties, and to enforce immediately. At the 20 January 2011 hearing—the applicant’s first and last—the applicant said no such supplement was in the file. Minutes stated the next hearing would be 2 February 2011; summons and confirmation forms allegedly showed handwritten corrections from 2 March to 2 February.

On 2 February 2011 the applicant was absent. The Chișinău Court of Appeal annulled the MCC valuation reports and the State Registration Chamber’s decision of 3 May 2007, reinstated the parties as before 3 May 2007, and excluded the applicant from company Q. Transactions after 3 May 2007 were unaffected. Immediate enforcement was ordered without stated reasons. On 3–4 February 2011 the State Registration Chamber enforced the judgment; officer A.B., later found to be the wife of the deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party, signed the decision. Company Q’s capital fell to MDL 236,662. The applicant’s action against the Chamber was dismissed. On 3 March 2011 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, complaining of late involvement, manipulated documents, unanswered arguments, wrong administrative jurisdiction and time-bar. On 20 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without addressing those arguments.

After 4 February 2011 company Q’s management changed; the recovery actions were withdrawn. The equipment continued to be used by company Q. A bank later sought possession of the pledged equipment. In 2013 the Supreme Court ordered its transfer to the bank; the CEO’s house was also taken, and in 2014 bankruptcy proceedings began against company Q.

case_name: CASE OF MORTIER v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicant, Tom Mortier, a Belgian national born in 1976 living in Rotselaar, is the son of G.T., who had chronic depression for about forty years and had been treated by psychiatrist B. The respondent is Belgium. In 2011 G.T. considered euthanasia; her general practitioner Dr W. did not wish to act as main doctor and referred her to Professor D. On 29 September 2011 Prof D saw her and agreed to become her main doctor, referring her to psychiatrist Dr V. On 17 November 2011 Dr V considered the request premature and referred her to Dr V.D. On 12 January 2012 Prof D referred her to psychiatrist Dr T, who met her on 17 January. On 20 January G.T. agreed to be assisted by Dr V.D.; it was suggested she inform her children. On 31 January she emailed the applicant and her daughter about her euthanasia request and suffering; her daughter respected her wishes, while the applicant did not reply. On 7 February Prof D contacted Dr B, who saw no chance of improvement; on 10 February Dr B wrote to Dr T describing serious chronic conditions and a bleak outlook. On 14 February G.T. lodged a handwritten euthanasia request; Prof D formally became main doctor, and Dr T reported G.T. was rational, informed, under no third-party pressure, and could be assisted. On 17 February Dr V.D. examined her and on 20 February reported she could be assisted. Prof D saw her again on 22 February and 8/12 March. On 27 February she drafted a body-donation statement. On 29 February she donated EUR 2,500 to LEIF, run by Prof D, whose members included Dr T and Dr V.D. On 12 March Dr B concluded there was no point contacting her children. On 20 March P.D. became a person of trust. On 3 April a meeting set euthanasia for 19 April. On 10 April Prof D assured her that her wishes would be respected. On 19 April 2012 Prof D performed euthanasia; G.T. died at 11:15 a.m. in a public hospital in the presence of friends. The hospital informed the applicant on 20 April 2012.

On 20 June 2012 the Federal Euthanasia Board received Prof D’s registration document. On 26 June 2012 the Board, co-chaired by Prof D, found the euthanasia complied with the Euthanasia Act. Dr C later examined G.T.’s medical file on 2 August 2013 and noted the euthanasia declaration was not in it. The applicant requested a copy of the registration document from the Board on 23 October 2013 and 4 March 2014; on 19 March 2014 the Board refused, citing legal confidentiality. On 16 February 2014 he complained to the Medical Association; he says the outcome was not communicated because of confidentiality. On 4 April 2014 he lodged a criminal complaint against persons unknown. On 8 May 2017 the Crown Prosecutor discontinued for insufficient evidence. On 2 May 2019 the investigation was reopened. An expert report of 5 May 2020 concluded G.T. had intolerable, incurable mental suffering, requested euthanasia freely and constantly, the statutory waiting period was respected, and two psychiatrists were consulted; it noted the applicant learned of the death unfortunately and the file lacked the Board declaration and assessment. Prof D was interviewed by police on 16 June 2020. The Crown Prosecutor found compliance and sought closure; the applicant declined to have Prof D summoned. On 11 December 2020 the Pre-Trial Division found no grounds for prosecution and closed the investigation; no appeal was lodged. The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 13.

case_name: CASE OF MARCINKEVIČIUS v. LITHUANIA
summary:
Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, born in 1971, lives in Vilnius and is a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba. In 2015 he lodged a complaint with law-enforcement authorities alleging that Vilniaus Prekyba had, through financial deals, avoided taxes, damaged the State and unjustly enriched N.N., another founder and major shareholder. A pre-trial investigation opened in August 2015. On 19 August 2016 the prosecutor discontinued it, finding no grounds that the deals were unlawful; the senior prosecutor upheld that decision on 21 November 2016. On 23 November 2016 the applicant asked to reopen the investigation, citing new facts. On 1 December 2016 he answered written questions from a Delfi journalist for an article about his conflict with N.N. and the proceedings. On 21 December 2016 the prosecutor dismissed the reopening request and forwarded the material to the tax authorities. On 2 January 2017 a pre-trial investigation judge upheld the discontinuation; the same day Delfi published the article quoting the applicant. On 10 January 2017 the applicant sent his allegations to the tax authorities. On 17 February 2017 the Vilnius Regional Court finally upheld the discontinuation. On 1 March 2017 the senior prosecutor dismissed his complaint, and on 9 March 2017 the tax authorities opened an inquiry into N.N.’s tax compliance; it was still pending as of December 2021.

In the article, the applicant said documents showed that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba had allegedly been used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoiding Lithuanian taxes and appropriating other shareholders’ funds; that one company, T., had allegedly laundered more than EUR 20 million and hidden at least EUR 3 million in taxes; and that the main goal had been to appropriate profit without paying taxes in Lithuania. He also said: “It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.” N.N. sued, alleging false and defamatory statements of fact. He complained of three statements but not the following sentence about contacting the company, shareholders’ meetings and the prosecutor. He argued the statements were unsupported and formulated as facts, and asked for a public retraction. The applicant argued they were value judgments, based on documents submitted to authorities, not insulting, and that N.N., as a public figure, had to tolerate criticism.

On 22 December 2017 the Vilnius District Court partly allowed N.N.’s claim. It found the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments with sufficient factual basis and not insulting. It found the second sentence of the third statement (“It is obvious…”) a verifiable statement of fact, false and insulting: the applicant knew prosecutors had twice declined to confirm his allegations and had not proved damage. It ordered retraction. The applicant appealed. On 18 February 2019 the Vilnius Regional Court quashed that finding, treating the phrase in context as subjective, abstract and exaggerated opinion; it dismissed N.N.’s appeal. N.N. appealed on points of law. On 2 October 2019 the Supreme Court quashed the Regional Court decision because it had admitted new documents without allowing N.N. time to respond, and remitted the case.

In fresh proceedings, the applicant submitted additional financial reports. On 25 February 2020 the Vilnius Regional Court refused the new evidence and upheld the District Court: the sentence was affirming, lacked concrete facts and denigrated N.N. On 4 March 2020 Delfi published a retraction. The applicant’s appeals on points of law were refused by the Supreme Court on 12 March, 29 April and 27 May 2020 as raising no important legal issues. The applicant complained that the statement was a value judgment and that the retraction order violated his freedom of expression.

On 1 March 2017 the senior prosecutor dismissed his complaint, and on 9 March 2017 the tax authorities opened an inquiry into N.N.’s tax compliance; it was still pending as of December 2021.

He also said: “It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.” N.N. sued, alleging false and defamatory statements of fact. He complained of three statements but not the following sentence about contacting the company, shareholders’ meetings and the prosecutor. He argued the statements were unsupported and formulated as facts, and asked for a public retraction. The applicant argued they were value judgments, based on documents submitted to authorities, not insulting, and that N.N., as a public figure, had to tolerate criticism.

It found the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments with sufficient factual basis and not insulting. It found the second sentence of the third statement (“It is obvious…”) a verifiable statement of fact, false and insulting: the applicant knew prosecutors had twice declined to confirm his allegations and had not proved damage. It ordered retraction. The applicant appealed. case_name: CASE OF PEJŘILOVÁ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, Hana Pejřilová, a Czech national born in 1983, lodged application no. 14889/19 against the Czech Republic on 12 March 2019. She married in 2012. Because the couple could not conceive naturally and her husband had a serious disease, they approached an assisted reproduction centre. On 26 June 2014 the husband’s sperm was cryopreserved; he signed a consent form for preservation for infertility treatment. The form stated further written consent was required before each thawing and that, unless clearly determined otherwise, storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death. On 15 December 2014 the applicant and her husband signed informed consent forms for IVF, thawing his sperm and ICSI; they agreed to notify the centre of relationship changes that could cause treatment to end. The husband died on 16 June 2015 before further steps; the record does not show the applicant had begun hormone treatment or had ova collected.

On 7 September 2015 the applicant asked the centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm. The centre refused, saying this was contrary to law, and suggested court proceedings for a settlement. On 26 October 2015 she sued the centre, seeking an order to perform the treatment in accordance with his wishes as shown by the consent forms. At a 4 April 2016 hearing both parties were ready to settle, but the Plzeň-City District Court did not approve the settlement because it contravened section 6 of the SHS Act, which required consent less than six months old.

On 22 July 2016 the Plzeň Regional Court upheld that decision. It said the SHS Act allowed infertility treatment only for a couple, not a single woman without a partner; the aim was to give a child an initial chance to grow up with both parents. The applicant and her husband ceased to be a couple upon his death. His later wishes could not be prejudged or replaced by a court, and his earlier consent was not a binding “previously expressed wish” because it was not in the required form. On 28 November 2016 the district court dismissed her action: she was no longer part of a couple and there was no valid informed consent from her late husband.

On 30 May 2017 the regional court upheld the dismissal. It found the request contrary to sections 6 and 8 of the SHS Act: assisted reproduction could be performed only on the application and written consent of the infertile couple, with consent less than six months old. Even the initial consent did not mean the husband would not have changed his mind, and further consent could not be replaced by a court decision. On 21 February 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on points of law. It considered family life required an actual family and a mere wish to found one was not protected; the failure to complete the procedure could interfere with private life. It referred to comparative legislation and the explanatory report. It found it in the child’s best interests to be born to a complete family with both parents at least at conception; after the man’s death the infertile couple no longer existed. The six-month consent rule protected the sperm provider and allowed revocation. It was unclear whether the husband would have wished fatherhood after death, as he had signed a form containing an explicit destruction-on-death provision. The centre was not obliged to perform the procedure. The applicant was not deprived of all opportunities to become a mother; she could conceive naturally or with another partner.

On 8 November 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal. It held the lower courts had adequately examined her arguments and reasoned their findings; the Supreme Court had considered the constitutional dimension and Court case-law; the conclusions were compliant with the Constitution; there was no European consensus. Legislation on assisted reproduction was based on moral, cultural, religious and ethical values, primarily for the legislature. A dissenting judge considered the law should only prevent a child being born against a man’s will; in his view the legislation had been misused and the courts should have determined the husband’s wishes.

case_name: CASE OF HUMPERT AND OTHERS v. GERMANY
summary:
The applicants are four German nationals—Karin Humpert, Kerstin Wienrank, Eberhard Grabs and Monika Dahl—who were State school teachers with civil servant status employed by different German Länder. They were members of the Trade Union for Education and Science and participated, during working hours, in strikes and a demonstration organised by that union to protest worsening working conditions for teachers. They were subsequently reprimanded or fined in disciplinary proceedings for breaching their duties as civil servants. On 10 December 2018 they lodged applications against Germany, complaining in particular about those disciplinary measures and about the prohibition on strikes by civil servants, which they considered incompatible with their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention.

The individual measures were as follows. Ms Humpert, a primary school teacher, was reprimanded by the Schleswig-Holstein Ministry for Education and Culture on 5 July 2011 for participating in a strike on 3 June 2010 and not teaching one lesson; it was later found she had missed two classes. Ms Wienrank, a vocational school teacher, and Mr Grabs, a secondary school teacher, were each fined EUR 100 by the Lower Saxony School Authority on 10 and 11 January 2011 respectively for unauthorised absence during a strike on 25 February 2009, when they did not give about five lessons each. The strike aimed, among other things, at securing a collective agreement for contractual State employees in the public educational sector and transferring its results to civil servants. Ms Dahl, a secondary school teacher, was fined EUR 1,500 by the Cologne District Government on 10 May 2010 for unauthorised absence during 12 lessons because of her participation in strikes on 28 January and 5 and 10 February 2009; those strikes had the same aims.

The applicants’ actions in the administrative courts were unsuccessful. The administrative courts found that they had breached their professional duties by participating in strikes. They considered that the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5 of the Basic Law restricted civil servants’ freedom of association under Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law through a prohibition on strike action. At first instance, the Schleswig-Holstein, Stade and Osnabrück Administrative Courts upheld the decisions against the first, second and third applicants by judgments of 8 August 2012, 6 December 2012 and 19 August 2011 respectively. The Düsseldorf Administrative Court, by judgment of 15 December 2010, initially considered that the employing State entity had to avoid a breach of Article 11 by discontinuing proceedings against the fourth applicant. On appeal, the Lower Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal, in a judgment of 12 June 2012 in the third applicant’s case, found the prohibition on strikes by civil servants part of the essence of Article 33 §§ 4 and 5 of the Basic Law and not alterable by interpretation in line with Article 11. On 16 May 2013 it rejected the second applicant’s request for leave to appeal by reference to that judgment. In the fourth applicant’s case, the North Rhine-Westphalia Court of Appeal overturned the first-instance judgment on 7 March 2012. On 27 February 2014 the Federal Administrative Court found the disciplinary decision against her lawful, though the fine should have been EUR 300; it considered that Article 33 § 5 could not be interpreted in a Convention-compliant manner and that the legislature had to resolve the conflict. The Schleswig-Holstein Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s appeal on 29 September 2014, and on 26 February 2015 the Federal Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicants lodged separate constitutional complaints, arguing that the decisions breached Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and that the administrative courts had failed to interpret national law in line with public international law, because the prohibition on strikes by teachers with civil servant status who did not exercise core public authority violated Article 11. On 12 June 2018 the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints (file nos. 2 BvR 1738/12 and others). It found no violation of Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and considered the prohibition on strikes by civil servants compatible with Article 11, based on the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5, and serving a functioning public administration and the State’s educational mandate.

case_name: CASE OF GUÐMUNDUR GUNNARSSON AND MAGNÚS DAVÍÐ NORÐDAHL v. ICELAND
summary:
Mr Guðmundur Gunnarsson (born 1976, Kópavogur) and Mr Magnús Davíð Norðdahl (born 1982, Reykjavík) lodged applications against Iceland on 6 and 20 May 2022. The case arose from the 25 September 2021 elections to Althingi. In the Northwest constituency, the smallest in Iceland, Gunnarsson stood as the top candidate for the Liberal Reform Party (Viðreisn), and Norðdahl as the top candidate for the Pirate Party (Píratar).

According to the Northwest constituency’s senior electoral commission, the initial vote count was finalised in the early morning of 26 September 2021. The reported result was that Liberal Reform received 1,072 of 17,666 votes, meaning Gunnarsson qualified for a levelling seat, while the Pirate Party received 1,082 votes, leaving Norðdahl a few votes short of a constituency seat.

At around noon that day, the National Electoral Commission telephoned the Northwest senior electoral commission, noting a very narrow margin of two votes in the Northwest and South constituencies that could affect levelling-seat allocation, and suggested a recount. A recount of Liberal Reform’s votes in the Northwest reduced its tally to 1,063, nine votes fewer. A full recount followed in the early afternoon: six parties lost between one and nine votes and four gained between one and ten; Liberal Reform ended with 1,063 votes and the Pirate Party with 1,081, one vote less than initially. A recount in the South constituency produced no changes. The Northwest recount led to a national reallocation of levelling seats. Gunnarsson lost his levelling seat, and the Northwest levelling seat went from Liberal Reform to the Centre Party.

The applicants lodged separate complaints on 1 and 5 October 2021, along with fifteen other complaints. Gunnarsson alleged that the recount lacked a legal basis; that ballots had been improperly stored and handled between counts; that party agents were not informed of the recount and could not observe it; and that changes in votes, blank ballots and invalid ballots were inconsistent and unexplained. He also disputed Althingi’s role in deciding electoral disputes and argued the defects could have influenced the outcome. Norðdahl alleged improper storage and handling of ballots and failure to inform him, as his party’s list agent, about the recount, depriving him of the chance to observe it. He argued it was sufficient that the defects could have influenced the result.

The Preparatory Credentials Committee, composed of nine members none elected in the Northwest, adopted procedural rules on 8 October 2021. It conducted an extensive inquiry over less than two months, obtaining documents, comments and information, questioning witnesses and experts, holding thirty-four meetings and making field visits to the count facility. The applicants appeared before it on 22 October 2021 and were invited to comment on draft descriptions in November. Most material was published on Althingi’s website, except confidential material and closed-hearing material. Gunnarsson’s lawyer requested access to various items, including material from a pending criminal investigation; Althingi provided some materials but refused others as confidential, and later refused a repeated request.

On 23 November 2021 the Preparatory Credentials Committee issued a ninety-page report identifying irregularities in the Northwest recount. It found that ballots had not been sealed and were left unattended in open boxes in a closed but unsupervised hotel room; one entrance could not be locked, hotel staff had keys, cameras did not cover the area, and the commission chairman had been alone there for about half an hour. It also found defects concerning the absence or insufficient notification of agents, changed numbers of valid ballots, and failure to secure agents’ participation in validity rulings. Other deviations concerned verification, mixing and counting procedures, and incomplete minutes.

On 25 November 2021 the Credentials Committee issued recommendations. Its majority found no indication of tampering and no effect on results, recommending confirmation of all sixty-three newly elected members. Minority members recommended annulling the Northwest or nationwide results and holding re-elections. Althingi debated the recommendations for over five hours and rejected the minority proposals. By forty-two votes to five, with sixteen abstentions, it confirmed the credentials. Under domestic law, Article 46 of the Constitution leaves Althingi to decide whether members are legally elected; the Act on Parliamentary Elections and Standing Orders govern complaints and credentials scrutiny.

case_name: CASE OF SHIPS WASTE OIL COLLECTOR B.V. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
The applicants are six Dutch limited liability companies. They complained about the transmission of intercept data obtained in criminal investigations to competition authorities and about the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

**First group.** Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. were engaged in collecting waste liquids from ships in Rotterdam. In late 2006, the VROM-IOD began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company, a subsidiary of Port Invest, for forgery and environmental offences. With an investigating judge’s authorisation, telephone calls were intercepted, including calls between I. company employees and Ships Waste Oil Collector employees. Some calls indicated price-fixing. On 21 April 2008 an official record with transcripts was drawn up. On 21 October 2008 a public prosecutor approved transmission to the NMA under section 39f WJSG; transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further material was authorised on 23 October 2009 and transmitted in 2010 after contact between the NMA and VROM-IOD. NMA inspectors visited premises on 29 and 30 June 2010. The I. company and an employee settled criminal charges on 11 March 2010; on 5 July 2010 the Regional Court declared the prosecution inadmissible.

On 16 November 2011 the NMA found competition-law infringements and imposed fines: EUR 834,000 on Ships Waste Oil Collector; EUR 1,861,000 jointly and severally on the I. company, Port Invest and Burando, with Burando’s liability capped at EUR 621,000. Objections argued that the transmissions lacked a proper basis, that there had been no prior judicial review, that the NMA had no power to intercept, and that no ex post criminal review occurred after settlement. On 11 July 2013 the Regional Court quashed the NMA decisions, finding the data were “criminal data” but that there was no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment. It found the data were criminal data, the transmissions had a statutory basis, judicial review safeguards existed, there was a compelling general interest in competition enforcement, less intrusive means were unlikely, and the criminal case ended on 19 July 2010 so the destruction period had not passed. Later, on 20 October 2016 and 30 October 2018, domestic courts upheld the competition infringements and fines.

**Second group.** Janssen de Jong Groep B.V., Janssen de Jong Infrastructuur Nederland B.V. and Janssen de Jong Infra B.V. were construction companies. Around 2007, the Public Prosecution Service and Rijksrecherche investigated “Cleveland” into bribery of local officials. With an investigating judge’s authorisation, telephone and internet communications of Janssen employees were intercepted. Some conversations indicated price-fixing. From July 2008 police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts on police premises. On 19 August 2008 the prosecutor provided a CD of about thirty audio recordings for information only. case_name: CASE OF TSATANI v. GREECE
summary:
The applicant, Georgia Tsatani, born in 1952, was a prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2016 V.T., President of the Court of Cassation, informed her that she had opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation against her. This followed letters dated 24 February 2016 from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General expressing concern about the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a media-covered fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. sent the applicant evidence and reports and invited written defence within ten days.

On 30 March 2016 the applicant wrote to the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation, arguing that he had exclusive competence and asking him to launch a preliminary investigation. She also complained that D.P., Deputy Minister of Justice, had referred in Parliament on 29 March 2016 to the confidential disciplinary proceedings. On 1 April she replied to V.T., complaining that she had not been offered an oral defence and that the alleged disciplinary acts were unclear. On 4 April V.T. provided a detailed statement and invited written and oral defence within a fresh ten-day period. The applicant submitted written defence and a recusal request against V.T., alleging bias: V.T. had served as interim prime minister in September 2015 and allegedly had special relations with D.P. and the Cypriot officials; V.T. had allegedly leaked confidential information, asked prejudicial questions and supplied an incomplete file.

On 12 April 2016 V.T. referred the case to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation to continue the preliminary investigation. She stated that the recusal request was an abuse of process and unfounded, that her relations with the Cypriot officials and D.P. were official, that she had not acted under Cypriot pressure, and that she had conducted the investigation herself because of high socioeconomic interest. On 21 April the applicant complained to the Vice-President that V.T. had issued a press release about the recusal request and asked that no further action be taken pending a decision on recusal. On 5 May the Vice-President concluded the investigation and proposed disciplinary action; she declared the applicant’s reiterated recusal request inadmissible for lack of standing.

On 24 June 2016 V.T. brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant before the seven-member disciplinary council of the Court of Cassation. She maintained that the recusal request was inadmissible because it had not been lodged with the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation and was, at most, an invitation to withdraw; she had not dismissed it but had delegated the investigation. On 10 October 2016 the seven-member council found the applicant guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary: she had terminated investigations within the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s exclusive competence and breached a Greece–Cyprus EUROJUST agreement. It imposed sixty days’ salary deprivation. It found the recusal request inadmissible and the delegation lawful. The applicant appealed. On 16 March 2017 the nine-member disciplinary council dismissed her appeal. It held that the recusal request had not been validly submitted and was in any event unfounded; V.T. had not dismissed it but had lawfully referred the investigation. On 22 March 2021 the nine-member council rejected a request to reopen.

The record also notes V.T.’s press release of 18 April 2016, reported in the press on 18–19 April, in which she called the recusal request unfounded and an abuse of process, and D.P.’s parliamentary statements of 29 March 2016 mentioning the pending disciplinary investigation. The applicant complained that she had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because V.T., who had opened the investigation and dealt with the recusal request, subsequently brought the disciplinary action against her.

case_name: CASE OF KYRIAN v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
The applicant, David Kyrian, a Czech national born in 1982, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the mother that began in 2012. Because the mother was married, her husband became the child’s legal father by presumption; the child lived with the legal parents. The applicant’s biological paternity was confirmed by a DNA test he arranged in 2015. Until February 2016 he saw the child two to four times a month when the mother visited him.

In April 2016 the applicant applied to the Příbram District Court under Article 927 of the Civil Code for contact rights. On 18 May 2016 the court granted provisional contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer holidays. The Prague Regional Court upheld that decision on 9 November 2016, noting an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father. Conflicts during visits led to supervised visits in July and August 2016. From September 2016 to November 2017 contact mostly followed the judgment, but the child’s psychological condition worsened.

In September 2017 the applicant sought more contact; the mother sought prohibition, alleging verbal abuse and that the child refused visits, was anxious and seeing a psychologist. The legal father alleged the applicant had physically assaulted him. A judgment of 3 October 2017 dismissing both requests was quashed by the Regional Court for insufficient fact-finding; it noted a weakening bond and recommended counselling. After mediation in April 2018, contact continued until mid-July 2018. On 17 July 2018 the District Court approved a mediated agreement granting contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer. Later visits were missed because the child refused; an incident with the legal parents led to police being called. Two supervised visits in October 2018 ended in conflict. A psychologist report of 10 October 2018 described the child as strongly attached to his mother and legal father and stressed by imposed contact.

In December 2018 the legal parents requested prohibition. In 2020 the Český Krumlov District Court and České Budějovice Regional Court ruled that no contact regime should be set, finding no positive emotional bond or harm from lack of contact. An expert opinion cited the child’s developmental delay, attachment to his legal father, the applicant’s pressure and conflicts, and considered no contact in the child’s best interests at that time. A constitutional appeal was dismissed on 13 October 2022.

On 23 April 2021 the applicant lodged a new application seeking contact every Wednesday afternoon. At a hearing on 24 August 2021, the legal parents described the child’s anxiety; the guardian ad litem advised dismissal. An expert report of 18 March 2022 found previous conflicted visits traumatic and did not recommend contact, though future contact was not excluded. A psychologist report of 20 March 2022 noted anxiety attacks. At a hearing on 24 March 2022, the applicant alternatively sought written communication via the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, citing distress and alleging he lingered near the child’s kindergarten or their home, bordering on stalking. The guardian opposed all requests.

On 24 March 2022 the Příbram District Court dismissed the claim but warned the legal parents about non-cooperation and ordered respect for the applicant’s biological parenthood. It found contact contrary to the child’s best interests and no basis for information rights. On 12 September 2022 the Prague Regional Court upheld that judgment. On 24 January 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal.

Subsequently, the legal parents divorced in April 2022 but shared custody and continued living together. The mother later moved out and resumed a relationship with the applicant, who had occasional contact through her. In 2024 shared-custody proceedings, the child said he did not want to see the mother mainly because he feared the applicant; the court placed the child with the legal father, and the mother’s contact application was dismissed because she would not meet without the applicant.

case_name: CASE OF MOGYLA AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
summary:
The case concerns three applications lodged against Ukraine: no. 1129/18 by Vadym Mykolayovych Mogyla, born in 1986 and introduced on 21 December 2017; no. 50410/18 by Petro Ivanovych Stetsenko, born in 1974 and introduced on 9 January 2019; and no. 34853/24 by Firma Svitlana, TOV, a company registered in 1996 and represented by Pleskach Vyacheslav Yuriyovych of Gozhuly, introduced on 8 November 2024. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention that their access to a court had been restricted. In application no. 1129/18, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention.

Mogyla filed an administrative claim on 24 November 2008 challenging a local council’s refusal to allocate him a plot of land. The claim was reconsidered several times. On 26 January 2011 the Higher Administrative Court confirmed that it should be examined within administrative proceedings. On 30 September 2014, in the second round of consideration, the Higher Administrative Court remitted the case to the first-instance administrative court for a new consideration. On 21 June 2017, however, the Higher Administrative Court ruled that the claim fell to be examined in civil proceedings and terminated the case. Consequently, Mogyla’s claim was not determined on the merits.

Stetsenko’s complaint arose from proceedings concerning his claim about a local court’s refusal to grant him access to a case file relating to his property. On 21 June 2018 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal ruled on his request for full or partial exemption from, or deferral of, payment of court fees of approximately EUR 34. He relied on an alleged lack of funds and submitted official tax certificates showing his family’s monthly income of approximately EUR 139, which was significantly lower than the applicable minimum family subsistence level. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the request, holding that he had “failed to provide relevant evidence to prove his allegedly difficult financial situation,” without further explanation. The Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 17 September 2018.

Firma Svitlana’s complaint concerned commercial proceedings relating to registration of property. On 26 July 2024 the Poltava Regional Commercial Court dismissed the company’s request for exemption from or deferral of a court fee of UAH 27,252 (approximately EUR 650), based on its alleged lack of funds, income or assets. In support, the company provided copies of financial reports and bank statements. The court reasoned that under Article 8 of the Court Fee Act only individuals, not legal entities, could be released from the obligation to pay court fees. On 31 July 2024 the court returned the claim for failure to pay the court fee. On 12 August 2024 the Eastern Commercial Court of Appeal dismissed the company’s request for deferral of the appellate court fee of UAH 2,422 (approximately EUR 60), applying the same reasoning. On 11 September 2024 the appellate court returned the company’s appeal against the 26 July 2024 decision for failure to pay the appellate court fee. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court refused to open cassation proceedings, essentially upholding the appellate court’s reasoning.
